To Christopher and Raina# Preface

The editors believe long prefaces are not likely be read to the end. However, the preface cannot be ignored. So, we intend to keep it brief.

This book is intended to serve as a text for graduate or senior students or as a reference for practicing engineers. The book develops the root cause approach to reliability - often referred to as physics of failure in the reliability engineering field. It differs from other books in reliability in that it approaches the subject from the point of view of a process and integrates the necessary methods and knowledge to support the process. As a text, the book can be used to teach seniors and first or second year graduate students in mechanical, electrical, manufacturing, materials or reliability on how to address reliability issues in product development. As a reference, the book will serve practicing engineers involved in design and development of electrical or mechanical systems and components.

We hope the book is an important contribution to the field as it is intended to emphasize concepts that can be integrated into design and places less emphasis on traditional reliability assumptions and analysis as a separate development activity. The book takes an interdisciplinary view that is in tune with Systems Engineering approaches. To emphasize the concepts, several case studies are discussed and real failures are provided as examples. These case studies emphasize understanding of failure mechanisms and failure prevention and underscore how to integrate reliability methodology, including simulation and testing, into design and development.

Concepts# Introduction to Product Integrity and Reliability Assessment

John W. Evans, Jillian Y. Evans and Dong-su Ryu

The goal of any product development and design effort is to produce a product that will be successful in the marketplace, resulting in maximum value or utility to the producer of the product. In order to effectively achieve this goal, products must be rapidly and efficiently designed and developed and must be of high integrity. We can define product integrity as the ability of a product to meet or exceed a customer's expectations for performance, quality and durability over the life of the product. The term product integrity was adapted for the text title in order to produce a focus on failure prevention in design and development, rather than on reliability calculations, which are often emphasized in reliability engineering texts. In this context, we will introduce a process for reliability assessment.

### 1.1 Introduction to Product Integrity

As markets become more global in nature and competition intensifies, product integrity becomes increasingly important to success in the marketplace. The economic importance of product integrity overall cannot be underestimated. A high degree of reliability contributes to brand recognition. In the absence of significant price advantages, reliability and quality issues will be the basis of consumer decisions in a given market.

The landmark studies bench-marking the world auto industry by Clark and Fujimoto (1991) clearly showed the importance of product integrity in the highly competitive world auto industry, as it developed through the late 1980s. In the case of the auto industry, the factors contributing to product integrity differentiated the highly successful companies. Clark and Fujimoto pointed out that addressing reliability and quality issue was as important as time to market and engineering productivity in achieving competitiveness in development. This extends to consumer electronics, consumer appliances, computers, photographic equipment and many other product types. In fact, significant resources are being expended to achieve a high degree of product integrity by many companies, in order to compete more effectively.

More recent studies on the success factors in the world electronics industry by the World Technology Evaluation Center also show that successful companies focus on product integrity. In particular sophisticated manufacturing quality control and high reliability by virtue of good design are key elements of success. More specifically, we can examine the success of Japanese companies in maintaining a large market share in consumer electronics. Japanesemarket share world wide is on the order of $49 \%$ [JTEC 1994]. This success is attributed in part to brand name recognition achieved through addressing product integrity-high reliability and product quality.

Let's examine the elements of product integrity. They are shown in Figure 1.1. These include quality, reliability and performance factors. We all have a sense of reliability, performance and quality as consumers. We desire the products we select to operate without failure and without unexpected degradation of performance. However, we will need to adopt more definitive meanings for these terms to develop our methodology.

We can define reliability as the probability of successful operation of a product over its intended design life under the loads encountered in the life cycle. In other words, reliability is the primary measure of uncertainty in product integrity. Certainly, a high degree of product integrity, or low probability of failure, must be achieved through good design and development practices. Quality in our context, can be defined as consistent product of low defect content. Quality is then built in through manufacturing process control. It is measured in terms of defect content in the product and variability in critical product factors, such as dimensions and materials properties, which affect the risk of failure. Performance factors are highly product dependent. One measure of performance is whether or not a product satisfies its functional requirements over the life cycle (Pecht 1995). Clearly performance is compromised by failure of components in the product before the end of its life.

Figure 1.1 Elements of product integrity. Our focus will be on the right hand branch of the diagram.Now, in order to achieve market success, we must address these issues through an appropriate process. A good process to address product integrity in design and development must be able to focus on the concept of Figure 1.2. An effective process must address root cause. Only through understanding the root cause of failure can effective corrective action and proactive prevention be implemented successfully. In addition, an effective process will have the following characteristics:

- Facilitate engineering productivity in development
- Afford easy integration with the overall product development process
- Focus on product failure and mitigation
- Provide for rapid root cause identification for manufacturing and product improvement
- Be comprehensive in its approach to reliability assessment
- Address uncertainties that contribute to product failure

Figure 1.2 A focus for product integrity and reliability in design.
In this text, we will focus on achieving product integrity in development, through a reliability assessment process that addresses these issues. We will introduce the process and develop the concepts and methodology concerned with failure mechanisms and mitigating failure in design. This approach is known as physics of failure.

Key concepts necessary for us to understand the implementation of physics of failure and the reliability assessment process for designing in product integrity are presented in the first section of this book. This chapter will introduce the process and Chapters 2 and 3 will build our fundamental understanding of variation, component failure and the relationship between component and system failure.

# 1.2 Failure Mechanisms in Products and Components

Before we introduce the process, we must gain a better understanding of failure mechanisms, their classification and nomenclature and their relationship to components and the system. An obvious loss of product integrity occurs with failure of the system. The consequences of failure can range from customer dissatisfaction to devastating loss of life and property, depending on how the failure manifests itself. The root cause of failure can generally be traced to one or more mechanisms acting on a component in the system.

### 1.2.1 Definitions and Nomenclature

A failure mechanism can be defined as a physical process acting on a component to produce failure of one or more system components. The system can be thought of as containing a seton $n$ components both electrical and mechanical. A component may have one or more dominant failure mechanisms excited by the loads on the system. This perspective is summarized in Figure 1.3. In the figure, a failure mechanism is abbreviated $F M_{i, j}$; the first subscript $i$ refer to a component in the system while $j$ refers to a failure mechanism active in the component.

Failure mechanisms can generally be divided into overstress failures and wear out failures. Examples of overstress failures include structural overloads that may cause structural col-

Figure 1.3 The physics of failure perspective of a system necessary to mitigate failure in design. Each component may have one or more dominant failure mechanisms (FM (s)). The subscripts denote the component and failure mechanism index.lapse due to a large single loading event or dielectric breakdown in a capacitor due to an excessive voltage transient. Wear out failures include those failure mechanisms which cause degradation in product or system components over time. Fatigue processes and corrosion are examples of wear out mechanisms that may occur in electronic or mechanical components. The well known process of electromigration in microcircuits is an example of wear out in electronic systems. The conductor in the microcircuit degrades over time under the influence of the applied load. A taxonomy of failures for a system with electronic and mechanical components is shown in Figure 1.4, as classified by load types.

Figure 1.4 represents many of the mechanisms that may occur in components of various systems but may be expanded in further consideration of electronic semiconductors or other types of components.

In many instances various forms of corrosion and fatigue are responsible for early wear out failures of components. These two mechanisms should be understood in some detail by engineers engaged in development and design activity for electronic or mechanical systems. They are explained in detail in later Chapters.

Loads on the system produce stresses in the components. The stresses then excite the various failure mechanisms producing failure of a component. The nomenclature of failure mechanics is summarized in Figure 1.5. A similar nomenclature is accepted by many other investigators in the field of reliability and physics of failure and is important to progress an

Figure 1.4 Taxonomy of failure mechanisms by loads on a system.

Figure 1.5 Nomenclature of component failure.understanding of failure (Lee, Katz, Hillman 1998). In this example, the load is an external time dependent force which produced a stress in the beam. Localized stresses excited the process of crack development. Crack growth eventually caused fracture. This failure process is a wear out mechanism we have mentioned above: fatigue.

In our example depicting the nomenclature of failure mechanics, the load is easily visualized an external force on the beam. But as we see above in our taxonomy of failure mechanisms, the term load can be more broadly applied to mean the external operational environment acting on the system, including ambient temperature, temperature range, humidity levels or moisture, chemical contact, vibration, mechanical shock, radiation levels, voltage and current. Examples of loads and potential stresses are shown in Table 1.1. One or more loads may excite various failure mechanisms.

Table 1.1 Examples of loads that can occur on a system.

| Load types | Loads                                                |
| :--------- | :--------------------------------------------------- |
| Mechanical | External Forces <br> Mechanical Shock <br> Vibration |
| Thermal    | Temperature <br> Temperature Gradient                |
| Chemical   | Humidity <br> Chemical Exposure                      |
| Electrical | Voltage <br> Current                                 |

The location of failure is the failure site. A defect may be associated with a failure site, but not always. There are many potential failure sites in a system but the list of mechanisms is finite. A component may have one or more potential failure sites at which different failure mechanisms are active.

The failure mode must be differentiated from the failure mechanism. The failure mode is how the mechanism manifests itself. We encounter the mode first and the mechanism may have to be ascertained by analysis. It is the symptom and not the root cause. As an example, we can again look at Figure 1.5. The failure mode is fracture; the beam has separated into two parts. A failure mode may have more than one mechanism that can cause the symptoms. Failure analysis is then an essential element of reliability assessment.

In the process of design, product integrity is achieved by systematically addressing failure mechanisms that may occur in the product. When a detailed understanding of potential failure mechanisms has been achieved, proactive design measures can be taken. When the process is performed early in the development and design, considerable cost savings can be achieved through failure prevention and control.

Failures in design must be addressed in consideration of the life cycle of the product. Figure 1.6 shows the elements of the life cycle of a typical product. Various stages of the life cycle can contribute to loads which may produce overstress or wear out failures. In design, we must not overlook issues such as the impact of manufacturing loads, such as temperature experienced in joining or loads occurring in deployment, such as shock occurring in shipment. Anticipation of operational conditions is of course essential. The second part of this book will further explain failure mechanisms and loading.

Figure 1.6 Elements of the product life cycle.

# 1.2.2 The Impact of Uncertainty

There are many sources of uncertainty that must be considered in designing a product. The loading applied to a system that produces component stresses, may take on a significant range of possible values. Also, materials properties and component dimensions that define the component strength are inherently variable. As we know, manufacturing processes result in variations in all dimensions and various processes may produce a range of defects. The accumulation of these uncertainties gives rise to statistical distributions for failure processes. Hence, reliability is the probability of success and unreliability then is the probability of failure. As we will see, these probabilities are defined in terms of the probability density function, $f(t)$, that describes the failure distribution. Each failure mechanism will have a unique probability density function.

For now observe Figure 1.7 to see why we must consider the failure distribution, $f(t)$, in our assessment process. Figure 1.7 shows two separate probability distributions for two different failure mechanisms acting on a component. They are denoted by the distribution parameters, $\beta$, of the function $f(t)$, where $f(t)$ is the two parameter Weibull distribution function. The means of these two distributions are indicated by the vertical lines and fall near 90 and 95 hours for $\beta=2$ and $\beta=5$, respectively. In other words the mean time to failure is relatively the same. So, which mechanism deserves resources for corrective action?

We must recall that the probability of failure at time $t$ is $F(t)=\int_{0}^{t} f(t) d t$.
If our component life was 20,000 hours for example, it should be clear that we must expend our resources to first correct $\beta=2$. Comparison of the means of two distributions, does not provide adequate information on where to focus corrective action. In addition, the mean life provides no information concerning risk and reliability. We can be more effective with more information. So, it is important to address uncertainty directly in design. The fundamental concepts for understanding probability are presented in Chapter 2.

Figure 1.7 Comparisons of two probability distributions of failure in a component, caused by two different failure mechanisms.

# 1.2.3 Defects

A defect occurs in the product as a result of the manufacturing operations used to fabricate and assemble a product. An example of a defect is shown in Figure 1.8. Here we see an assembly process which has resulted in two lead wires nearly touching in a multi-leaded transformer. The result was early failure under changing environmental temperatures. The failure mode was of course a short circuit. The leads were brought together as the temperature was reduced, due to differences in thermal coefficients of expansion of the materials.

Radiograph

Macrophoto

Figure 1.8 An electrical transformer with multiple lead wires. One lead wire was deformed during assembly resulting in a defect. The external case and coating has been removed to reveal the defect site.The nature of defects is to produce undesirable early failures in the life cycle of the product. They may arise due to reductions in strength of the component due to the defect resulting in susceptibility to overstress or defects can result in early wear out.

We will not focus specifically on manufacturing control to eliminate defects. There are many good texts on statistical process control. However, we will focus on identifying the relationship between manufacturing defects and variability and reliability, so that appropriate corrective actions for manufacturing operations can be devised through our assessment process.

# 1.3 Introduction to the Reliability Assessment Process

Cost effective and timely reliability assessment must involve a comprehensive structured process that is implemented early in the overall system development. The process can be applied to one or more competing technologies during product development, leading to an understanding of the suitability of a technology for a particular system or range of system applications. Hence, the right technologies are implemented for products early in development - a key to cost effectiveness. In addition, the technology is well characterized for application and design in future products. In order to effectively reduce risk, however, the process must be comprehensive and focus on root causes of failure.

The elements of an effective assessment process involve six key steps: (1) a technical assessment needed to characterize the materials and processes; (2) identification of potential failure sites and their associated failure mechanisms; (3) modeling of the mechanisms under the influence of accelerated and expected life cycle loads; (4) test matrix development; (5) execution of accelerated testing; and (6) detailed failure analysis. These critical process elements fit together, as shown in Figure 1.9.

A new technology assessment or new product development may begin with the technical assessment or ongoing materials characterization and testing as an entry point to the

Figure 1.9 The reliability assessment process forming the basis of this text book.process. However, if improvement is an initiative, then the process may begin with failure analysis as an entry point with field failures or defective components.

In any case, the successful implementation of this process involves a necessary understanding of system performance requirements and anticipated environmental loading conditions. An understanding of the life cycle of the system and its components is essential. This includes the potential impact of assembly stresses, storage environments, system operational testing, shipping, deployment and operational duty cycle. The loading conditions and their variabilities must be characterized including: absolute temperature, temperature range, humidity, vibration and other environmental considerations, such as pressure differential, the presence of some corrosive environmental conditions or the presence of radiation.

Once implemented, the process shown in Figure 1.9 is carried on continuously. New materials are always characterized and loading conditions assessed and updated for each new development or product improvement effort. The blocked region may be thought of as a continuous loop of testing and analysis often referred to as Test, Analyze and Fix (TAAF) A product of the process is not explicitly shown. However, if we think of the right-hand rule for a moment, the product of continuous TAAF activity, fueled by updating the materials and process data base, is effective corrective action emerging from the process in our direction.

The remainder of this chapter will further explain this process. In general, this book is intended to teach and provide reference to the techniques needed to implement the process shown. As with any systematic approach, this process serves as a model which can be tailored to suit specific product development goals.

# 1.3.1 Technical Assessment - Materials and Process Characterization

The initial step in implementation of an assessment is to identify loads on the system and develop an understanding of candidate technologies that may fulfill system performance and application requirements. Examples include speed, size and weight for a computing system or weight to strength ratio for a structural component. Candidate technologies must then be understood in terms of their physical architecture, manufacturing processes and materials properties. The potential variability in materials properties and dimensional variabilities resulting from fabrication and assembly are also important. Much of this information is compiled in other development activities. Hence, reliability assessment must be planned and conducted in parallel with other design activities.

Materials characterization is essential and should become a natural part of any upstream reliability program. Accurate material's properties are needed to effectively model failure processes. For example, the accuracy of a finite element model in assessing stresses acting on a failure site is dependent upon accurate constitutive relationships. In complex structures, the linear assumption may not be valid - particularly if polymers are involved. Often, creep behavior of polymers must be characterized over temperature, in order to provide effective constitutive relationships in modeling the impact of temperature. From a structural reliability perspective, fatigue performance and fracture toughness, and their variabilities, are critical material properties. As there are many excellent books on the details of materials testing, we will not devote discussion of specifics in this area. However, we will see throughout the book the importance of carrying on the effort of materials testing as a valuable input to the assessment process.

Also, the variability in materials properties cannot be neglected. Neglecting materials property variability is neglecting the nature of materials. Strength and strength related properties, such as fatigue and fracture toughness, are inherently dependent on defects. Defects are distributed in size and number giving way to a statistical distribution of the property.Manufacturing variabilities are also of critical importance. Variations expected in a particular process may be characterized from prototypes or pilot line production. Past performance of processes used to fabricate or assemble the components or subsystems may also provide information for estimating the expected variations.

# 1.3.2 Failure Site and Failure Mechanism Assessment

A failure mechanism may be described as a physical process, resulting from the application of chemical, mechanical or electrical loads, which leads to failures in system components. A variety of failure mechanisms, as we see in Figure 1.4, are possible and one or more may act on a single component in a system. Solder joints, for example, currently form the structural basis of the attachment of electrical parts to printed wiring boards in an electrical system. The failure of solder joints occurs from a combination of fatigue and creep, as solder is a material used at high temperature relative to its melting point. In mechanical systems, a structural component may undergo processes of corrosion and fatigue, depending on its application environment.

A systematic approach to assessment of potential failures and their associated sites in a system is a key part of the overall reliability assessment process. Given an understanding of system loads and the architectures of potential candidate technologies, fault tree analyzes can be performed. Fault trees can be used to relate system, subsystem or component failure modes to their respective sites and mechanisms. Fault trees also provide the opportunity to model the probability of top level events in terms of specific failures and their associated distributions. Failure Modes and Effects Analysis (FMEA) is also useful in systematically breaking down the architectural elements of a component or subsystem in order to ascertain potential failure mechanisms and their associated failure sites. These two methods compliment each other and can be performed in parallel during design activity. These methods are explained in Chapter 3.

### 1.3.3 Modeling

Modeling of potential failure mechanisms acting on key sites provides significant information concerning which mechanisms may dominate a particular technology. An effective modeling process will also yield the expected life, reveal the potential for overstress and provide an associated statistical distribution for each given mechanism. This provides the key to selecting a technology or component design that provides the necessary life, at an acceptable risk, under the anticipated operating conditions. The implementation of modeling provides for the development of robust designs. In a given technology, application of modeling of failure mechanisms provides the opportunity for proactive implementation of corrective actions in the development process through focusing on root cause.

Failure mechanism modeling may require two steps, as we see in Figure 1.10. First, the influence of system loads component stresses may need to be determined in a stress model. The stress model serves as an input to a damage model that relates component life to the stresses. The two parts are combined into the overall failure mechanism model which relates loads and stresses, material properties and component geometry to component life-time. Defects may also be considered. We can also operate on the model to estimate the component life distribution.

In many cases, a damage model exists relating stress to life (Evans, Lall Bauernschub 1995). Knowledge of materials properties as a result of materials and process characterization provides the necessary input for implementation of modeling. A familiar model thatdescribes the mechanical failure process of fatigue is Basquins Equation, which is the basis of modeling the linear region of the well known S-N curve :

$$
\frac{\Delta \sigma}{2}=\sigma_{f} N^{b}
$$

where $\Delta \sigma$ is the stress range and N is the number of cycles to failure. We can see that we must create a stress model to estimate the mechanical stress in the component, as depicted in Figure 1.10. Materials properties are also important. $\sigma_{f}$ and $b$ are materials constants which must be determined from fatigue testing.

Certainly mechanical and structural designers are familiar with this expression. However, an overall systems view must be taken in the development process and the architectural elements of electrical and electronic components must be subjected to the same scrutiny as elements of an aerospace structure. Closed form models exist for many electronic component failure mechanisms. In addition, addressing variability directly with the application of appropriate statistical and stochastic methods need to be extended to structural design rather than relying on safety factors. As we have seen, understanding variability can increase our effectiveness and ability to employ our resources wisely. Concepts in modeling are also explained in Chapter 3, while many specific failure mechanisms and their models are presented in later chapters in the second part of this text. Overstress, fatigue and corrosion are explained in Chapters 4,5 and 7 respectively.

In some cases, finite element modeling (FEM) can be very useful in stress modeling by assessing the impact of loading on a complex component. FEM modeling can reveal the distribution of temperature, stress and strain that are inputs to damage models (Evans, Evans and Ryu 1997). As we explain in Chapter 6, the application of finite element models, however, must clearly recognize the importance of accurate materials property data, realistic assumptions of boundary conditions and proper meshing. FEM is also deterministic and techniques to evaluate the impact of variations must be applied in concert with FEM to make this a valuable reliability assessment tool.

Figure 1.10 Simple example of failure mechanism modeling. The external loads and geometry determine the component stresses. The stress can be related to life through a damage model, in this case a simple S-N curve for fatigue life assessment.As an example, the power of finite element modeling can be extended through virtual experiments (Evans, Evans, Ryu 1995). In a virtual experiment, a factorial or fractional factorial statistical experimental design is set up around the geometric and materials variables comprising a particular failure site. The ranges of the variables of interest can be extracted from materials testing and process characterization. The model is then exercised in accordance with the design. A regression analysis reveals which factors are dominant and yields a closed form model which can be used for further analysis. The factors dominating the reliability or life of the structure then become the focus of improvements in processing, fabrication or design.

The propagation of uncertainty in materials and architecture can be managed by application of the Monte Carlo method. Inputs of the materials and process characterization can be used to estimate the statistical distributions of materials and architecture of a given technology (Evans, Evans, Ryu 1997, Hazelrigg 1995). These distributions are then sampled and the deterministic model is exercised. The process is repeated keeping track of each result. After many repetitions, the distribution of failure is revealed. A sensitivity study will show which factors contribute to the most to variability in the life of the technology and which failure mechanisms control the life. Adequate computing capability enables the Monte Carlo methodology. However, a PC is adequate for many situations. Chapters 2 and 3 explain the concepts in applying Monte Carlo simulation while Chapter 14 shows how this technique fits into actual reliability assessments.

# 1.3.4 Test Effectiveness and Testing

Design of a developmental testing program should be based upon potential failure modes and mechanisms acting on a system, sub-system or component of a given technology and architecture. A complete test effectiveness analysis will yield a ranking of which tests are most effective at exciting the dominant failure mechanisms. Appropriate accelerated tests can then be selected and executed. This approach results in an expedient cost effective test program. Issues in testing are presented in the final part of the book.

Test effectiveness analysis employs a relational matrix similar to a quality function deployment matrix. As shown in Figure 1.11, the matrix is used to correlate the results of the failure mechanism assessment to available test methods. Each test is scored in its ability to excite a failure mechanism active in the system. As in the QFD process, ranking symbols are used. Each test method is then scored. Those methods which are most effective are highly correlated to the dominant failure mechanisms. This approach can be extended to analyze the effectiveness of of the full range of verification methods including prevention, analysis, process controls and tests (PACTS). This technique is explained in detail in Chapter 10.

Testing to failure of new technologies in the system development process is important and preferred. Testing to failure allows confirmation of the dominant failure mechanisms and with sufficient samples will provide the data necessary to confirm the statistical distribution of the product life for each dominant failure mechanism. It may be necessary to test the same subsystem to induce more than one failure mode. If testing to failure cannot be performed, then modeling can effectively provide a minimum test time to qualify or demonstrate an appropriate level of risk for a technology. Caution should be employed in the application of standard tests developed for older technologies. Simply applying past practices may not address key problems. The impact of accelerated environments on the architecture and materials comprising a technology should be understood.

Figure 1.11 Concept of a relational matrix used in Test Effectiveness analysis.

Selection of test loads and conditions is highly important. Accelerated testing is desirable as it reduces test time. Accelerated testing is performed by elevating the test loads above the load levels normally encountered in use of the product. For example, semiconductors may be tested at elevated temperature and voltage levels to shorten test times. The acceleration factor of a test is then defined as the ratio of the field life to the test time:

$$
A F=\frac{t_{\text {field }}}{t_{\text {test }}}
$$

The importance of modeling in concert with testing is essential in assessing the impact of accelerated test conditions and projecting test data to field conditions. Also, over acceleration is a risk. For example, selecting a large temperature range above the glass transition temperature of a printed wiring assembly may produce unrealistic results. Accelerated testing and the analysis of data from such tests is explained in Chapter 11.

Multiple test conditions can be performed using designed experiments. Statistically designed experiments provide the advantage of fully exploring the experimental space of the factors of interest, using the minimum number of test conditions [Box et. al. 1978]. The number of runs can increase rapidly, however. In this case, screening designs can be used to initially identify key factors and fractional factorial designs can be used to still gain considerable information. Two level factorials are generally very useful in reliability investigations of new technologies. In this case the number of experimental runs can be calculated from the following equation:

$$
i_{\mathrm{r}}=2^{k}
$$

where $i$ is the number of runs and $k$ is the number of factors. An example of a layout used to evaluate new types of solder alloys is shown in Table 1.2.

Statistical experiments for reliability assessment are explained in Chapter 11.Table 1.2 Example of Multiple Factors and Test Conditions Evaluated using SED

# 1.3.5 Failure Analysis

Completion of a developmental test program should conclude with a detailed failure analysis of test articles. The process of failure analysis provides confirmation of the dominant mechanism and the failure site. As discussed previously, this is critical to ensuring that testing is representative of 'field conditions' or anticipated environments. The results of failure analysis can also provide data needed to improve failure mechanism models. It is also the entry point of our process when product improvement is the focus to correct field failures.

Failure analysis employs many different techniques to ascertain the cause of a failure. It is the goal of failure analysis to extract as much information about the circumstances as possible. The characteristics of various failure mechanisms can be matched to the evidence collected in the process of failure analysis and the mechanism can be determined. Information about the loading conditions is also obtained.

As an example, Figure 1.12 shows a typical fracture surface of a bolt. The characteristics of fatigue are immediately apparent. The shape and relative size of these features reveal the

Figure 1.12 The many features identified in failure analysis of this fractured bolt confirm the mechanism and the nature of the loading conditions. (Fuchs and Stevens 1980). Courtesy of Münchener Rückversicherungs - Gesellschaft).loading was moderate in comparison to the strength of the bolt material and that stress concentration played a role in crack initiation. This information is useful in confirming the failure mechanism and loading conditions, which are essential to developing the proper corrective action for the problem.

Chapter 13 explains the techniques used in failure analysis. While this chapter focuses more on electronics component failure analysis, however, many of the techniques applied to analyze mechanical failure are the same. Chapter 9 shows many examples of failures and how they manifest themselves in both mechanical and electronic components and systems and can be consulted in conjunction with Chapter 13 to provide a complete understanding of failure analysis and practical manifestation of failures.

# 1.4 Summary

Products, which are competitive in the market place, require the careful consideration of factors contributing to the integrity of the product early in the design. The implementation of new technologies in products requires appropriate methodologies which are timely and cost effective. A comprehensive approach to reliability assessment must be employed, which can be implemented 'upstream' in the system development to insure a high degree of product integrity. In addition, continuous improvement in the next generation of products is essential and requires an ongoing systematic process. A comprehensive process focusing on root cause of failures in system elements and employing effective test programs ensures that reliability and product life goals will be met.

In this chapter we have introduced the process. We have discussed the elementary definitions and nomenclature of failure and we are now ready to move on to understanding the techniques necessary to implement the process. We will further discuss concepts in physics of failure and reliability assessment in the remainder of Part 1 in Chapters 2 and 3. Part 2 will address specifics of failure mechanisms, including stress analysis, in Chapters 4 through 8, with many actual examples of failures presented in Chapter 9. Part 3 will discuss testing and analysis of test results, including failure analysis, in Chapters 10 through 13. Finally, the process in action will be presented in several case studies shown in Chapter 14.
