Hyung S. Hahn

Although engineers do their best to create systems and components with the best possible integrity, $100 \%$ reliability is not likely to be obtained due to many causes. As we discussed in Chapter 1, failure mechanisms may become active in products due to defective components under unexpected loading conditions, errors or defects in manufacturing processes, and even inadequate design of the system and its components, as some of the causes commonly found. Generally, we can classify some common factors resulting in a loss of product integrity. These may include: ignorance of the loading conditions or actual environmental conditions subjected to the system, inability to maintain control of the system in its operation, and inherent randomness embedded in the system from variations in materials properties and the geometry which describes the components in the system. All these factors work in combination or separately to create uncertainty for the performance and life of the products and systems engineers endeavor to develop.

We say there is uncertainty because we cannot predict outcomes precisely. Reliability is then a measure related to the life of a system that is basically a measure of uncertainty. In this chapter, we will present the basic mathematics and processes needed to deal with the reliability of a system. Reliability theory is to provide a quantitative measure for the possibility that a system or component will function as designed. Probability is the best measure that describes and allows us to understand and manipulate the level of uncertainty. The mathematics dealing with uncertainty is probability theory which we review in the next sections. In addition, the Monte Carlo method provides us with a framework helpful to link the probability theory with failure mechanism models to build up information needed to deal with the uncertainty in design. In this chapter, we will build our understanding of these key concepts through a review of probability theory and concepts. For further in depth study, the reader is encouraged to consult the references listed.

### 2.1 Random Events and Uncertainty

Let's now review and examine some of the fundamental concepts related to understanding uncertainty and probability theory.

### 2.1.1 Probabilities and Uncertainty

Before we turn to the study of probability, we need to define the concept of set. A set is defined as any collection of objects we choose. Each one of the objects within a set is calledan element. Given set $A$, the notation $a \in A$ implies that $a$ is an element of $A$. We denote $A \subset B$ to indicate that set $A$ is a subset of set $B$. Set $A$ becomes a subset of set $B$ when each element of $A$ is also an element of $B$. By this definition, a set is a subset of itself. If set $A$ has no elements, $A$ is called a null set, and is often denoted by $A=\varnothing$. The union of the two sets $A$ and $B$ is defined as the collection of all the elements that $A$ and $B$ have, and is denoted by $A \cup B$. The intersection of the two sets $A$ and $B$ is defined as the collection of elements common in $A$ and $B$, and is denoted by $A \cap B$ or simply $A B$. If two sets have no common elements, they are called mutually exclusive or disjoint. If two sets $A$ and $B$ are mutually exclusive, $A \cap B=\varnothing$.

An experiment is the process by which we observe or measure something of interest. We conduct experiments to obtain information on the process or phenomena of interest if we do not have sufficient information on it. While we cannot predict the outcome of an experiment, let's assume that we know all the possible outcomes. This set of 'all the possible outcomes' of an experiment is referred to as the sample space of the experiment, and is often denoted by $S$. An event is defined as a subset of the sample space. In other words, an event is the set of points that belong to a subset of the sample space. For example, let's consider an experiment of tossing a coin. In a single toss of a coin, the outcome will be either a head $(\mathrm{H})$ or a tail $(\mathrm{T})$. It follows that the sample space is $S=\{H, T\}$. If we toss the coin twice consecutively, the sample space would be $S=\{H H, H T, T H, T T\}$. In this case, some of the possible events include two heads, one head and one tail, and two tails, etc.

Based on the concept of an event, we define the union and intersection of events. For a set of events $E_{1}, E_{2}, \ldots, E_{n}$, the union of these events, denoted by $\bigcup_{i=1}^{n} E_{i}$ is defined as the event consisting of all the outcomes of the events $E_{1}, E_{2}, \ldots, E_{n}$ while their intersection, denoted by $\bigcap_{i=1}^{n} E_{i}$ is the event consisting of those outcomes common in all the events $E_{1}, E_{2}, \ldots, E_{n}$. The complement of $E$, often denoted by $E^{\mathrm{c}}$ or $\overline{\mathrm{E}}$, is defined as the event consisting of all the outcomes in the sample space, which do not belong to $E$. In the example of tossing a coin, the sample space $S=$ $\{\mathrm{H}, \mathrm{T}\}$. If event $E$ were one head, then $E^{\mathrm{c}}$ would be one tail. Based on the notion of set and experiment, we can now define the concept of probability.

There are a couple of major perspectives on the concept of probability. The classical perspective takes the ratio of the number of successes to the total number of trials:

$$
P(\text { success })=\frac{\text { number of successes }}{\text { total number of trials }}
$$

This perspective is conceptually easy to understand. However, it has some ambiguities that limit its wider application: it is not often possible to repeat the experiment, and even if it could be repeated, it's not clear how many times we need to repeat the experiment in order to obtain the exact probability.

The other important perspective is the axiomatic probability. It is based on the following three axioms.
(i) $0 \leq P(E) \leq 1$
(ii) $P(S)=1$
(iii) If events $E_{1}, E_{2}, \ldots, E_{n}$ are mutually exclusive, $P\left(\bigcup_{i=1}^{n} E_{i}\right)=\sum_{i=1}^{n} P\left(E_{i}\right)$

Since it is simple to use and mathematically clear, it is widely applied in analysis. We will take this perspective for our discussion on probabilities. In this context, the probability of an event can be defined as a quantitative measure over a $0-1$ scale, representing the frequency of the occurrence of the event relative to the sample space. Further, the probability of an event $E$ is the sum of the probabilities of the elements in $E$. In terms of the probabilities, uncertaintytakes place when the sample space has more than one element with nonzero probability of occurrence, which prevents us from predicting the outcome of an experiment.

# 2.1.2 Rules of Probability

In order to calculate the probabilities of a specific or combination of events, we need to understand some basic rules or properties of probabilities. We can derive the following properties of probability based on the probability axioms in (2.2).

Since $E$ and $E^{\mathrm{c}}$ are mutually exclusive, and $E \cup E^{\mathrm{c}}=S$ by definition,

$$
P\left(E \cup E^{\mathrm{c}}\right)=P(S)=P(E)+P\left(E^{\mathrm{c}}\right)=1
$$

For any two given events $A$ and $B$, the probability of the union of $A$ and $B$, that is the probability of any one of the events $A$ and $B$ taking place is calculated by

$$
\begin{aligned}
& P(A \cup B)=P(A)+P(B)-P(A \cap B) \\
& \quad=P(A)+P(B)-P(A B)
\end{aligned}
$$

since all points in $A \cap B$ are counted twice in $P(A)+P(B)$.
In the case where we calculate the probability of the union of three events $A, B$, and $C$, we can see the following

$$
\begin{aligned}
& P(A \cup B \cup C)=P[(A \cup B) \cup C]=P(A \cup B)+P(C)-P[(A \cup B) C] \\
& \quad=P(A)+P(B)-P(A B)+P(C)-P(A C \cup B C) \\
& \quad=P(A)+P(B)+P(C)-P(A B)-P(B C)-P(A C)+P(A B C)
\end{aligned}
$$

The above calculation process can be extended in the case of union of multiple events $E_{1}, E_{2}$, $\ldots, E_{n}$. By induction, we can obtain,

$$
\begin{aligned}
& P\left[\bigcup_{i=1}^{n} E_{i}\right]=\sum_{i=1}^{n} P\left(E_{i}\right)-\sum_{i<j}^{n} P\left(E_{i} E_{j}\right)+\sum_{i<j<k}^{n} P\left(E_{i} E_{j} E_{k}\right) \\
& \quad-\sum_{i<j<k<l}^{n} P\left(E_{i} E_{j} E_{k} E_{l}\right)+\ldots+(-1)^{n+1} P\left(E_{1} E_{2} \ldots E_{n}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

## Conditional Probabilities

Another important concept of probability is conditional probabilities. Suppose that we toss a fair coin twice consecutively, and that one head and one tail occur. Given this information, what will be the probability that the head occurs first. We can interpret this question as to asking the probability of having a head first, on the condition that one head and one tail occur in the consecutive tosses. The conditional probability deals with the probability of an event $A$ given that another event $B$ takes place, and is often denoted by $P(A \mid B)$.

In this example, the solution can be obtained through the following process. It is easy to conjecture that the sample space of this experiment is $S=\{(\mathrm{HH}),(\mathrm{HT}),(\mathrm{TH}),(\mathrm{TT})\}$. From here, we know that the event that one head and one tail occurs is $B=\{(\mathrm{HT}),(\mathrm{TH})\}$. And, the event of having a head first is limited to $A=\{(\mathrm{HT})\}$. Since each of the four outcomes of the sample space is equally likely (fair coin) to occur, the probability of occurrence for each outcome is $1 / 4$. Since the above question is asking the probability of event $A$ out of event $B$, the answer would be $\frac{1}{4} / \frac{1}{2}=1 / 2$.

The reasoning in the example above can be applied to derive a general formula for the calculation of $P(A \mid B)$. The condition that one head and one tail occurs in this experiment has the effect of compressing our sample space to $\{(\mathrm{HT}),(\mathrm{TH})\}$, which makes the event $B$ the newsample space. On the other hand, given that event $B$ occurs, if event $A$ is to occur, the actual incident should be an outcome of both $A$ and $B$, namely the event $A B$. Thus, the probability of $A$ given $B$ is the probability of $A B$ relative to the probability of $B$. It follows that,

$$
P(A \mid B)=\frac{P(A B)}{P(B)}
$$

It should be noted that $P(A \mid B)$ can be defined only if $P(B)>0$. It follows that,

$$
P(A B)=P(A \mid B) P(B)
$$

We say that events $A$ and $B$ are independent if and only if

$$
P(A B)=P(A) P(B)
$$

It follows that, if events $A$ and $B$ are independent,

$$
P(A \mid B)=P(A) \text { and } P(B \mid A)=P(B)
$$

This result implies that the occurrence of event $A$ is not affected by the occurrence of event $B$ and vice versa, if events $A$ and $B$ are independent.

The usefulness of conditional probabilities is in that many real life events are combined in a manner where each event works as a condition to others, and thus we can often obtain the probability of events more easily by expressing them in terms of conditional probabilities.

# Bayes'Formula

Based on the definition of conditional probabilities, we can now define Bayes' Formula. Given two events $A$ and $B$, we can write $A$ as

$$
A=A B \cup A B^{c}
$$

This equation implies that in order for an outcome to be in $A$, it must occur either in $A B$ or $A B^{c}$. Since $A B$ and $A B^{c}$ are mutually exclusive,

$$
\begin{aligned}
& P(A)=P\left(A B \cup A B^{c}\right)=P(A B)+P\left(A B^{c}\right)-P\left(A B \cap A B^{c}\right) \\
& \quad=P(A B)+P\left(A B^{c}\right)=P(A \mid B) P(B)+P\left(A \mid B^{c}\right) P\left(B^{c}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

This equation implies that the probability of $A$ can be calculated as the weighted average of the probability of $A$ given that $B$ occurs and the probability of $A$ given that $B$ does not occur, and the probability of each conditional event is given as the weight.

The above formula is a simple form of Bayes' formula. We can extend the above reasoning process to obtain the generalized formula. Suppose that the occurrence of event $A$ depends on the occurrence of a number of events $B_{i} \mathrm{~s}$, and the events $B_{1}, B_{2}, \ldots, B_{n}$ are mutually exclusive events such that $\bigcup_{i=1}^{n} B_{i}=S$ as shown in the Venn diagram of Fig. 2.1. Then, it is clear that,

$$
\begin{aligned}
A & =\sum_{i=1}^{n} A B_{i} \\
P(A) & =\sum_{i=1}^{n} P\left(A B_{i}\right)=\sum_{i=1}^{n} P\left(A \mid B_{i}\right) P\left(B_{i}\right) \\
P\left(B_{i} \mid A\right) & =\frac{P\left(A B_{i}\right)}{P(A)}=\frac{P\left(A \mid B_{i}\right) P\left(B_{i}\right)}{P(A)} \\
& =\frac{P\left(A \mid B_{i}\right) P\left(B_{i}\right)}{\sum_{j=1}^{n} P\left(A \mid B_{j}\right) P\left(B_{j}\right)}
\end{aligned}
$$

Figure 2.1 A Venn diagram of an event whose occurrence depends on a number of mutually exclusive events. Equation (2.9) is known as Bayes' Formula. Bayes' Formula is the result of manipulating the concept of conditional probabilities.

Equation (2.9) is known as Bayes' Formula. Bayes' Formula is the result of manipulating the concept of conditional probabilities.

Example 2.1 An electronics company purchases a component from two vendors, A and B. A supplies $30 \%$ and B supplies $70 \%$ of the total number of the components to this company. On average, the percentage of defective components supplied by A and B are known to be $3 \%$ and $4 \%$, respectively. What is the probability that a randomly selected component is defective? If a selected component is defective, what is the probability that it was supplied by vendor A or vendor B?

# Solution:

(i) The Bayes' formula indicates,

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \mathrm{P}(\text { defective })=P(\text { defective and from } A)+P(\text { defective and from } B) \\
& \quad=P(\text { from } A) P(\text { defective from } A)+P(\text { from } B) P(\text { defective } \mid \text { from } B) \\
& \quad=(0.3)(0.03)+(0.7)(0.04)=0.037
\end{aligned}
$$

(ii) If the selected component is defective, it follows that,

$$
\begin{aligned}
& P(\text { from } A \mid \text { defective })=\frac{P(\text { from } A, \text { Defective })}{P(\text { defective })}=\frac{(0.3)(0.03)}{0.037}=0.243, \text { and } \\
& P(\text { from } B \mid \text { defective })=\frac{P(\text { from } B, \text { Defective })}{P(\text { defective })}=\frac{(0.7)(0.04)}{0.037}=0.757
\end{aligned}
$$

Example 2.2 Suppose that a piece of test equipment has a $98 \%$ probability of identifying a defective part correctly, and a $4 \%$ probability of identifying a good part as defective. A box containing 100 parts including 3 defectives is selected to be tested. When the equipment identifies a part as defective, what is the probability that it is truly defective?

Solution: Let A and B represent the event that the equipment identifies a part as defective and that the part is truly defective, respectively. Then, we have

$$
P(A \mid B)=0.98, P(A \mid \bar{B})=0.04, \text { and } P(B)=0.03
$$It follows that,


$$

\begin{aligned}
P(B \mid A) & =\frac{P(B) P(A \mid B)}{P(B) P(A \mid B)+P(\bar{B}) P(A \mid \bar{B})} \\
& =\frac{(0.03)(0.98)}{(0.03)(0.98)+(0.97)(0.04)}=0.431
\end{aligned}

$$

# 2.1 Random Variables

We can now move on to the concept of the random variable.

### 2.2.1 Random Variables and Distribution Functions

## Random Variable

In conducting experiments, we are often more interested in some functions of the outcome than the outcome itself. Suppose that an electronic device consists of three key components, and if any one of the three components breaks, the device will be disposed. If we want to know the average life of this device, we should know the life of the component, which is the minimum of the three, and we will not be concerned about the lives of the other two. In other words, we will be interested in knowing that the minimum is 9.2 months, and not be concerned if the lives of the other two are $(10.3,12.6)$ or $(10.5,18.3)$, etc.

As shown in the above example, the values of interest are defined as random variables. Formally a random variable is defined as real valued functions defined on the sample space. This definition indicates that since a random variable represents a set of events in an experiment, we may be able to assign probabilities to its values. Applying the concept of random variables facilitates the manipulation of event in mathematical form.

We can classify random variables into two categories: discrete and continuous. A discrete random variable is one that can have either a finite or countable number of possible values. This definition implies that there is a one-to-one correspondence between the possible values that the random variable can take on and a set of positive integers $1,2,3, \ldots$ A continuous random variable is one that is defined over a range of numerical values so that it can take on a continuum of possible values. For example, a random variable representing the sum of two dice is discrete since it has only 11 possible values: $2,3,4, \ldots, 12$. On the other hand, a random variable denoting the life of an electric light bulb is continuous since it can take on any values between 0 and $\infty$. We can assign probabilities to each possible value of a discrete random variable or to each range of a continuous random variable.

## Cumulative Distribution Function(cdf)

Cdf is defined as the probability that random variable $X$ is less than or equal to the real value $x$. Mathematical expression of the $\operatorname{cdf} F($.$) is given by$


$$

F(x)=P(X \leq x)

$$

where $x$ is any real value, $-\infty<x<\infty$
It is easy to understand that $F$ is a monotone non-decreasing function of $x$ since the event $\{X \leq y\}$ is included in the event $\{X \leq x\}$ if $y \leq x$. And it follows that,
$$

\begin{aligned}
& \lim _{x \rightarrow-\infty} F(x)=F(\infty)=1, \text { and } \\
& \lim _{x \rightarrow-\infty} F(x)=0
\end{aligned}

$$

Using the above properties of cdf, we can calculate the probability of events easily. For example, the probability that $X$ is less than or equal to $b$ and greater than $a$ is calculated easily by


$$

P(a<X \leq b)=F(b)-F(a)

$$

# Probability Density Function(pdf)

In accordance with the concept of cdf, we can define the concept of pdf $f(\cdot)$ as a marginal probability assigned to an incremental value from $x$. By definition, the pdf is the derivative of cdf. The pdf enables us to calculate the distribution of random variables easily. In the case of continuous random variables, we have


$$

F(x)=\int\_{-\infty}^{x} f(y) d y

$$

For a small value $\varepsilon>0$, we have


$$

P\left\{x-\frac{\delta}{2} \leq X \leq x+\frac{\delta}{2}\right\}=\int\_{x-\frac{\delta}{2}}^{x+\frac{\delta}{2}} f(y) d y \cong \delta f(x)

$$

Thus, $f(x)$ can be interpreted as a measure of the likelihood of the random variable being near $x$.

For discrete random variables, the expression of pdf is slightly different since $P\left\{X \leq x \pm \frac{\delta}{2}\right\}$ converges to $P(X \leq x)$ as $\delta \rightarrow 0$. For a discrete random variable $X$, the pdf, often denoted by $p(x)$, is defined as


$$

p(x)=P(X=x)

$$

It should be noted that $p(x)$ is positive only for a countable number of values of $X$. It follows then, that the distribution function $F(x)$ of discrete random variables will be,


$$

F(x)=\sum*{a l l x*{i} \leq x} P\left(X=x\_{i}\right)

$$

### 2.2.2 Moments of Random Variables

The density or distribution function of a random variable provides all the information about the random variable. However, there are many cases where the exact form of distribution of a random variable is not available. In this case, some numerical values that characterize the distribution are enough to manipulate the random variables. The moments of random variables are those that enable us to obtain such values. The $\boldsymbol{n}$-th moment of a random variable $X$ is defined as


$$

E\left[X^{n}\right]=\left\{\begin{array}{lll}
\int*{-\infty}^{\infty} x^{n} f(x) d x & \text { if } & X \text { is continuous } \\
\sum*{x \in \mathbb{Z}} x^{n} P(x) & \text { if } & X \text { is discrete }
\end{array}\right.

$$

The first moment is referred to as the mean or expected value of the distribution, and is often denoted by $E[X]$ or simply $\mu$. Variance $\operatorname{Var}(X)$, often denoted by $\sigma_{x}^{2}$, is defined as
$$

\operatorname{Var}(X)=E\left[(X-\mu)^{2}\right]= \begin{cases}\int*{-\infty}^{\infty}(x-\mu)^{2} f(x) d x & \text { if } X \text { is continuous } \\ \sum*{x \in S} x^{n}(x-\mu)^{2} P(x) & \text { if } X \text { is discrete }\end{cases}

$$

$E\left[(X-\mu)^{n}\right]$ is often called the $\boldsymbol{n}$-th central moment of the random variable $X$. The square root of the variance, $\sigma_{x}$ is called the standard deviation. Both variance and standard deviation are the measure indicating the variability of the distribution. The mean and the variance are widely used as parameters characterizing the distribution of random variables.

When random variable $X$ is continuous, we have,


$$

\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{Var}(X) & =\int*{-\infty}^{\infty}(x-\mu)^{2} f(x) d x=\int*{-\infty}^{\infty}\left(x^{2}-2 \mu x+\mu^{2}\right) f(x) d x \\
& =\int*{-\infty}^{\infty} x^{2} f(x) d x-2 \mu \int*{-\infty}^{\infty} x f(x) d x+\mu^{2} \int\_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x) d x \\
& =E\left[X^{2}\right]-2 \mu E[X]+\mu^{2}=E\left[X^{2}\right]-\mu^{2}
\end{aligned}

$$

We can derive the same relationship easily for discrete random variables.

# 2.2.3 Random Vectors

So far, we have developed an analogy for the distribution of a single random variable. However, if the mathematical system models we use include more than one random variable, we need to understand how the functions of random variables work.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be two random variables. We can define joint distribution of these two random variables. The joint cumulative distribution function of $X$ and $Y$, which is the probability that the event of $\{X \leq x\}$ and the event of $\{Y \leq y\}$ take place jointly, is defined by


$$

F\_{x y}(x, y)=P(X \leq x, Y \leq y)-\infty<x, y<\infty

$$

We call $X$ and $Y$ jointly continuous if there exists a function $f(x, y)$ such that for every sets $A$ and $B$ of real numbers, it satisfies,


$$

P[X \in A, Y \in B]=\int*{y \in B} \int*{x \in A} f(x, y) d x d y

$$

The function $f(x, y)$ is called joint density function of $X$ and $Y$. From the above equation, it follows that,


$$

P[X \in A]=\int*{x \in A} \int*{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x, y) d y d x=\int*{x \in A} f*{x}(x) d x

$$

where $f_{x}(x)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x, y) d y$ is the marginal probability density function of $X$.
For discrete random variables $X$ and $Y$, we can also define the joint probability density function of $X$ and $Y$ as


$$

p(x, y)=P(X=x, Y=y)

$$

The marginal probability density function of $X$ can be obtained by


$$

p*{x}(x)=\sum*{y} p(x, y)

$$

Based on the above notions, we can deal with the mathematics of random variables. For a given function $g(x, y)$ of the two random variables $X$ and $Y$, we will have,


$$

E[g(x, y)]=\left\{\begin{array}{ll}
\int*{-\infty}^{\infty} \int*{-\infty}^{\infty} g(x, y) f(x, y) d x d y & \text { if } X \text { and } Y \text { are continuous, } \\
\sum*{y} \sum*{x} g(x, y) p(x, y) & \text { if } X \text { and } Y \text { are discrete }
\end{array}\right.

$$
Then, let's derive the expected values of some functions of random variables.


$$

\begin{aligned}
E(X+Y) & =\int*{-\infty}^{\infty} \int*{-\infty}^{\infty}(x, y) f(x, y) d x d y \\
& =\int*{-\infty}^{\infty} x\left[\int*{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x, y) d y\right] d x+\int*{-\infty}^{\infty} y\left[\int*{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x, y) d x\right] d y \\
& =\int*{-\infty}^{\infty} x f*{x}(x) d x+\int*{-\infty}^{\infty} y f*{y}(y) d y=E[X]+E[Y]
\end{aligned}

$$

The two random variables $X$ and $Y$ are called independent if they satisfy that, for any real values $x$ and $y$,


$$

P[X \leq x, Y \leq y]=P[X \leq x] P[Y \leq y]

$$

Thus, the independence of the two random variables $X$ and $Y$ implies the independence of the two events $\{X \leq y\}$ and $\{Y \leq y\}$. If $X$ and $Y$ are independent, we have for any real-values $x$ and $y$,


$$

F*{x y}(x, y)=P[X \leq x, Y \leq y]=P[X \leq x] P[Y \leq y]=F*{x}(x) F\_{y}(y)

$$

If $X$ and $Y$ are jointly continuous and independent, then


$$

f(x, y)=f*{x}(x) f*{y}(y)

$$

and, if X and Y are discrete, then


$$

p(x, y)=p*{x}(x) p*{y}(y)

$$

Using the above equations of joint cdf's and pdf's, we can derive useful equations for the functions of random variables. If $X$ and $Y$ are independent, and $h$ and $g$ are any functions, then


$$

\begin{aligned}
& E[g(x) h(y)]=\int*{-\infty}^{\infty} \int*{-\infty}^{\infty} g(x) h(y) f(x, y) d x d y \\
& \quad=\int*{-\infty}^{\infty} g(x) f*{x}(x) d x \int*{-\infty}^{\infty} h(y) f*{y}(y) d y=E[g(x)] E[h(y)]
\end{aligned}

$$

Given two independent random variables $X$ and $Y$, we will have


$$

E[X Y]=E[X] E[Y] \text { and } E\left[\frac{X}{Y}\right]=E[X] E\left[\frac{1}{Y}\right]

$$

The above equations for the expected values of the functions of random variables are useful when obtaining the expected values of mathematical models including complex forms of random variables' functions. We close this section with emphasis on the fact that


$$

E\left[\frac{x}{Y}\right]=\iint*{X} \frac{x}{y} f(x) g(y) d x d y \neq \frac{E[X]}{E[Y]}=\frac{\int*{x} x f(x) d x}{\int\_{y} y g(y) d y}

$$

# 2.3 Probability Distributions of Random Variables

Probabilities are defined as any real values from 0 to 1 , such that the sum of the probabilities of all the elements in the sample space is 1 . Since there are no other restrictions on what form the distribution can take, we can define a large number of different probability distributions. However, there are some important forms of distributions that enable us to enjoy the convenience of utilizing them to describe many observed phenomena found in real life. From this point forward, we will explore the properties of some important distributions. We will follow the convention of describing the probability distributions by classifying them discrete or continuous.# 2.3.1 Discrete Distributions

## Discrete Uniform Distribution

We say that a random variable X has discrete uniform distribution if it is defined over a sample space $S=\left\{x_{1}, x_{2}, x_{3}, \ldots, x_{n}\right\}$ that is countable or finite, and has the probability density function of the form,


$$

P\left(X=x*{i}\right)= \begin{cases}\frac{1}{n} & \text { if } x*{i} \in\left\{x*{1}, x*{2}, x*{3}, \ldots, x*{n}\right\} \\ 0 & \text { otherwise }\end{cases}

$$

Fig.2.2 (a) shows the density function of a discrete uniform distribution when the sample space has five elements. The uniform random variables have the property that the occurrences of all the components in the sample space are equally likely. The example of tossing a fair coin can be described by the discrete uniform distribution, where each of the outcomes (head and tail) has the probability of $1 / 2$.

## Bernoulli Distribution

The Bernoulli distribution is used to model the occurrence of events where exactly one of two possible outcomes takes place. The two outcomes of the Bernoulli random variable $X$ are often associated with $X=0$ and $X=1$ referred to as 'failure' and 'success', respectively. The parameter $p(0 \leq p \leq 1)$ denotes the probability of success. It follows that the probability of failure becomes $1-p$. Thus, the density function of a Bernoulli random variable is defined by


$$

P(\mathrm{X}=x)= \begin{cases}p & \text { if } x=1 \\ 1-p & \text { if } x=0\end{cases}

$$

## Geometric Distribution

The geometric distribution is a simple extension of the Bernoulli distribution. It is often associated with the number of repeated trials needed to obtain the first success, where the outcomes of each trial have the Bernoulli distribution. It follows that the probability density function of the Geometric distribution is given by


$$

P(X=n)=(1-p)^{n-1} p, n=1,2, \ldots

$$

where $p$ is the probability of success on a trial, and $n$ is the number of trials needed to obtain the first success. Fig.2.2 (b) shows the pdf of a geometric distribution.

Example 2.3 Suppose that 10 identical lots numbered from 0 to 9 are contained in a black box. We continue to draw the lots one by one until we draw the number 7 lot. If we return the lot into the box every time we draw one, what is the probability of finishing this game on the fourth draw? And what is the probability if we do not return the drawn lots?

## Solution:

(i) If we return, the probability to select the number 7 lot at each draw is 0.1 . Thus, we get:


$$

P(X=4)=(1-p)^{4-1} p=(0.9)^{3}(0.1)=0.0729

$$
(ii) If we do not return, the probability to select the number 7 lot changes at each draw:


$$

\begin{array}{ll}
P(\text { do not select } 7 \text { at } 1 \text { st draw })=\frac{9}{10} & P(\text { do not select } 7 \text { at } 2 \text { nd draw })=\frac{8}{9} \\
P(\text { do not select } 7 \text { at } 3 \text { rd draw })=\frac{7}{8} & P(\text { select } 7 \text { at } 4 \text { th draw })=\frac{1}{7}
\end{array}

$$

It follows that,


$$

P(X=4)=\left\{\left(\frac{9}{10}\right)\left(\frac{8}{9}\right)\left(\frac{7}{8}\right)\right\}\left(\frac{1}{7}\right)=\frac{1}{10}

$$

# Binomial Distribution

A discrete random variable $X$ is said to have the binomial distribution when its probability density function is given by


$$

f(x)= \begin{cases}n C\_{x} p^{x}(1-p)^{n-x} & x=0,1,2, \ldots, n, \& 0 \leq p \leq 1 \\ 0 & \text { otherwise }\end{cases}

$$

Fig.2.2 (c) shows the pdf of a binomial distribution. It applies to the cases where we repeat the experiment $n$ times and random variable $X$ represents the number of successes in the $n$ experiments, given $p$ and $1-p$ as the probability of success and failure at each trial, respectively. That formula is derived from the equation that,


$$

(a+b)^{n}=\sum*{x=0}^{n} C*{x} a^{x} b^{n-x}

$$

If we replace $a$ and $b$ by $p$ and $1-p$, respectively, we would have


$$

[p+(1-p)]^{n}=1=\sum*{x=0}^{n} C*{x} p^{x}(1-p)^{n-x}

$$



Figure 2.2 Pdfs of some discrete probability distributionsThe binomial distribution is often denoted by $b(n, p)$, where the two parameters $n$ and $p$ represent the number of trials and the probability of success at one trial, respectively. The binomial distribution becomes an excellent mathematical model for experiments where the trials are repeated many times with identical conditions at each trial.

Example 2.4 Suppose that we toss a fair die seven times. Let $X$ be the number of ' 6 's appeared in this experiment. Then, $X$ is a binomial random variable whose density function is given by


$$

P(X=x)= \begin{cases}c*{x} C*{x}\left(\frac{1}{6}\right)^{x}\left(\frac{5}{6}\right)^{7-x} & x=0,1,2,3, \ldots, 7 \\ 0 & \text { otherwise }\end{cases}

$$

# Poisson Distribution

We say that a random variable $X$ has the Poisson distribution with parameter $\lambda(\lambda>0)$ if its density function is given by


$$

P(X=x)=\frac{\lambda^{x} e^{-\lambda}}{x!} \quad x=0,1,2,3, \ldots

$$

Fig.2.2 (d) shows the pdf of a Poisson distribution. Poisson distribution is widely used to express the number of events occurring in a time period. Specifically, it is known that the Poisson distribution provides a good mathematical model for the pattern of the occurrence of failures in many systems and components. It can be also used as an approximation to the binomial distribution when the binomial parameter $n$ is large.

Example 2.5 Assume that the number of defects produced from a production line in one day follows the Poisson distribution with a mean of 5 . What is the probability that we have fewer than three defects today?

Solution: Since $\lambda=5$, we have


$$

\begin{aligned}
& P(X<3)=\sum*{k=0}^{3} P(X=k)=\sum*{k=0}^{2} \frac{5^{k} e^{-5}}{k!} \\
& =e^{-5}+5 e^{-5}+\frac{5^{2} e^{-5}}{2}=\frac{37 e^{-5}}{2}=0.1247
\end{aligned}

$$

Example 2.6 Let $X_{1}$ and $X_{2}$ be two independent Poisson random variables with parameters $\lambda_{1}$ and $\lambda_{2}$, respectively. What is the distribution of $X_{1}+X_{2}$ ?

## Solution:


$$

\begin{aligned}
& P\left(X*{1}+X*{2}=n\right)=\sum*{k=0}^{n} P\left(X*{1}=k, X*{2}=n-k\right)=\sum*{k=0}^{n}\left[\frac{\lambda_{1}^{k} e^{-\lambda_{1}}}{k!}\right]\left[\frac{\lambda_{2}^{n-k} e^{-\lambda_{2}}}{n-k!}\right] \\
& \quad=\frac{e^{-\left(\lambda*{1}+\lambda*{2}\right)}}{n!} \sum*{k=0}^{n} \frac{n!}{k!(n-k)!} \lambda*{1}^{k} \lambda*{2}^{n-k}=\frac{e^{-\left(\lambda*{1}+\lambda*{2}\right)}}{n!}\left(\lambda*{1}+\lambda\_{2}\right)^{n}
\end{aligned}

$$

Therefore, $X_{1}+X_{2}$ has the Poisson distribution with the parameter $\lambda_{1}+\lambda_{2}$.# 2.3.2 Continuous Distributions

Continuous distribution functions, including the Weibull distribution, are very important to describing the reliability of components over the life of a system or product.

## Continuous Uniform Distribution

The uniform distribution can also be defined over a range $(a, b)$ instead of a set of points $\left\{x_{1}\right.$, $\left.x_{2}, x_{3}, \ldots, x_{n}\right\}$. The one defined over a range is called a continuous uniform distribution. The density function of a continuous uniformly distributed random variable X is given by


$$

f(x)= \begin{cases}\frac{1}{b-a} & \text { if } a \leq x \leq b \& a<b \\ 0 & \text { otherwise }\end{cases}

$$

Example 2.7 Suppose that a random variable $X$ is uniformly distributed between 0 and 2. What is the probability that $X$ is less than or equal to 1.5 ?

Solution: Since the density function of $X$ is given by


$$

f(x)=1 / 2 x \in[0,2]

$$

the probability would be calculated as:


$$

P(X \leq 1.5)=\int\_{0}^{1.5} \frac{1}{2} d x=0.75

$$

## Normal Distribution

We say that a random variable $X$ has normal (or Gaussian) distribution with parameters $\mu$ and $\sigma^{2}$ when the density function of $X$ is given by


$$

f(x)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2 \pi} \sigma} \exp \left[-\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{x-\mu}{\sigma}\right)^{2}\right] \quad-\infty<x<\infty

$$

The normal distribution is often denoted by $N\left(\mu, \sigma^{2}\right)$, where these two parameters represent the mean and variance of $X$, respectively. Fig. 2.3(a) shows the two density functions of normal distribution when $\mu=2, \sigma=1$ and $\mu=2, \sigma=2$. As shown in Figure 2.3a, the normal distribution is symmetric around the mean, and the standard deviation indicates the level of deviation from the mean.

Due to the complexity of normal density function, it is not possible to derive a closed form expression for cdf by integration. However, if we define another random variable $Z$ as


$$

Z=\frac{X-\mu}{\sigma}

$$

Then, since $X=Z \sigma+\mu$, the density function of $Z$ will be obtained as


$$

f(z)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2 \pi}} \exp \left[\frac{-(z \mathrm{~s}+\mu-\mu)^{2}}{2 \sigma^{2}}\right]=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2 \pi}} \exp \left[\frac{-z^{2}}{2}\right] \quad-\infty<z<\infty

$$

Therefore, we know that $Z$ has normal distribution with a mean of 0 and variance 1 (which is called the Standard Normal Distribution). We often denote the distribution function of the standard normal distribution by $\Phi($.$) . We can calculate the probability using the Normal$ Table for the standard normal distribution.Example 2.8 Suppose that $X$ is a normal random variable with a mean $\mu$ and a variance $\sigma^{2}$. What is the probability that $X$ is less than or equal to $x$ ?

Solution: Let $z=\frac{x-\mu}{\sigma}$. Then, we have,


$$

P(X \leq x)=P\left(\frac{X-\mu}{\sigma} \leq \frac{x-\mu}{\sigma}\right)=P\left(Z \leq \frac{x-\mu}{\sigma}\right)=\Phi\left(\frac{x-\mu}{\sigma}\right)

$$

The importance of the normal distribution is that many real-life phenomena can be approximated by the normal distribution, as the number of samples increases. We will dwell on this issue later in this section. Finally, it must be mentioned that the normally distributed random variables are defined over a range from $-\infty$ to $\infty$. Since we generally deal with positive values in probability assessment, this fact restricts the applicability of the normal distribution. However, we can control the distribution of the normal random variables apart from 0 when we have a relatively small variance.

# Exponential Distribution

We say that a random variable $X$ has an exponential distribution with parameter $\lambda$ if its density function is given by


$$

f(x)= \begin{cases}\lambda \exp (-\lambda x) & \text { if } x \geq 0 \\ 0 & \text { if } x<0\end{cases}

$$

The exponential distribution is often denoted by $\exp (\lambda)$. The parameter implies the rate of the occurrence in the event that the random variable $X$ represents. Fig. 2.3(b) shows the density functions of the exponential distribution when $\lambda=1$ and $\lambda=2$. The exponential distribution is widely applied in the analysis of the life of systems.


Figure 2.3 Pdfs of Some Continuous Probability DistributionsExample 2.9 Suppose that a random variable $X$ represents the life of a component, and it is exponentially distributed with parameter $\lambda$. What is the probability that this component will survive at least $s$ hours more, given that it has already survived $t$ hours so far?

Solution: Since $t+s>t$, we have,


$$

P(X>t+s \mid X>t)=\frac{P(X>t+s)}{P(X>t)}

$$

For any $t(t \geq 0)$, we have,


$$

P(X>t)=1-P(X \leq t)=1-\int\_{0}^{t} \lambda e^{-\lambda x} d x=1-\left(1-e^{-\lambda t}\right)=e^{-\lambda t}

$$

Thus, it follows that,


$$

P(X>t+s \mid X>t)=\frac{e^{-\lambda(t+s)}}{e^{-\lambda t}}=e^{-\lambda s}=P(X>s)

$$

This equation shows that the probability that the component survives at least $s$ additional hours, given that it has already survived $t$ hours, is the same as the probability that it survives at least s hours. The distribution of the remaining life of the component is independent of the time used, so it is 'memoryless'. Therefore, a random variable with this property is said to have a memoryless property. It was proven that the exponential distribution is the only distribution with this property (Ross 1993).

Example 2.10 Suppose that $X$ and $Y$ are independent and identically distributed exponential random variables with parameter. Then, what is the distribution of the sum of $X$ and $Y$ ?

Solution: Let $Z$ be the sum of $X$ and $Y$. Then, for any positive real value $z$, we have,


$$

\begin{aligned}
& P(Z \leq z)=P(X+Y \leq z)=\int*{0}^{z} \int*{0}^{z-x} \lambda e^{-\lambda x} \lambda e^{-\lambda y} d x d y \\
& \quad=\int*{0}^{z} \lambda^{2} e^{-\lambda x}\left(\int*{0}^{z-x} e^{-\lambda y} d y\right) d x=\int\_{0}^{z} \lambda e^{-\lambda x}\left(1-e^{-\lambda(z-x)}\right) d x=1-(1+\lambda z) e^{-\lambda z}
\end{aligned}

$$

Thus, the density function of $Z=X+Y$ would be,


$$

f(x)=\frac{d F(z)}{d z}=\lambda^{2} z e^{-\lambda z}

$$

# Gamma Distribution

We say that a random variable $X$ has a gamma distribution with parameters $\lambda$ and $k$ if its density function is given by


$$

f(x)=\frac{\lambda(\lambda x)^{k-1} e^{-\lambda x}}{\Gamma(k)} x \geq 0

$$

where is the scale parameter, $k$ is the shape parameter, and $\Gamma(k)$ is the gamma function defined as


$$

\Gamma(k)=\int\_{0}^{\infty} x^{k-1} e^{-x} d x

$$

Fig. 2.3(c) shows the density functions of gamma distribution with different values of $k$. In the case where $k$ is an integer greater than 1 ,
$$

\Gamma(k)=(k-1)!

$$

The gamma distribution is widely applied to model the duration of time needed to finish an activity. From the example $2-10$, we derived the density function of the sum of two identically distributed exponential random variables as


$$

f(k)=\lambda^{2} x e^{-\lambda x}

$$

This is the same as the density function of a random variable that has the gamma distribution with the parameters $\lambda$ and 2 . This result can be generalized by induction as that if $X_{1}, X_{2}$, $\ldots, X_{n}$ are independent and identically distributed exponential random variables with parameter $\lambda$, then $X_{1}+X_{2}+X_{3}+\ldots+X_{n}$ has a gamma distribution with parameters $\lambda$ and $n$.

# Weibull Distribution

We say that a random variable X has a Weibull distribution with a scale parameter $\mu$, and a shape parameter $\beta$, if its density function is given by


$$

f(x)=\left\{\frac{\beta}{\mu} \left\|\frac{x}{\mu}\right\|^{\beta-1} \exp \left[-\left(\frac{x}{\mu}\right)^{\beta}\right]\right\} \quad x \geq 0

$$

If the Weibull random variable X shifts left or right from 0 , we can redefine the density function of the Weibull distribution with one more parameter $v$, the location parameter $(-\infty<v<\infty)$ as follows.


$$

f(x)=\left\{\frac{\beta}{\mu} \left\|\frac{x-v}{\mu}\right\|^{\beta-1} \exp \left[-\left(\frac{x-v}{\mu}\right)^{\beta}\right]\right\} \quad x \geq v

$$

The location parameter does not affect the variance. This modification is often referred to as the Three Parameter (3-P) Weibull Distribution or Modified Weibull Distribution.

The cdf of the 3-P Weibull distribution is derived as


$$

F(x)= \begin{cases}0 & \text { if } x<v \\ 1-\exp \left[-\left(\frac{x-v}{\mu}\right)^{\beta}\right] & \text { if } x \geq v\end{cases}

$$

Fig. 2.3(d) shows some density functions of the Weibull distribution when $v=0$. As shown by the Figure, we can generate many different shapes by manipulating the values of the two parameters $\mu$ and $\beta$. Thus, the Weibull distribution provides us with convenience to fit experimental data. It can be shown easily when $\mu=\frac{1}{\lambda}, \beta=1$, and $v=0$, the density function would be $f(x)=\lambda e^{-\lambda x}$. This is the same as the density function of the exponential distribution. Therefore, we can say that the exponential distribution is a special case of the Weibull distribution. The reader should note that different authors use various notations for the parameters in the Weibull distribution.

Example 2.11 Suppose that the failure time of an electronic component is known to have a Weibull distribution with $\mu=400$ hours, $\beta=1 / 2$, and $v=0$. Calculate the probability that a component fails before 1000 hours.

Solution: Using the cdf given above, we have,


$$

F(1000)=1-\exp \left[-\left(\frac{1000}{400}\right)^{0.5}\right]=1-e^{-1.581}=0.794

$$
# 2.3.3 Extreme Value Distribution

In dealing with the reliability of a system, we may face many situations where the extreme value(minimum or maximum) of a set of random variables will be our primary interest. In this section, we will explore the distribution and the density of the minimum and maximum of random variables.

Suppose that $X_{1}, X_{2}, X_{3}, \ldots, X_{n}$ are independent random variables with distribution functions $F_{1}, F_{2}, \ldots, F_{n}$, respectively, and, $Y$ is the random variable that is the maximum of those $n$ variables. Then, let's calculate the distribution function $F_{y}(y)$ of $Y$.


$$

F*{Y}(y)=P(Y \leq y)=P\left[\left(X*{1} \leq y\right) \cap\left(X*{2} \leq y\right) \cap \ldots \cap\left(X*{n} \leq y\right)\right]

$$

Since $X_{1}, X_{2}, X_{3}, \ldots, X_{n}$ are independent, we have,


$$

F*{Y}(y)=\prod*{i=1}^{n} P\left(X*{i} \leq y\right)=\prod*{i=1}^{n} F\_{i}(y)

$$

If all the $n$ random variables are identically distributed with a distribution function $F(x)$, we have,


$$

F\_{Y}(y)=F^{n}(y)

$$

It follows that the density function of $Y$ can be derived by


$$

f*{Y}(y)=\frac{d F*{Y}(y)}{d y}=n F^{n-1}(y) f(y)

$$

where $f(y)=\frac{d F(y)}{d y}$
The distribution of the minimum of random variables can be derived by a similar approach. Let $Z$ be the random variable that is the minimum of $n$ independent random variables $X_{1}, X_{2}$, $X_{3}, \ldots, X_{n}$.


$$

\begin{aligned}
& F*{Z}(z)=P(Z \leq z)=1-P(Z>z) \\
& \quad=1-P\left[\left(X*{1}>z\right) \cap\left(X*{2}>z\right) \cap \ldots \cap\left(X*{n}>z\right)\right]
\end{aligned}

$$

Since $X_{1}, X_{2}, X_{3}, \ldots, X_{n}$ are independent,


$$

\begin{aligned}
& F*{Z}(z)=1-\prod*{i=1}^{n} P\left(X*{i}>z\right)=1-\prod*{i=1}^{n}\left[1-P\left(X_{i} \leq z\right)\right] \\
& \quad=1-\prod*{i=1}^{n}\left[1-F*{i}(z)\right]
\end{aligned}

$$

Thus, if these $n$ variables are identically distributed with the distribution function $F(x)$, we have


$$

F\_{Z}(z)=1-[1-F(z)]^{n}

$$

It follows that the density function of $Z$ can be derived by


$$

f*{Z}(z)=\frac{d F*{Z}(z)}{d z}=n[1-F(z)]^{n-1} f(z)

$$

where $f(z)=\frac{d F(z)}{d z}$# 2.3.4 Laws of Large Numbers

Suppose that $\left\{X_{1}, X_{2}, X_{3}, \ldots,\right\}$ is the sequence of outcomes in an experiment where $X_{i}$ is the outcome of the $i$-th trial and each trial is conducted under identical conditions. Since each event $\left\{X_{i} \mid i=1,2, \ldots\right\}$ in this experiment is independent to each other, $\left\{X_{1}, X_{2}, X_{3}, \ldots,\right\}$ is a sequence of independent trials. One of the main objectives in repeating trials in an experiment in scientific research is to obtain insights into the eternal truth of the phenomena with a prospect that the result will proceed closer to the truth as the number of trials increases. In this section, we will study the behavior of probability distributions for random variables, which are the outcomes of an experiment where the number of trials goes to infinity. Before moving into the limiting behavior of distributions, we will first explore some of the conditions of the probability distributions, which will provide us with useful insights into the boundaries on probabilities when information on only the mean or both the mean and the variance is available.

## Markov Inequality

Let $X$ be a nonnegative random variable. Then, for any positive value $a$,


$$

P(X \geq a) \leq \frac{E[X]}{a}

$$

This inequality provides a good upper bound for the probability $P(X \geq a)$ when the value of $a$ is greater than $E[X]$.

## Chebyshev Inequality

Let $X$ be a random variable with mean $\mu$ and variance $\sigma^{2}$. Then, for any positive value $k$,


$$

P[|X-\mu| \geq k] \leq \frac{\sigma^{2}}{k^{2}}

$$

This inequality holds when the mean and variance are finite.

## Strong Law of Large Numbers

Let $X_{1}, X_{2}, \ldots$ be a sequence of independent and identically distributed random variables with finite mean $\mu$ and variance $\sigma^{2}$. Then, with a probability of 1 ,


$$

\lim _{n \rightarrow \infty} \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} X\_{i}}{n}=\mu

$$

In other words, this law states that the average of a sequence of independent and identically distributed random variables will converge to the mean of the distribution with a probability of 1 .

## Central Limit Theorem

Let $X_{1}, X_{2}, \ldots$ be a sequence of independent and identically distributed random variables with finite mean $\mu$ and variance $\sigma^{2}$. Then, as $n$ goes to infinity,


$$

P\left[Z=\frac{\bar{X}-\mu}{\sigma / \sqrt{n}} \leq a\right] \rightarrow \int*{-\infty}^{a} \frac{e^{-x^{2} / 2}}{\sqrt{2 \pi}} d x
$$where $\bar{X}$ the mean of the $n$ samples $X*{1}, X*{2}, \ldots, X*{n}$.
In other words, if the number of samples n is sufficiently large, the distribution of the sample mean tends toward a Normal distribution with mean $\mu$ and variance $\frac{\mu}{n}$ regardless of the original distribution of $\left\{X_{i}\right\}$. This theorem explains why the distribution of many random variables found in real life looks similar to the normal distribution. The Central Limit Theorem and the Strong Law of Large Numbers together provide the theoretical basis of using sample mean in the estimation for statistical analysis.

# 2.4 Reliability and Reliability Functions

We can define the reliability and its related functions in terms of our specific density functions.

### 2.4.1 Definition of Reliability and Hazard Function

As we noted earlier, the term 'reliability' is related to the length of time that a system or component maintains its intended functionality. There are many factors or causes that affect the life of a system or component. Failures such as bolt breakage and short of an electric circuit can definitely terminate the life of a system. Poor programming or logical errors(often referred to as 'bugs') can interrupt the functionality of a computer software. However, we need to point out that the definition of failure is very important in defining the life and reliability. Emotional factors such as fashion or aesthetics can also be important in determining the life of a system, but such factors are not as easily defined in terms of failure.

A system or product will generally consist of many components, parts and/or subsystems with different life cycles. Some of the components, parts or subsystems may have a critical effect on the life of the system. It is easy to find a case where the whole system halts due to the failure of a small and trivial component. For example, a T.V does not work if its fuse is blown. On the other hand, we can also find many examples where a system works fine even though one or more of its components fail. A passenger car runs fine while its door lock or automated safety belt system are broken; a clock works fine even though the alarm stops working; a radio may work, but with sizable static. As is hinted in these examples, the practical definition of reliability, as well as failure, can be rather conditional and relative.

However, in this section, we will define the mathematical model of reliability based on the probability concept and we will refer to well defined causes of failure. Hence we will define reliability as the probability that the system or component will function as designed for a specified amount of time under specified conditions. We will need to understand the mechanisms that comprise the reliability of a system in order to create a system with better reliability at minimal cost. We will conduct a detailed discussion on failure mechanism modeling in Chapter 3 and discuss key causes of failure in Part II of the book.

## Reliability Function

In the reliability analysis, random variable $T$ representing the time to failure is one of our primary concerns. The distribution of $T$ is completely derived by the cumulative distribution function $F(t)$ of failure time:

$$
P(T \leq t)=F(t)=\int_{0}^{t} f(s) d s \quad(\mathrm{t}>0)
$$

where $f(t)$ is the density function of $T$.The reliability function denoted by $R(t)$ is defined as

$$
R(t)=1-F(t)=\int_{t}^{\infty} f(t) d t
$$

Since the reliability function $R(t)$ implies the probability that the system survives by time $t$, it is also called the survivor function.

# Hazard Function

The hazard function denoted by $h(t)$ is defined as

$$
h(t)=\frac{f(t)}{\mathrm{R}(t)}=\frac{f(t)}{1-F(t)}
$$

The hazard function is the conditional probability that a system fails, given that the system does not fail by time $t$. Since it indicates a change in the system failure rate over the life cycle of a system, the hazard function is also called the hazard rate function or instantaneous failure rate function. In conjunction with the hazard function, we can define the cumulative hazard function $H(t)$ as

$$
H(t)=\int_{0}^{t} h(s) d s=\int_{0}^{t} \frac{f(s)}{1-F(s)} d s
$$

### 2.4.2 Reliability Functions of Common Distributions

We can now apply the concept of reliability and hazard function to the probability density functions we have already examined. We begin with the Exponential distribution.

## Exponential Distribution

The density function of the exponential distribution $f(t)$ was defined as the equation (2.38). Then the reliability function can be calculated as

$$
\begin{aligned}
& R(t)=1-F(t)=1-\int_{0}^{t} \lambda e^{-\lambda s} d s=1-\left|-e^{-\lambda s}\right|_{0}^{t} \\
& =1-\left(1-e^{-\lambda t}\right)=e^{-\lambda t}
\end{aligned}
$$

It follows that the hazard function can be calculated as

$$
h(t)=\frac{f(t)}{R(t)}=\frac{\lambda e^{-\lambda t}}{e^{-\lambda t}}=\lambda
$$

As shown, the hazard function of the exponential distribution is constant and the failure rate of systems having an exponential failure distribution does not change over time. This result matches the 'memoryless property' of exponential random variables.

## Normal Distribution

The density function of a normal random variable was defined in equation (2.35). Then the reliability function will be

$$
R(t)=1-F(t)=1-\int_{-\infty}^{t} \frac{1}{\sqrt{2 \pi} \sigma} e^{\frac{-(s-\mu)^{2}}{2 \sigma^{2}}} d s
$$As noted earlier, we cannot calculate the integral part of the above equation in closed form, but can obtain the probability by converting it into the distribution $\Phi(\cdot)$ of the standard normal random variables.

Let $Z=\frac{t-\mu}{\sigma}$, then we have,


$$

R(t)=1-\int\_{-\infty}^{t-\mu} \frac{1}{\sqrt{2 \pi}} e^{-\frac{z^{2}}{2}} d z=1-\Phi\left(\frac{t-\mu}{\sigma}\right)

$$

Thus, the hazard function would be calculated as


$$

h(t)=\frac{f(t)}{R(t)}=\frac{1}{1-\Phi\left(\frac{t-\mu}{\sigma}\right)}\left[\frac{1}{\sqrt{2 \pi} \sigma} e^{\frac{-(t-\mu)^{2}}{2 \sigma^{2}}}\right]

$$

# Weibull Distribution

The density function of the Weibull distribution was defined as equation (2.41) or (2.42). Then, the reliability function $R(t)$ can be calculated as


$$

\begin{aligned}
& R(t)=1-F(t)=1-\int\_{0}^{t} \frac{\beta}{\mu}\left(\frac{s}{\mu}\right)^{\beta-1} e^{-\left(\frac{t}{\mu}\right)^{\beta}} d s \\
& \quad=1-\left[1-e^{-\left(\frac{t}{\mu}\right)^{\beta}}\right]=e^{-\left(\frac{t}{\mu}\right)^{\beta}}
\end{aligned}

$$

because $\frac{\beta}{\mu}\left(\frac{s}{\mu}\right)^{\beta-1} e^{-\left(\frac{t}{\mu}\right)^{\beta}}=\left[-e^{-\left(\frac{t}{\mu}\right)^{\beta}}\right]^{\nu}$
Hence, we obtain,


$$

h(t)=\frac{f(t)}{R(t)}=\frac{\beta}{\mu}\left(\frac{t}{\mu}\right)^{\beta-1} e^{-\left(\frac{t}{\mu}\right)^{\beta}} e^{-\left(\frac{t}{\mu}\right)^{\beta}}=\frac{\beta t^{\beta-1}}{\mu^{\beta}}

$$

For the 3-P Weibull, where the location parameter $v \neq 0$, we would have,


$$

R(t)=e^{-\frac{(t-v)}{\mu} \beta}

$$

and $h(t)=\frac{\beta}{\mu}\left(\frac{t-v}{\mu}\right)^{\beta-1}$ for $t \geq v$

| 3-P Weibull | $\begin{aligned} & \mu>0, \beta>0 \\ & \delta v \neq 0 \end{aligned}$ | $\frac{\beta}{\mu}\left[\frac{t-v}{\mu}\right]^{\beta-1} \exp \left[\frac{t-v}{\mu}\right]^{\beta} t \geq v$ | $\exp \left[\frac{(t-v)}{\mu} \beta\right]$ | $\frac{\beta}{\mu}\left(\frac{t-v}{\mu}\right)^{\beta-1}$ |# 2.5 The Monte Carlo Method

The Monte Carlo method is an excellent means of manipulating variability in a set of parameters which contribute to uncertainty in product life. We will refer to the use of this technique throughout the book, including a general design approach in Chapter 3. We contend that this method can be used very effectively in design due to the availability low cost computing power and its very simple approach to the manipulation of random variables.

### 2.5.1 Introduction

Monte Carlo method is a technique using random or pseudo-random numbers to derive a solution for a model. For example, it has been used to solve complex integrals and equations. However, combined with the power of modern computers and the mathematics of probability theory, the Monte Carlo method has emerged as the most powerful tool for analyzing complex problems including stochastic simulations. Stochastic simulation is often called Monte Carlo simulation since it includes the use of random numbers. Conceptually the method is simple. For example, let's calculate the area below a curve $g(x)$ as shown in Fig. 2.4 using the Monte Carlo method.

The area of the rectangle containing the curve $g(x)$ is,


$$

A\_{r}=a b

$$

Since the area under the curve is a fraction of the rectangle, we can say that,


$$

A*{u}=\mu A*{r}=\mu a b

$$

where $\mu$ is a number $0 \leq \mu \leq 1$
If we know the value of $\mu$, we can solve the area. It is relatively easy to evaluate the value of $\mu$ by the following procedure. Suppose that we hang the rectangle including the curve on the wall, and that we are positioned 3 meters apart from the wall and blindfolded. Then, standing in the direction of the wall, we begin throwing darts on to the wall. If the darts are thrown in a random direction, then we expect that $\mu$ would be the ratio of the number of darts that land below the curve to the total number of darts that land inside the rectangle. According to the


Figure 2.4 Calculation of the Area under the Curve $g(x)$ by the Monte Carlo methodlaw of large numbers, if random, this process converges toward the correct value of $\mu$ as the number of darts thrown increases. This process is called the hit-or-miss Monte Carlo method. This simple process includes the essence of the Monte Carlo method. We only need to replace the physical process of throwing darts with the computer process of selecting and using random numbers.

Now suppose that we input information into a computer to generate uniformly distributed random numbers between 0 and 1 . Let the numbers represent the fractional distance along a side, and let two successive numbers give the horizontal-vertical position on the rectangle. Then, by merely checking to see if the position is below the curve or not, we count the number of tries that land below the curve along with the total tries. The ratio of the latter number to the former is $\mu$. The advantage of the computer is that it can conduct many tries in a short period of time, as well as keep track of the statistics simultaneously.

# 2.5.2 Random Number Generators

From the above, we know that the Monte Carlo method relies on random numbers to work on a computer simulation. The first problem we face in performing the Monte Carlo simulation is to obtain a very large set of random numbers. If our model includes more than one process, which is independent, we need to provide different sets of random numbers for each process.

One simple method to obtain this large set of random numbers is to design some truly random processes, and keep records of the numbers generated by the processes. However, it can be very costly as well as time-consuming to keep records of the random numbers since huge memory space is needed. In addition, it is often meaningless to keep such memory since we generally consume millions to billions of random numbers in a simulation. Another method, which is more practical and inexpensive, is to design algorithms by which the computer can generate pseudo-random numbers as needed. It is inevitable to sacrifice the randomness to some extent as long as we depend on this approach since it depends on the mathematical models that are deterministic in nature. However, some mathematical models that generate fairly random pseudo-random numbers have been developed and are now available.

We can consider some measures to evaluate the randomness of the outputs generated by an algorithm. First, we want them to be uniformly distributed. No one number or group of numbers is to be favored than others. Second, the random numbers should be independent to each other. They should not show any tendency or cyclic variation: auto-correlation between numbers, periodicity (i.e. numbers sequences repeat, numbers successively higher or lower than adjacent numbers), etc. If we use poor random number generators for simulation, the result of the analysis can be seriously distorted.

A commonly applied class of random number generation model is called the linear congruential generator. This model basically generates a sequence of integers, $X_{1}, X_{2}, \ldots$ between zero and $m-1$ in accordance with the following recursive formula


$$

X*{i+1}=\left(A^{\*} X*{i}+C\right) \operatorname{Mod}(m) \quad i=0,1,2, \ldots

$$

where $A$ and $C$ are constants, and $\operatorname{Mod}(m)$ refers to the modulo operation.
The modulo operation gives the result as the remainder of the calculation $\left(\frac{A^{*} X_{1}+C}{m}\right)$. Therefore, it is inevitable that the random numbers generated will be cyclic with the maxi-mum length of $m$. We need to determine only three parameter values: $A, C$, and $m$, to define a linear congruential random number generator. We call the initial value $X_{0}$ the seed.

Example 2.12 In case $A=5, C=3, m=16$, and 0 for the seed, the corresponding linear congruential generator will yield random number stream as follows.

Table 2.2 Results for Example 2.12.

| $\boldsymbol{i}$ | $\boldsymbol{X}_{\boldsymbol{i}}$ | $\mathbf{5}^{\boldsymbol{*}} \boldsymbol{X}_{\boldsymbol{i}}+\mathbf{3}$ | $\boldsymbol{X}_{\boldsymbol{i}+1}$ |
| :--: | :--: | :--: | :--: |
| 1 | 0 | 3 | 3 |
| 2 | 3 | 18 | 2 |

| 5 | 4 | 23 | 7 |
| 6 | 7 | 38 | 6 |

In this case, we find that each number between 0 to 15 appears exactly once in the sequence of 16 numbers. Thus, the uniformity requirement is met. However, Fig. 2.5 shows strong evidence of correlation existing among the generated numbers. This correlation provides predictability, so this violates the randomness condition.


Figure 2.5 Plots of the successive random numbers showing correlation.Aside from the above example, Thesen (1992) presents many other potential problems we face when utilizing the linear congruential generators including short cycles and seed dependence, degeneracy, and nonrandom sequences, etc. The performance (randomness of generated numbers) of the linear congruential model depends heavily on the selection of the values for three parameters. As long as we depend on the mathematical model implemented on computers to obtain random numbers, the periodicity is unavoidable due to the modular operation. Within this limitation, we need to select a model that guarantees the maximum periodicity, which equals the value of the modular operation parameter $m$, and has minimum correlation. In this regard, there are some widely applied linear congruential models. Among them, the Lewis algorithm has been noted for its good performance. The parameter values for this model are 16807,0 , and 2147483647 for $A, C$ and $m$, respectively. It should be noted that 2147483647 is $2^{31}-1$, the largest integer that can be stored in a standard 32-bit computer. The C code for the Lewis model is given below. This generator returns normalized random numbers between 0 and 1 by dividing the generated integers by $2^{31}-1$. Fig. 2.6 shows the low correlation between random numbers successively generated by the Lewis algorithm.

```
Float Lewis( ) \(\{\)
    static long double seed \(=12345\);
    seed \(=\operatorname{fmod}\left(\operatorname{seed}^{*} 16807 ., 2147483647 .\right)\);
    return(seed/2147483647.);\}
```

In conclusion, we close this section by heeding some words of advice in selecting random number generators from Thesen (Thesen, 1992).

1. Do not use unknown random number generators
2. Check the generators you use very carefully, using several different types of tests
3. Do not use ad hoc approaches to improve a random number generator.


Figure 2.6 Plots of successive random numbers showing low correlation by the Lewis Algorithm.# 2.5.3 Monte Carlo Models and the Sampling Process

Now, we are ready to consider how to combine the random number generators with the Monte Carlo model for computer simulation. Since simulation models generally include many events with different patterns of probability distribution other than uniform distribution, we need to know how to convert uniformly distributed random numbers into random variates in a general distribution. In order to do this, we need to design a process that consistently samples values in the random variable of interest that correspond to the uniform random numbers $[0,1]$ generated. For example, let's consider a discrete random variable $X$ whose density function is given by


$$

\begin{array}{ll}
P(X=1)=0.2, & P(X=2)=0.4, \quad P(X=3)=0.2 \\
P(X=4)=0.1, & P(X=5)=0.1
\end{array}

$$

If the generated uniform random number value $U$ is 0.1534 , what is the corresponding random variate with this distribution? Since $P(X=1), P(X=2)$ and $P(X=3)$ are greater than $0.1534,1,2$ and 3 can be the candidate comparable to this random number. One easy approach to consistently match the value for a random number is to use the cumulative probability instead of the density function. In this context, the conversion mechanism can be designed as


$$

X=\left\{\begin{array}{ll}
1 & \text { if } 0.0 \leq U<0.2 \\
2 & \text { if } 0.2 \leq U<0.6 \\
3 & \text { if } 0.6 \leq U<0.8 \\
4 & \text { if } 0.8 \leq U<0.9 \\
5 & \text { if } 0.9 \leq U<1.0
\end{array}\right.

$$

There is no law in the order of the arrangement, as long as we keep the order consistent. This process can be applied to generate random variates with many other distributions. Fig. 2.7 summarizes the concept of this conversion process. Conceptually, this process is very simple to understand. If cdf of $X$ is $F(x)$, and let


$$

U=F(X)

$$

Then, it follows that


$$

X=F^{-1}(U)

$$



Figure 2.7 Generation of a Random Variate from cdf.Example 2.14 Suppose that a random variable $X$ has an exponential distribution with parameter $\lambda$. What is the comparable exponential random variate for the uniform random number $U(U \in[0,1])$ ?

Solution: Since the density function of $X$ is $f(x)=\lambda e^{-\lambda x}$, its cdf can be obtained by


$$

\begin{aligned}
& F(x)=\int*{0}^{x} \lambda e^{-\lambda t} d t=\left|-e^{-\lambda t}\right|*{0}^{x} \\
& \quad=1-e^{-\lambda x}
\end{aligned}

$$

Thus, from


$$

\begin{aligned}
& U=F(x)=1-e^{-\lambda x} \\
& e^{-\lambda x}=1-U
\end{aligned}

$$

It follows that


$$

x=\frac{-1}{\lambda} \operatorname{Ln}(1-U)=\frac{-1}{\lambda} \operatorname{Ln}(U)

$$

We call this process the inverse transform method. However, the above process cannot always be applied to generate random variates in general distributions. The greatest problem is to obtain the closed form mathematical expression of cdf to easily calculate its inverse function. For example, we cannot derive a closed expression of cdf in normal distribution. Fortunately, some approximation models are available for those probability distributions whose cdfs are not easily calculated in closed form. These approximation models provide efficiency (in terms of the number of random variates generated per time unit) and convenience at the cost of sacrificing accuracy a bit. Since we can improve the accuracy of the simulation analysis by increasing the number of simulations, we can justify the loss in accuracy from the application of approximation models. Readers interested in these approximation models are encouraged to read the reference (Brately et. al. 1987).

As we are able to generate random variates in general distributions, we are now prepared to consider the general scheme of the Monte Carlo simulation. Fig. 2.8 shows the logic flow in a typical Monte Carlo simulation model. We may apply the Monte Carlo simulation either to estimate the value of some specific parameters or to obtain the appropriate values of some input parameters that meet the predetermined conditions given to systems. The calculation $\mu$ of in estimating the area under a curve in Fig. 2.4 is a typical example when seeking the value in the parameter of interest. Suppose that the results of the subsequent throw of darts is $h($ hit $), m($ miss $), m, m, h, m, h, \ldots$ Then, the value of $\mu$ will be calculated as $1,0.5,0.333,0.25,0.4$, $0.333,0.429, \ldots$ If we run the simulation using different random number stream (by the same random number generator with a different seed), we may have $m, h, h, m, h, m, m, \ldots$, resulting in $0,0.5,0.6,0.5,0.428, \ldots$ as the value of $\mu$. As we repeat the simulation, we can increase credibility in our estimation of the true value of $\mu$.

On the other hand, when designing certain systems, we often face problems when requested to find the values of certain input parameters that maximize or minimize some performance measures. For example, shrinkage is often selected as a quality measure in injec-tion-molded plastic products. Injection speed, holding pressure, mold temperature, and cooling time, etc. are the design parameters that process engineers can control to develop a mathematical model to forecast the shrinkage of the molded products. They can apply the Monte Carlo simulation to determine the values of these input parameters that meet the requirements in product shrinkage. In this case, it is not simple to obtain such values due to large degree of freedom for the values of input parameters and possible interactive effects among them.

Figure 2.8 The Logic Flow of a typical Monte Carlo model.

It should be noted here that simulation is not a tool that can give an optimal solution by itself. Each time we run a simulation, the result will be a value: hit or miss, or shrinkage of 0.26 mm , etc. Each one of these values fails in providing insights into the true value or optimal solution. However, as the number of values increases due to repeated simulation runs, we can improve our knowledge about the distribution of the values, which results in more effective choices. Hazelrigg defined the knowledge that enables us to make effective choices in design as information (Hazelrigg, 1996). Simulation is basically a tool for helping us build up information based on the concept of 'trial-and-error'. In order to obtain good information efficiently, we need to know how to repeat the simulation, and when to stop. In addition, we need a mathematically sound base to derive a meaningful conclusion from the data. Statistical experimental design techniques enable us to run the simulations, analyze and compare the results, and reach the conclusion soundly and efficiently.

# 2.5.4 The Triangular Distribution

As shown previously, random variate generation of general distributions includes complex calculations associated with cdf and pdf, and often the closed form expression of cdf is not available. In this case, we can apply some approximation models to many general probability distributions. When we apply such an approximation model, there is a trade-off between the sacrificed accuracy and the improved efficiency. The resulting gain often justifies this exchange. Since triangular distribution is simple to define and easily fits into any specific distribution, it may be the most widely applied approximation model. Triangular distribution is based on the following three parameters.1. Your best guess of the variable $(\beta)$
2. Your guess of the confidential lower bound $(\alpha)$
3. Your guess of the confidential upper bound $(\gamma)$

Fig. 2.9 shows the density function of a triangular distribution. Since we can define the range and skewness in density function by controlling the above three parameters, we can derive a relatively good approximation fitting the data we obtained from the experiment. Hazelrigg argues that we can also improve the state of our information if we apply a triangular approximation to the events whose distributions are not known rather than leaving them unknown. (Hazelrigg, 1996).

It is easy to derive the density and cumulative distribution functions of the triangular distribution using the premise that the area under the curve is 1 . The pdf of the triangular distribution is given by


$$

f(x)=\left\{\begin{array}{cl}
0 & \text { if } x<\alpha \\
h \frac{x-\alpha}{\beta-\alpha} & \text { if } \alpha \leq x \leq \beta \\
h \frac{\gamma-x}{\gamma-\beta} & \text { if } \beta \leq x \leq \gamma \\
0 & \text { if } \gamma<x
\end{array}\right.

$$

where


$$

h=\frac{2}{\gamma-\alpha}

$$

and cdf can be derived as


$$

P(X \leq x)=F(x)=\left\{\begin{array}{cl}
0 & \text { if } x<\alpha \\
\frac{(x-\alpha)^{2}}{(\beta-\alpha)(\gamma-\alpha)} & \text { if } \alpha \leq x \leq \beta \\
1-\frac{(\gamma-x)^{2}}{(\gamma-\beta)(\gamma-\alpha)} & \text { if } \beta \leq x \leq \gamma \\
1 & \text { if } x>\gamma
\end{array}\right.

$$



Figure 2.9 Probability density function of a triangular distribution.# 2.5.5 Analysis and Interpretation

As noted previously, we can obtain a set of numerical data from our simulation. The mean and variance of the parameters of interest can be easily calculated from these data. In addition, we can identify the distribution from the data using the histogram. A histogram is a graphic technique that collects and compares the number of data in bins. It enables us to reconstruct the distribution of data. In order to do this, we first need to divide the range of data by some number of equal-sized bins. Sorting all the data into the bins by their value, we can count the number of data contained in each bin. Finally, the probability density in each bin can be calculated by dividing its data count by the total number of data. The relative frequency in each bin is used as the estimator of its probability density. Cumulative distribution can be derived from the density function by calculating cumulative probabilities from each bin. Fig. 2.10 is an example of the histogram constructed from the data in the following table.

| :--: | :--: | :--: | :--: | :--: | :--: |
| 1 | $0-99$ | 37 | 37 | 0.37 | 0.37 |
