Figure 2.10 Histogram of data.There is no guideline as to the appropriate size of a bin order to draw the histogram. If it is too small (narrow), we may have too many bins. Some may have relatively small data or even be empty. The resulting curve would be very rugged. We need a large amount of data in order to obtain a smooth curve showing the distribution. On the other hand, if it is too large, it is hard to conjecture the true shape of the distribution. Since there is a trade-off between the smoothness of the curve and the number of data needed, we need to select a bin size, taking into consideration of the number and state of the data obtained. We may draw several histograms with different bin sizes, and select one among them.

We can obtain the mean and variance, and reconstruct the distribution of the output data. Then, we can derive some conclusions from them. We may have to answer to many questions. Can we conclude that $\mu$ is 0.46 ? How much does shrinkage change if pressure or temperature changes? What factors affect shrinkage of the product? Which combination of temperature, pressure and velocity minimizes the shrinkage? In addition, we may use the Monte Carlo simulation to compare the performance of some alternative designs. Once again, statistical techniques, such as confidence intervals and hypothesis testing provide useful and mathematically sound frameworks that can answer these questions. In general, 2-factorial experimental designs are widely applied in the evaluation of main and interaction effects of control variables. These topics are discussed in further detail in later chapters.

# 2.5.6 Monte Carlo Application Example

We now turn our attention to an example of the Monte Carlo method. Understanding the probability distribution of a load, acting on a component, is an important part of design and reliability assessment. Many factors can contribute to the uncertainty in load. We will discuss the implications of load distributions to the concept of load - strength interference in greater detail in Chapter 4. At present, however, let's show the utility of the Monte Carlo method, as one way to study the propagation of uncertainties through a load model.

Let's consider the design of a spherical pressure vessel, known as a Hortonsphere, that may be used for natural gas storage. Let us also assume that the pressure P in the vessel, the load, is known to be a function of ambient temperature and operator interactions during the filling cycle of the vessel. Let's assume that testing has shown that pressure in the Hortonsphere will be predicted by the following hypothetical model


$$

\frac{500}{P}=0.88\left(\frac{298}{T*{\text {emp }}}\right)+\frac{0.60}{t*{\text {operator }}}

$$

where $T_{\text {emp }}$ and $t_{\text {operator }}$ represent the temperature and interaction time of the operator or fill time, respectively.

In this application, the temperature and the operator fill time have associated uncertainties. As an example, assume that the vessel must be designed to operate in both Saudi Arabia and in the Port of Pusan in Korea. We might expect from studying the weather at these locations that temperature on the Hortonsphere surface may be anywhere from $-15^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ to $+50^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$, depending upon the time of year. In addition, let's assume that different operators behave differently. The fill time is defined as the operational parameter of interest. In this hypothetical case, fill time has been found to be nominally 4 minutes with a standard deviation of 0.5 minutes, among experienced operators. In other words, we have a two parameter model where the parameters of interest are random variables.From the distribution of ambient temperature and operator fill time, we can estimate the pressure by using the Monte Carlo simulation.

1. The ambient temperature range is between $-15^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ to $+50^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$. For simplicity, we apply the triangular distribution for the ambient temperature, assuming $+25^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ as the most common temperature. Then, the pdf of ambient temperature is calculated as


$$

f(T)= \begin{cases}0 & \text { if } T<258 \\ \frac{2}{65}\left(\frac{T-258}{40}\right) & \text { if } 258 \leq T \leq 298 \\ \frac{2}{65}\left(\frac{323-T}{25}\right) & \text { if } 298 \leq T \leq 323 \\ 0 & \text { if } T>323\end{cases}

$$

2. Though the operator fill time is normally distributed, we may approximate it by a triangular distribution for simplicity. In this case, the most likely would be 4 minutes with a range from 3.0 minutes to 6.0 minutes. The pdf would be calculated as


$$

g(t)= \begin{cases}0 & \text { if } t<3.0 \\ \frac{2}{3}(t-3) & \text { if } 3.0 \leq t \leq 4.0 \\ \frac{1}{3}(6-t) & \text { if } 4 \leq t \leq 6.0 \\ 0 & \text { if } t \geq 6.0\end{cases}

$$

Fig. 2.11 shows the pdfs of the ambient temperature and operator fill time.
Accordingly, the cdfs of the ambient temperature and operator fill time can be easily calculated as,


$$

F(T)= \begin{cases}0 & \text { if } T<258 \\ \left(\frac{T-258}{2600}\right)^{2} & \text { if } 258 \leq T<298 \\ 1-\left(\frac{323-T}{1625}\right)^{2} & \text { if } 298 \leq T<323 \\ 1 & \text { if } T \geq 323\end{cases}

$$

and,

(a) pdf of the ambient temperature $\beta=25 \mathrm{C}, \alpha=-15 \mathrm{C}, \gamma=50 \mathrm{C}$

(b) pdf of the operator fill time $\beta=4 \mathrm{~min}, \alpha=3 \mathrm{~min}, \gamma=6 \mathrm{~min}$

Figure 2.11 The triangular approximation pdfs of the ambient temperature and operator fill time for our example problem of the Hortonsphere pressure distribution.
$$

G(t)= \begin{cases}0 & \text { if } t<3.0 \\ \frac{(t-3)^{2}}{3} & \text { if } 3.0 \leq t<4.0 \\ 1-\frac{(6-t)^{2}}{3} & \text { if } 4 \leq t<6.0 \\ 1 & \text { if } t \geq 6.0\end{cases}

$$

We would derive the pdf of pressure by using the Monte Carlo method. We need two random number generators assuming the independence of ambient temperature and operator fill time. We may create two uniform random number generators by giving different seed value to each. Afterward, the inverse transform method can be used in order to derive conversion mechanisms that consistently assign triangular random variates of ambient temperature and operator fill time to the uniform random numbers generated. Applying the values of ambient temperature and operator fill time to the empirical model of the pressure vessel, we can obtain the pressure values.

Figure 2.12 shows the histogram(bar) constructing the pdf of pressure based on 1,000 pressure values obtained by the above process. The mean and variance of the pressure are calculated as 481.7 kPa and 447.8 kPa , respectively. Fig. 2.12 also shows that the curve of normal pdf with mean 481.7 and standard deviation 21.16 fits the histogram very closely. Readers who are interested in the precision of the curve fitting are encouraged to refer to the 'goodness-of-fit' test (Thesen 1992).

In the case of the Hortonsphere, we may wish to improve the reliability of the design by installing a relief valve. Effectively, the relief valve will truncate the load distribution. One of the parameters we need to determine in installing a relief valve is the threshold value(often called 'cracking pressure') at which the relief valve begins to release the gas out of the vessel lest the pressure exceed the limit.

Assuming the normal distribution of the pressure as above, we would like to design the relief valve to keep closed up to $99 \%$ of the pressure distribution and release for the remaining $1 \%$. Using the standard normal distribution, we can have,


Figure 2.12 Histogram showing the pdf of pressure for the Hortonspere based upon a Monte Carlo Simulation.
$$

Z=\frac{X-\mu}{\sigma}=\frac{X-481.7}{21.16}

$$

Since $Z_{0.01}=2.327$, we can calculate the solution as


$$

X=481.7+21.16 \times 2.327=530.9(k P a)

$$

# 2.6 Summary

In this chapter, we have discussed the elements of probability theory and their application to the concept of reliability. We have defined reliability in terms of the probability of success and we have learned that the reliability function is defined in terms of a specific probability distribution function. These concepts are crucial to understand how to directly deal with uncertainty during design of systems and components and we will explore their application further, in subsequent chapters. In addition, we have seen, that the Monte Carlo simulation technique can be readily applied to design problems for directly estimating the impact of uncertainties in design parameters. The reader is encouraged to refer back to sections of this chapter, as needed, to assist understanding, throughout the book.

Jillian Y. Evans and John W. Evans

In Chapter 3, we will turn our attention to some key concepts in reliability analysis for design. This will continue to build our foundation for reliability assessment in product design and development. In Chapter 2, we developed the principles of probability, as they apply to reliability engineering mathematics. These concepts will now be put into perspective in understanding component failure and its relationship to system reliability.

We will begin our discussion by reexamining component hazard rate over the full life cycle of component application. The classic description of hazard rate for a component over its full life cycle is represented by the mortality or bath tub curve, which takes its name from its characteristic shape. While the bath tub curb is an ideal model, it gives a great deal of insight into what factors may be dominating failure processes and limiting the reliability of the components over the life cycle. As this simple model shows, hazard rate can exhibit decreasing, increasing or constant behavior over time. This makes the Weibull distribution an excellent starting point for modeling component reliability from field data, test data or simulations. However, other distributions, such as the log-normal, are frequently used by convention, particularly for wear out type failure mechanisms.

The component reliability and hazard rate behavior result from the dominant failure mechanisms acting on the component over the life cycle. Each mechanism will have a unique probability distribution. The individual failure mechanism probabilities of failure, at any point in time, $t$, in the life cycle of the component, combine to render the overall component reliability and probability of failure. Component reliability can be estimated from the individual failure mechanism probability density functions by a number of different methods, which are discussed in succeeding sections. One frequently used method is to assume a constant hazard rate and apply the exponential distribution to the components and then extend this to the system. As we shall see, this assumption must be applied with caution, as the exponential distribution only applies to overstress failure mechanisms. The dominant failure mechanism and their associated pdfs can, of course, be extracted from test data, as discussed in later chapters. It is extremely useful, however, to be able to model failure mechanism pdfs through Monte Carlo simulations and extract information about the design or manufacturing parameters contributing the most to the dominant failure mechanisms. This requires knowledge of the failure mechanism and its associated model.

With knowledge of individual component failure probabilities, we can estimate the reliability of any system consisting of various components. Components arranged in serial or parallel fashion can be analyzed using block diagrams or fault tree models. Fault trees are particularly useful in examining system reliability and behavior, as the failure of individual components can be related to the system level failure modes and system level consequences of failure. Hence, weak points and critical components in the design can be identified. Inaddition, the probability of failure, as identified by the top level event in the fault tree, can be estimated. The complementary method of Failure Modes and Effects Analysis (FMEA) is also very useful in identifying the potential modes of failure and associated mechanisms for each component selected for a system or product. These methods are introduced below. Chapter 3, then, is an important chapter linking component reliability and failure assessments to system failure, through our concepts in reliability mathematics.

# 3.1 Component Hazard Rate vs. Time: the Mortality Curve

Let's begin our discussion by examining the occurrence of failures of the components in a product or system, over the life cycle of the system. As we defined in Chapter 2, the hazard function or hazard rate for a component is defined in terms of the probability density function or $p d f$ that describes the distribution of failures in a given time period. The hazard rate is then expressed in equation 3.1:


$$

h(t)=\frac{f(t)}{1-F(t)}

$$

where $t$ is our random variable, $f(t)$ is the $p d f$ of the distribution of failures for a given failure mechanism and, $F(t)=\int_{0}^{t} f(t) d t$. The hazard function allows us to estimate the hazard rate or instantaneous failure rate at any point in time, $t$, for a failure mechanism, fitting the given $p d f$, $f(t)$, and acting on the components in the system. In other words, the hazard rate $h(t)$ is the conditional probability that a component will fail in the time interval $d t$, between $t+d t$, given that it has successfully operated until time $t$. If we are able to examine the behavior of hazard rate data over time we can ascertain significant information about the failure mechanisms acting on a component.

It is important note that different failure mechanisms and defect types will produce different $p d f s$. In addition, different loading conditions will shift the distribution. Figure 3.1 shows a series of probability plots at three different loading conditions. As we will discuss later, the combination of different failure distributions from the dominant failure mechanisms, describes the reliability of the component. A constant failure rate assumption is often made in practice regarding this distribution from which the rate of occurrence of failures in the system are estimated. However, caution must be applied to this assumption. Understanding the dominant failure mechanisms and the uncertainties affecting processes of failure is an important part of effectively deriving corrective action and design improvement.

If we examine the combined hazard rate for various mechanisms acting over the entire life cycle on a group of components under load, we can generate a mortality curve, as shown in Figure 3.2. This curve is commonly referred to in reliability engineering as the bath tub curve given its characteristic shape.

Three distinct regions are shown comprising the curve that reflect the dominant mechanisms acting at various points in the life cycle.

### 3.1.1 Defects, Useful Life and Wear Out

Let us examine these three distinct regions in Figure 3.2 that comprise the classic description of hazard rate or failure rate over time for components. Early in the life cycle of the product, Region I, we may see a high component failure rate that will decrease to nominal level at $t_{0}$. This region is often referred to as the region of infant mortality, debugging-period or burn-in

Figure 3.1 A plot showing probability distributions for a single wear out failure mechanism, electromigration, in a microcircuit. The data were accumulated from testing. The distribution applied here by convention is the log-normal distribution. Note that the three levels of loading result in three different distribution of failures. However, the plotted distributions are parallel indicating the same mechanism is acting (Evans et. al. 1989)


Figure 3.2 The Hazard Rate or Mortality Curve. The characteristic shape lends the name bath tub curve.
period in which we would expect substandard or weak components to fail early with the application of system loads. We should note that the term infant mortality is a misnomer as it refers to human life (Katz 1999). Early life is perhaps a better description. From $t_{0}$ on to $t_{d}$ Region II, we may have a period of a low, nearly constant failure rate. This is of course a desirable condition and is achieved only by good design. This region is the region of useful life. Finally, the component will began to wear out. For many wear out failure mechanisms, this period will exhibit increasing failure rates, as reflected in Region III of our bath tub curve.

Early life behavior, as reflected in Region I in the components of a product or system is largely the result of defects in the manufacture or design. Clearly, as a producer, it is desirable to release a product to market at time $t_{0}$, with low levels of defects. To achieve this, the devel-opment and production of the product, must have controls in place to reduce component defects. Development testing, commonly referred to as debugging the design and assuring quality through process control are essential. Early failures and a decreasing hazard rate might also be attributed to poor control of product or component shipping and distribution to market, (e.g. handling, storage and transport) or improper start-up due to lack of knowledge of proper system operation, so that system loads are much higher than anticipated until problems are resolved.

Early life behavior due to defects may be difficult to eliminate in new component technologies where the manufacturing history is short, in situations where the production output is small or where human involvement is intensive. In these cases, there may difficulty in establishing control of critical manufacturing parameters. We often turn to screening prior to assembly of components into the product or prior to putting a system into service. This may be achieved by nondestructive inspection of parts. An example of this is inspection of weldments by x-ray or other means to insure low defect content before a system is brought on line. Screening methods also include the application of testing under a given level of accelerated stress, so as precipitate defective product from the screened lot of components. This is typical in electronics where semiconductor devices are tested at elevated temperature and voltage, to weed out infant mortality. The effectiveness of screening procedures is directly related to the maturity of the production process and technologies that comprise the component.

The period of useful life, from $t_{o}$ to $t_{d}$, in well designed components, will exhibit a low failure rate which may be nearly constant. In this region, failures occur primarily due to overstress failure mechanisms. Overstress results from a random load exceeding the designed strength of the component. As an example, a transient voltage spike may exceed the dielectric strength of a capacitor. A shock load may occur to an automobile during operation due to a road hazard. This may produce failure of one or more suspension components of the system by overstress fracture or perhaps excessive plastic deformation. A good design will anticipate the potential for overstress failure. For example, a mechanical component, such as a shaft, will be designed to have adequate strength to survive a large random torque load, at an acceptable level of risk or probability of failure. Electronic components may also be selected for a system design that have adequate strength to survive a given random load, such as a transient voltage or short term high temperature exposure, at an acceptable level risk.

The wear out period, denoted by Region III, is characterized by rapidly increasing hazard rate or component failure rates. Wear out failures begin to occur as the component materials degrade with time. They will dominate the hazard rate behavior when the risk of wear out exceeds the risk of overstress. Corrosion is a common wear out failure mechanism in many components of a system. Time dependent dielectric breakdown and electromigration are also wear out mechanisms that occur in electronic components. In a good design, wear out failures are anticipated, and the system is designed so that these types of failures will not be likely before the desirable product lifetime is reached. The useful life time $t_{d}$, at a hazard rate, $h\left(t_{d}\right)$ may also be defined as the component durability.

The mortality curve shown in Figure 3.2 is an ideal model. In the useful life, depending upon the dominant failure mechanism and applied loads, a constant component failure rate may not be exhibited. If a wear out mechanism is not anticipated for a given loading condition, a component may exhibit an increasing failure rate or hazard rate in its intended useful life. In addition, wear out may commence in some components, as soon as product is placed in service. A bearing race in a rolling bearing assembly may begin to wear out as soon as it is placed in use. In such cases, we must anticipate the effect on the life and risk of failure of the product we are designing and specify appropriate repair and maintenance actions to be taken on the components.We might also note that in the case of fatigue fracture of structural metal components, also a common wear out mechanism, a steadily increasing failure rate behavior may not be observed. Rather, after an initial failure free period, the failure rate will generally increase abruptly and then gently decrease for a long period of time (Carter 1986). This can be seen in one of our case studies presented in Chapter 14 where long life behavior is simulated by the Monte Carlo method. When fatigue fracture then dominates wear out in the life cycle, the simple increasing failure rate in Region III may not observed. An exception is the case of solder fatigue where increasing failure rates are normally observed in electronic assemblies. This may be largely due to the creep-fatigue interaction as discussed in Chapter 8.

The effects of increasing system loads on the ideal hazard rate model is characterized by Figure 3.3 As increasing system load levels increase component stresses, the mortality curve will shift upwards. This should not surprise us, as we know that increasing component stress levels shifts the component failure distribution. In addition, we can see that the useful life period can be anticipated to decrease. As we will describe later, we can take advantage of this behavior during testing. This behavior also shows that it is essential to properly characterize the system loads by defining the use environment in order to properly anticipate the reliability in service.

# 3.1.2 Do's and Dont's in Design

In the remainder of the book, do's and don'ts will be generally presented at the end of the various chapters, however, the implications of Figure 3.2 to achieving a good design are many. We can summarize some of these in general, as follows:

## Region I:

- Consider the need for screening by burn-in, inspection or non-destructive evaluations
- Insure manufacturing issues are addressed early in the design
- Apply statistical process controls to manufacturing and assembly processes
- Anticipate the effects of defects as stress concentration points


Figure 3.3 The effects of increasing load levels on the ideal Mortality Curve.# Region II:

- Carefully anticipate system loads and corresponding stress levels over the life cycle, that selected and designed components will be exposed to, including: shipping, storage, handling, manufacturing and operation
- Anticipate overstress failures and quantify overstress risks
- Select and design components with adequate strength to meet overstress conditions at acceptable risks
- Qualify by testing components to ensure anticipated overstress conditions will be met


## Region III:

- Anticipate wear out failures
- Design and select components with adequate durability or life, at an acceptable level of risk
- Conduct component life testing to ensure life goals will be met by the design
- Consider maintainability and repairability issues to ensure maintenance goals are met by the design

Much of the remainder of the text is devoted to enabling the list above, through reliability assessment for product development and design.

### 3.2 Component Hazard and Reliability Models

Our previous discussion shows that the hazard rate of a component can be very indicative of the failure mechanisms that can occur in the life of a component. Equation 3.1 shows that we define the hazard rate in terms of the probability density function describing the probability distribution of failures. Several useful and commonly applied distributions are discussed in Chapter 2; the hazard functions and reliability functions for these distributions are also presented in Chapter 2 and the reader should review these.

A continuous probability density function or $p d f$, describes the distribution of failures of a component in time, under given load conditions, for a single failure mechanism and defect type. If we can appropriately model these failure processes and their associated uncertainties we can model pdfs of each mechanism and determine the reliability of the components. This information can be invaluable in assessing where corrective action or design improvements can most effectively be implemented. Recall our discussion of Figure 1.7 in Chapter 1. It also becomes possible then to model the reliability of the system or product we are designing by appropriate combinations of the probabilities of failure for each mechanism, under the rules we described in Chapter 2.

The Weibull distribution is among the most useful distributions to describe the hazard functions and reliability functions associated with a failure mechanism in a component. If we do not know the best distribution for a failure mechanism, it may be the safest place to start.

### 3.2.1 Applying the Weibull Distribution

As we have seen in Chapter 2, the hazard function for the 3-P Weibull distributions is given by three parameters. We will adopt the notation in equation 3.2 below:


$$

h(t)=\frac{\beta}{\eta}\left[\frac{t-\gamma}{\eta}\right]^{\beta-1}
$$$\beta$ represents the shape parameter; $\eta$ is the scale parameter and $\gamma$ is the location parameter, which may be used to represent a failure free period.

The reliability function of the 3-P Weibull is then:

$$
R(t)=e^{-\left|\frac{t-\gamma}{\eta}\right|^{2}}
$$

Let's initially consider the case of $\gamma=0$ and examine the effect of the shape parameter $\beta$ on the hazard rate to show the utility of the Weibull distribution. By an inspection of Figure 3.4, we see that depending upon the values of $\beta$, we can model the failure distribution for any type of behavior that can occur over the life cycle of a component. For $\beta<1$, defects are likely to be dominant. If $\beta=1$, the Weibull distribution will reduce to the simple exponential distribution. This is the special case of constant failure rate, which may apply to the useful life of a well designed component or Region II behavior. It may also indicate the undesirable condition that our data indicates a combination of failure mechanisms are acting on a component. This special case will be discussed further in following section. If $\beta>1$, then many types of wear out failures are indicated. In assessing parameters during analysis of test data, simulations or field performance data, determining the Weibull slope can be an important indication of the dominating mechanisms and of corrective action.

In considering $\gamma$, we can gain further information from the 3-P Weibull Distribution. In the special case of $\beta<1$ and $\gamma>0$ fatigue failure is indicated. As noted by Carter (1986), failure by fatigue fracture in metal structures and mechanical elements will often exhibit a failure free period followed by an abrupt increase in failure rate and a period of decreasing failure rate.

In general, the indications of the 3-P Weibull and its flexibility are indicated in Table 3.1.
The parameters of the Weibull distribution can be evaluated by conducting tests on components, subsystems or systems. Failure times are accumulated for components or systems under test. Component failure data are then plotted on probability paper and the Weibull parameters are determined. This process is discussed in detail in Chapter 12. The Weibull distribution can also be fit to data generated from a Monte Carlo simulation.

Accumulations of system or sub system level test or field performance data should be segregated by the different failure modes and their associated mechanisms. The application of failure analysis on test samples exhibiting various failure modes will ascertain the associated failure mechanism. The cumulative hazard for each failure mode and its associated mecha-

Figure 3.4 Schematic showing the general effects of the Weibull Shape Parameter on hazard rate. The Weibull Distribution can be used as a model for any region of the Mortality Curve.Table 3.1 Indications of the 3-P Weibull Distribution Parameters

| Location Parameter | Shape Parameter | Indications                                                                |
| :----------------- | :-------------- | :------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| $\gamma=0$         | $\beta<1$       | Weak or defective components                                               |
|                    | $\beta=1$       | Random overstress failures or several combined or mixed failure mechanisms |
|                    | $\beta>1$       | Wear out beginning at introduction of service or test                      |
| $\gamma>0$         | $\beta<1$       | Fatigue                                                                    |
|                    | $\beta>1$       | Corrosion or similar erosion mechanisms                                    |
| $\gamma<0$         | $\beta<1$       | Defective components                                                       |
|                    | $\beta>1$       | Aging and degradation before service or test                               |

nism may then be plotted and the parameters of individual competing failure mechanisms may be determined. A comparison of the test conditions to operational conditions in an acceleration factor model will then allow a projection of test data to operational conditions. Again, this analysis process is covered in detail in Chapter 12. Once again, it is important note that from the Weibull distribution as a starting point, the need for other distributions can be assessed as necessary.

Other distributions are applied to modeling hazard rate and reliability. For example, the log-normal Distribution has been applied to various wear out mechanisms for electronic components and to fatigue in mechanical components. The normal distribution has also been applied to fatigue. In the face of existing practices in various industries, or if test data are not available and too costly to generate, various distributions and estimated parameters may be used in the course of modeling the hazard rate and reliability of a component or product in design. Many standardized approaches in electronic component and system design call for the assumption of a constant hazard rate and the application of the exponential distribution. Such standards include the widely used military handbook MIL-HDBK-217. However, the constant hazard rate assumption applies only in certain circumstances and the assumption must be validated and used with caution.

# 3.2.2 The Constant Hazard Rate

Let us now turn out attention to this special case of the constant hazard rate. Application or assumption of this condition can greatly simplify reliability calculations, as we will see in succeeding sections. In part for this reason, the constant failure rate assumption is widely applied and the exponential distribution is then used to for hazard rate models for components and it is then extended to systems and products. An examination of the relationship between the Poisson distribution and the exponential distribution will give some insights into the physical significance of a constant hazard rate and how it should be appropriately applied.

Consider the concept of independent random shock loads occurring in a time interval, $t$. Then, from the Poisson distribution, we can express the probability of the random variable $x=n$ as:

$$
\operatorname{Pr}(x=n)=\frac{\exp (-\lambda t)(\lambda t)^{n}}{n!}
$$

The conditions here are subject to the Homogeneous Poisson Process (HPP). Each random shock load is independent; $n$ shocks will occur in the interval $(0, t)$ and $\lambda$ is the average rate at which the shocks will occur. Now, suppose a single shock load will kill the component. The reliability of the component must then be $R(t ; \lambda)=\operatorname{Pr}(x=n=0)$.It follows that from equation 3.2 that:

$$
R(t)=e^{-\lambda t}
$$

You will recognize that this is the reliability function for the exponential distribution. Then, $f(t)$ is

$$
f(t)=\lambda e^{-\lambda t}
$$

Recalling our definition of the hazard function:

$$
h(t)=\frac{f(t)}{R(t)}=\frac{\lambda e^{-\lambda t}}{e^{-\lambda t}}=\lambda
$$

As shown, the hazard rate function for the exponential distribution reduces to a constant failure rate.

The implication here is that a constant failure rate implies that the loading conditions and failure process that induce component failure must conform to the rules of the Homogeneous Poisson Process. A single random shock load, that is independent of other loads, and induces component failure, is by definition an overstress load. In other words, from a physical perspective, the exponential distribution and constant failure rate assumption is suitable to describe the risk of overstress failures in time. Hence, in the useful life of the well designed component, where we do not expect significant degradation of strength, we can appropriately model the probability of overstress failures in time, using a constant failure rate approximation. This does not apply to a condition where wear out failure mechanisms dominate the failures of the components.

However, it is also important to note that a combination of failure mechanisms acting over time on a component, wear out or overstress, may cause the combined hazard rate for the component to appear to approach a constant failure rate. As discussed by O'Connor (1991), a collection of non-HPP identically distributed random variables may lead the combined effect to approach an HPP condition. The implication is that lumping a collection of failures from different causes and perhaps different failure process and failure starting times, into an analysis, may show a constant failure rate and hence may fit an exponential distribution. As we shall see, assuming this condition, simplifies reliability calculations. However, combining failure mechanisms is of little value in trying to ascertain corrective actions and make improvements in components during development. It is also one of the reasons why the exponential distribution is widely misapplied.

For example, a complex semiconductor device may exhibit a constant failure rate in modeling field data variability, if no attention is paid to isolating failure mechanisms. This is not surprising, since a complex semiconductor is a system unto itself, which can fail from many different mechanisms, as discussed in Chapter 8. Depending upon the applied loads, different mechanisms may activate at different times. Lumping all data together may show a constant hazard rate in the results of the analysis leading to an assumption of the exponential distribution. However, the analysis of the lumped data for this component, really has little value here, since we cannot make a judgement about improvements in the processing of the device or design of the device to improve the product or system that uses it and there is little physical significance in doing so. In actuality, the exponential distribution is appropriate to model the risk of electrical overstress failures, such as the risk of electrical overstress from a voltage transient, during the useful life of this component.# 3.3 Failure Mechanisms and Competing Causes of Failure Model

The physics of failure or failure mechanics approach is an approach to modeling and reliability analysis involving separate treatment of the failure mechanisms acting upon the product. To some extent, this is already done by the conventional design process. For example, a shaft designed for an electric motor would certainly consider fatigue, bearing wear and potential for excessive twist under the applicable torque loads. However, during the design of this nature we would generally apply a safety factor approach to assure the shaft will meet its application requirements. We might not consider treatment of uncertainties or assessment of shaft reliability through the fatigue, wear or deflection model. In the case of a printed wiring board, a system failure rate might be generated from constant hazard rate assumption for each component and may be applied to estimate reliability of the assembly. The part hazard rate may be modified for a given environment but the individual failure mechanisms acting on the assembly and their life may not be directly considered. The system reliability may then be estimated by summing the part hazard rates through the various indenture levels. Both of these approaches are lacking in their ability to provide sufficient information and generally do not apply anytime a new technology or new material is introduced.

In addition, an assessment of product reliability under intended life cycle loads from data obtained under accelerated tests is a key to reliability assessment in design. This necessarily involves explicit and separate treatment of failure processes or mechanisms to interpret the test. In addition, as we have already discussed, separate treatment of failure mechanisms can be very revealing as to the need for corrective action.

Consider the microelectronic device we discussed earlier which is subject three dominant failure mechanisms acting at associated failure sites within the device. The time to failure from of each of the failure mechanisms may be influenced by variations in several parameters, including loads, geometries, material properties, defect magnitudes and stresses. Figure 3.5 depicts the relationship between the time-to-failure distribution of each

Figure 3.5 The desirable state of information for designing a reliable component with three dominant mechanisms of failure.of the three failure mechanisms, and the stress on which each mechanism depends. Explicit consideration of the three dominant failure mechanisms, geometries and material properties, will provide the insight required to design and build reliability into the device.

In general, Evans et. al. [Evans, Cushing. Lall and Bauernschub 1995] have identified several important steps in the competing failure mechanism modeling approach. The modeling approach will include the following steps:

- Determine the likely failure mechanisms and damage model for each potential mechanism.
- Review the loads and stresses and their limits for the models of each failure mechanism
- Estimate model parameters for each failure mechanism
- Etrapolate use stresses for each failure mechanism.
- Use the competing-risk model to combine the times-to-failure distributions of the failure mechanisms.

Damage models characterize the various mechanisms in components. Failure mechanisms may include mechanical, electrical or chemical degradation. In Chapter 1, we presented the classic damage model used in modeling fatigue failures. Defects and geometry would be considered in the estimation of the mechanical stress in the component. Similarly, each failure mechanism will have an associated model. Models for may different mechanisms are presented in later chapters of this book. For our present discussion lets assume a general model for time to failure may be constructed as shown in equation 3.8 below, where $t_{f}$ is a function of a matrix of critical component variables, including material properties, geometry and loads or stresses:

The general damage model is then:

$$
t_{f}=f\left[\begin{array}{llll}
g_{11} & g_{12} & g_{13} & \ldots & g_{1 n} \\
m_{21} & m_{22} & m_{23} & \ldots & \ldots \\
p_{31} & p_{32} & p_{33} & \ldots & \ldots \\
e_{41} & e_{42} & e_{43} & \ldots & \ldots \\
\delta_{l r} d_{51} & \delta_{l r} d_{52} & \delta_{l r} d_{53} & \ldots & \delta_{l r} d_{m n}
\end{array}\right]
$$

where $t_{f}$ is the time to failure due to a failure mechanism; $g_{1, i}$ are the geometric parameters; $m_{2 i}$ are the material properties and $p_{3 i}$ are the operational parameters; $e_{4 i}$ are applied loads and $d_{5 i}$ are the defect magnitudes or load/stress concentration factors; $l$ and $r$ are indices the at indicate the existence or non-existence of a defect.

$$
\delta_{l r}=0 \text {, for } l=r \text { and } \delta_{l r}=1 \text { for } l \neq r
$$

Uncertainty in the time to failure arrises due to uncertainties and variations in $g, m, p$ and $d$. In other words, $t_{f}$ is a continuous random variable that arrises from the fact that the factors contributing to failure are also random variables. As an example, once again consider the electric motor drive shaft. Variations in the shaft diameter, an $m$ factor, naturally arise from the manufacturing processes used to fabricate the shaft. In addition, the surface condition will vary according to the processes used to finish the surface of the component, $a d$ factor. These variations affect the stress distribution and, hence, the crack development that initiates fatigue failure in service.

As shown in the process in Figure 3.6, the variations in the parameters of a damage model can be treated directly by Monte Carlo simulation to develop an estimate of the time to failure distribution for a given mechanism. The deterministic failure mechanism model is embedded in the simulation. The probability density function for each model parameter must be determined or estimated as an input to the simulation. The $c d f s$ of these distributions are then sampled using a random number generator. The deterministic model is run for

Figure 3.6 Process of Monte Carlo simulation to estimate component reliability from $n$ failure mechanisms acting on a component.
each sample and the results of each time to failure calculation is saved in a data cell. The results can then be viewed in the form a frequency histogram and fitted to an appropriate distribution. Of course, adequate testing can also provide a time to failure distribution for a given mechanism.

A component then has a random time to failure, $T_{\text {comp }}$ from $n$ different mechanisms acting on the component. In a case where any of the $n$ mechanisms will cause the component to fail (e.g. $F M_{1}$ or $F M_{2}$ or $F M_{n}$ ) failure will occur when the first of the $n$ times to failure occurs. This is the weakest link concept that gives rise to the competing failure mechanism model for component reliability Evans et. al. (1995). The mechanics of dominant failure processes and their various damage models are covered in succeeding chapters.

Once again, considering $n$ failure mechanisms, the weakest link concept indicates that:

$$
T_{\text {comp }}=\min \left(T_{1}, T_{2}, T_{3} \ldots \ldots \ldots . T_{n}\right)
$$

where $T_{1}, T_{2}$ to $T_{n}$ are the times to fail for a set of $n$ failure mechanisms. By our definition, the reliability of the component is the probability that the component survives to our desired life, $t$. We can express this as: $R(t)=\operatorname{Pr}\left(T_{\text {comp }} \geq t\right)$. Then, for our set of $n$ failure mechanisms acting on the component:$$
R(t)=\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\left(T*{1} \geq t\right) \cap\left(T*{2} \geq t\right) \cap\left(T*{3} \geq t\right) \cap \ldots \ldots \cap\left(T*{n} \geq t\right)\right\}

$$

If the $n$ failure mechanism are independent then we can combine the probabilities according to the rules we covered in Chapter 2:


$$

R(t)=\operatorname{Pr}\left(T*{1} \geq t\right) \bullet \operatorname{Pr}\left(T*{2} \geq t\right) \bullet \operatorname{Pr}\left(T*{3} \geq t\right) \bullet \operatorname{Pr}\left(T*{n} \geq t\right)

$$

and


$$

R(t)=R*{1}(t) \bullet R*{2}(t) \bullet R*{3}(t) \bullet \ldots \cdot \bullet R*{n}(t)

$$

In this special case, the hazard function can be determined from the sum of the hazard functions for the different failure mechanisms. Hence, the hazard rate at time, $t$, for the component becomes:


$$

h*{\text {comp }}(t)=\sum*{i=1}^{n} h\_{i}(t)

$$

In most cases, the failure mechanisms acting on a component are not likely to be independent. Variation in material properties, geometry or loading will effect more than one mechanism. Hence, the independent competing risk case is not always appropriate. It will, however, yield a conservative estimate. This will provide a lower bound of the reliability when the $n$ times to failure are positively correlated. Then, the reliability of the shortest time to failure can express an upper bound to bracket the reliability of the component.

The problem of dependence can best be addressed by using Monte Carlo simulation. In this case, appropriate probability distributions describing variations of physical dimensions or material property variations can serve as the inputs to more than one failure mechanism reliability model.

The are several methods of estimating or bounding the reliability of a component from the failure mechanism times to failure. The bounds can be made increasingly more accurate with greater information about the $p d f s$ of each failure mechanism acting on the component. If the case where we know only the mean times to failure, $\mu_{i}$, for $n$ mechanisms, we can estimate the component reliability as:


$$

R(t) \geq e^{-t \sum*{i=1}^{n} \frac{1}{\mu*{i}}}

$$

In most cases, this will provide a very conservative estimate. However, this method does provide a link between the failure mechanisms and the reliability of the component and the mechanism need not be assumed to be independent.

The following assumptions must hold to apply equation 3.14 .

- The failure mechanisms have constant or increasing hazard rates (e.g wear out or overstress failures)
- The failure mechanisms must be associated. Associated implies that the mechanisms act similarly with respect to increasing loads. The mechanisms may or may not be independent.
- The time period of interest or component life, $t$, must be less than the minimum of the known means.
- The means of each of the $n$ failure mechanisms are known $\left(\mu_{1}, \mu_{2}, \mu_{3} \ldots \ldots . \mu_{n}\right)$.
- The component of interest is coherent which implies that improving the reliability of one mechanism will not decrease the reliability of the component.
Another method of bounding with limited information about the time-to-failure distribution of interest, uses the mean and variance of a the time to failure for a given mechanism. Then, ifwe assume the mechanisms are independent, we can apply equation 3.14 to bound the reliability. This method was developed by Barlow and Marshall (1965) and applies to a non-decreasing hazard rate situation. This method uses tables prepared by Barlow and Marshall which can also be found in Tobias and Trindade (1986); these tables are not reproduced in this book. The tables are utilized by normalizing the mean of the distribution of interest to 1 . The second moment about the distribution origin must also be calculated.

In general, the moments of a distribution are related as follows:


$$

\mu*{r}=\sum*{i=0}^{i}\binom{r}{i} \mu*{r-1}^{\prime}\left(-\mu*{1}^{\prime}\right)^{i}

$$

where $\mu_{r}$ is the $r$ th moment about the mean and $\mu_{r}{ }^{\prime}$ is the $r$ th moment about the origin of the distribution of interest. If we set $r=2$, then we can see that relationship between the mean, $\mu$, which is the first moment about the origin, the variance, $\sigma^{2}$, the second moment about the mean, and the second moment about the origin, $\mu_{2}{ }^{\prime}, 3.15$ becomes:-


$$

\mu^{2}=\mu\_{2}^{\prime}-\sigma^{2}

$$

Dividing through by $\mu^{2}$ yields the useful equation for the Barlow-Marshall Tables.


$$

1=\frac{\mu\_{2}^{\prime}}{\mu^{2}}-\frac{\sigma^{2}}{\mu^{2}}

$$

To use the Barlow-Marshall Tables we also divide the time of interest, $t$, by the mean of the time to failure distribution. Now, using the Barlow-Marshall Tables we can bound the reliability of each mechanism of failure with only limited information about the failure distribution. We can then apply the competing failure mechanism model to estimate component reliability.

Example 3.1 Recalling Figure 1.7, let us assume that this figure describes the failure distributions of two failure mechanisms in an electronic device. Calculate the device reliability by direct calculation using the Weibull distribution at $50,000,65,000$ and 75,000 hours of device use. Then, estimate the reliability using the Barlow-Marshall Tables and compare the results. The distributions have the following parameters:

Table 3.2 Data Table for Example 3.1

|  | $\boldsymbol{p d f - 1}$ | $\boldsymbol{p d f - 2}$ |
| :-- | :-- | :-- |
| Mean | 88,600 hours | 91,800 |
| Variance | $2.14 \times 10^{9}$ hours $^{2}$ | $4.423 \times 10^{8}$ hours $^{2}$ |
| Shape Parameter | 2 | 5 |
| Scale Parameter | 100,000 hours | 100,000 hours |

From equation 3.3, we can calculate the reliability of each failure mechanism from the Weibull parameters. The results are:

Table 3.3 Results of Reliability Calculation from Weibull Distribution Parameters

| $\boldsymbol{t}$ (hours) | $\boldsymbol{R}_{\boldsymbol{F} 1}(\boldsymbol{t})$ | $\boldsymbol{R}_{\boldsymbol{F} 2}(\boldsymbol{t})$ | $\boldsymbol{R}_{\text {comp }}=\boldsymbol{R}_{\boldsymbol{F} 1} \cdot \boldsymbol{R}_{\boldsymbol{F} 2}$ |
| :-- | :-- | :-- | :-- |
| 50,000 | 0.78 | 0.97 | 0.75 |
| 60,000 | 0.70 | 0.93 | 0.65 |
| 75,000 | 0.57 | 0.79 | 0.45 |To use the Barlow-Marshall Tables, we calculate $\mu_{2}{ }^{\prime}$ for each distribution. For failure mechanism $1, \mu_{2}{ }^{\prime}=10^{10}$ and for failure mechanism $2, \mu_{2}{ }^{\prime}=8.873 \times 10^{9}$. Then dividing these values by the square of the mean and our times of interest by the mean we estimate the lower bound of the reliability of each failure mechanism; we can then estimate the component reliability.

Table 3.4 Results of Reliability Calculation from Barlow-Marshall Tables

| $\boldsymbol{t}$ (hours) | $\boldsymbol{R}_{\boldsymbol{F} \boldsymbol{t}}(\boldsymbol{t})$ | $\boldsymbol{R}_{\boldsymbol{F} \boldsymbol{t}}(\boldsymbol{t})$ | $\boldsymbol{R}_{\text {comp }}=\boldsymbol{R}_{\boldsymbol{F} \boldsymbol{t}} \cdot \boldsymbol{R}_{\boldsymbol{F} \boldsymbol{t}}$ |
| :-- | :-- | :-- | :-- |
