| 60,000 | 0.64 | 0.86 | 0.55 |
| 75,000 | 0.49 | 0.71 | 0.35 |

By inspection of Tables 3.3 and 3.4, we can see the lower bound compares quite favourably to the reliability calculations from full information of the failure mechanism distributions. In either case, we can also see that Failure Mechanism 1 is the weakest link and should be the initial focus of corrective action. If we examine only the means of the two distributions, we may conclude there is little difference in the two failure mechanisms and that failure is not likely if the device life is far less than 90,000 hours.

This example then shows three important concepts. First, we can estimate the reliability of the failure mechanisms and, hence, the device with limited knowledge of the failure distributions. Second, we must treat failure mechanisms separately to derive effective corrective action. Finally, we must consider uncertainty in the separate treatment of failure mechanisms in order to derive effective corrective action in design.

# 3.4 System Reliability Prediction and System Models

A system reliability model can be constructed from its components. For most engineering systems, a series model applies. In this case, the failure of a single component in the series will cause the system to fail. Some systems may be comprised of parallel arrangements of components. In this case, one of the components in the parallel arrangement may fail, without causing system failure. This can be a way of increasing reliability by adding redundancy of a critical component. In any case, we can generally construct a block diagram describing the interaction between the components of the design.

### 3.4.1 Series and Parallel Systems

First, lets consider the simple series system. As we see Figure 3.7 the arrangement of components will result in system failure if a single component fails. We can describe the reliability of the series system at time $t$, as the probability of the event that each component will operate successfully to time $t$.


Figure 3.7 A simple series system. The series system model describes many types of systems.Hence:


$$

R*{s}(t)=\operatorname{Pr}\left(E*{1}\right) \cap \operatorname{Pr}\left(E*{2}\right) \cap \operatorname{Pr}\left(E*{3}\right) \cap \ldots \ldots \cap \operatorname{Pr}\left(E\_{n}\right)

$$

where $R_{s}(t)$ is the system reliability and $E_{i}$ is the event of successful operation of component $i$ to time $t$.

We quickly see that, for independent events:


$$

R*{s}(t)=\operatorname{Pr}\left(E*{1}\right) \bullet \operatorname{Pr}\left(E*{2}\right) \bullet \operatorname{Pr}\left(E*{3}\right) \bullet \ldots . . \bullet \operatorname{Pr}\left(E\_{n}\right)

$$

And for a total of $n$ components:


$$

R*{s}(t)=\prod*{i=1}^{n} R\_{n}(t)

$$

$R_{n}(t)$ is the reliability at time $t$, as described by the individual component reliabilities. If we apply the Exponential distribution to describe the failure distribution of the $n$ components, the system failure rate, $\lambda_{s}$, is the sum of the component failure rates and the system Mean Time Between Failures or MTBF is simply:


$$

\begin{aligned}
& \lambda*{s}=\sum*{i=1}^{n} \lambda*{n} \\
& \text { MTBF }=\frac{1}{\lambda*{s}}
\end{aligned}

$$

Applying the Exponential distribution to the series systems greatly simplifies the calculation, but it should be applied only as appropriate. Its application often leads to MTBF as a descriptor of system reliability. However, in complex systems there may be no reason to expect repeated failure patterns of the same components, particularly when overstress failures dominate. MTBF is therefore not a system property as is weight or size.

As stated, the series model description fits most types of systems. The model tells us that individual component reliability must be very high to achieve reasonable probabilities of successful system operation.

Example 3.2 Consider system of 40 devices on 2 printed wiring boards used for a consumer appliance. What is the component reliability, if the system must have an operational life of 7 years and at an end of life unreliability of 1 unit per 1000 units requiring repair?

Solution: For the purposes of demonstration, we assume all the components are similar. Then, from equation 3.20 above:


$$

\begin{aligned}
& R*{s}=\left(R*{\text {component }}\right)^{n} \\
& R*{\text {comp }}=\left(R*{s}\right)^{\frac{1}{n}} \\
& R*{\text {comp }}=(0.999)^{\frac{1}{n, 2}} \\
& R*{\text {comp }}=0.99998
\end{aligned}

$$

Lets examine a parallel arrangement of components shown in Figure 3.8. Whereas, before we examined the reliabilities of the individual components, let us now examine the potential for failure of the individual components in the system.
$F_{s}(t)$ is the unreliability of the system or probability of failing to operate to time $t$. Then, we can say that:


$$

F*{s}(t)=\operatorname{Pr}\left(\bar{E}*{1}\right) \cap \operatorname{Pr}\left(\bar{E}_{2}\right) \cap \ldots \ldots \cap \operatorname{Pr}\left(\bar{E}_{n}\right)

$$

Figure 3.8 A parallel arrangement of components. If unit 1 fails, the system will continue to operate as long as at least 1 of the $n$ units functions. A sensing and switching system may be used to switch from a failed to a functioning component.
where $\overline{E_{i}}$ is the complement of event $E_{i}$ or the event that the component will fail to operate to time $t$.

In the case of independent events, we see the system unreliability is:


$$

F*{s}(t)=\operatorname{Pr}\left(\overline{E*{1}}\right) \bullet \operatorname{Pr}\left(\overline{E*{2}}\right) \bullet \ldots . . \cdot \operatorname{Pr}\left(\overline{E*{n}}\right)

$$

or


$$

F*{s}(t)=\prod*{i=1}^{n} F*{i}(t)=\prod*{i=1}^{n}\left[1-R_{i}(t)\right]

$$

Most systems can be represented by a combination of series and parallel arrangements of components.

Example 3.3 Lets consider a spacecraft data handling system consisting of a transmitter, data storage sub-system and receiver. What is the reliability improvement for a redundant transmitter, given the following sub-system reliabilities?

| Sub-system/Component | Function | Reliability |
| :-- | :-- | :-- |
| 1 | Data Transmission | 0.84 |
| 2 | Data Storage | 0.99 |
| 3 | Command Receiver | 0.95 |

The block diagram is as shown below and considering the system with a single transmitter, The system reliability is:


$$

R*{s}=R*{1} \bullet R*{2} \bullet R*{3}=(0.84)(0.99)(0.95)=0.79

$$
Now, modifying the block diagram to allow for the redundant transmitter, as shown below, we see the reliability of the data transmission subsystem, with two transmitters, will be:


$$

R*{1}=1-\left(1-R*{\text {trans1 }}\right)\left(1-R\_{\text {trans2 }}\right)=1-(1-0.84)^{2}=0.9744

$$

Then, the system reliability becomes:


$$

R*{s}=R*{1} \bullet R*{2} \bullet R*{3}=(0.9744)(0.99)(0.95)=0.9164 \cong 0.92

$$

A large gain in reliability is evident. This significant increase in reliability often justifies added redundancy. In the example shown above, the system will successfully operate if either or both of the components is operational to time $t$. This is known as active redundancy.

The model above is relatively simple. However, when redundancy is added, a sensing and switching sub-system may be required to sense failure and switch to the redundant component which is in a non-energized or dormant state. This is referred to as stand-by redundancy. The sensing and switching subsystem may significantly effect the system reliability. In addition, while in the de-energized or dormant state, the redundant components may not be free from environmental loads inducing failure mechanism to act on the components. Hence, the hazard rate and failure distribution may be different before the switching time as compared to the failure distribution and hazard rate after the switching time. These complexities may be accounted for in the modeling process.

Refering to Figure 3.9, we can see the reliability or probability of successful operation of the system is the probability that unit 1 functions until the desired time $t$ or that unit 1 will fail and the switch will activate to energize unit 2 at some point in time, $t_{1}$. In this case, we see the reliability is the probability that unit 1 fails at time $t_{1}$ and the sensing and switching unit does not fail to time $t_{1}$ and unit 2 operates successfully from time $t_{1}$ until the desired time $t$.

If we assume independent events, we can write the equation for reliability of the system as follows:


$$

R*{s}=R*{1}(t)+\int*{t*{1}=0}^{t*{1}=t}\left[h*{1}\left(t*{1}\right) d t*{1}\right] R*{s / s}\left(t*{1}\right) R*{2}\left(t*{1}\right) R*{2}\left(t-t*{1}\right)

$$

Another form of redundancy, is the $k$ out of $n$ system. In this case, at least $k$ units must operate out of a total $n$ redundant units for the system to function. This is described by the binominal distribution.


Figure 3.9 Redundant system with sensing and switching element. Unit 2 remains dormant until Unit 1 fails.It should be noted that the law of diminishing returns applies to redundancy. For each redundant unit added, there will be less added improvement in reliability. After the fourth level of redundancy, the marginal improvement is very small. In addition, we must consider the added cost of each redundant component. The costs of redundancy are then traded off against the cost of designing or selecting a component or sub-system with better reliability.

A more complete description of block diagrams and their analysis is discussed in Moddares (1993) or Pecht (1995). However, the methods of Fault Tree Analysis and Failure Modes and Effects Analysis are more powerful in their ability to relate system failure to component failure mechanisms.

# 3.4.2 Repairable System Behavior

Until now we have discussed the potential application of various distributions, including the Weibull distribution and exponential distribution to determining the hazard rate and reliability of components that comprise our system or product. We then discussed building system level models from our knowledge of component failure distributions. In this case, a continuous probability density function is applicable to each single failure mechanism acting on a component with associated defect types and we are concerned about the risk of the first failure in a given component. However, in many systems or products we may want to replace the component to repair the system when it fails. Hence, let us now turn to developing a basic understanding of repairable systems.

As discussed by O'Connor, (1991) we cannot in actuality represent a repairable system by continuous probability distribution function. Rather, a group of unrelated failures in a repairable system of various types of components, failing from different mechanisms, occur as a series of discrete events in a time continuum. We refer to this as a stochastic point process. If the events occur randomly at a constant average rate, we can represent the occurance of failures by the Poisson distribution. As we discussed before, a Homogenous Poisson Process (HPP) is a process in which the number of events in a fixed interval does not vary regardless of when or where a sample is taken. This may lead us to representing the system reliability by the exponential distribution (constant failure rate). However, this assumption should be validated by appropriate analysis of data.

In considering a series of unrelated failures, we refer to the time at which the failure occurs as the arrival time and the time between failures as the interarrival time. We must examine the arrival times closely in a set of data to determine wether or not there are trends in the data. If a trend exists, then the data indicate that system failure is not HPP. We can test for a trend in a series by using the Laplace or Centroid Test. The calculated statistic, $U$, is used a basis for the test:


$$

U=\frac{\left[\sum_{i=1}^{N_{o}} T_{i}-\frac{T_{o}}{2}\right]}{T\_{o} \sqrt{\frac{1}{12(n-1)}}}

$$

The value of $U$ compares the centroid of the discrete failure arrival times, $T_{i}$, to the mid-point of the observation period, $T_{o} ; n$ is simply the number of observations, with the last observation defining the observation period. If $U<0$ there is a decreasing trend in the failure arrival times. If $U=0$ there is no trend and if $U>0$ there is a trend toward an increasing arrival time for the series of discrete failure arrival times. Statistical significance can be tested using the Standard Normal tables.Let examine by a diagram, the failure arrival times for a simple hypothetical system of four components. We can see similar analyzes in Moddares (1993) or O'Connor (1991). In our example, the four components are all replaceable upon failure. As Figure 3.10 shows, each component has been replaced at the time indicated. Component 1 has a small increasing trend, while component 2 has a significant increasing trend. Component 3 has a decreasing trend and Component 4 has a significant increasing trend. The combined system trend at the observation time is an increasing rate of occurrence of failures, as we see the influence of two components on the system. It is frequently the case, that a few components dominate the failure of system. In this case, we must initiate failure analysis and trace down the root cause through proper reliability assessment. The individual failure trends can be valuable in helping identify causes.

Continuous monitoring of more complex system may show a tendency towards an constant rate of occurrence of failures in the system, regardless of the individual trends of the components, once most of the components have been replaced more than once. However, this is not likely to occur in most types of systems, since the service life will end well before all the components are replaced. Here we see the danger of getting an erroneous estimate of system reliability by assuming a constant failure rate for the components and summing up the indenture levels to find the system rate of occurance.

The use of such data, with the lumping of various failure modes together under a single distribution, for a repairable, maintained system, under the constant failure rate assumption in design of systems, however, is generally restricted to evaluation of logistics issues. There is seemingly no physical basis for lumping failure modes and mechanisms together under a single distribution. In addition, the value in making decisions for a design or to develop corrective action for design improvements is limited. However, this approach may provide a first order estimate appropriate for an initial warranty cost estimate or estimates of required spares.


Figure 3.10 Representation of a repairable system. Each component exhibits a trend in failures influencing the overall trend of the system. In this example we see an increasing trend in the system owing to increasing failure rate trends in two of the components.The onset of wear out of a system can be prolonged by maintenance. Maintenance action can be taken to remove a component from service before failure. This can be done through periodic inspections. In addition, changing the conditions of service, through periodic lubrication or other maintenance actions may prolong the onset of wear out. But it is important to note that any maintenance action or repair action does not necessarily make the equipment as good as new. Maintenance is not discussed in detail here as it is not within the scope of the book. However, the process and methods can be used to identify maintainability issues. Maintainability issues are further discussed by O'Connor (1991) and in Blanchard and Fabrycky (1990).

# 3.5 System Failure Assessment

Two approaches which are powerful in relating component failures to system failure and the resulting consequences of component failure are the methods of Fault Tree Analysis (FTA) and Failure Modes and Effects Analysis (FMEA). These methods play an important role in reliability assessment during design and development.

These methods are known as event oriented, as they anticipate failure of the system. There are essentially two different groups of event-oriented evaluation methods. In the one group the relations between cause and event are set up the casual direction. These evaluation methods are called 'forward methods' or 'bottom up evaluation' or induction. The most important one of this methods is FMEA. The second group of evaluation methods is characterized by the fact that its basic reasoning is anti-causal, which are called 'top-down' or deductive methods, because this stems from the logic reasoning of deduction in which one derives from the general (or more global) information the particular (or detailed) information. The major method is FTA.

The implementation of these methods is discussed below with examples.

### 3.5.1 Fault Tree Analysis

Fault Tree Analysis(FTA) has been widely used in various industries for system reliability assessment. It has been used significantly in aeronautics, telecommunications, nuclear power generation and transport system development. This approach was initially developed by H. A. Watson of the Bell Telephone Laboratories in 1962 for the analysis of the availability of rocket launch control systems, and was later revised by D. F. Haasl of the Boeing airplane company.

Fault Tree Analysis(FTA) is both qualitative and quantitative. Qualitatively, it can be used to improve the system reliability by identifying components in the system that may contribute the most to system unreliability or failure. As an example, Walker and Cavallaro (1996) have successful applied FTA to analysis of robot reliability with the objective of design improvement. FTA is particularly powerful in that the fault tree is composed of a logical arrangement of the events that cause the system to fail. The fault tree logic is represented by using a set of standard graphical symbols as described below. The logical structure can then be simplified using Boolean Algebra and from our knowledge of how probabilities can be combined, we can estimate the probability of system failure due to a catastrophic top level event.

If the overall system is too complex to easily represent, it is usually split into several manageable subsystems. The procedure and analysis method of FTA are described below, and a simple example is presented. The analysis by means of fault tree consists of an oriented graph representing the causes and consequences of events in relation to each other. The relationbetween events is presented by means of standardized symbols. The primary symbols used in the construction of the fault tree are shown below

# Basic Event

The symbol in Figure 3.11a, indicates an end point of a fault tree. The circle indicates a basic fault event; the failure mode of the most elementary component, an environmental failure, or a human failure (operation, repair). For a quantitative analysis the probability of this event or its probability distribution must be known or determined from the component failure mechanisms responsible for the failure mode.

## Resultant Event

The rectangle, as shown in Figure 3.11b, indicates an event resulting from a combination of events, at the input of the associated logic.


Figure 3.11a Basic Event Symbol b Resultant Event Symbol c Undeveloped Event Symbol d Trigger Event e AND Gate f OR Gate $\mathbf{g}$ and $\mathbf{h}$ Transfer symbols.# Undeveloped Event

The diamond symbol, which we see in Figure 3.11c indicates an event, the causes of which will not be further developed.

## Trigger Event

The house symbol shown in Figure 3.11d, indicates an event that is implied during normal use, or an event that is expected not to occur during such a case. It can function as the trigger for a number of other events.

## AND-Gate

The symbol in Figure 3.11e is used when the output event occurs only if all the gate's input events occur.

## OR-Gate

This symbol in 3.11 f is used when the output event occurs if one or more of the input events occurs.

## Transfer Symbols

Transfer out or transfer in, shown in Figures 3.11 g and 3.11 h , are used to avoid repetition of parts of the fault tree. These symbols connect parts of fault trees that may extended over several consecutive pages.

## Fault Tree Analysis Procedure

The evaluation procedure of reliability and failure analysis by the fault tree analysis method can be described as follows.

- Select the system boundary and identify system components
- Construct the System Block Diagram
- Develop the fault tree from the block diagram
- Define the top fault event of the system
- Develop the resultant events that cause the top event and connect them in terms of appropriate logic symbols (AND or OR gate)
- Continue until resultant events are divided into the basic events which can no longer be divided
- If necessary, simplify the fault tree by means of Boolean operators
- Determine/Calculate failure probabilities and identify failure modes
- Identify critical fault paths


## Calculation of Failure Probability

The probability of an event is calculated from the logic of the fault tree. Lower events are combined to give an estimate of the probability of the top event from the known probabilities of the lowest events. Most situations can be dealt with by the appropriate use of the two simple cases shown below in Figure 3.12 and 3.13. Complex situations require the use of both rules, and the application of some common sense and experience to describe the situation in terms of the basic events.

Suppose we have a simple situation in which two elements are in series. Call them $C_{1}$ and $C_{2}$ with associated probabilities of failure. Recalling our previous discussion of series sys-

Figure 3.12 Simple series system showing OR Gate application


Figure 3.13 Simple parallel system showing AND Gate application.
tems, we know the system will fail if either $C_{1} O R C_{2}$ fail. Then, the logic of the fault tree dictates the OR gate. Our probabilities of failure of the lower basic events then combine to describe the probability of the top event, as follows:$$
\begin{aligned}
& \operatorname{Pr}(\text { System Failure })=\operatorname{Pr}\left(C_{1} \text { Fails }\right) \text { OR } \operatorname{Pr}\left(C_{2} \text { Fails }\right) \\
& \operatorname{Pr}\left(F_{s}\right)=\operatorname{Pr}\left(C_{1}\right) \cup \operatorname{Pr}\left(C_{2}\right) \\
& \operatorname{Pr}\left(F_{s}\right)=\operatorname{Pr}\left(C_{1}\right)+\operatorname{Pr}\left(C_{2}\right)-\operatorname{Pr}\left(C_{1}\right) \cdot \operatorname{Pr}\left(C_{2}\right) \\
& \operatorname{Pr}\left(F_{s}\right)=1-\left[1-\operatorname{Pr}\left(C_{1}\right)\right]\left[1-\operatorname{Pr}\left(C_{2}\right)\right]
\end{aligned}
$$

Suppose that our simple system made up of two components, $C_{1}$ and $C_{2}$ in parallel. This may represent a case of redundant components. Then the probability of failure of the simple system shown below is the event that $C_{1}$ AND $C_{2}$ fail dictating the AND gate logic for the fault tree.

Our failure probabilities then combine as follows, assuming independent events:

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \operatorname{Pr}\left(F_{s}\right)=\operatorname{Pr}\left(C_{1}\right) \text { AND } \operatorname{Pr}\left(C_{2}\right) \\
& \operatorname{Pr}\left(F_{s}\right)=\operatorname{Pr}\left(C_{1}\right) \cap \operatorname{Pr}\left(C_{2}\right) \\
& \operatorname{Pr}\left(F_{s}\right)=\operatorname{Pr}\left(C_{1}\right) \bullet \operatorname{Pr}\left(C_{2}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

Any combinations of lower events for which the probabilities of occurrence are known can be combined through the logic of the fault tree using the methods of combining probabilities as shown above. This is further illustrated in the next example.

Figure 3.14 Electric motor system with a redundant switch

Example 3.4 Consider the simple system shown above, comprised of an electric motor and redundant switch. Construct a fault tree and estimate the probability of failure.

The block diagram for this simple system is show below.

Figure 3.15 Block diagram for the electric motor system in Figure 3.14Let 'No Motor Output at Point A' be the top event. Lets now construct the fault tree.
For this example, we have adopted a letter convention for the physical element or subsystem that is within our system boundary. We have used a subscript for the components associated with each sub-system, where it is necessary. The same convention has been applied to the schematic, block diagram and fault tree for comparison. On the fault tree, each gate has

Figure 3.16 FTA of the simple electric motor with redundant switch.also been identified with the letter G and a subscript. The probabilities of failure for each component or primary failure event are shown on the fault tree. We can now reduce the fault tree and estimate the probability of the top event. We will assign the probabilities of the event with their letter designation on the fault tree.

Beginning at gate $G_{1}$, we see the output event, Motor fail ( $F$ ). This OR gate has 4 separate input events. Applying the rules we learned earlier:

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \operatorname{Pr}\left(F \text { fails })=\operatorname{Pr}\left(F_{1}\right) \cup \operatorname{Pr}\left(F_{2}\right) \cup \operatorname{Pr}\left(F_{3}\right) \cup \operatorname{Pr}\left(F_{4}\right)\right. \\
& \therefore F=1-\left[1-F_{1}\right]\left[1-F_{2}\right]\left[1-F_{3}\right]\left[1-F_{4}\right]
\end{aligned}
$$

Moving to AND gate $G_{2}$, we see it has output event, Switch fail ( $C$ ), with two input events. $C_{1}$ and $C_{2}$. The AND gate is the result of the redundant switch in the switching sub-system. Then:

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \operatorname{Pr}\left(C \text { fails }\right)=\operatorname{Pr}\left(C_{1}\right) \cap \operatorname{Pr}\left(C_{2}\right) \\
& \therefore C=C_{1} \bullet C_{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

At OR Gate $G_{3}$, we see 3 inputs and the output event, No current at B. Keeping our convention:

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \operatorname{Pr}(\text { No current at } B)=\operatorname{Pr}(E) \cup \operatorname{Pr}(C) \\
& \therefore B=1-[1-E][1-C]
\end{aligned}
$$

Note that the tree indicates that Event D, No Input Power, is elected to be an undeveloped event. There is of course no associated probability. This may be the case for an event external to the system for which we have no information. We can also immediately see that event $C$ links Gate $G_{3}$ and $G_{2}$ through our equations above.

At gate $G_{4}$, we have the top level event as the output of the gate:

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \operatorname{Pr}(\text { No Motor Output } A)=\operatorname{Pr}(B) \cup \operatorname{Pr}(F) \\
& \therefore A=1-[1-B][1-F]
\end{aligned}
$$

Combining the equations above with the known probabilities of failure, we can estimate $\operatorname{Pr}$ (No Motor Output at $A$ ) $=A=0.07$ and the reliability of the system as $R=1-A=0.97$. The logic in a fault tree of this nature can also be reduced by Boolean Algebra. For further information on fault trees, we can consult Pecht (1995), Moddarres (1993) or O'Connor (1991).

# Minimum Cut Set

A cut set is a set (or collection) of component failures that will produce system failure, and a minimum cut set is a cut set that has no subsets that are cut sets. This means that a minimum cut set is the limiting case of a cut set, i.e. it is a set of component failures that will produce system failure, with the further property that any single repair is sufficient to bring the system back to the functioning condition again. A list of all the minimum cut sets of a system tells the designer or user all there is to know about the reliability structure of the system, and if the data are available, the probability of failure of the system can be calculated. The probability of occurrence of each cut set is the product of the failure probabilities of each component in the set, and the failure probability of the system is the sum of the probabilities of occurrence of each cut set.

### 3.5.2 Failure Modes and Effects Analysis (FMEA)

FMEA is powerful complementary method to the Fault Tree. Whereas, FTA identifies each potential failure sites or critical component, FMEA is used to identify each failure mode, mechanism and contributing causes, associated with the components of a system or product.The corrective action necessary to prevent the failure mode and method to detect the failure are also part of the FMEA process.

The FMEA procedures is a straightforward qualitative analysis, centered around a worksheet that acts as an accounting tool. An example of the typical FMEA worksheet is shown in Table 3.5. This type of analysis can be performed at various level of abstraction during the development process and can be updated as the design progresses. A FMEA can also be performed from different points of view of the life cycle, such as human interaction with the product, maintenance or service activity, normal operation and manufacturing processes.

A successful analysis will involve several key steps. Functional and reliability block diagrams begin the analysis. In addition, this type of analysis can best be performed using an interdisciplinary team approach, with a cross functional team make-up.

# FMEA Procedure

The procedure to preform a Failure Modes and Effects Analysis may be described as follows: , Select the system boundary and identify system components

- Construct the system functional block diagram
- Consider loading environment
- Identify failure modes of components leading to loss function
- Identify mechanisms, contributing factors or component defects
- Assess local effects and effects on subsystem and system levels
- Assign a severity classification
- Identify compensating provisions or corrective actions,

# Failure Modes and Causes

One of the most important aspects of the FMEA process is the identification of modes and mechanisms. This requires experience and a solid knowledge base of the product type, loading conditions, defects and potential mechanisms. However, the typical modes for many components can be understood in terms of their functions. Reference materials, analysis of field failures and warranty claim data are good places to begin. Moddares (1993) and Pecht (1995) list modes and mechanisms for many electronic and simple mechanical components. An abbreviated list of modes is summarized below in Table 3.6. Careful consideration of modes, mechanisms and effects of fasteners, metallurgical joining, polymers components and surface finishes should be made. One can see the benefit of a team approach in this effort in which service personnell, manufacturing engineers and designers are involved.

## Effects

The consequences of the failure mode should be evaluated at the part level or lowest level of abstraction, the sub-system or intermediate level and the final system. Local effect may mean the loss of the component and its function. This may or may not cause the sub-system to fail. The final or system level effect may involve consideration of multiple failures depending upon the impact. For example, consider a space craft. A power transistor may short. If there is no redundant component, the power conditioning unit will fail. As a result, batteries will not be charged and the spacecraft will be lost in short order.

## Detection and Compensating Provisions.

These efforts comprise the proactive corrective action which makes FMEA a powerful part of the assessment process. Detection simply identifies how a failure mode and mechanism will be detected in the system. For example, an air cleaner element for a diesel engine may require periodic inspection to detect loss of air flow. Compensation refers to the action needed to avoid the mode and its impact on the system. Once again, refering to the spacecraft power unit, we may wish to have a redundant power transistor.

## Severity Class

The severity class is an indication of the magnitude of an effect of a given failure mode and cause. The most severe classification would be assigned to failure modes that are identified as causing complete loss of the system under analysis or human loss of life and injury. Lesser severity is assigned to system degradation or unscheduled maintenance and repair.

We have already mentioned that standards are employed for the FMEA Procedure. Standards will vary between industries. However, as an example, we can examine the severity classification scheme used in a US military standard. This is summarized in Table 3.7, below. We can also imagine a severity class considering different criteria, such as cost of warranty repair.

Upon completion of the analysis we can address the modes and mechanisms with the most severe consequences.Table 3.6 Common Failure Modes of Selected Components

# 3.5.3 Benefits and Limitations of System Failure Assessment

While FMEA is a bottom-up approach, FTA is a top-down analysis, and the two techniques complement each other. The benefits of performing these analysis can be summarized as follows:

- Critical failure modes and mechanisms are identified
- Systems weaknesses are identified
- Proactive corrective actions are evaluated

These methods impose a discipline on the designers. The design team is forced to think of the system in terms of how it may fail, and how the subsystems and components interact in the event of failure. It also gives insight into the structure of the system and components.

However, these methods do have limitations. FMEA for example can provide very little information about probabilistic risks. A weak point of the FTA method is that it is easy to overlook a possible cause of the top event. In addition, FTAs can become very unwieldy for a complex system. In any case, software becomes essential as the system complexity increases beyond a few components.

## Failure Mechanics# Overstress Failure and Load - Strength Interference

John W. Evans

We now begin our discussion of the mechanics of failure in Part II of this text. Part II provides the background necessary to understand many of the major failure mechanisms encountered in product design and reliability assessment, which is inturn necessary to implement the concepts presented in Part I. Mechanisms, models, factors contributing to uncertainty and mitigation are presented. We begin with overstress.

As shown in Chapter 3, one of our major concerns in design and selection of components is preventing overstress failures in the useful life of the product. We can define overstress failure as the event that the demanded load exceeds the available strength of a component. In our framework of classifying failures, we consider that overstress failures do not result from degradation of the strength of a component with time. We can then evaluate reliability during an assessment, on the basis of load and strength as random variables. Of course, we are also concerned with assuring a product will meet the durability requirements of the design and we must account for degradation of the component strength over time. But, we will leave this subject to later chapters.

As an example of overstress, we can consider electronic and electrical components. In this case, overstress may occur as result of excessive current in a conductor or excessive voltage applied to a dielectric, leading to rupture and an electrical short circuit. In mechanical devices, the definition of overstress will depend upon the component service requirements and behavior of the material. We can generally classify these as excessive elastic deformation, plastic deformation and overstress fracture, as defined by the primary strength parameter we must consider for the component.

We must design the strength of components to assure that we meet the load conditions for a reasonable level of risk. The approach often taken for mechanical parts and components is to apply the concept of safety factors. We estimate the load and then apply a safety factor. Our safety factor is often based upon accumulated design and service experience. We rely on it to account for the potential variations in load and strength when designing the component. Similarly, we may derate electronic components for given conditions of applied loads, where the loads may be temperature and voltage, constraining the system to operate well below specified limits of the components. In these conventional approaches, we do not explicitly consider the variations in load or strength. An alternative approach is to utilize a probabilistic model. We then design the component, explicitly considering the probability distribution functions of the applied or demanded load and the available strength. This is known as a load-strength interference model.In this chapter we focus on overstress failures. We examine the mechanisms, the sources and effects of variations in strength. From this perspective, the load-strength interference approach to modeling the reliability of a component, based upon knowledge of load and strength probability distribution functions, is developed and applied to design of components. We can also understand design for quality issues in the context of this model. Finally, we will leave this chapter with a greater understanding of overstress.

# 4.1 Overstress Failure Mechanisms

As we discussed in Chapter 1, we can think of the applied loads to a system as an environmental load or an operational load. The environmental loads may include absolute temperature, temperature range and cyclic temperature changes, humidity levels or ambient pressure differences. Operational loads can include external forces applied to a structure or voltage and current applied to an electronic component. The strength is the ability of the component to resist the loads applied to the system, as defined by corresponding materials properties of the component, which respond to the applied load. As we have discussed, overstress is the event the demanded load on a component exceeds the available strength.

### 4.1.1 Electrical Overstress Mechanisms

Lets examine one of the fundamental structures used in electronic components. As we see in Figure 4.1, a voltage applied across a dielectric represents a simple capacitor or perhaps the gate structure on a CMOS integrated circuit. The dimensions of these structures are very different, but the mechanics of failure is similar. The voltage is the load which induces an electric field in the dielectric. This electric field, then, represents the stress in the simple component shown, with electric field lines drawn in the dielectric.

The field in the material, $D$, is a function of the applied eternal field, $E$. From electrostatics, we see that:

$$
D=\varepsilon E
$$

where $\varepsilon$ is the dielectric constant of the material. For our simple geometry, $E \approx \frac{V}{h}$ where $h$ is the spacing between conductors. Then, we see that the field induced in a dielectric, when it is inserted between the plates is:

$$
D=\varepsilon \frac{V}{h}
$$

The expression above shows that, as we expect, the stress is related to the material properties, $\varepsilon$, and the geometry of the structure, $h$.

Figure 4.1 Simple dielectric structure that is the building block of many electronic devices, including capacitors and CMOS gate structures in integrated circuits.Failure by overstress occurs when the available dielectric strength, or maximum sustainable field in the material, is exceeded by the stresses demanded, when a voltage is applied to the structure.

$$
D_{\text {Demand }}>D_{\text {Available }}
$$

Equation 4.3 expresses the condition of failure in terms of stress. We can also express failure in terms of load, which in design, may be more useful. In addition, we note that tests are conducted to determine the eternally applied field at the breakdown point of a material, $E_{B}$. In this case, we express failure as occuring when $V_{\text {Demand }}>V_{B}$ or this may be expressed as:

$$
V_{\text {Demand }}>E_{B} \cdot h
$$

When 4.4 is satisfied, electrons will be encouraged to cross the dielectric and current will be induced to flow in the dielectric. This usually occurs in a localized region, where the field is concentrated by the presence of a manufacturing defect or material flaw. As an example, process variations may result in thickness variations; thinner regions will sustain a greater field. As the current builds, the localized temperature rises. The dielectric subsequently ruptures, with increasing current flow and localized melting, burning or charing of the dielectric. A short circuit results in the component and it no longer performs its intended function.

Excessive voltages that can induce overstress failure can come from several sources. For example, human being can build up a large electrostatic field by walking across a carpet. The voltage can easily exceed 10,000 volts. This can be discharged into a system input, resulting in a large field induced in dielectrics used in microcircuit components, leading to short circuits. This is called electrostatic discharge failure or simply ESD. It is of great concern in the manufacturing environment when people come into direct contact with sensitive components. In addition, large transients can be induced into the components of a system through electromagnetic interference, EMI, or even a lightening event. Errors in testing the system can also be a cause of an unintended overstress event. Figures 4.2 a and 4.2 b show a dielectric breakdown site in a simple high voltage capacitor, that occurred due to test error.

If we examine the design of a dielectric component for a moment, we can see that we will select a material and design the thickness so that the component meets our electrical performance requirements. We are left with a risk of failure due to overstress by a transient voltage or perhaps an ESD event. This contributes to the Region II or useful life hazard rate of our component and in turn effects the reliability and frequency of repair our system experiences. Of course, we have the option of controlling to some extent the operational loads that might be applied to our system. In this case, we can filter out some range of large transient voltages, using a filtering circuit or a surge protector. We can also train our assembly people in proper handling and use conductive materials around us to prevent ESD events.

Another form of electrical overstress is excessive current. Once again, we can see that a conductor has a maximum capacity to endure the application of current, or maximum available current density. In this case the applied current, $I$, is related to the current density, $j$, simply by:

$$
j=\frac{I}{A}
$$

where $A$ is the cross sectional area of the conductor. Failure occurs when the demanded current density exceeds the current carrying capacity of the conductor, $j_{\text {Demand }}>j_{\text {Available }}$. Localized heating followed by melting of the conductor generally results.

Figure 4.2 a Optical photomacrograph of an overstress site in a ceramic capacitor, resulting in localized dielectric breakdown. Note the discoloration and localized melting due to current flow in the region. b SEM micrograph showing localized melting of the dielectric that is typical of dielectric breakdown.

The overstress of a tungsten lightbulb filament is shown in Figure 4.3. The melting and formation of a metal ball is characteristic of excessive current failures. More on electronic component overstress, as well as various wear out mechanisms, is presented in Chapter 8.

Figure 4.3 SEM micrograph of a tungsten light bulb filament. (Courtesy H. J. Lee, Daewoo Electronics, Ltd.)# 4.1.2 Mechanical Overstress

Mechanical overstress failures result when the demanded load in service, such as an applied eternal force, exceeds the available strength of a mechanical component. As an example, a metal fastener can fail due to an excessive torque applied during assembly. In general, we can define three types of mechanical overstress in terms of the required strength parameter of a component. A component may fail from excessive elastic deformation, without yielding. A component may fail as a result of plastic deformation or by fracture.

Lets examine the stress stain curve of some typical materials to understand these forms of overstress. The stress strain curves are shown in Figure 4.4. Now, let us consider a simple component design. We will refer to a typical connecting rod structure shown in Figure 4.5, which is axially loaded, to examine the types of mechanical overstress failures that may occur.

Lets review our knowledge of basic mechanics of materials for the simple structure in our example. If we apply a load $P$ to the structure, it will change in length by the amount $\Delta L$. The stress and corresponding strain developed are simply:

$$
\sigma=\frac{P}{A} \text { and } \varepsilon=\frac{\Delta L}{L_{o}}
$$

If the stresses generated by the application of load P are below the yield strength, $\sigma_{y}$ shown on the stress strain curve, then the material will change back to the original length $\mathrm{L}_{o}$, when the load is released. This is elastic deformation.

Most materials are used below their yield strength in structural applications and will experience only elastic deformations. However, if the elastic deformation is greater than desirable,

Strain, $\varepsilon$
Figure 4.4 Engineering stress-strain curves for ductile and brittle materials.

Figure 4.5 A simple axially loaded bar or connecting rod of circular cross section.
then we may experience failure. In this case, we say that component does not have adequate stiffness. As an example, consider two shafts with mating gears, if one shaft undergoes excessive elastic deformation under the demanded load, then the gears may bind. Hence, a component must be designed to ensure that elastic deformations are not excessive.

We must also recall that more complex stresses will occur with more complex geometry and various loading conditions, such as bending and torsion. However, all stress components can be reduced to the principal stresses and combined into a single equivalent stress in accordance with basic principles of mechanics. The reader may refer to Higdon et. al. (1976) for discussions of elementary mechanics. However, we will use simple components and axial loading to demonstrate the concepts of this chapter, as well as later chapters.

Lets return to our simple component shown in Figure 4.5. In the event the change in length under the demanded load $P$, exceeds the yield strength, the component will experience a permanent change in length. When the load is released, only the elastic portion of the deformation is recovered. The resulting permanent change in length is the plastic deformation. Plastic deformation is undesirable in most components. For another simple example, considers a bolt. The threads of a bolt, or any other threaded fastener, are not likely to remain functional, if the bolt undergoes any appreciable permanent axial deformation as the result of overstress during installation of the bolt.

When a material deforms plastically so that the stresses exceed the ultimate tensile strength, $\sigma_{u}$, our simple component will began to experience necking. In this case, deformation in the axial direction becomes so substantial, that deformation will also occur in a plane perpendicular to the applied axial load. The state of stresses in this region are no longer simply described by the axial stress.

Eventually, after further deformation, the component will fracture or separate into two pieces. The failure of a ductile metal component by fracture is summarized in Figure 4.6.

If a component is manufactured from a less ductile material, we can of course expect that the necking and plastic deformation will be significantly less. Ceramics for example are brittle and will not exhibit a significant amount of deformation prior to fracture. Hence, the strength of ceramic materials is described in terms of their ultimate strength or fracture strength.

Figure 4.6 Process of ductile overstress fracture in a simple axially loaded component.

In some cases, defective manufacturing processes will result in unexpected brittle failure in metals. The light bulb filament in Figure 4.7 is an example. Note that there is no necking or evidence of plastic deformation.

Figure 4.7 Overstress failure of a light bulb filament caused by mechanical shock to the component. In this case, the lack of any necking or evidence of plastic deformation indicates defective material.The fracture surface characteristics can tell us a significant amount about the behavior of a material in a failed component. As we mentioned in Chapter 1, failure analysis is an important aspect of reliability assessment. Fractography is the failure analysis process dealing with documenting and interpreting the information that a fracture surface provides. As an example, we can view Figure 4.8 a and 4.8 b . These photographs are high magnification views of overstress fracture surfaces. Figure 4.8 a is what we expect to see in a ductile overstress fracture. Figure 4.8 b is also an overstress failure. However, as we can see the fracture surface clearly exhibits a a different fracture pattern. The grains of the alloy are clearly visible indicating intergranular fracture. Look again at Figure 4.7. We can also see this is an intergranular fracture.

Intergranular fracture occurs only under special circumstances. It is generally indicative of poor manufacturing due to improper materials processing, plating or heat treatment. Clearly failure by overstress due to excessive loads would necessitate different corrective action then overstress failure due to embrittlement and reduced strength from poor component manufacturing. Proper interpretation of the overstress conditions along with failure analysis is essential to arriving at the right conclusion about an overstress event.

We also cannot forget the combined effects of mechanical and environmental loading conditions on the potential for mechanical overstress. Polymers in particular will exhibit sensitivities to temperature. Polymers may also be much less linear in their elastic deformation than a metal. Examine Figure 4.9. The strength properties of the material shown vary significantly over temperature. As depicted, at lower temperatures the material is less ductile. Less total strain occurs before the onset of appreciable permanent deformation, then at

Figure 4.8 a Ductile overstress fracture of a metal component. b Brittle intergranular fracture in steel component, indicating defective materials processing.

Figure 4.9 Deformation of a polymer at two different temperatures.
higher temperatures. If the load is a fixed deformation, then the material may respond favourably at high temperature, but may fail at the lower temperature.

One of the most infamous failures of this nature is the Challenger Disaster. In this case, the stress-strain behavior of the elastomer O-ring seal designed to prevent the hot gasses from escaping the rocket casing, did not respond as anticipated at the colder than normal conditions at Kennedy Space Center, on that fateful day. As a result, hot gases blew past the O-ring, eventually causing the destruction of the entire spacecraft (NASA 1986).

# 4.2 Load - Strength Interference

As we have stated, the failure of a component will occur when the applied or demanded load exceeds the available strength. In general we can write this condition as:

$$
\mathrm{L}_{\text {Demand }}>\mathrm{S}_{\text {Demand }}
$$

where $\mathrm{L}_{\text {Demand }}$ represents load and $\mathrm{S}_{\text {Available }}$ is the strength. Loads may be operational, such as voltage, current or external forces or they may be environmental. These may include: temperature, temperature change or humidity levels. The strength of a component is defined by physical dimensions and materials properties that are responsive to the loading.

It should be apparent that there may be significant uncertainty in the load and the strength. As an example of uncertainty in loading, consider the possible deflection of a suspension spring in an automobile. It will deflect according to the surface roughness and objects encountered on the roadway during operation of the vehicle. We may also think of the wind loads buffeting an aircraft wing or the amplitude of an earthquake event. In an even simpler case, the force applied to the rungs of a ladder will be in response to the the variation in the weights of the users. In design, we may try to anticipate the worst case load conditions and apply them accordingly.

Strength also has associated uncertainty. In particular, materials properties have significant associated variation. We can examine the plots of percent failure versus strength for two ceramics as shown in Figure 4.10. The range of fracture strength in bending is considerable for the two materials. In addition, both materials behave differently, as we see by the variation in slope of the two curves. Hence, we see it is important to be fully aware of the effects of introducing new materials technology into systems.

Even familiar materials may exhibit considerable variation. Table 4.1 illustrates the ranges of tensile properties for a common 1035 steel alloy. In this case, a large number of manufacturing runs or heats of hot finished steel bars were tested for yield strength, ultimate tensile strength and elongation at fracture.

Figure 4.10 Comparison of the Weibull probability plots of the strength of two different ceramics. The addition of TiC to alumina may be considered a technology improvement. (Adapted from Saito 1985)

Table 4.1 Variations in Properties of 1035 Steel Bars (Carter 1986)

| Property                         | Minimum | Mean | Maximum |
| :------------------------------- | :-----: | :--: | :-----: |
| Yield Strength (Kpsi)            |   40    |  49  |   61    |
| Ultimate Tensile Strength (Kpsi) |   75    |  87  |   95    |

The reader should now be able visualize that the demanded load, $\mathrm{L}_{\text {Demand }}$ and available strength $\mathrm{S}_{\text {Available }}$ in our equation describing overstress failure are random variables. A variety of $p d f s$ may describe $\mathrm{L}_{\text {Demand }}$ or $\mathrm{S}_{\text {Available }}$. However, it is easy to imagine a strength parameter fitting a Weibull distribution and a load parameter fitting a Normal distribution. We can plot these two distributions as shown in Figure 4. 11. The two distribution may overlap or interfere, as shown. This overlapping region represents our risk of overstress failure.

# 4.2.1 Overstress Reliability Models

Lets examine the interference region and evaluate the general expression for the reliability of a component. The pdf of $\mathrm{L}_{\text {Demand }}$ can take any appropriate functional form $f_{L}(s)$ and $\mathrm{S}_{\text {Available }}$ can take any functional form $f_{S}(s)$. Of course, the two distributions must share a common set of units on the ordinate axis. For example, the units for an applied load, where the load is an external force, must be in Newtons.

The region of overlap is our area of interest. Now, consider a common value between the two distributions, $s_{o}$, which falls in this area, as we see in Figure 4.11. In analysis of the interference region, first, consider the $p d f$ of the strength, $f_{S}(s)$, for a parameter $s$. Then, the probability that the available strength of a component is greater than $s_{o}$ is expressed by the following integral:

$$
\operatorname{Pr}\left(S_{\text {Avail }}>s_{o}\right)=\int_{s_{o}}^{\infty} f_{s}(s) d S
$$

Figure 4.11 Load and strength pdfs plotted on a common set of axes. The overlap region, or region of interference between the two pdfs, defines the risk of overstress failure.

Now, turning our attention to the load distribution, the probability that the value $s_{o}$ lies within a small region $d L$ under the load distribution is simply the area defined by $f_{L}\left(s_{o}\right) d L$. Assuming these two probabilities are independent, we can say that the probability that the strength is greater than the value $s_{o}$, and falls within $d L$, is the product of the probabilities of the two events. We see that:

$$
f_{L}\left(s_{o}\right) d L \int_{s_{o}}^{\infty} f_{s}(s) d S
$$

Now considering all values of the demanded load, we can see that the reliability in consideration of load and strength, as random variables is:

$$
R=\int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} f_{L}(L)\left[\int_{S}^{\infty} f_{s}(S) d S\right] d L
$$

The probability of failure is $F=1-R$ and can be expressed as:

$$
F=1-R=\int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} F_{s}(s) \bullet f_{L}(s) d s
$$

where $F_{s}(s)$ is the cumulative distribution function (cdf) of available component strength for values of parameter $s$ and $f_{L}(s)$ is the pdf of the demanded load distribution, evaluated for parameter $s$. The resulting function is evaluated by integrating over all values of parameter $s$.

Our two distributions in Figure 4.11 can also be plotted in terms of component stress, developed under an applied load and the strength of the material from which the component is manufactured. In this case, common units for stresses under an eternally applied force, would be $\mathrm{N} / \mathrm{m}^{2}$. This approach is taken by many other texts discussing this subject.

We can immediately see that the evaluation of the integrals above is not an easy task for the complex forms of the various pdfs we may encounter. For the case of a normally distributed demanded load and a Weibull distributed available strength, Kapur and Lamberson (1977) evaluated the probability of failure as:$$
1-\Phi\left(\frac{\gamma*{s}-\bar{L}}{\sigma*{L}}\right)-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2 \pi}}\left(\frac{\eta*{s}}{\sigma*{L}}\right) \int*{-\infty}^{+\infty} \exp \left[-y^{\beta*{s}}-\frac{1}{2}\left\{\left(\frac{\eta*{s}}{\sigma*{L}}\right) y+\frac{\gamma*{s}-\bar{L}}{\sigma*{L}}\right\}^{2}\right] d y

$$

where $y$ is a substitution variable and:


$$

y=\frac{L-\gamma*{s}}{\eta*{s}} \text { and } d y=\frac{d L}{\eta\_{s}}

$$

The parameters of the normally distributed demanded load are the mean load, $\bar{L}$ and standard deviation of the load $\sigma_{L}$. The parameters of the Weibull distributed available strength are $\beta_{s}, \eta_{s}$ and $\gamma_{s}$; these are the shape parameter, scale parameter and location parameter, respectively, for the three parameter Weibull distribution. $\beta_{s}$ is sometimes referred to as the Weibull Modulus, particularly in relating the Weibull distribution to strength of materials.

The integral above cannot be solved in closed form, but may be solved by numerical integration or by the aid of the tables published by Kapur and Lamberson (1977). It is the contention of the author, that we can make good use of low-cost computing power at our disposal to facilitate the method of load-strength interference for analysis, by using numerical techniques.

# 4.2.2 Safety Margin and Loading Roughness

Let's examine Figure 4.11 and define two simple parameters that describe the relationship between the interfering distributions. There is obviously a difference between the means, $\bar{S}-\bar{L}$. But we can see by inspection that the variances of the distributions are also of significant influence on the region of interference. In consideration, we can define the Safety Margin as:


$$

S M=\frac{\bar{S}-\bar{L}}{\sqrt{\sigma*{S}^{2}+\sigma*{L}^{2}}}

$$

where $\sigma_{S}$ and $\sigma_{L}$ are the standard deviations of the available strength distribution and demanded load distributions, respectively. Do not confuse the use of $\sigma$ for mechanical stress in a component.

The demanded load standard deviation is a key parameter. We must deal with the demanded load and its variance to select components or design the dimensions of components used in systems and products. Hence, we define the Loading Roughness in terms of the standard deviation of the demanded load, $\sigma_{L}$, as:


$$

L R=\frac{\sigma*{L}}{\sqrt{\sigma*{S}^{2}+\sigma\_{L}^{2}}}

$$

In terms of these two parameters, we can see that a high loading roughness and small safety margin are quite undesirable. The effects of Safety Margin and Loading Roughness are shown in Figures 4.12a and 4.12b. In the first case, a significant risk of component failure exists, where the strength is defined by the distribution $f_{S}(s)$. A large $S M$ and low degree of $L R$ is desirable. However, the $L R$ is may not necessarily be something we can control. Rather, we are often faced with the challenge of properly anticipating it and designing accordingly.

In Figure 4.12b, there is no overlap in the two distributions. In this case, the component can be said to be intrinsically reliable.

Figure 4.12a Undesirable condition of low safety margin and high loading roughness. b Desirable condition of high safety margin and low loading roughness.

# 4.2.3 Normally Distributed Demanded Load and Normally Distributed Available Strength

In the special case where both the demanded load and available strength of the component are both normally distributed, we can easily show that the reliability of the component can be expressed as:


$$

R=\Phi[S M]=\Phi\left[\frac{\bar{S}-\bar{L}}{\sqrt[2]{\sigma*{S}^{2}+\sigma*{L}^{2}}}\right]

$$

As we can recall from Chapter 3, the function $\Phi(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function of the Standard Normal Distribution. Hence, in this simple case, we can calculate the SM and estimate the reliability from the Standard Normal Distribution Tables. While this is a useful exercise to demonstrate the concept of Load - Strength Interference, the author contends this is an unlikely combination of load and strength, since strength of materials is more likely to fit a Weibull distribution. Consequently, in practice, our simple model in Equation 4.16 must be used with caution. Lets now look at an example in the application of load strength interference.

Example 4.1. An applications engineer is tasked with approving or qualifying a special high voltage capacitor for a switching circuit. Three manufacturers provide this device in the desired configuration and capacitance, at different costs. The nominal rated voltage is 1000 V and the design load is 850 V . A primary concern is voltage overstress failure. How should she proceed?

One solution may be to sample each manufacturers product, conduct an accelerated test and evaluate the reliability of each manufacturer. The engineer samples 20 devices from each manufacturer and measures the breakdown voltage, $V_{B}$. She finds by plotting, that the breakdown voltage is normally distributed. In addition, she cross sections several devices from each manufacturer to measure the thickness of the dielectric and finds the following data in Table 4.2.

In order evaluate the reliability, however, she must know something about the loading roughness. She finds the load may be normally distributed with a standard deviation of 150 V. She makes the following calculations and compares them to part cost, using our simple load strength model in Equation 4.16. The results are shown in Table 4.3.Table 4.2 Initial Test Results- High Voltage Capacitor Example

| Manufacturer | $\boldsymbol{V}_{\boldsymbol{B}}$ <br> (Volts) | $\sigma_{V B}$ <br> (Volts) | $\boldsymbol{h}$ <br> $(\mathbf{m m})$ | $\boldsymbol{\sigma}_{\boldsymbol{h}}$ <br> $(\mathbf{m m})$ |
| :-- | :-- | :-- | :-- | :-- |
| $A$ | 1550 | 110 | 0.349 | 0.010 |
| $B$ | 1568 | 114 | 0.358 | 0.011 |
| $C$ | 1505 | 240 | 0.335 | 0.027 |

Table 4.3 Estimated Reliability for a Single Load Application High Voltage Capacitor

| Manufacturer | SM | $\boldsymbol{R}$ | Part Cost <br> $(\mathbf{S})$ |
| :-- | :-- | :-- | :-- |
| $A$ | 3.76 | 0.99991 | 0.73 |
| $B$ | 3.81 | 0.99993 | 0.76 |

Manufacturer $A$ and $B$ have similar reliability, while $C$ may present a significantly higher risk. We may interpret the results to show that, for C's parts, about 1 unit out of 100 deployed units may be expected to experience failure, due to the high voltage capacitor, on the application of the first load. Hence, the engineer's decision was to exclude manufacturer $C$ from passing the qualification and being used in the design, even though the part price was $5-10 \%$ less.

This example illustrates a few important concepts. Lets look a little more closely at the cause of the differences in reliability. The available strength, $\mathrm{S}_{\text {Available }}=\mathrm{V}_{B}$, is a function of the dielectric strength and thickness. Lets recall our model of the dielectric strength from equation 4.4. In the case of the dielectric component, we see that:


$$

V*{B}=E*{B} h

$$

Hence the strength is related to the materials properties and the thickness, $h$, of the dielectric.
If we examine part strength data, we see that Manufacturer $C$ produces a part with an average $V_{B}$ that is about $5 \%$ less than $A$ or $B$. This correlates to a lower dielectric thickness for C's parts. More importantly, however, the standard deviation of the strength is more that twice $A$ or $B$. This also correlates to thickness data; the standard deviation of the thickness, $\sigma_{h}$, for Manufacturer $C$ is also a factor of two greater than $A$ or $B$. As we see from our model of the strength, we can expect thickness variation to significantly effect our strength variation and, hence, the reliability. The control of the thickness variation is a quality issue related directly to control of manufacturing processes for this part and significantly effects the available strength of the component.

For other than the Normal distribution, the solutions may not be so easy, as we must resort to numerical methods for analysis. However, O'Connor (1991) presents a normal approximation of the Weibull distribution for the tail of the distribution. Consider the tail region between 0.01 and 0.10 of the CDF of a Weibull distributed strength. We can approximate the lower tail region of the strength distribution, using a normal distribution that coincides with these two points. The estimated normal equivalent will have the following parameters:


$$

\sigma*{s}^{\prime}=1.3 \eta*{s} \text { and } \mu*{s}^{\prime}=\gamma*{s}+0.9 \eta*{s}
$$where $\sigma^{\prime}{ }*{x}$ and $\mu^{\prime}{ }_{x}$ are the standard deviation and mean of the equivalent normal distribution for a three parameter Weibull strength distribution, with a characteristic strength, $\eta_{x}$, and a minimum strength, $\gamma_{x}$. Using this estimate we can apply equation 4.16 to a variety of problems to demonstrate the load-strength interference approach.

Example 4.2. Lets again examine Figure 4.13. Assume we will design a ceramic component subject to bending loads. The configuration is a simple cantilever, as shown. The demanded load P , is normally distributed and develops a mean stress of $150 \mathrm{MN} / \mathrm{m}^{2}$ with a standard deviation of $25 \mathrm{MN} / \mathrm{m}^{2}$. The distributed stress accounts for variations in the final component dimensions. We may select conventional $\mathrm{Al}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{3}$ with an average bending strength of $440 \mathrm{MN} / \mathrm{m}^{2}$ or we can select an advanced ceramic alloyed with $30 \%$ TiC. The advanced material has an average strength of $670 \mathrm{MN} / \mathrm{m}^{2}$. Compare the apparent safety factors and reliabilities for the two materials.-

Figure 4.10 is a two parameter Weibull probability plot for the strength of the two materials we are interested in. From the plot we can determine the characteristic strength of each material at the probability of failure of $63 \%$.

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \eta_{A l_{2} \mathrm{O}_{3}}=450 \mathrm{MN} / \mathrm{m}^{2} \\
& \eta_{A l_{2} \mathrm{O}_{3}+T i C}=725 \mathrm{MN} / \mathrm{m}^{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

The plots show that the data apparently fit the two parameter Weibull and we will let $\gamma_{x} \rightarrow 0$ for both materials. Now apply Equation 4.18 and determine the equivalent normal distribution parameters for the two materials.

Next, using component stress and materials strength, with the appropriate units of $\mathrm{MN} / \mathrm{m}^{2}$, we can then apply equation 4.16 .

Finally, the apparent safety factor is:

$$
S F=\frac{\text { Reported Average Material Strength }}{\text { Average Max Stress }}
$$

The results of our calculations are shown in Table 4.4.
We have made several assumptions to complete this example. With this mind, we can see some interesting results. The advanced ceramic material, $\mathrm{Al}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{3}+\mathrm{TiC}$, does provide an increase in reliability of the component. However, the increase may not be as significant as we expect from

Figure 4.13 Simple cantilever component to be made from ceramic.Table 4.4 Data and Results of Calculations for a Ceramic Component Design

|                                                                                                      | $\mathrm{Al}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{3}$ | $\mathrm{Al}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{3}+\mathrm{TiC}$ |
| :--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | :------------------------------: | :-------------------------------------------: |
| Reported Average Strength $\left(\mathrm{MN} / \mathrm{m}^{2}\right)$                                |               440                |                      670                      |
| Weibull Characteristic Strength, $\mathrm{n}_{\mathrm{c}}\left(\mathrm{MN} / \mathrm{m}^{2}\right)$  |               450                |                      725                      |
| Equivalent Normal Mean Strength, $\mu^{\prime}\left(\mathrm{MN} / \mathrm{m}^{2}\right)$             |               405                |                      652                      |
