observing the difference in the apparent safety factors. The advanced ceramic shows an apparent safety factor that is 1.5 times greater than the conventional ceramic. This also shows the risk of relying on safety factors, particularly for materials like ceramic. This example also illustrates the risk of relying on safety factors where we are introducing new materials technology. In the example shown, the final choice of material must consider the cost trade off between the materials and the risk of system failure from component overstress.

# 4.2.4 Safety Factors and Derating

The example above illustrated some of the problems with relying on safety factors in design. Safety factors have been widely applied in many industries. The concept works when we have significant experience with the materials commonly used for components in our systems and when we can anticipate the worst case loading conditions. Common steel alloys for example are well characterized materials and their use includes a wide variety of application.

The Safety Factor may be defined as the ratio of available component strength to the demanded load:

$$
S F=\frac{S_{\text {Available }}}{L_{\text {Demand }}}
$$

In general, we would anticipate the worst case conditions and compare our safety factor to our desirable design margin. An acceptable margin or value for SF is of course based upon experience with the product and components under consideration.

During component design, a fixed level of the safety factor is used to reduce the allowable stress developed in a component, which effectively increases the component strength. The safety factor, SF , is then applied as:

$$
\sigma_{\text {Allowable }}=\frac{\sigma}{S F}
$$

where $\sigma$ is the material strength, such as yield strength for a metal component or ultimate strength for a ceramic material, and $\sigma_{\text {Allowable }}$ is the allowable stress that can developed in the component under the demanded load. A typical safety factor used for a steel shaft in an industrial electric motor design, for example, may be 1.5 or 2 .

As Smith (1976) indicated, anticipating the maximum load and applying a fixed SF based upon experience with the materials being considered, generally lead to conservative designs. However, when there is little experience with the materials, such as in the case of introducing new technology, the safety factor may not assure a good design. The same concept applies tothe introduction of new manufacturing methods. New technologies require adequate characterization of the uncertainties in the strength of components and variations in the strength of the materials.

A safety factor contains no information about the actual risk or probability of failure. Two components with the same safety factor could have very different reliabilities. As an example, the same steel part could be supplied by two different manufacturers with different heat treatment operations. As equation 4.16 would predict, the manufacturer with stricter process control and therefore less variation in the strength, would produce a more reliable component.

Derating in electronic components is equivalent to the safety factor in mechanical design. In this case, a selected component is used below its rated load level by controlling the design of the system, as to effect the loads on the components, or by selecting components with higher than the required rating. Hence, a parameter we use to select components for a design can be derated as follows:

$$
P_{\text {Allowable }}=D R F \bullet P_{\text {Rated }}
$$

where $P_{\text {Allowable }}$ is a specific component parameter of interest, such as operating voltage, $D R F$ is derating factor and $P_{\text {Rated }}$ is the supplied value of the parameter. Capacitors for example may be derated for applied voltage by a factor of 0.8 for an industrial application or by as much as 0.5 for a spacecraft application. Semiconductors may be constrained to operate at junction temperature of $80^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ or $100^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$, when they are rated to operate at $125^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$. Derating may reduce the potential for overstress and may also increase life, if the wear out mechanisms of the device are sensitive to the derated parameters.

Once again, $D R F$ values are generally selected by experience with components in a specific application. However, as technologies change, rules to select a $D R F$ for a component may no longer be applicable. Derating may be over conservative or may not provide the anticipated increase in design margin even though they will significantly affect the system design. As an example, temperature reduction through active cooling systems to control junction temperature, can impart significant costs. In general, $D R F$ s effectively suffer from the same problems as the safety factor approach to mechanical design.

# 4.2.5 Multiple Load Reliability

Equations 4.10 and 4.11 were derived for a single load application. In the event we have multiple load applications, we must modify our integral as follows:

$$
R=\int_{0}^{\infty} f_{L}(S)\left[\int_{0}^{2} f_{L}(L) d L\right]^{n} d S
$$

where $n$ represents the number of loading applications on the component. Equation 4.18 cannot be solved in closed form, but can be integrated using numerical methods, given functions for the available strength $p d f$ and demanded load $p d f$.

Lets reconsider our case of a normally distributed demanded load and a normally distributed available strength. We can plot the solution of equation 4.18, as shown in Figure 4.14. Here the probability of failure per load application is plotted against the Safety Margin. Each contour represents a line of constant Loading Roughness. Figure 4. 14 is developed considering that values of $n$ are large. Similar plots can be seen in Carter (1986) and O'Connor (1991).

The reliability for $n$ load applications is then:

$$
R=\left(1-p_{f}\right)^{n}
$$

Equation 4.20 may be used to calculate reliability, given a value, $p_{f}$, extracted from Figure 4.14.

Figure 4.14 Safety Margin versus Probability of Failure per Load Application at different values of Loading Roughness. The demanded load and variable strength pdfs were taken as normally distributed

# 4.2.6 A Method Design for Intrinsic Reliability Against Overstress

If we examine our plot of probability of failure per load application versus the safety margin. We can see that there is a critical value, $S M_{C}$, at the point our loading roughness curve approaches a vertical asymptote. The region to the right of this value, defines the region of intrinsic reliability, where the probability of failure per load application, $p_{f}$, approaches zero. This is summarized in Figure 4.15. We can also see that immediately to the left of $S M_{C}$, that small changes in the Safety Margin result in large changes in the probability of failure, $p_{f}$. This region is not very practical for design purposes. However, if we can determine $S M_{C}$, at a given value of $L R$, we can design a component to be intrinsically reliable for multiple load applications, against overstress failure. Design curves can be generated for various distributions, as shown in Carter (1986) and O'Connor (1991). This concept can be illustrated clearly, using an example.

Example 4.3. Lets look again at a variation of our simple, axially loaded, connecting rod component. We will evaluate the thickness needed for a small component, of a square cross section, with a width, $w$, of 15 mm , as shown in Figure 4.16. The design is intended to be intrinsically reliable against overstress failure under a random load, $P$.
$P$ is normally distributed with a mean of 4.8 kN and standard deviation of 0.3 kN . The rod is to be designed against yielding by overstress. The yield strength of the material is Weibull distributed and has the following parameters:

Characteristic Strength: 416 MPa
Minimum Strength: 320 MPa
In order to demonstrate our design concept. Lets apply the normal approximation to the Weibull data and use Figure 4.14.

We initially estimate the equivalent normal distribution parameters for material strength, as the following:

Figure 4.15 Concept of Intrinsic Reliability for designing a component.

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \sigma_{s}^{\prime}=0.3 \eta=0.3(416 \times 106)=124.8 \times 10^{6} \mathrm{~N} / \mathrm{m}^{2} \\
& \mu_{s}^{\prime}=0.9 \eta_{s}+\gamma_{s}=0.9\left(46 \times 10^{6}\right)+120 \times 106=694.4 \times 10^{6} \mathrm{~N} / \mathrm{m}^{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we must estimate the strength of the connecting rod component and its standard deviation. We assume that variation is contained in the strength of materials variation and solve for $t_{\text {min }}$

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \bar{S}=w t_{\min } \cdot \mu_{s}^{\prime}=\left(15 \times 10^{-3}\right) 694.4 \times 10^{6} t_{\min }=10416 \times 10^{3} t_{\min } N \\
& \sigma_{s}=w t_{\min } \cdot \sigma_{s}^{\prime}=\left(15 \times 10^{-3}\right) 124.8 \times 10^{6} t_{\min }=1872 \times 10^{3} t_{\min } N
\end{aligned}
$$

Using equations 4.14 and 4.15 , we now solve for the $S M$ and $L R$ in terms of our design parameter $t_{\text {min }}$.

$$
\begin{aligned}
& S M=\frac{1872 \times 10^{3} t_{\min }-4800}{\left(1872 \times 10^{3} t_{\min }\right)^{2}+300^{2}} \\
& L R=\frac{300}{\left(1872 \times 10^{3} t_{\min }\right)^{2}+300^{2}}
\end{aligned}
$$

We can now calculate values of $L R$ and $S M$ for $t_{\text {min }}$. We determine if our value of $S M$, at a given $t_{\text {min }}$, is less than or greater than $S M_{C}$. All designs with $S M>S M_{C}$, as shown in Figure 4.15, are within the intrinsically reliable region. However, we select the smallest value of $t_{\text {min }}$ that provides an intrinsically reliable design, so as not to over design and incur unnecessary cost.Our calculations are summarized in the Table 4.5.

Table 4.5 Calculations for Example 4.3

| $t_{\min }(\mathrm{mm})$ | 1.0  | 1.3  | 1.5  | 1.9   | 3.0  |
| :----------------------- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :---- | :--- |
| $S M$                    | 2.96 | 3.56 | 3.83 | 4.20  | 4.70 |
| $L R$                    | 0.16 | 0.12 | 0.11 | 0.084 | 0.05 |

In plotting our results for $t_{\min }=1.0 \mathrm{~mm}$ on Figure 4.14, we can quickly see that at an $L R=$ $0.16, S M_{C} \approx 3.7$. Obviously, $S M<S M_{C}$ and this is not intrinsically reliable. At $t_{\min }=3.0 \mathrm{~mm}$, we are well within the intrinsic region, but over designed. At $1.3 \mathrm{~mm}, S M \approx S M_{c}$. So we can select a $t_{\text {min }}>1.3 \mathrm{~mm}$. Considering available sheet stock materials for manufacturing our component, we would likely select $t=1.5 \mathrm{~mm}$ and assign the appropriate tolerances. We would also want to assure the defined width is maintained as a minimum and that our design also posses adequate stiffness.

In summary, we have selected a design based on our approximation to a normal distribution and we have assumed all of the variation in component strength resulted from variation in materials. In regard to the later assumption, in practice, we would want to assure that our dimensions remain within the specified minimum values, given dimensional tolerances that are appropriate to the manufacturing processes.

# 4.3 Time Dependent Stress-Strength Reliability Models

If we examine, Equation 4.19, we can easily surmise that $n=f(t)$. Then, it follows that the hazard rate for our component, $h(t)$, is a function of $p_{f}$. But, we can expect for an intrinsically reliable component, designed against overstress, that in the useful life:

$$
\begin{aligned}
& h(t) \rightarrow 0 \\
& R(t) \rightarrow 1
\end{aligned}
$$

Figure 4.16 Connecting rod component for Example 4.3. The minimum thickness, $t$, for intrinsic reliability of the component must be selected for the design.This of course assumes that there is no degradation of the materials and no unaccounted for defects that may reduce the strength outside of the lower limits of our strength distribution. It also assumes we have fully anticipated the load distribution.

As we have seen in Chapter 3, when we apply the Poisson process, we derive a constant failure rate for overstress failures. We then can expect the reliability, $R(t)$, of a component to decline in accordance with the exponential distribution. That is:

$$
\begin{aligned}
& h(t) \rightarrow \lambda \\
& R(t)=e^{-\lambda t}
\end{aligned}
$$

Carter (1986) points out that in accordance with equation 4.19 , this occurs only in the limiting case where the loading roughness, $L R \rightarrow \infty$. Recalling our definition of loading roughness, $L R$ will become very large when the standard deviation of the load, $\sigma_{L}$, becomes very large or $\sigma_{L} \gg>\sigma_{S}$

In a practical sense, then, we see that equations 4.21 represents the upper bound reliability, that is possible in the design, if we undertake an intrinsic design process against overstress failure. Achieving intrinsic reliability in service depends on our ability to predict the loads during design. In practice, we are likely to incur uncertainty in characterizing the load distribution. As an example, consider the difficulties in developing a distribution for electrical overstress. Operational voltages may be well defined, but predicting ESD events and test errors may be difficult. Hence, in some cases, infinite loading roughness may represent practical service, and we will accumulate overstress failures according to a limiting value of $\lambda$, that is dependent upon frequency and magnitude of random loading events. This is of course why our definition of reliability includes the statement that it is the probability of success under defined conditions of service.

We may also ask, that if we can apply the load strength model to overstress, why can't we use such a model for wear out? The condition that failure occurs at time $t^{*}$ when:

$$
L_{\text {Demand }}>S_{\text {Available }}\left(t^{*}\right)
$$

is certainly true. However, to apply this condition, we must know how the wear out failure mechanism shifts the strength pdf over time. This is summarized in Figure 4.17. It may be far easier and useful to apply a damage model concept and utilize Monte Carlo simulation to generate a life distribution, as we discussed in Chapter 3. On the other hand, the model below is a useful construct to visualize the effects of component degradation.

Figure 4.17 Degradation in strength shifts the strength distribution with the onset of wear out.At time $t_{0}$, the component is intrinsically reliable. It would remain in that state, in the event there is no degradation of materials. However, as wear out processes become active, the distribution will shift to the left. At time $t^{*}$, we can see that there is sufficient degradation, so that the demanded load $p d f$, overlaps the available strength $p d f$ of the component. Thus at time $t^{*}$, there is considerable risk of failure.

# 4.4 Design for Quality

As we have seen from our example of overstress in capacitor dielectrics, manufacturing quality issues are directly related to product reliability. The distribution of the strength of a component depends upon the manufacturing processes that effect the geometry and the strength of the materials. Applications of statistical process control (SPC) to reduce variations in manufacturing processes is extremely important to achieving high reliability. As we can see from equation 4.14 , the safety margin of a design can be increased by reducing strength variations. In our simplest reliability model, the Normal Load Distribution and Normal Strength Distribution, the immediate benefit to reliability is apparent. In development, reductions in materials strength variation can be achieved with the application of SPC to processes effecting strength, such as alloying or heat treatment of mechanical components or deposition of dielectric films for microcircuits. In addition, as the variation in strength of a finished component also depends upon variation in geometric parameters, application of SPC to tighten geometric parameter variations can have a similar effect. Further discussions on SPC are beyond the scope of our discussion, but many references can be found on this subject.

In addition to ensuring the implementation of $S P C$, other actions to enhance the reliability of a design can be taken during design and development. In consideration of our loadstrength model, we can see in Figure 4.18, that truncation of the right tail of the load distribution or truncation of the lower or left tail of the strength distribution will reduce the potential for overlap and enhance the reliability.

Control of the load distribution may be somewhat difficult to envision. However, if we return to our pressure vessel example in Chapter 2, Section 2.5 .6 we can see that installing a relief valve is one way to ensure the load does not exceed a critical value. This in effect truncates the right tail of the load distribution for the pressure vessel. Another example, in an electrical product is to utilize a surge protector to cut-off large voltages. Finally, in some cases, it may be possible to install sensors of various types to sense loads including forces, pressures, voltages or temperatures. A sensor can then be used to trigger a shut-off circuit or to warn operators that human intervention is necessary.

In the case of strength, it may possible to eliminate the lower end of the strength distribution. If we consider a group of components, we may be able to effectively weed out weaker components through application of a single overstress load in a controlled test environment, as shown in Figure 4.18. Any weaker components failing the load application are rejected or discarded. This is the concept of proof testing of ceramic components or pressure vessels. In the case of electronic components, elevated voltages and temperatures are applied to burn-in new devices or environmental stress screening (ESS) is applied to assemblies, using thermal cycling. Devices or assemblies failing burn-in or ESS are discarded and those passing are utilized. Another approach is to inspect for variations in critical parameters and eliminate parts or components that do not pass the inspections. As an example, radiographic inspection may be specified for weldments.

It should be noted that screening tests, burn-in, inspection or ESS on finished products may become less effective as a product matures. This is particularly true in manufacturing where

Figure 4.18 Concepts in design for quality based on a Load-Strength interference model.

SPC is utilized in a program of continuous improvement to reduce variation. Hence, the effectiveness of screening specified in development must be re-evaluated later in a product's life cycle. Roettgering and Kyser (1999) present a methodology for this type of decision making.

# 4.5 Summary

This chapter initiated Part II of our book by beginning to develop and explain the mechanics of failure. In this chapter we have presented the concept of overstress failure for both mechanical and electronic component failures. We defined overstress as failures which occur when the demanded load exceeds the available strength of a component and the component strength has not degraded in time. This leads to the concept of Load-Strength interference models for evaluating or designing products or components, when we have knowledge of the strength and load probability distributions. In today's environment of low cost computational power, this method can be developed and may overcome the shortcomings of safety factors or derating in the application and development of new materials and technologies.

In addition, we have explored the relationship of the Load-Strength interference model to our time domain. If the loading roughness becomes infinite, we are likely to accumulate overstress failures according to the constant failure rate, as we discussed in Chapter 3. This is likely the case for such mechanisms as electrostatic discharge (ESD) failures in electronic devices.

Other related topics, such as design for quality have also been explained in the context of the Load-Strength interference model.

### 4.6 Do's and Don'ts in Design

Do seek to evaluate loading conditions and load probability distributions for products in the field. Do continuously evaluate new materials including strength parameter probability distributions. Do consider using load-strength interference models in design and for reliability assessment for overstress failures.Do apply the concept of intrinsic reliability when designing critical mechanical components against overstress failure.
Do adequate testing to qualify new components and materials against overstress failure.
Do implement preventive measures to reduce electrostatic discharge failures in electronic components.
Do consider the impact of the human contribution to the case of infinite loading roughness
Do carefully think through quality and reliability relationships during product development.
Do consider methods of truncating the load distribution in design for reliability enhancement, fuses and surge protectors in electronic circuits or load-sensors and shut-off switches and warning signals.
Do carefully evaluate the benefits of the specification of strength distribution control, such as proof testing, screening, burn-in or inspections.
Do widely implement statistical process controls.
Do remember lessons learned from overstress failures experienced in the past.
Do not indiscriminately apply safety factors or derating in new designs when new technologies in manufacturing or materials are employed.
Do not assume a safety factor provides a failure free situation.
Do not forget to do adequate failure analysis including fractographic examinations, when fractures are encountered.
Do not forget to evaluate effectiveness of screening and burn-in when technologies mature.
Do not forget that adequate stiffness may be more important than preventing yielding when designing the strength of a machine element or structure.
Do not forget to consider the environmental influences on materials strength parameters, especially when using polymers and elastomers.
