John W. Evans

In Chapter 4, we focussed on overstress. We presented the Load-Strength interference concept as a method to evaluate reliability and only briefly discussed the time regime as it related to this concept. We will now turn our attention to wear out, beginning with fatigue. Wear out failures result from degradation of component strength over time. In fatigue, this occurs by crack development followed by failure by fracture.

Fatigue includes a major class of wear out mechanisms occurring in both mechanical structures and mechanical elements of electronic systems. In fact, fatigue along with corrosion, often determine the useful life of a system. Fatigue may also govern the necessity for maintenance and inspection to prevent failure. Carter (1986) repeats an interesting assertion that $80 \%$ of all mechanical failures are fatigue related and $80 \%$ of electronic system failures are mechanical in nature. The author would modify this based on experience, since it seems to underplay the role of corrosion. However, the general assertion is correct in that fatigue and its interaction with aging phenomena is a major problem in achieving high reliability and integrity in systems and products.

Fatigue occurs when loading conditions change with time. This occurs in rotating machine elements, vibration environments and with changing temperature. Time dependent loading gives rise to crack initiation, growth and eventually failure of the component. The processes of crack initiation and growth represent degradation in the strength of the component. Final failure occurs when the loads can longer be endured by the component. Early fatigue failure, in the desired useful life of the component, must be prevented by good design. Reliability assessments cannot ignore the necessity of fatigue analysis. Characterization of any new materials for fatigue related properties is also essential.

In this chapter will examine the process of fatigue, fatigue models and their uncertainty and discuss the elements of fatigue testing. We will also examine the interaction of fatigue with aging phenomena including creep, grain growth and embrittlement.

### 5.1 The Mechanism of Fatigue

The American Society of Testing and Materials (ASTM) definition of fatigue states the essential elements of the fatigue process. The definition states in ASTM E-206:

Fatigue is the process of progressive localized permanent structural change occurring in a material subjected to conditions which produce fluctuating stresses and strains at some point or points and which may culminate in cracks or complete fracture after a sufficient number of fluctuations.The process described by the ASTM definition can be divided into three distinct regions of crack initiation, development and final failure, as shown in Figure 5.1. We will again refer to our simple axially loaded connecting rod component. In Stage I of the fatigue process, localized plastic deformation initiates the onset of failure. The initial damage usually occurs at the surface of the component. Near the surface, some grains of a polycrystalline metal are likely to be preferentially oriented to allow localized slip to take place under the application of an external load. As the load fluctuates over time, slip bands will slide in and out relative to each other, creating both micro-extrusions and micro-intrusions. Regions of intrusion may form v-grooves or micro-notches which serve as crack initiation sites. A crack will grow a very short distance, on the order of a few grain diameters under the application of the localized shear stresses. This process will be accelerated in the presence of stress concentrations and surface flaws. Hence, crack initiation is sensitive to surface finish conditions and manufacturing processes that affect the final finish for components.

In Stage II, the crack will begin to propagate in a direction normal to the tensile stresses developed in the component, under load. The crack will continue to grow in a stable manner under the fluctuating load. Each tensile load application will tend to propagate the crack one small step. At some point, the load will be too large for the reduced cross section of the component to bear. The crack will grow rapidly in an unstable manner. The component will then fail by fracture. This is stage III.

The processes of crack development, growth and final fracture will tend to leave distinctive features on the fracture surface. Knowledge of these features plays an important role in the confirmation of fatigue as the failure process and identification of root cause in failure analysis. If we examine once again the failed bolt we first saw in Chapter 1, we can see the typical features that often appear on fatigue fracture surfaces, as shown in Figure 5.2. Each of these features are summarized in Table 5.1.

Figure 5.1 Three stages of fatigue for a simple axial loaded component made from a ductile polycrystalline metal.

Figure 5.2 Fatigue failure exhibiting common fatigue fracture characteristics (Fuchs and Stephens 1980). (Courtesy of Münchener Rückversicherungs-Gesellschaft

Table 5.1 Summary of Macro-features Visible on Fracture Surfaces

| Crack Stage | Nomenclature        | Macro-Features | Description                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |
| :---------- | :------------------ | :------------- | :---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| I           | Crack Initiation    | Ratchet Marks  | Crack initiates due to localized plastic deformation at the <br> surface of the component. Crack develops under shear stress.                                                                                                                                                 |
| II          | Stable Crack Growth | Beach Marks    | Crack propagates under stable growth conditions along <br> plane perpendicular to stresses in the component. Crack <br> grows to point of failure. Crack will often grow by striation <br> formation in ductile materials or by microcleavage in less <br> ductile materials. |
| III         | Final Fracture      | Shear Lip      | Rapid crack growth occurs when component cannot endure <br> applied load, causing fracture or separation of the <br> component. Final fracture may occur by ductile modes.                                                                                                    |

As Table 5.1 shows, common fracture surface features are associated with the different stages of crack development. Crack initiation can occur at more than one point. However, initiated cracks will coalesce in stage II. The starting branches can give rise to ratchet marks near the origin, which are indicative of the multiple initiation sites. These features are often associated with high stress concentration. Beach marks, sometimes called clamshell markings, are the most distinct fatigue fracture surface characteristic; they may form during stable crack growth. They are generally indicative of the arrested crack growth, during changes in the applied load in service. Rubbing of the opposite fracture surfaces and oxidation also promote the formation of beach marks. In stage II or final fracture a shear lip may form. The shear lip is often more prominent in ductile metals and thinner sections and forms as a result of ductile overstress at the final failure.

Figure 5.3 shows the usefulness of macroscopic features in the process of failure analysis. The relative size of the final fracture region in comparison to the region of stable crack growth can reveal useful information about the load. In addition, we can see that the shape of fracture features, like beach marks, may reveal the role of designed-in notches in the process of crack development.

Figure 5.3 Diagrams useful for comparing fracture surface features to determine relative load and stress concentration effects. The cross hatched region represents the region of final fracture. (Courtesy of Society of Experimental Mechanics).

Crack growth in polycrystalline engineered metals can occur by several different mechanisms. We can determine the mechanisms of crack growth by microscopic examination of the fracture surface, usually at near 1000 X magnification. This requires a scanning electron microscope to effectively evaluate fracture surface features.

Generally, fatigue growth will occur by transgranular crack growth. There are three basic mechanisms of transgranular, stable fatigue crack growth. These include striation formation, microvoid coalescence and microcleavage. Striation formation is among the most common and is observed in metals ranging from solder to copper to steel. An example of striations is shown in the electron micrograph in Figure 5.4. It is characterized by lines across the grains which may be at different orientations in different grains. A single linear marking represents a single step of crack growth. Hence, determining the spacing of striations by high magnification electron microscopy can be useful in understanding the rate of crack growth.

Microcleavage is observed in high strength steels. Microcleavage is undesirable, as it is a relatively low energy absorbing process and is indicative of poor toughness and lower ductility. This process occurs by separation of crystallographic planes along the weakest planes of the crystal. On the other hand, microvoid coalescence is a ductile mechanism of growth. The process is described by the name. Void formation may initiate at several sites, which coalesce into a crack.

Identification of the crack growth mechanism is an important aspect of failure analysis. The mechanism of crack growth will confirm the failure process and may yield information about the condition of the material. Information from macroscopic and microscopic features can be combined to yield data about the loading conditions causing failure in components.

Figure 5.4 Striations in the fracture surface of a steel fastener.

# 5.2 Fatigue Loading

Fatigue arises when the loading conditions are time dependent or cyclic. Cyclic loading produces cyclic stresses in the component, which activate crack initiation and growth. Cyclic loading occurs under several different situations. They will occur in components when a system encounters externally induced vibration, such as in the suspension of an automobile or the fluctuations of a printed wiring board assembly during take-off and landing of an aircraft. Rotating components are also subject to cyclic loads, including bearings, shafts and gears. Cyclic loads also occur as a result of temperature changes during operation of systems. For example, semiconductor devices heat up and cool down with each on and off cycle of the system. Large mechanical stresses can also be induced by moisture absorption in polymers. Absorption and desorption of moisture can result in cyclic loading.

Let's examine a simple case of a constant amplitude loading. Fatigue is easily discussed in terms of the mechanical stresses induced in the component, as a result of one of the loading conditions we have previously described. Lets examine the simple case of a sinusoidal stress induced by a constant amplitude mechanical load, as shown in Figure 5.5.

Figure 5.5 shows some of the key quantities and nomenclature for fatigue and cyclic stresses. The stress range is $\Delta \sigma$ and the amplitude is $\sigma_{A}$. We can easily see that for the simple case of a constant amplitude:

$$
\sigma_{A}=\frac{\Delta \sigma}{2}=\frac{\sigma_{\max }-\sigma_{\min }}{2}
$$

The mean stress is $\sigma_{\text {mean }}$. When $\sigma_{\text {mean }}=0$, we have fully reversed loading and the stresses will include compressive stresses. Its important to note that crack growth will halt when the driving normal stress becomes compressive and the crack surfaces close together.

The stress ratio, $R$, is defined as:

$$
R=\frac{\sigma_{\min }}{\sigma_{\max }}
$$

Figure 5.5 Simple cyclic stress condition resulting from a constant amplitude load. The general nomenclature of cyclic fatigue stress is shown on the plot.

In the special case of fully reversed, constant amplitude loading, we see that:

$$
\sigma_{\max }=-\sigma_{\min } \text { and } R=-1
$$

Fatigue characterization is often conducted under these conditions on test samples. However, loading on actual components in the field may be significantly different. A complex load spectrum may look more like Figure 5.6.

In general, for reliability assessment, we test materials under simple loading spectra. Component loading conditions are then carefully evaluated and the stresses in the component are modelled. We then compare the stress conditions in the component to materials test data, to evaluate the life of the component. Components may also be tested to ensure their integrity. Fracture characteristics are also analyzed following tests.

In evaluating a complex loading spectra, we must define an additional term. A reversal occurs each time the direction of the load changes. For a simple cycle we define two reversals per cycle. Hence, the number of reversals to failure is twice the number of cycles to failure. This is a simple concept but important in trying to deal with complex spectra and modeling fatigue in real components.

Figure 5.6 A complex loading spectrum for a component.# 5.3 Fatigue Tests

There are several methods of executing fatigue tests for characterizing materials. ASTM standards define specimens and conditions for executing theses tests. Two common methods for which data are reported, include the rotating bending test and the axial fatigue test.

### 5.3.1 Test Methods

The rotating bending test is rather simple and involves applying a single direction load to a rotating specimen. This results in fully reversed bending loads, as the specimen rotates. The number of cycles to fracture the specimen is recorded. A simple test jig is shown schematically in Figure 5.7.

Axial tests usually involve more complex equipment. Hydraulic test equipment is used to apply an axial load to a specimen. This type of testing can be much more versatile. Mean stresses can be applied. In addition, twisting loads can be combined to evaluate multi-axial stresses. Load and deflection can be controlled. Failure can be defined as being a fraction of load reduction under a constant deflection.

Specimen configuration is an important issue in fatigue testing. Materials characterization is usually performed on specimens with a polished surface. Recall that fatigue crack initiation is associated with the surface condition. A polished surface is ideal and will not represent many components. The manufacturing processes used to fabricate components will significantly effect the surface condition. This results a reduction in fatigue life of the component in comparison to materials characterization test data.

Tests may also be conducted on components. Testing conducted at the component level, usually requires specialized equipment. Components may be significantly larger and complex in shape. Test equipment must be capable of applying a representative load. Component level testing can therefore be much more expensive then materials characterization tests performed on smaller standardized specimens.

### 5.3.2 Fatigue Test Data Analysis

Fatigue data will generally show significant variations, for a given test condition. The most uniform specimens may exhibit large variations in fatigue life. This indicates the importance of materials property variations and their influence on fatigue life. Testing of components

Figure 5.7 Diagram of a simple rotating bending test jig.will exhibit even larger variations in the fatigue life. This reflects the added influence of manufacturing process variation on the component fatigue life.

Variations in fatigue life are often described by the Weibull distribution. The number of cycles to failure are recorded for the samples. The data are then plotted on Weibull probability plots. Plotting techniques for test data are discussed in detail in Chapter 12. Fatigue data are sometimes represented by the lognormal distribution as well. The best fit distribution must be determined from a Goodness of Fit Test. Variation in fatigue data are shown in Figure 5.8 for a given load condition.

The Weibull distribution is appealing for fatigue, as it is an appropriate distribution to represent the probability of the weakest link failing. The weakest link in a materials test specimen, may be the point where we encounter the largest materials defect or where the grains of the polycrystalline metal are aligned favourably for slip processes to initiate a crack. Hence, we see that the Weibull distribution has a basis for utilization for fatigue analysis.

Albekis (1967) developed an alternative distribution for low probabilities of failure. Data have shown that the Weibull may be non-conservative for very low probabilities of failure (Fuchs and Stevens 1980). The selection of distributions for analysis must be carefully considered in anticipating probabilities of failure below about 0.1 .

Example 5.1 Fatigue tests were conducted on a solder alloy. The data were found to be Weibull distributed with the following parameters:

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \beta=1.6 \\
& \eta=1517 \text { cycles }
\end{aligned}
$$

where $\beta$ is the shape parameter and $\eta$ is the characteristic life of the test data. Determine the mean life and number of cycles to failure at a failure probability of 0.1 , under the test conditions.

As we recall from Chapter 2, the mean life can be calculated as follows:

$$
\mu=\eta \Gamma\left(1+\frac{1}{\beta}\right)
$$

where $\Gamma$ is the gamma function.

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \mu=1517 \Gamma\left(1+\frac{1}{1.6}\right) \\
& \mu=1517 \Gamma(1.62)
\end{aligned}
$$

Tabulated values for $\Gamma$ can be found in Hildebrand (1976) or other similar texts. Hence, the mean life is:

$$
\mu=1517(0.8959)=1359 \text { cycles }
$$

Again, recalling Chapter 2, the cumulative failure distribution for the data can be defined as:

$$
F(N)=1-\exp \left[-\left(\frac{N}{\eta}\right)^{\beta}\right]
$$

At a probability of failure of 0.1 we can solve for $N$. Substituting our known values:

$$
\begin{aligned}
& 0.1=1-\exp \left[-\left(\frac{N}{1517}\right)^{1.6}\right] \\
& N=371 \text { cycles }
\end{aligned}
$$Figure 5.8 Weibull plot of fatigue test data. The data are taken from a large data set of more than 1800 samples. (Fuchs and Stevens 1980)


# 5.4 Fatigue Models

Fatigue modeling of components is essential to designing reliable components. There are three different approaches to fatigue modeling. These include the S-N Diagram, the MansonCoffin Equation and Linear Elastic Fracture Mechanics. We will review the basic elements of each of these in turn.

### 5.4.1 S-N Diagrams for Materials

Let's begin our discussion of fatigue models with the simplest approach. The S-N diagram is easiest to understand and manipulate and is widely used for design purposes. The S-N diagram is created by plotting the log of cycles to failure versus the log of the stress amplitude created by the fluctuating load. Let's initially consider a rotating bending test on small materials characterization samples of low alloy steel with polished surfaces. If we test several conditions recording the cycles to failure, we can construct a plot of mean cycles to failure versus applied stress amplitude. We will observe the characteristics shown in Figure 5.9.

Figure 5.9 S-N Curve that would be typical of a low alloy steel.

On the S-N diagram, we will define the stress amplitude for $N_{f}$ cycles to failure. We will also adopt $S$ for stress. We then define the fatigue strength, $S_{f}$ as the alternating stress causing failure at $N_{f}$ cycles and $S_{e}$ as the notation for the endurance limit. These are common notations used in design of mechanical components when using the S-N diagram.

The S-N curve can be characterized by three distinct regions. From 1 cycle to approximately $10^{3}$ cycles is the region of low cycle fatigue in which the applied stress amplitude results in relatively short life. A break point or change in slope will occur at about $10^{3}$ cycles. From this point, until approximately $10^{6}$ cycles, we have a region of high cycle fatigue in which the applied stress amplitude produces longer, but limited life. Beyond $10^{6}$ cycles, we can see that the applied stress amplitude approaches a constant value and does not limit the life of the material. This point, at which we transition to infinite life, is known as the endurance limit, $S_{e}$.

The S-N curve approach to modeling fatigue behavior in design of structural components is usually applied to the high cycle regime. We should also note that not all materials will have an endurance limit. Most non-ferrous materials will not have a distinct endurance limit. However, we can see that it may be desirable to design a steel structural component with infinite life, provided we can tolerate the extra weight and cost and appropriately measure the endurance limit.

The straight line behavior from $10^{3}$ to $10^{6}$ cycles on the S-N Diagram is often represented by the following simple power law relationship:


$$

S*{f}=C N*{f}^{b}

$$

where, C and b are materials properties and $N_{f}$ is the number of cycles to failure. The two constants can be extracted from our S-N Diagram.

As we can imagine, the fatigue life at $10^{0}$ cycles will closely correlate to the ultimate strength of the material. In fact, as previously discussed, $\frac{1}{2}$ cycle is a single stress reversal. This is approximately the condition of a tensile test. So, we can expect that the ultimate strength, $\sigma_{u}$, to approximate the fatigue strength at a single stress reversal.The break point at $10^{3}$ cycles is often taken as a fraction of the ultimate strength for estimating the high cycle $\mathrm{S}-\mathrm{N}$ curve for a small rotating bending test specimen. For steels, the average value is approximately 0.8 of the ultimate strength, $\sigma_{u}$. The lower limit may be estimated at $0.65 \sigma_{u}$. Also for steels, the endurance limit is approximately $0.5 \sigma_{u}$. These estimating values, however, should not be used to replace test data for the purposes of component design.

Example 5.2 The following data are available for a structural steel alloy. Tensile test data show the average ultimate strength to be 1580 MPa . A rotating bending test was conducted on samples. The samples reflected a mean fatigue limit of 230 MPa . Estimate the mean fatigue strength at $10^{5}$ cycles.

If we simply take the log of both sides of equation 5.9:


$$

\log S*{f}=\log C+b \log N*{f}

$$

This simple linear relationship requires 2 conditions to solve for $C$ and $b$. Recall that for estimating purposes:


$$

S*{f}=0.8 \sigma*{u} @ 10^{3} \text { cycles }

$$

The known data are organized in Table 5.2.

Table 5.2 Data for Example 5.2

|  | $S_{f}(\mathrm{MPa})$ | $N_{f}$ (Cycles) |
| :-- | :-- | :-- |
| Condition 1 | $0.8(1580)=1264$ | $10^{3}$ |
| Condition 2 | 230 | $10^{6}$ |

Substituting into 5.10:


$$

\begin{aligned}
& \log 1264=\log C+3 b \\
& \log 230=\log C+6 b
\end{aligned}

$$

Solving simultaneously we find that:


$$

\begin{aligned}
& \log C=3.84 \\
& b=-0.247
\end{aligned}

$$

Substituting equations 5.13 into 5.10 , we see that at $10^{5}$ cycles:


$$

\begin{aligned}
& \log S*{f}=3.84-0.247(5)=2.60 \\
& S*{f}=403 M P a
\end{aligned}

$$

This example represents an approach to estimating the mean fatigue strength. At various conditions.

As shown in previous discussions, fatigue life, like other failure mechanisms is statistically distributed with its variation dependent upon materials property variations and variations arising from manufacturing processes. For polished test specimens, materials property variations dominate. Manufacturing variations and processing influence are added for real components. We will discuss the manufacturing influences further in later sections.

As shown in Figure 5.10, we can expect the curve to shift downward with decreasing probability of failure or increasing reliability. We can construct the lower curves by extracting the cycles to failure at the desired probability of failure from test data at different test conditions, by the method shown in Example 5.2.

Figure 5.10 Effect of decreasing failure probability on the $S-N$ curve. The mean life is of little value in designing a reliable product and we must determine the lower boundary at a reasonable risk of failure.

In the absence of adequate test data, a reliability factor, $k_{c}$ can be calculated as an estimate to construct fatigue curves. The calculation of $k_{c}$ is shown in the classic design text by Shigley and Mitchell (1983), and is based upon the normal distribution. Shigley and Mitchell (1983) apply $k_{c}$ to calculating the endurance limit for a material or component for a given level of reliability. $k_{c}$ is expressed as:


$$

k\_{c}=1-0.08 \Phi(z)

$$

where $\Phi(z)$ is the Standard Normal random variable at the desired level of reliability. Then, $k_{c}$ is applied as follows:


$$

S*{e}=k*{c} S\_{e}^{\prime}

$$

where $S e$ is the endurance limit at the desired reliability and $S_{e}^{\prime}$ is the endurance limit determined from test data.

Example 5.3 A material exhibits an average endurance limit of 200 MPa in a rotating bending test. What is the endurance limit at a desired reliability of $99 \%$ ?

We must first examine the cumulative Standard Normal tables. $\Phi(z)=2.33$ for $\mathrm{R}=0.99$. Applying equations 5.15 and 5.16 , we see that:


$$

\begin{aligned}
& k*{c}=1-0.08(2.33)=0.814 \\
& \text { and } \\
& S*{e}=0.814(200) \\
& S\_{e}=146 M P a @ R=0.99
\end{aligned}

$$
# 5.4.2 S-N Diagrams for Components

As we have discussed, the manufacturing processes and component configuration will significantly effect the fatigue life. We can expect the following factors to significantly effect fatigue life, when a material is processed into a component:

- Surface condition
- Size
- Stress Concentration
- Temperature
- Stress State
- Environment

Each of these factors will reduce the fatigue strength of a material. Hence, we can modify our simple power model relating the fatigue strength, $S_{f}$ to the number of cycles to failure, incorporating a fatigue strength reduction factor for each item on our list that will affect our component, as shown in equation 5.17.


$$

S*{f}=C^{\*} \prod*{1}^{a} k*{a} \mid N*{f}^{b}

$$

Shigley and Mitchell (1983) suggest a method for calculation of correction factors for fatigue design of components. They suggest that each factor be applied to reduce the fatigue limit, $S_{e}^{\prime}$, determined from a rotating bending test using polished specimens, to determine the component fatigue limit, $S_{e^{\prime}}$


$$

S*{e}=k*{a} \bullet k*{b} \bullet k*{c} \bullet k*{d} \bullet k*{e} \bullet k*{f} \bullet S*{e}^{\prime}

$$

Where


$$

\begin{aligned}
& S*{e}=\text { Endurance limit of the component } \\
& S*{e}^{\prime}=\text { Endurance limit of rotating-beam specimen } \\
& k*{a}=\text { Surface factor } \\
& k*{b}=\text { Size factor } \\
& k*{c}=\text { Reliability factor } \\
& k*{d}=\text { Temperature factor } \\
& k*{e}=\text { Modifying factor for stress concentration } \\
& k*{f}=\text { Miscellaneous-effects factor }
\end{aligned}

$$

Each $k$ factor must be determined according to the manufacturing processes, component geometry and desired reliability. Surface condition is among the most important factors in fatigue. Reduction factors for fatigue limits for components vary according to process, surface roughness and notch sensitivity. As an example, $k_{a}$ will range from 0.2 for high strength steels to 0.5 for more ductile steels, for as forged components. Figure 5.11, shows the relationship between $k_{a}$ and strength for different manufacturing processes.

Component size is also significant. Components can be much larger than simple test specimens. The larger surface area and greater volume increase the number of locations a fatigue crack may initiate from. The size reduction factor, $k_{b}$, can be expressed as follows for bending loads:


$$

k\_{b}=1.189 d^{-0.097} \text { for } 8 \mathrm{~mm}<\mathrm{d} \leq 250 \mathrm{~mm}

$$

In the case of axial loading, $k_{b}=0.71$ when the tensile properties are taken from actual testing. Non circular sections require the determination of an effective size dimension for the

Figure 5.11 Diagram showing the effects of surface condition on fatigue life of steel components. (Courtesy of McGraw-Hill)
application of equation 5.19. The reader is referred to Shigley and Mitchell (1983) for greater details.

We have already discussed the application of $k_{c}$ in our previous examples. The same equation applies here.
$k_{d}$ is the temperature factor. Unless temperatures are very high in proportion to the melting point of the material, $k_{d}=1$. For steels, temperature will generally not be a factor unless it exceeds about $450^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$. For the case of steel alloys, $k_{d}$ can be expressed as:


$$

k\_{d}=1-5.8 \times 10^{-3}(T-450)

$$

where T is the temperature of the component in ${ }^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$.
$k_{e}$ is the effect of stress concentration or notch effect. For most situations,


$$

\begin{aligned}
& k*{e}=\frac{1}{K*{t}} \\
& K*{t}=\frac{\sigma*{\text {NotchRoot }}}{\sigma*{\text {Nominal }}}
\end{aligned}
$$$K*{t}$ is the stress concentration factor. This is the ratio of the local stresses occurring at the root of the notch to the nominal stresses in the component. Values for stress concentration are widely tabulated and can be found in various handbooks (Fuchs and Stevens 1980). As an example, $K_{t}$ is plotted for a circular hole in a plate in Figure 5.12. A portion of the plate is shown. The diagram shows the relative stress gradient as well as values for $K_{t}$ at the edge of hole for different designs under tensile loading.
$k_{f}$ is a general correction for corrosion conditions or other environmental effects. As an example, $k_{f}$ may range from 0.24 to 0.90 under conditions of fretting. Fretting is form of cor-rosion-wear interaction described in Chapter 7. The general effects of corrosion on fatigue behavior are also explained in Chapter 7.

Example 5.4 Let us consider the fatigue life of a simple connecting rod component made of 1020 steel. We assume that there is a small hole in the connecting rod to be used for some additional assembly. In our example, we will calculate the fatigue limit for reliabilities of 0.95 and 0.9999 using the procedure in Shigley and Mitchell (1983).

Figure 5.12 Plot of stress concentration around a circular hole in a flat plate.For our example component, we will consider forging as the manufacturing process. From our equations above:

$$
\begin{aligned}
k_{a} & =0.5 \text { as forged. } \\
k_{b} & =0.71 \\
k_{c} & =1-0.08 Z_{r}=1-0.08 \times 1.645=0.868, \text { when } \mathrm{R}=0.95 \\
& Z_{r}=1-0.08 \times 3.719=0.702, \text { when } \mathrm{R}=0.9999 \\
k_{d} & =1.0(\mathrm{~T} \leq 450) \\
k_{e} & =\frac{1}{k_{t}}, \text { since } \frac{d}{w}=0.2 \text { then, } k_{t} \approx 2.5 \\
& =0.4 \\
k_{f} & =1.0
\end{aligned}
$$

For a 1020 steel $\quad S_{u}=450 \mathrm{Mpa}$ and $S_{e}^{\prime}=240 \mathrm{Mpa}$.

$$
\begin{aligned}
\therefore S_{e} & =k_{a} \bullet k_{b} \bullet k_{c} \bullet k_{d} \bullet k_{e} \bullet k_{f} \bullet S_{e}^{\prime} \text {, in the case of } R=0.95 \\
& =0.5 \times 0.71 \times 0.868 \times 1.0 \times 0.4 \times 1.0 \times 240 \mathrm{Mpa} \\
& =0.123 \times 240 \mathrm{Mpa}=29.5 \mathrm{Mpa} \\
\therefore S_{e} & =k_{a} \bullet k_{b} \bullet k_{c} \bullet k_{d} \bullet k_{e} \bullet k_{f} \bullet S_{e}^{\prime} \text {, in the case of } R=0.9999 \\
& =0.5 \times 0.71 \times 0.702 \times 1.0 \times 0.4 \times 1.0 \times 240 \mathrm{Mpa} \\
& =0.0996 \times 240 \mathrm{Mpa}=23.9 \mathrm{Mpa}
\end{aligned}
$$

This example shows the intricate relationship between manufacturing processes, component configuration and geometry to the reliability. For this reason, the Shigley and Mitchell (1983) method was presented in some detail. The dramatic differences in life between polished specimens and real components is also apparent here. This underscores the need to carefully evaluate how materials test data may be used in design.

It is probably apparent to the reader that an equivalence between equation 5.17 and 5.18 was not made. This is because some caution must be taken in applying the Shigley and Mitchell (1983) method to the general case. As can be seen, some of the relationships apply only to certain conditions, such as steel components under small elastic stresses. Of particular interest are the magnitude of stresses and strains that might arise. If plasticity occurs, than the Manson-Coffin approach should be utilized. Plastic deformation, for example, may occur in notches. In such cases, a notch strain analysis is needed.

# 5.4.3 Mean Stress Effects

One can probably envision many situations in which fatigue is of crucial concern other than rotating machinery. In such cases, the mean stress is not likely to be zero. When there is a mean stress that is greater than zero, the fatigue life will be reduced. In other words, we expect the S-N curve to shift down to the left. Then, the Modified Goodman relationship can applied as a conservative measure to limit the design, if the only fatigue data available are from fully reversed rotating bending tests. This relationship is expressed in equation 5.22:

$$
\frac{\sigma_{a}}{S_{e}}+\frac{\sigma_{m}}{S_{u}}=1
$$

In the Modified Goodman equation, $\sigma_{a}$ is the stress amplitude, $\sigma_{m}$ is the applied mean stress, $S e$ is the fatigue limit and $S u$ is the ultimate strength of the material.# 5.4.4 More on Notches

A notch or stress concentration can appear in many forms. Essentially any change in the cross section of a component will result in a stress concentration or a local increase in the stress field in the component. Examples include a hole in a plate, as we have just seen, or threads of fasteners, irregularities caused by processing, grooves, keyways or splines, changes in a shaft diameter or the toe of a weldment. Indeed many kinds of stress concentrations may be present in design of machine elements, structural components or electronic assemblies. It is these elements which tend most often to result in failure and require more attention in design and analysis.

As an example of a notch, let's examine the case of a groove in a shaft. This is shown in Figure 5.13. The notch clearly has a significant effect on the life of the component. This is due to the increased stress at the root of the notch. We can define the fatigue notch factor, $K_{f}$, as the ratio of the alternating stresses between the two curves plotted above, at a given life, usually a long life situation. Now, if $K_{f}=K_{s}$ the material is said to be fully notch sensitive. This is the case of the low alloy steel shown in Figure 5.13. In general, higher strength materials tend to be more notch sensitive then softer, lower strength materials. So, without data on the effect of the notch on fatigue life, a conservative estimate is often made allowing $K_{f}=K_{f}$. This is the basis of our fatigue limit reduction factor in the Shigley and Mitchell (1983) approach. However, a better estimate for softer materials at long life conditions can be formulated based upon the expected stress gradients. The reader is referred to Fuchs and Stevens (1980) for a detailed discussion.

As we shall see in the next section, as plastic strains dominate the process of fatigue damage, it is more important use a strain-life approach. We will need to know the strain at the root of notch. This may be evaluated using finite element methods or estimated using Neuber's Rule in which we segregate the strain and stress concentration factors for the notch root and define the following relationship:

$$
K_{i}^{2}=K_{e} K_{\sigma}
$$

Figure 5.13 Notch effect on a low alloy steel.An example of the application of this rule is discussed Chapter 14 and in detail in Fuch and Stevens (1980). While we have only introduced the subject of notches here, the importance of notches to the reliability of components exposed to alternating loads must be taken very seriously in practice. Many failures occur in the field due to inadequate fatigue strength of notched components, such as threaded fasteners.

# 5.4.5 Strain Life Models

Up to this point, we have developed the S-N or stress life approach to design and analysis of fatigue life. This is the most common approach to component design for long life or high cycle fatigue. Using the methods shown we can approach the the consideration of uncertainty and the analysis of reliability in the design. This can be achieved through the method of Shigley and Mitchell (1983) or through Monte Carlo simulation, considering variations in loads, materials properties and geometric variables.

In the low cycle regime, the strain-life approach or $\varepsilon-N$ approach is more appropriate to determine structural life, as we know plastic strains are likely to develop and dominate the process of failure.

Lets examine Figure 5.14. The solid line on the figure shows the log of the strain amplitude, $\frac{\Delta \varepsilon}{2}$, plotted against the log of the number of reversals, $2 N$, which will produce failure. The strain may be divided into the elastic component and plastic component. In each case, we can see there is a linear dependence, defined by the slope of the line. The intercept of the plastic component, $\varepsilon_{f}^{\prime}$ is the strain ductility coefficient and the slope, $c$, is the strain exponent. The intercept of the elastic component is $\sigma_{f}^{\prime} / E$, where $\sigma_{f}^{\prime}$ is the fatigue strength coefficient and $E$ is the elastic modulus; $b$ is the fatigue strength exponent.

Hence the relationship between strain range and cycles to failure, $N$, is expresses as:

$$
\frac{\Delta \varepsilon}{2}=\frac{\Delta \varepsilon_{\text {elastic }}}{2}+\frac{\Delta \varepsilon_{\text {plastic }}}{2}=\frac{\sigma_{f}^{\prime}}{E}(2 N)^{b}+\varepsilon_{f}^{\prime}(2 N)^{c}
$$

Equation 5.24 is the well known Manson -Coffin Equation.
The coefficients and exponents are cyclic materials properties, determined from fatigue testing small polished specimens in fully reversed axial loading conditions. Hence, the Manson-Coffin equation can be used to generally predict the life to small detectable cracks in real structures.

Figure 5.14 The strain life approach to modeling fatigue life.# 5.4.6 Accumulating Damage: Miner's Rule

In actual environments, loading conditions may change. Clearly, in examining our relationships for life prediction we must consider the accumulation of fatigue damage under each loading regime. Miner's Rule is one useful approximation for the accumulation of damage under different loading conditions.

This approach is based upon partitioning the damage occurring at each loading condition. We assume the damage done at a specific alternating load is the ratio of the number of cycles accumulated on the component at the alternating stress level, $n_{1}$, to the expected life at the same stress level, $N_{f 1}$. In other words, $n_{1}$ is the number of cycles expected in the field for a given load on a component. $N_{f}$ is estimated from a stress life or strain life model as the expected number of cycles to failure that would occur at the same given load. The fractions of damage accumulate at each loading condition, according to equation 5.25 :

$$
\frac{n_{1}}{N_{f 1}}+\frac{n_{2}}{N_{f 2}}+\ldots \ldots \ldots+\frac{n_{i}}{N_{f i}}=1
$$

### 5.4.7 Stress Intensity Factor and Crack Growth Models

Lets now turn our attention to crack propagation. Linear Elastic Fracture Mechanics (LEFM) is generally applied to model fatigue crack growth. LEFM models will be applicable only if the stresses developed in the component, assuming no crack, are roughly less than $80 \%$ of the yield strength of the material. Under these conditions, the crack tip plastic zone will usually be within limits that make application of LEFM valid to estimating crack growth.

Lets examine a component with a crack, as shown in Figure 5.15. This component is similar to the test specimens used to study crack growth and is convenient to understand the parameters governing the extension of a crack. A crack of length $a$ can extend when the tensile load $P$ is applied. Under the conditions shown in the figure, a load is applied in the $z$ direction of our defined coordinate system. The crack opens and propagates normal to the direction of the stresses, as in stage II fatigue crack growth. This is Mode I crack growth and, is the most common mode of crack growth in fatigue and will be the general case of our discussion about crack growth modeling.

However, we should be aware that cracks can also extend under the influence of in- plane shear stresses. If the opposing forces, $P$, are applied in the $x$ direction of our coordinate system for the simple component, the crack will propagate in Mode II growth. If the loads are applied in the $y$ direction, the crack will propagate under conditions of tearing or Mode III crack growth.

In any mode of growth, the stresses developed in the tip of the crack, which drive the growth, depend upon the stress intensity factor, $K$. This parameter in turn depends upon the loading, crack length and specimen geometry. In general, $K_{f}$, the subscript denoting Mode I crack growth, can be determined from the following expression:

$$
K_{I}=\alpha \cdot \sigma \sqrt{\pi a}
$$

$\alpha$ is function of the ratio of the crack length, $a$, to the width of the component $\mathrm{W} . \sigma$ is the normal stress developed in the component, assuming no crack is present. The units for $K$ are $M P a \sqrt{m}$.

Figure 5.15 A singled edge crack in a component under tensile loading.

For the component shown in Figure 5.15 lets consider the limiting case of a semi-infinite plate where $\mathrm{W}>>a$, under a tensile load $P$. This might occur in various components where a defect is present at the edge of the structure. In this case, $a / W \rightarrow 0$ and the expression for $\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{j}}$ becomes:

$$
K_{j}=1.12 \frac{p}{W h} \sqrt{\pi a}
$$

The value $\alpha=1.12$ is known as the free edge correction for the single edge crack shown in Figure 5.15. The stress intensity factors for various load configurations, crack opening modes and geometric configurations can be modelled from theory of elasticity and are compiled in many references on LEFM. (Fuchs and Stevens 1980, Sih 1973). We can confirm by inspection, that the ratio of the crack length to the width of the specimen is an important quantity. A numerical solution for $K_{j}$ for our simple single edge crack, in terms of this ratio is:

$$
K_{j}=\sigma \sqrt{a}\left[1.99-0.41 \frac{a}{W}+18.7\left(\frac{a}{W}\right)^{2}-38.48\left(\frac{a}{W}\right)^{3}+53.85\left(\frac{a}{W}\right)^{4}\right]
$$

For analysis and design, it is then convenient to plot $\alpha \cdot \sqrt{\pi}$ against the ratio of $a / W$. From plots of this type we can utilize equation 5.26 to model simple structures. An example plot for our single edge crack is shown in Figure 5.16.

Figure 5.16 A plot of $\alpha \cdot \sqrt{\pi}$ against the ratio of a/W for a specimen or component with a single edge crack as shown in Figure 5.15.

At the point of abrupt failure, a crack will rapidly propagate resulting in fracture of the component. The onset of failure occurs at the critical stress intensity, $K_{C}$, for the material used for the component. The limiting value of $K_{C}$ occurs under tensile loading, when the thickness of the component allows for the condition of plane strain. This value is a critical material property known as the fracture toughness, $K_{I C}$ of the material, and is determined by materials testing. Hence, we can determine for a given loading condition, what the critical crack size, $a_{c}$ will be at the point of failure, by setting $K_{I}=K_{I C}$ for our material and structural configuration. As an example, for our simple component in Figure 5.15:

$$
a_{c}=K_{I c}^{2} \cdot \frac{1}{(\alpha \sqrt{\pi})^{2}} \cdot\left[\frac{W h}{P}\right]^{2}
$$

The equations shown above have been developed for the single edge crack. A center crack in a two dimensional plate is another important configuration that we should be familiar with. This type of crack is shown in Figure 5.17. Equation 5.26 applies here as well. However, the quantity $a$ is half the crack length and for a semi-infinite plate, $\alpha=1.0$.

Example 5.5. Let's consider a situation in which we must estimate the minimum crack size in a welded aluminum structure. We may be concerned with how large a crack will need to grow before the structure would fail catastrophically by fracturing.

The structure is to be manufactured from 2024-T351 plate stock of 10 mm thickness that will be under a loading that will produce a uniform tensile stress in the plate. We have some data concerning the material property variations and manufacturing tolerances of the plate and welding process. These are reflected in Table 5.3. The width of the plate is 1 m and the maximum applied load is $900 \mathrm{kN} / \mathrm{m}$. The weld is a transverse butt weld and the loading is applied normal to the weldment. We could expect some significant stress concentration at the toe of the weld.

Figure 5.17 A center crack in a semi-infinite plate under tensile loading.

Table 5.3 Data for Example 5.5

|         | Stress Concentration from Weldment $\left(K_{s}\right)$ | Fracture Toughness MPa $\sqrt{\mathrm{m}}$ | Thickness mm |
| :------ | :------------------------------------------------------ | :----------------------------------------- | :----------: |
| Minimum | 1.0                                                     | 31                                         |     9.5      |
| Typical | 1.5                                                     | 34                                         |      10      |
| Maximum | 3.0                                                     | 44                                         |     10.5     |

An initial approach to this situation may be to estimate the minimum flaw size from worst case conditions. We will model the weld defect as a center crack in a semi-infinite plate and apply equation 5.26 . Our assumptions are that the crack is small in comparison to the width of the plate and let $\frac{a}{W} \rightarrow 0$ and $\mathrm{a}=1.0$.

$$
a_{c}=1.77 K_{f c}^{2} \cdot\left[\frac{W h}{K_{r} P}\right]^{2}
$$

Then $a_{c}$ can be estimated as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
& a_{c}=1.77\left(31 \times 10^{6}\right)^{2}\left[\frac{9.5 \times 10^{-3}(1)}{3\left(900 \times 10^{3}\right)}\right]^{2} \\
& a_{c}=0.021 \mathrm{~m}=2.1 \mathrm{~cm}
\end{aligned}
$$

The critical crack size is then $2 a_{c}$ or about 4.2 cm . Clearly, such a crack is easily detectable.
However, our analysis in the above example does not directly consider the variations in materials properties or manufacturing. An alternative approach is to analyze 5.30 is by embedding it in a Monte Carlo simulation. As far as Monte Carlo simulations are concerned, this is not a difficult problem. We can apply the methods illustrated in Chapters 2 and 3, constructing triangular distributions for the geometric and materials parameters in Table 5.3.The results of such a simulation are shown in Figures 5.18a and Figure 5.18b. The plots show the parameter $a_{c}$ as an output from the analysis. The data from the simulation were fit to a log-normal distribution as shown in Figure 5.18b. The fit is acceptable. At a probability of failure of $0.01 \%$, the critical crack size is $2 a_{c}$ or about 3.0 cm . This result is considerably less than our worst case analysis. But, we can see that the results might be considered conservative relative to the plotted data at the lower end of the log-normal curve. In this case, we may want study further the influence of our initial assumption of the triangular distribution on the tail of our log-normal fit.

Figure 5.18 a Frequency histogram showing the distribution of the data from a Monte Carlo simulation of crack length. b Monte Carlo simulation data from crack length simulations fit to a logNormal distribution. (Plotting techniques for fitting data to a distribution are described in greater detail in Chapter 12.)# 5.4.8 Fatigue Crack Propagation

As we have discussed, a fatigue crack will grow in a stable manner until it reaches a critical length. This is stage II fatigue crack growth. Then, the remaining supporting section will fail by fracture. We can estimate this critical crack size, as we have shown in the previous example problem. Let's now turn our attention to estimating the number of cycles a crack will take to grow from crack initiation to fracture over the course of stage II stable crack growth.

Under fluctuating loads, we can estimate the stress range which a component will see in service or test. We can expect that the stress intensity factor will have a corresponding range and that equation 5.26 can be modified to reflect this as follows:

$$
\Delta K_{I}=a \bullet \Delta \sigma \sqrt{\pi a}
$$

where $\Delta \sigma$ is the stress range under fatigue conditions and $\Delta K_{I}$ is the corresponding stress intensity range.

A plot of the log of stress intensity range versus the log of the rate of crack growth per cycle, $\frac{d a}{d N}$, will yield a sigmoidal curve similar to the plot in Figure 5.19.

The linear region of this curve will fit the power law model known as the Paris Equation (Paris and Erdogan 1963).

$$
\frac{d a}{d N}=A\left(\Delta K_{I}\right)^{n}
$$

where $A$ and $n$ are constants that are material properties. $n$ is the slope of the linear region of the sigmoidal crack growth curve. Another important feature of the crack growth curve is the limiting or threshold value of the stress intensity range, $\Delta K_{I t h}$. The crack will not propagate at stress intensities below this level.

Figure 5.19 Crack growth rate plotted against stress intensity. This type of plot is commonly called da/dN curve.We should recall that fatigue testing used to characterize the stress-life or $S-N$ curve for materials is generally performed using fully reversed loading, where the stress ratio $\mathrm{R}=-1$. However, crack growth experiments are conducted under different conditions. Generally, materials tests are conducted on compact specimens similar to our component in Figure 5.15, under conditions of $R=0$. This is due to the fact that the crack will not propagate under compressive loads. $K_{j}$ has no real physical meaning for $\sigma<0$. We can expect for components, that the $\frac{d a}{d N}$, curve will shift to the left for $R \geq 0$.

In order to apply the Paris Equation (equation 5.32), we must integrate to find the value of the number of cycles to failure. We integrate from the initial suspected crack size to the critical crack size:

$$
N_{f}=A \int_{a_{i}}^{a_{f}} \frac{d a}{(\Delta K)^{n}}
$$

Example 5.6 Lets look at an example of the application of the Paris Equation. Barsom (1971) found that a conservative approximation of for common pearlitic steels fit the following relationship:

$$
\frac{d a}{d N}=6.9 \times 10^{-12} \Delta K^{3.0}
$$

Considering the case of a single edge crack in a 1015 sheet steel where a $>>$ W. We will apply equation 5.31 for the stress intensity factor range. In this case, let $R=0$. From the methods previously shown we can estimate the critical crack size from the fracture toughness of our alloy. The initial crack size is often taken as the minimum flaw size that might occur as a result of assembly, fabrication or manufacturing operations.

In addition, we may estimate the life to detectable crack size from an analysis of the Manson Coffin equation taking the minimum crack size to be the size of a typical test specimen.

Integrating Barsom's Equation for our single edge crack, we obtain:

$$
N_{f}=\frac{a_{i}^{-0.5}-a_{i}^{-0.5}}{\left[\frac{-1.12^{3} * 6.9 \times 10^{-12}}{2} *\left(\sigma_{\max }-\sigma_{\min }\right)^{3} * \pi^{\frac{3}{2}}\right]}
$$

In the case of the single edge crack, the integration is not difficult and is left as an exercise for the reader. However, when $\alpha$ is a function of $a$, we may require numerical techniques for integration.

Now, considering the following data in Table 5.4, we can estimate the number of cycles to failure for our component.

Table 5.4 Data for Example 5.6

| Initial Crack Size             | $a_{i}$                 | 5 mm    |
| :----------------------------- | :---------------------- | :------ |
| Critical Crack Size at Failure | $a_{f}$                 | 70 mm   |
| Maximum Stress                 | $\sigma_{\text {max }}$ | 210 MPa |
| Minimum Stress                 | $\sigma_{\text {min }}$ | 0 MPa   |

$$
\begin{aligned}
N_{f}= & \frac{0.07^{-0.5}-0.005^{-0.5}}{\left[\frac{-1.12^{3} * 6.9 \times 10^{-12}}{2} *(210)^{3} * \pi^{\frac{3}{2}}\right]} \\
& N_{f}=41,480 \text { cycles }
\end{aligned}
$$Once again, we can consider the solution to this problem using a Monte Carlo Simulation. The application of Monte Carlo Simulations to crack propagation has been investigated by many different researchers and had proved to be a valuable approach in considering crack propagation in structures.

# 5.5 Related Mechanisms and Interactions

The follow sections discuss related mechanisms and their interaction with fatigue including: aging, rolling wear, creep and grain growth.

### 5.5.1 Wear of Rolling and Sliding Elements

The surfaces of sliding elements, roller bearing and their associated races are also subject to fatigue failure. In this case, bearing elements may not fracture into two pieces. However, metal particles may flake from the surface. This is known as spalling. Usually the roughened surface created by spalling, impedes the function of the bearing and results in increased noise and vibration and possible further secondary damage. The mechanism for spalling involves the formation of small cracks which interconnect resulting in flakes of metal, as shown in Figure 5.20.

### 5.5.2 Aging Interactions and Polymers

Aging implies that a critical material property of a component is changing over time. Aging may be very important if the changes in strength or crack propagation resistance are substantial within the life of the component. Aging processes are driven by elevated temperature and can be related to diffusion of one or more constituents of the material or by other thermally activated processes, such as scission of polymer molecules or other chemical reactions.

We can consider changes in the material properties of polymers and elastomers, as an example. While we have devoted much of our discussion in this chapter to metals, polymers are also subject to fatigue. The mechanism of crack development is different, however, we can understand crack growth in much the same way. Aging in polymers is important to fatigue crack propagation. The properties of polymers can change over time, with environmental conditions, such as temperature, exposure to ultraviolet light or radiation. These changes may then impede the ability of the polymer to resist growth of cracks.

Figure 5.21 shows hardness plotted as a function of time at three different temperatures for an elatomeric vibration damper made of natural rubber. The hardness increases with time and corresponds to a loss of ability to absorb strain energy. At a critical level, the vibration damper will crack, and fracture will eventually result. This process of embrittlement corresponds to the loss of volatile plasticisers in the rubber, through diffusion. The embrittled component cannot absorb the strain energy imparted to it during vibration and it eventually cracks and loses its function.

### 5.5.3 Creep

Creep can be defined as time dependent deformation of a component, under load. Strain accumulates, as time progresses, leading to permanent plastic deformation and if the load is continuously applied, fracture by creep rupture may occur. The name itself implies that deformations occur very slowly, which may be the case for many structural applications. However, the rate of deformation is dependent upon the temperature and load. In metals,

Figure 5.20 The sequence shows the development of spalling in a rolling bearing assembly. Small surface cracks are aggravated by lubricant penetration followed by flaking. (Chapter 14 presents a case study in the life of a bearing assembly in a gear mechanism.)
creep process are usually not active unless the application temperature is an appreciable fraction of the melting point of the metal. If the absolute temperature of application is above approximately $0.3 T_{m}$ to $0.45 T_{m}$, where $T_{m}$ is the absolute melting temperature creep will be of concern. As an example, creep readily occurs at near room temperature for lead based alloys and solders used for electronic assembly, but usually it is not consideration for steels, unless temperatures exceed about $400^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$. In practice, creep deformations can be of significant concern in plant applications, such as petroleum processing, where high temperature and constant pressure limit component life due to creep, necessitating maintenance to prevent rupture (Reed-Hill 1973).

Creep occurs in metals by one of several different mechanisms of deformation. Mechanisms may interact and mechanism shifts can occur depending upon the temperature and load conditions. Creep deformation mechanisms may include:

Figure 5.21 Aging of elastomer vibration dampers. Increasing hardness, to critical level for failure, follows an Arrhenius function. Under fixed loading conditions, the aged material can no longer absorb the energy of vibrational loading.

- Screw Dislocation Climb
- Grain Boundary Diffusion
- Grain Boundary Sliding

The latter is significant at higher temperatures in relation to the melting point and will produce crack nucleation between grains leading to intergranular fracture under constant load. In testing, intergranular fracture is often noted in creep rupture of many different types of metals.

There are several constitutive relationships that are applied to model creep deformations. Models of creep generally relate the strain rate to the applied stress and temperature, using an Arrhenius relationship or mixed power-law Arrhenius model. One common model, the Feltham Model, is presented in Chapter 6.

In practice, creep testing is usually conducted under constant load. Creep curves similar to Figure 5.22 are generated in testing. Stage II creep occurs at constant rate and the data for stage II creep is usually extrapolated from the accelerated conditions of testing, to less severe load conditions that occur in the field or by extrapolation of the early results of creep tests.

# 5.5.4 Fatigue - Creep Interactions

Creep can occur within a cyclic loading regime. As a result, complex interactions between creep and fatigue occur, which impart greater damage to the material, than would be expected for the cyclic loading regimes in which fatigue is the only concern. We can refer to the loading spectra for sinusoidal stresses that we discussed in earlier sections. In comparison, Figure 5.23 shows a loading spectrum in which the load is held constant for a time period, $t_{D}$, at each extreme of the cycle. The time, $t_{D}$, is called the hold time for the cycle. In this case, the hold time is symmetrical. If operational temperatures allow creep processes to be active within the hold time, additional strain will be imposed upon the component during

Figure 5.22 Creep curves generated by constant load testing of a material at three different temperatures.


Figure 5.23 Loading spectrum that includes a hold time at the cyclic extremes. If creep is active at the operational temperatures, added creep strains will occur.
the hold time. This increases the cyclic damage. If there is a fixed deformation of the structure, which may occur in thermal cycling, added creep strains will cause the stresses in the structure to relax. Once again, the increased strain energy will impart greater damage per cycle to the material than with fatigue alone. Careful consideration must be given to modeling fatigue damage when creep plays a substantial role. The work of Coffin (1977) was fundamental to understanding the relationship between hold time and total strain history for purposes of modeling. High temperature fatigue is also explained in further detail in Fuchs and Stevens (1980).One notable example of creep-fatigue interaction occurs in electronic assemblies. Thermal deformations in solder connections occur due to changes in temperature, which are driven by differences in coefficients of thermal expansion of the surrounding materials (Evans 1989). Cyclic deformation, with significant hold time at elevated temperature, occurs due to the operational duty cycle of electronic equipment. Stress relaxation is then inevitable, imparting significant cyclic and creep damage to solder joints. This makes the life prediction of soldered assemblies in equipment design necessary and yet difficult. The problem of solder joint fatigue is presented in further detail in Chapter 8.

# 5.5.5 Grain Growth Effects

Grain growth and related changes in microstructure occur in metals at elevated temperature. Grain growth is an aging phenomena fuelled by diffusion, with grain boundary diffusion perhaps being most significant. In the microstructure of a polycrystalline metal, larger grains will generally grow at the expense of smaller grains. The rate of microstructural changes or grain growth will be substantial when the absolute temperature of the metal exceeds about $0.3 T_{m}$ to $0.5 T_{m}$. In deformed or cold worked structures, grain growth will be preceded by re-crystallization, where new crystals will be nucleated in the deformed, cold worked grain structure.

The effect of grain size on mechanical properties is well known. Ductility and strength both decrease with increasing grain size. Therefore, we would expect corresponding changes in fatigue behavior to occur with grain growth and microstructural development, depending upon the loading regime. Significant recrystallization of a cold worked structure, in which the net strength of the metal depends upon cold working will likely be detrimental in any case. However, changes in fatigue performance, due simply to increasing grain growth, will depend on the loading regime. Reduced ductility will adversely effect low cycle fatigue, while reduced strength will have its greatest effect on long life behavior. The case of fatigue with substantial creep deformation, however, may not be easily resolved since increased grain size may reduce creep deformation.

### 5.6 Fatigue Mitigation

The foremost preventive measure for fatigue related problems is proper anticipation of loading, thorough materials characterization, followed by careful design and development of the both manufacturing processes and component geometry. One must recognize that the design factors influencing fatigue, including materials properties, are random variables that influence the life distribution of a component. The influence of manufacturing on component life was detailed earlier in the chapter. This once again underscores the relationship between quality issues, manufacturing processes and reliability.

There are several important design issues that deserve careful consideration in the development of a component or product, that can mitigate fatigue failure. These include:

- Selection of improved surface finishing
- Proper notch design and stress gradient mitigation
- Introduction of self-stresses

The subject of surface finishing was discussed in some detail in previous sections. As Figure 5.11 shows, selection of a finishing process that yields a smooth. surface, such as polishing,can improve the fatigue life of a component. In addition, if corrosion - fatigue interaction is a significant concern, an electroplated metal finish can be considered. Corrosion fatigue interactions are explained in Chapter 7. Some caution is warranted, since some electroplated finishes may induce undesirable residual stresses that may potentially reduce fatigue life.

Notches represent a major source of fatigue life reduction. Therefore, proper notch design is of critical importance in achieving adequate component life and may often be a necessary focus of improvement when failures occur in mechanical equipment. In general, the notch effect can be reduced by the use of generous radii in fillets and by designing cross sections of components that tend to reduce stress gradients. The many aspects of stress concentration improvement can be summarized by comparing a conventional bolted joint design to a bolt design which considers improvements at all regions of stress concentration, as shown in Figure 5.24. In general, stress gradient reduction can be accomplished by several methods. Removing material from around a primary notch, hole or shoulder, through stress relieving grooves or undercuts, can be highly beneficial to fatigue life. Holes, splines and keyways in shafts may require increased diameter at their location, with generous radii to accommodate the change in section of the shaft. Connections of wheels, pulleys and gears can be handled similarly or added fillets on hubs at the shaft connection can be of considerable benefit to reducing stress concentration in the connection.

Self stresses or residual compressive stresses induced in the surface of a component can also be of substantial benefit to improving fatigue life. Cracks are much less likely to initiate and develop into Stage II fatigue under compressive stresses. This can be achieved with added manufacturing processes, including mechanical means and by heat treatments. Shot- peening is a typical mechanical process for inducing compressive stresses in components ranging from suspension springs in automobiles to crankshafts in diesel engines used in heavy equipment. Small metal balls called shot are caused to strike and impinge upon the surface of the component. The intensity of the shot- peening treatment is critical to attaining the desirable depth of compressive stress. Surface heat treatments, such as carburizing, nitriding or induction hardening are also effective in creating a hard surface finish, which is in a state of compressive stresses.


Figure 5.24 Bolted connection design. (a) Conventional. (b) Fatigue mitigating designImparting residual compressive stresses in the surface of a component will be effective only if the stress levels remain below the yield strength. In the short life regime, compresive stresses will not be very beneficial. However, in the long-life, high cycle fatigue situation they will significantly improve fatigue life of components. The added benefit of reduced deviation in life may also be realized in addition to increased expected life.

# 5.7 Summary

Fatigue is a major failure mechanism in many systems including electronic, mechanical and structural components subject to cyclic loading environments. Fatigue in metals initiates with localized deformations at surfaces and progresses with crack growth through the component, normal to the applied stresses. When the load exceeds the strength of the component fracture will occur. Fatigue failures of this nature may have devastating consequences.

There is considerable variation in fatigue life of materials and the variations increase with real components. The variation in fatigue life arises due to contributing variations in materials properties, that effect fatigue behavior, and manufacturing variabilities that effect component geometry. Models of fatigue for design and reliability assessment include the stress-life approach, strain-life approach and cyclic crack growth or Linear Elastic Fracture Mechanics (LEFM) approach. Uncertainties and variabilities can be incorporated into these approaches by several approaches, including Monte Carlo simulation, allowing for reliability estimates of designs.

Fatigue testing is necessary to gather sufficient data for modeling and to validate. Testing of materials, and in some cases components that comprise a system, remains an essential aspect of obtaining a reliable design against fatigue failure. Fatigue may interact with other mechanisms and phenomena including creep at elevated temperatures. This complicates life prediction and testing issues.

### 5.8 Do's and Dont's in Design

Do careful failure analysis of fatigue failures to ascertain contributing factors and load conditions. Do conduct fatigue tests on materials used in the development of components.
Do test components to validate fatigue life.
Do consider the importance of fatigue life uncertainty and characterize fatigue life distributions in testing.
Do carefully evaluate loading regimes and loading spectra expected for field conditions.
Do carefully evaluate mean stress effects and effects of changing loads and complex loading spectra.
Do use LEFM to estimate minimum flaw and crack sizes.
Do characterize fracture toughness of materials.
Do anticipate the effects of notches and changes in geometry on fatigue performance of components.
Do consider the use of generous radii for changes in sections.
Do consider surface heat treatments and shot-peening to improve fatigue life.
Do careful assessment of rolling and sliding element to prevent spalling.
Do careful design of bolted and welded joints to reduce stress and stress concentration.
Do grind welds flat and use peening to finish a weld.Do use fasteners with rolled threads.
Do assess potential interactions of fatigue with other mechanisms including creep and corrosion.
Do comparative analysis with past designs when developing new components.
Do reduce stress concentrations.
Do qualify manufacturing processes used for surface finishing, shot-peening and heat treatments.
Do remember that designs must have very low probabilities of failure.
Do carefully consider the selection of fatigue life probability distributions especially for low probabilities.

Don't underestimate the effects of manufacturing process variations and quality factors on component fatigue life.
Don't forget the importance of surface finish on fatigue life.
Don't forget to consider periodic inspection to monitor fatigue crack formation and development.
Don't forget welding and grinding may produce harmful tensile residual stresses.
Don't forget to anticipate environmental effects including high temperature, low temperature or humidity.
Don't fail to anticipate the highly degrading effects of fatigue corrosion interactions including fretting.
Don't use typical properties for designs. Materials parameters are random variables.
Don't expect shot-peening or compresive residual stresses to improve fatigue life for very short life situations.
Don't neglect consideration of variations in parameters and materials properties that effect the variation in fatigue life.
