Mark S. Fan

In Chapters 4 and 5 we discussed the mechanics of failure for overstress and fatigue related failure mechanisms. It should be clear to the reader at this point that stress analyses, mechanical, thermo-mechanical or perhaps thermal, will be necessary to model these failure mechanisms, during a reliability assessment and in design. Hence, we have placed our discussion of stress analysis here. The reader may again refer to this chapter at the completion of Part II of the text.

Our discussion focuses on applying the finite element method to estimate stresses under mechanical and thermal loading and to validation by whole field methods. While there are many books devoted to the basics and theory of these subjects, we have endeavored to focus on the essentials of application to aid in interpreting analysis results and on the subject of optically based, whole field methods for validation. Therefore we hope this chapter may be interesting to experts, as well as those less familiar with the Finite Element Method.

The Finite Element Method is a mathematical tool for numerical analysis. Commonly known as FEA (Finite Element Analysis), it is widely used to solve many types of governing equations of complex systems, either in differential format or variational integral format. The development of FEA was mainly associated with structural analysis in solid mechanics, but today its applications have been expanded into many branches of science and technology. FEA is applied to problems as varied as fluid flow to magnetics and electrostatics. Although the roots of FEA can be traced back to the work of Courant (1943), the foundation of modern finite element method was laid by Turner, et al. (1956) and more directly by Clough (1960). The development and improvement of FEA have been continuing since then, both in industry and academia.

## 6.I Finite Element Method

FEA as a numerical analysis method was mainly used in the early days for the performance evaluation of products that had already been built. This approach was commonly referred to as a design check. Today, FEA has become a critical tool in product development. FEA is used to evaluate electrical or mechanical devices, sub-systems and whole spacecraft during design. This allows designers to have a clear picture of performance. Any design faults or inadequacies that will result in possible malfunctions and even failures can be diagnosed and corrected prior to actual missions or product deployments, saving time and money in development.The optimization process is iterative in nature. Results from earlier optimization analyzes enable a designer to gain new insight into the issue upon which a newer design will depend. Based on analyzes, corrective actions that are part of an iterative design optimization process, are taken and design modifications are made. These measures will ultimately enhance the performance and improve reliability before the start of fabrication and system assembly, therefore saving millions of dollars of non-recurring engineering costs.

New generation airplanes and cars are thoroughly examined using various FEA techniques before the designs are finalized. This practice has expanded rapidly into many other areas of engineering and technology. For example, lap-top personal computer companies are using FEA for drop shock analysis, and biotechnology companies for stress analysis on artificial bones to be implemented into human bodies.

The basic philosophy of FEA method is that a geometrically complex physical object can be split up into many smaller and simpler objects. This is called spatial discretization, with each simple geometrical shape being known as an element and the total group of elements being known as a mesh. Element equations are written about fixed points on the elements known as nodes. The behavior of the object can be predicted by assembling the element equations and obtaining a solution to them. The procedures used are the same for all objects, regardless of their geometric complexity. These steps will be shown in more detail in the next section.

From a mathematical standpoint, there are three broad problem areas that design engineers need to be concerned with, which are equilibrium problems, eigenvalue problems and transient problems. Steady state thermal and static stress analyzes are typical equilibrium or time independent problems. Eigenvalue problems are an extension which analyze the fundamental characteristics of the system under examination. The method can be used to determine the natural frequencies, modal shapes and the buckling loads of the system. In transient or propagation problems, the loads are usually a function of time and the purpose of FEA is to analyze the forced response of the system. Obviously the range of engineering problems that FEA can solve is very large.

An important issue in interpretation is the accuracy of FEA results. It has become a major concern recently because more and more design engineers who are not trained as 'finite element analysts' are using commercially available FEA software packages to do their job. The advancement of the pre- and post-processors in these commercial packages has enabled design engineers to create visually impressive and apparently reliable models for analysis, and produce equally impressive and convincing graphical output. While these tools are very powerful, they can only generate accurate and reliable results when used correctly. Even though modern FEA software packages have made users remote from the underlying principles and methodologies, one has to remember that, as with any other numerical analysis techniques, FEA is an approximate method. The validity and accuracy of the solutions rely heavily on an accurate representation of the problem and correct analysis procedures. This issue will further be discussed and demonstrated later in the chapter.

# 6.1.1 Basic Description of Method: The simple one-dimensional finite element stress analysis

Let us introduce the basic concept and procedures of FEA by considering a pin-jointed bar with a length $L$, under loading force $F$, as shown in Figure 6.1a. Because of pin-joint, the bar can only transmit axial forces, namely, tensile or compressive forces. This physical bar can be represented by a one-dimensional element known as a bar element. A simple element of this type has only two nodes as shown in Fig. 6.1 b.

# Node $i$ Node $j$



Figure 6.1 a A pin jointed component, under tensile load $F$. b A single bar element with two nodes, representing the component shown in Fig. 6.1a.

For small axial loading, it is a good assumption that the displacement of the bar is linear. That is


$$

u=a+b x

$$

Thus displacement at each node can be written as


$$

\begin{aligned}
& u*{i}=a+b x*{i} \\
& u*{j}=a+b x*{j}
\end{aligned}

$$

Solving Eqn (6.2) for $a$ and $b$ yields


$$

\begin{aligned}
& a=\left(u*{i} x*{j}-u*{j} x*{i}\right) / L \\
& b=\left(u*{j}-u*{i}\right) / L
\end{aligned}

$$

where $L=x_{i}-x_{j}$.
Hence Eqn (6.1) can be rewritten as


$$

u=N*{i} u*{i}+N*{j} u*{j}

$$

where $N i=\left(x_{j}-x\right) / L$ and $N_{j}=\left(x-x_{i}\right) / L$, are known as the shape function of the element.
The strain energy stored in the above bar is defined as
$$

\Gamma=\frac{1}{2} \int*{x*{i}}^{x\_{i}} A \sigma \varepsilon d x

$$

A being the cross-sectional area of the bar. Using one-dimensional Hooke's law, $\sigma=E \varepsilon$, Eqn (6.5) becomes


$$

\Gamma=\frac{A E}{2} \int*{x*{i}}^{x\_{i}} A \varepsilon^{2} d x

$$

Differentiating Eqn (6.4) with respect to $x$, and using the relation $\varepsilon=d u / d x$, we have


$$

\varepsilon=\left(u*{j}-u*{i}\right) / L

$$

Substituting Eqn (6.7) into Eqn (6.6) and integrating yields


$$

\Gamma=\left(u*{j}-u*{i}\right)^{2} A E / 2 L

$$

We may write Eqn (6.8) in matrix form


$$

\Gamma=\frac{A E}{2 L}\left(u*{i} u*{j}\right)\left(\begin{array}{rr}
1 & -1 \\
-1 & 1
\end{array}\right)\left(\begin{array}{l}
u*{i} \\
u*{j}
\end{array}\right)=\frac{1}{2}(U)^{T}[k](U)

$$

where $[k]=\frac{A E}{L}\left(\begin{array}{rr}1 & -1 \\ -1 & 1\end{array}\right)$ is the stiffness matrix.
Because of the displacement, the external force has done work, which can be expressed as


$$

W=u*{i} F*{i}+u*{j} F*{j}=(U)^{T}(F)

$$

By definition, the total potential energy for the bar is


$$

P E=\Gamma-W=\frac{1}{2}(U)^{T}[k](U)-(U)^{T}(F)

$$

When the bar is at its equilibrium state, its potential energy has to be minimum. In other words, it must satisfy the following condition


$$

\partial P E / \partial U=[k](U)-(F)=0

$$

If the system consists of multiple bar elements, Eqn (6.12) will become


$$

\sum*{i}\left[k*{i}\right](U)-(F)=0

$$

where $\sum_{i}\left[k_{i}\right]$ is the system stiffness matrix.
Example 6.1 We can use a numerical example to demonstrate the use of the above results. For the same bar, assume the left end (node $i$ ) is fixed to a solid wall so that the nodal displacement is zero. A pulling force toward the right-hand side $(100 \mathrm{~N})$ is acting at node $j$. Also assume $E=10 \mathrm{GPa}, L=100 \mathrm{~mm}$ and $A=10 \mathrm{~mm}^{2}$. The stiffness matrix is


$$

[k]=\frac{A E}{L}\left(\begin{array}{rr}
1 & -1 \\
-1 & 1
\end{array}\right)=\left(\begin{array}{rr}
1000 & -1000 \\
-1000 & 1000
\end{array}\right) N / m m

$$

From Eqn (6.12), we have


$$

\left(\begin{array}{rr}
1000 & -1000 \\
-1000 & 1000
\end{array}\right)\binom{u*{1}}{u*{2}}=\binom{0}{100}

$$

In order to solve the matrix equations, the constraints on the bar need to be considered. Since node i is fixed to the wall, $u_{1}$ is zero. Further, there is a reaction force $F_{r}$ acting at node $i$ fromthe wall to keep the bar at its equilibrium. Incorporating those two conditions into Eqn (2.1.14) yields


$$

\left(\begin{array}{cc}
1000 & -1000 \\
-1000 & 1000
\end{array}\right)\binom{0}{u*{2}}=\binom{F*{r}}{100}

$$

and


$$

\begin{aligned}
& u*{2}=0.1 \mathrm{~mm} \\
& F*{r}=-100 \mathrm{~N}
\end{aligned}

$$

The strain in the bar can be obtained using Equation (6.7)


$$

\varepsilon=0.1 / 100=0.001

$$

and the stress is calculated with Hooke's law


$$

\sigma=E \varepsilon=10,000 \times 0.001=10 \mathrm{MPa}

$$

In fact, the stress can directly be calculated by definition for this simple one-dimensional problem


$$

\sigma=F / A=100 / 10=10 \mathrm{MPa}

$$

As shown from the above steps, for stress-strain type problems in a conservative structural system, the first task is to obtain an expression of the potential energy for the system. Next, we obtain the stiffness equations by applying the principle of minimum potential energy to the system. Solving these equations will give the stress-strain and displacement results. The following section briefly discusses the general forms of system equations for various problems that design engineers frequently face.

# 6.1.2 System Equations

A general equation of equilibrium can be written as follows


$$

[M]\{\ddot{u}\}+[B]\{\dot{u}\}+[K]\{u\}=\{P\}+\{N\}

$$

where $[M],[B]$ and $[k]$ are the mass, damping and stiffness matrices, and $\{P\}$ and $\{N\}$ denote static and time-dependent linear or nonlinear loads applied to the system, respectively. $\{u\}$ is the displacement vector. As we shall see, many engineering problems are simply special cases of Equation 6.16.

## Linear statics

When nonlinear or time-dependent loads do not present, and the system's inertia is neglected, the system is in static state and Eqn (6.16) reduces to


$$

\{K\}\{u\}=\{P\}

$$

This is the stiffness equation that is used in the above bar problem.

## Elastic buckling

Generally, the stiffness matrix $[K]$ consists of both elastic and geometric stiffness terms, namely, $[K]=\left[K_{e}\right]+\left[K_{g}\right]$. The elastic components are related to material properties, whereas the geometric components are associated with element geometry.

For elastic buckling, the equation becomes


$$

\left[K+\lambda K_{g}\right]\{u\}=0
$$where $\lambda$ is the magnification factor of the applied load. The smallest value for $\lambda$ determines the first buckling mode.

# Eigenvalues

If there are no loads and damping, and the structural displacement is of sinusoidal type, namely

$$
\{u\}=\{\varnothing\} \cos (\omega t)
$$

where $\varnothing$ is a vector commonly referred to as eigenvector. When this is the case, Eqn (6.16) reduces to

$$
[K-\lambda M]\{\varnothing\}=0
$$

where $\lambda=\omega^{2}$ is the eigenvalue. Solving eigenvalue problem is the basis for extraction of natural frequencies of a structure.

## Frequency response

If a structure is subject to sinusoidal time loads, and there are no nonlinear loads, the general equation becomes

$$
\left[-M \omega^{2}+i B \omega+K\right]\{u\}=[P]
$$

where $i$ is the unit imaginary number for a $90^{\circ}$ phase relationship. Note that in frequency response each load may be at an arbitrary phase angle, whereas in eigenvalue analysis the phase relationship is required to be the same.

## Linear transient response

When the material of the structure obeys Hooke's law, and there are no nonlinear loads applied to the structure, the general equation reduces to

$$
\left[M d^{2} / d t^{2}+B d / d t+K\right]\{u(t)\}=\{P(t)\}
$$

Equation (6.22) is the basis for two types of transient response analysis, i.e., direct transient response and modal transient response. The former solves the discretized form of Eqn (6.22) using all the degrees-of-freedom (dof) in the model, whereas the latter first extracts the eigenvalues and eigenvectors, and then integrates Equation (6.22) using every natural frequency and eigenvector as a dof. The time-dependent load is sampled with a small time step during the structural response analysis.

## Thermal system equations

A general form of thermal system equation can be written as

$$
[B]\{\uparrow\}+[K]\{T\}+[R]\{T\}^{4}=\{P\}+\{N\}
$$

where
$[B]=$ thermal capacity coefficient matrix
$[K]=$ combined conduction and convection coefficient matrix
$[R]=$ radiation matrix
$\{P\}=$ time-dependent heat flux
$\{N\}=$ temperature-dependent heat flux
$\{T\}=$ absolute temperature
For thermal analysis, no term with second-order time derivative presents in the system equation.# 6.1.3 Types of Elements

As mentioned earlier, when modeling any physical structure using FEA, the geometry is split into elements. Each element is the computational unit upon which the solutions of the system equations depend. Thus choosing appropriate elements for discretizing the model is an important step. If this step is not properly done, the analysis results could have large errors or even be completely misleading.

Generally speaking, there are five types of basic elements and each may have its own variations. Table 6.1 lists these basic elements. However, detailed explanations of each element type are beyond the scope of this discussion and the reader may wish to refer to one of the many referenced on FEA.

With major commercial FEA packages, users can choose from over 100 different types of elements. Depending on the problem to be analyzed, the engineer needs to narrow down the choices of elements, and pick the most suitable ones. Often this selection process requires a user to have a good understanding of the basic underlying principles and a reasonable prediction of what is going to happen in the problem set up for analysis. This step affects both solving process and the output. If selections are well made, not only can the solving procedures be simplified, but the results will be more accurate.

The first- and second-order elements are more frequently used than higher order elements in FEA modeling. In certain cases, higher order elements may deliver better results at the expense of larger model and longer solving time. Among the high order elements, the p-element is the one that is worth noting. Instead of using first- or second-order polynomials to describe the spatial dependence of solution variables within the element volume, p-elements use much higher order polynomials, for example, $p=8$. In an FEA model, p-elements with different orders of polynomials can be intermixed, thus providing great modeling flexibility. A very useful function of p-elements is the improvement of modeling accuracy. By varying the polynomial order, p-elements offer an easy way for improving accuracy of initial analysis

Table 6.1 The basic elements

| Dimensionality | Type                                                         | Geometry                  |
| :------------- | :----------------------------------------------------------- | :------------------------ |
| Point          | Mass                                                         | $\bullet$                 |
| Line           | Spring, beam, bar, gap, torsion                              | $\bullet \longrightarrow$ |
| Area           | 2D continuum, axisymmetric, <br> continuum plate, flat shell |                           |

| Curved area | Generalized shell |     |
| :---------- | :---------------- | :-- |
|             |                   |     |

Volume 3D continuum
without having to re-mesh. With p-elements, the iterative convergence and accuracy can be assessed by generating error estimates for a series of solutions with different p-order. Another feature is that the p-elements can handle shape distortion well, thus making the meshing job easier and reducing the need for remeshing. However, using high order pelements is expensive. When p-elements are used, the system matrices are no longer sparse and may contain large numbers of nonzero terms just for a single element. This will require much longer time for solving the equations. There are other limitations relating to the use of p-elements, such as severe discontinuities and nonlinearities.

# 6.2 Accuracy: Element, Mesh, Boundary Conditions and Material Properties

It was already discussed earlier that the accuracy of FEA results using commercial packages is a critical issue for the engineer, since the advancement of computer graphics technologies have enabled many 'non-FEA analysts' to perform various types of analyses and produce impressive graphical outputs. For any FEA work, attention must be paid to accuracy of results and interpretation of results. The former is determined by the reasonableness of the model set up, whereas the latter typically requires the analyst to have an in-depth knowledge of basic principles and a good insight into the problem analyzed. This section focuses on the first aspect. The second one is beyond the scope of this book.

In the following discussions, the error sources identified are from element selection, mesh geometry, boundary conditions in the model, and material properties used in the analysis. Numerical precision related errors caused by the computer algorithm utilized in the FEA software are usually very small and will not be included in the discussion.

### 6.2.I Errors Due to Element Selection

As an FEA software package user, one must remember that, although there are many options in selecting elements to be used for a particular model, not all elements are created equal. Some elements are more accurate than others. Even for a given element, the accuracy is not always the same in different applications. The second point is easier to understand because many elements were originally introduced for analyzing certain physical processes, such as acoustic elements or membrane elements. To illustrate the first point, let us use a simple example of static stress problem.

Figure 6.2 shows a simple cantilever beam, which is 200 units long, 50 units wide and 5 units thick. It is fully built-in at one end and a static point load, $P=1200$ units, is applied in the direction of its thickness, to the other end. Let's assume the cantilever beam is elastic with a Young's modulus of $2 \times 10^{5}$ units, and a Poisson's ratio of 0.3 .

From elastic beam bending theory, the strain energy in the bent beam is

$$
U=\int_{0}^{L} \frac{M^{2}}{2 E I} d x
$$

where $M$ is bending moment and $I$ is moment of inertia. In this case

$$
M=P x
$$

Substituting Eqn (6.24) into (6.23) gives

$$
U=\int_{0}^{L} \frac{P^{2}}{2 E I} x 2 d x=\frac{P^{2} L^{3}}{6 E I}
$$

Figure 6.2 A simple built in cantilever beam under bending force $P$. The results of analyzing this simple structure with various elements us shown in Table 4.

The maximum deflection at the tip can be found using Castigliano's theorem

$$
\delta=\frac{\partial U}{\partial P}=\frac{P L^{3}}{3 E I}=\frac{4 P L^{3}}{E b h^{3}}
$$

With the above values, the maximum deflection is 30.72 units.
The maximum stress occurs along the built-in end and the analytical solution is

$$
\sigma_{\max }=\frac{M d}{I}=\frac{6 P L}{b h^{2}}
$$

where $d$ is the distance measured from the neutral axis. The value of the maximum stress is 1152 units. These stress and deflection results may be considered exact deterministic solutions. With the commercial FEA package ABAQUS, several different types of elements and mesh densities were used to model the above beam. The FEA results are summarized in Table 6.2.

From the results in Table 6.2, it is clearly demonstrated that the selection of proper elements for modeling is of critical importance. Huge errors could be induced when inappropriate elements are used in the analysis. In most practical applications, the system is complicated and a theoretical solution that can be used to check the FEA results is not possible to obtain. Therefore the accuracy of the FEA results is in the hands of the software user who is expected to know the behavior of various elements very well. An experienced user is guided, perhaps intuitively, by some rules that he or she has acquired. Examples of these rules may include:

- Avoid constant strain triangles in a bending problem
- Avoid large aspect ratios, severe tapers, and large skew angles in quadrilateral elements
- Avoid known deficiencies of particular elements

If learned only by rote, there is little chance that the user will be able to apply them successfully to new and complex problems. In other words, the user needs to have an appreciation for the reasons behind those rules in order to build a good FEA model and deliver reasonable results.Table 6.2 Comparison of FEA with different elements

# 6.2.2 Errors Due to Mesh

Even if the selection of elements is proper, unacceptable errors could still occur because of the meshing procedure for the object under analysis. As has been described earlier, each element is a divided region of the structure or geometry and the mesh is the total collection of the elements. It is not enough to only take care of the small regions. There are many global issues that need special attention, such as the correct way to put all the right elements together.

One of the most fundamental issues is the density of the mesh. If it is too coarse, the accuracy of the results will be in question. However, time and cost penalties will occur if the mesh is unnecessarily too fine. If the use of use the FEA tool is to be practical engineering design, not to perform an academic numerical analysis, an optimized mesh will reasonably ensure the accuracy of the final results, while requiring a reasonable amount of time to solve. Overly fine meshes, significantly increase the degrees of freedom ( $d o f$ ) in the model and the computational time becomes too long to be practical. It is the author's experience and observation that, in most engineering designs involving FEA work, designers often use very fine meshes, rather than a reasonable coarse mesh, as an assurance for accuracy at higher expenses.

Another reason for using finer mesh as common practice in engineering design is the auto-meshing capability available in commercial FEA packages. While auto-meshing is

Figure 6.3 a Silicon film sensor element with support structure. This assembly was analyzed by eigenvalue extraction for its vibration characteristics using FEA. b Side view of the silicon sensor and support.
convenient in building the model especially for inexperienced users, it commonly has poor control over the variations of mesh density. Often the mesh is too fine across the whole model. In reality, only localized fine mesh is needed based on the rapid gradient changes of the variables to be modeled. Thus the auto-meshing should be used with great care.

Errors can still be induced due to improper meshing even if the above issues are taken care of. Let us illustrate this point with an octagon, thin-film, silicon sensor design. Figure 6.3a and 6.3 b show this silicon sensor design used in spaceflight missions. The thickness of the silicon film is $70 \mu \mathrm{~m}$. For silicon, $\mathrm{E}=161 \mathrm{GPa}, v=0.279$ and $\mathrm{p}=2330 \mathrm{~kg} / \mathrm{m}^{3}$. The circumference of the bottom side of the silicon disk is glued to the solid base made from G-10, and the width and thickness of the glue are 0.8 mm and $60 \mu \mathrm{~m}$ respectively. The modeling task here is to obtain the natural frequencies of the disk ranging from 20 to 1000 Hz .

Once the element type and mesh density have been decided, the silicon disk is meshed as shown in Figure 6.4. It is a quarter-symmetric mesh and generally works well in most FEA models. An eigenvalue extraction procedure gives the following natural frequencies

$$
\begin{aligned}
& f(1)=285.40 \mathrm{~Hz} \\
& f(2)=594.48 \\
& f(3)=595.02 \\
& f(4)=974.39 \\
& f(5)=979.42
\end{aligned}
$$

However, examining the modal shapes corresponding to these frequencies in Figures 6.5a through 6.5 e quickly raises questions about the above results.

Figure 6.4 Quarter symmetric mesh for analysis of the vibration characteristics of the silicon sensor.

Figures 6.5a through 6.5e show two pairs, namely, mode 2 and 3, and mode 4 and 5, which are two-fold degenerate modes. Mathematically, their natural frequencies should be the same, but the above FEA results show frequency splitting. This cannot be true. Recall that the mesh we built for the disk was a quarter-symmetric mesh, and the usual two-fold degenerate modes are rotationally symmetric. This reminds us that a rotationally symmetric mesh may help solve this problem.

A new mesh that is rotationally symmetric is shown in Figure 6.6. Note that the same element type is used and the mesh density is about the same as the quarter-symmetric. We rerun the eigenvalue analysis and it yields the following results:

$$
\begin{aligned}
& f(1)=285.06 \mathrm{~Hz} \\
& f(2)=593.85 \\
& f(3)=593.85 \\
& f(4)=973.26 \\
& f(5)=973.26
\end{aligned}
$$

The new mesh indeed delivers reasonable results as theoretically predicted. This example shows that the FEA errors could be induced by the mesh pattern despite the proper selection of element type and mesh density.

# 6.2.3 Errors Due to Boundary Conditions

No matter how good the model is built, analytical results are highly dependent on the boundary conditions applied to the model. Boundary conditions are required to obtain a unique solution of the system equations. If the boundary conditions were not properly applied, the results will not be accurate. Applying different boundary conditions to the model will give different answers.

Most boundary conditions, such as nodal displacements, force loading, isothermal or convective thermal boundaries, are quite straightforward to apply. However, care must be taken when the boundary conditions are associated with unrestrained rotational dof, thermal radiation, multi-point constraint (MPC), and two-dimensional cross-section analysis of threedimensional structures. Improper setup of these boundary conditions could cause large errors. The following example demonstrates how the boundary conditions affect the FEA results.

Figure 6.5 a Model shape of the sensor. The calculated natural frequency is 285.40 Hz . b Mode 2 shape of the sensor. The calculated natural frequency is $f 594.48 \mathrm{~Hz}$ using the quarter symmetric mesh. Compare to 6.5 c . The natural frequency should be equivalent. c Mode 3 shape of the sensor. The calculated natural frequency is 595.02 Hz using the quarter symmetric mesh. Compare to 6.5 b . The natural frequency should be equivalent. d Mode 4 shape of the sensor. The calculated natural frequency is 974.39 Hz using the quarter symmetric mesh. Compare to 6.5 e . The natural frequency should be equivalent. e Mode 5 shape of the sensor. The calculated natural frequency is 979.42 Hz using the quarter symmetric mesh. Compare to 6.5 d . The natural frequency should be equivalent.

Figure 6.6 A rotationally symmetric mesh for the silicon sensor that corrects the error in the natural frequency calculation for the degenerate pairs: Modes 3 and 4 and Modes 4 and 5.

Let us again perform an eigenvalue analysis for a bare circuit card, as shown in Figure 6.7. A multiple-pin connector fixes the left side of the card, and two 5-piece wedge locks restrain the top and bottom edges. The card thickness is 2.0 mm . Assuming $\mathrm{E}=60 \mathrm{GPa}, v=0.32$ and $\mathrm{p}=2700 \mathrm{~kg} / \mathrm{m}^{3}$.

In the first run of the analysis, the wedge lock edges are treated as totally fixed. This is the common way of modeling wedge locks in practice, for simplicity. Thus three edges of the card are totally restrained and only one edge is free. Figure 6.8 plots the fundamental mode, under the boundary conditions. The resonant frequency is 727.9 Hz .

However, recent studies have concluded that treating wedge locked edges, as totally fixed is incorrect (Fan and Niemeyer 1997 and Barker 1992). A typical multiple-piece wedge lock provides a fixity to the circuit card edge, somewhere between simple support and total fix.

Figure 6.7 Diagram of a printed wiring board assembly employing wedge locks to support its edges. The connector edge remains free.

Figure 6.8 Vibration characteristics of the assembly in Figure 6.7. The calculated resonant frequency for the case of fixed edges, used to represent the wedge locks, is 729.9 Hz .

The fixity depends on several variables, such as number of pieces of the wedge lock and the torque of tightening the locking screws. For situations like this, regular displacement boundary constraints are invalid and spring elements with rotational stiffness must be introduced into the wedge locked edge of the model. The rotational stiffness of the spring element is then directly related to the fixity of the wedge lock, and determination of this stiffness is the key to accurate modelling of the wedge lock. This is an important step in the dynamic analysis because the fixity of the card edge plays an essential role in dynamic responses of the circuit card.

To account for the effect of the two wedge locks, the eigenvalue analysis should be rerun with the following conditions along the wedge-locked edges

$$
\begin{aligned}
& D_{x}=D_{y}=D_{z}=0 \\
& R_{x}=\beta, R_{y}=R_{z}=0
\end{aligned}
$$

where $P$ is the rotational stiffness with a units of $\mathrm{N} / \mathrm{rad}$.
For this purpose, we introduce a non-dimensional rotational stiffness $K$, where

$$
K=\beta(a / D)
$$

$a$ is the card lateral length, and $D$ is the card flexural rigidity defined as

$$
D=\frac{E h^{3}}{12\left(1-v^{2}\right)}
$$

$h$ being the card thickness. Using the above values, $D$ is found to be $44.56 \mathrm{~N}-\mathrm{m}$.
For this type of wedge lock, $K$ has been determined to be 4 (Fan and Neimeyer 1997). Hence:

$$
\beta=K D / a=990.2(\mathrm{~N} / \mathrm{rad})
$$

Returning to the eigenvalue analysis, with this rotational stiffness value, yields the fundamental frequency of 348.4 Hz . The modal shape is shown in Figure 6.9. The validity of using such a boundary constraint for modeling typical wedge locks has been confirmed in several studies (Fan and Niemeyer 1997). One can see that, with different boundary treatment, for wedge-locked edges, the difference between the two resonant frequencies is substantial.

Figure 6.9 Vibration characteristics of the assembly in Figure 6.7 with modified boundary conditions. The calculated resonant frequency for the case of wedge lock edge model, with lower fixity, is dramatically different at 348.4 Hz .

# 6.2.4 Errors Due to Material Properties

FEA users must be well aware of the importance of using good property data for the materials involved in the analysis. A wealth of property data for common engineering materials can be found in various handbooks. Major problems for the users in this area include:

- new materials that have not been well characterized
- nonlinear properties such as temperature-dependency
- materials with the feature of rate dependency

If the quality of property data is poor for any given material, the FEA outputs are usually meaningless and should not be used for design purposes. Without reasonable materials data perhaps is better not to run an analysis. A more common situation is that available data are good only at the room temperature. However, the design application involves large temperature variations. Quite often we see analyzes performed based on the room temperature data, and the results are mistakenly applied to high or low temperature regions. Depending on the materials, this practice could cause enormous errors in FEA results, if the temperature dependence of the property data is not taken into consideration. These are called data-related errors, since the main source of error is from the materials data. The errors can be minimized, if good property measurements are taken. It is not uncommon that the cost of data measurement is much higher than that of FEA analysis, mainly because many measurements require sophisticated or specialized instruments.

Another source of error related to the materials is model-related, namely, the accuracy of the modeling results depends on the constitutive model of the material to be used in the design. For instance, a mechanical component made from standard structural steel may be reasonably treated as linear elastic with no temperature dependence for routine design. But if the component is subject to a severe overload, it is necessary to analyze how it may deform under the given load, and whether the material has enough ductility to withstand the load without catastrophic failure. In this situation, a metal plasticity model must be included inthe modeling and a nonlinear analysis is needed. If the structure under that load might buckle or undergo large geometry changes, the geometric nonlinearity must be considered.

Furthermore, if a severe overload occurrs, suddenly inducing rapid straining in the structure, the inelastic response of the metal could exhibit strain rate dependence. In such circumstances, a rate dependent plasticity model should be incorporated into the FEA. It is sometimes argued that the rate dependency can be ignored as a conservative analysis, because it has a strengthening effect. This argument in general is undoubtedly wrong, since strengthening of one part of the structure could cause the load to be shed to another part, which proves to be weaker in the event. Depending on the event to be modeled, the material constitutive model can be from simple nonlinear to a more complex type. For the latter case, a good example is if the component is failing by wear out, rather than a sudden overload, because of creep at elevated temperatures, low cycle fatigue, or a combination of both. The structural response during several loading cycles, in which a certain amount of inelastic deformation would be accumulated, must be modelled. This modeling can be difficult and tedious, but it is necessary to model wear out conditions.

At elevated temperatures, both metallic and nonmetallic materials exhibit creep phenomenon. For metals, creep occurs when temperature is above its recrystallization temperature at which the atoms are quite mobile. It is characterized by the fact that most of the structural deformation is irreversible. If creep is maintained for a sufficiently longtime, excessive deformation (creep failure) or fracture (creep fracture) will occur. It is therefore critical to include a proper creep model when the application temperature is sufficiently high, in relation to the melting temperature.

Nonmetals, such as glass and polymers, also creep at high temperatures. However, the mechanical behavior of these nonmetallic materials during creep is somewhat simpler than that of metals. This is mainly because these nonmetals are more isotropic than metals and large creep strains are needed in order to induce anisotropy in them. A unique feature of these nonmetals is the rate dependent viscoelastic behavior, which should be incorporated into the modeling. Note that the creep behavior for other nonmetals, such as concrete, asphalt and wood, is highly complex.

To give readers a general idea about constitutive models of materials, two commonly used equations are shown below.

# Deformation Plasticity

Plastic deformation of a metal can be modeled by the the Ramberg-Osgood model:

$$
E \varepsilon=\sigma+\alpha\left(\frac{|\sigma|}{\sigma_{0}}\right)^{n-1} \sigma
$$

where $\alpha$ is the yield offset, $\sigma_{0}$ is the yield stress, and n is the hardening exponent $(n \geq 1)$.
This model can be generalized to multi-axial stress states using Hooke's law for the linear term, and the von Mises stress potential and associated flow laws for the nonlinear term

$$
E \varepsilon=(1+v) S-(1-2 v) p I+(3 / 2) \alpha\left(q / \sigma_{0}\right)^{n-1} S
$$

where
$\varepsilon$ is the strain tensor
$\sigma$ is the stress tensor
$p=-(1 / 3): \mathrm{I}$ is the equivalent hydrostatic stress
$q=[(3 / 2) \mathrm{S}]^{0.5}$ : is the Mises equivalent stress
$S=\sigma+p I$ is the stress deviator
This model is generally good for static loading cases, where the displacements are small.Table 6.3 Units for common varibles

# Metal Creep

One constitutive relation for creep is the Feltham model:

$$
\boldsymbol{\ell}_{c r}=A[\sinh (B q)]^{n} \exp \left(-\frac{Q}{R T}\right)
$$

where $\boldsymbol{\ell}_{c r}$ is the creep strain rate, $q$ is the uniaxial equivalent deviatoric stress, $T$ is temperature, in absolute scale, and $A, B, Q, n$ and $R$ are material parameters.

Finally, it is of great importance to unify the consistency of all the units of any quantities involved in the modeling. Almost all the commercial FEA packages are developed with units neutral, meaning that it is user's responsibility to use consistent units throughout the analysis. Users of most FEA packages can freely choose the basic set of units to make the modeling easier, but any inconsistent units used during the analysis will produce wrong results. Table 6.3 lists the commonly used quantities in various FEA problems in both SI and English units.

### 6.3 Applications in Reliability Assessment

In this section, we discuss practical FEA design and development problems, encountered frequently. We will examine a specific problem for microelectronics-heat dissipation and thermo-mechanical stress evaluations for a GaAs power monolithic microwave integrated circuit or MMIC device. We will treat all quantities in this analysis as deterministic, in order for us to focus on the application of analysis procedures. The modeling object has been modified and simplified, due to proprietary data restrictions, but no generality of FEA application, for such a reliability assessment, is lost.Power MMIC devices differ from the small signal devices mainly in that they dissipate higher power, within several very tiny regions of current flow called channels. Understanding the thermal characteristics of MMIC devices is essential because temperature variations will influence the operation of the circuits in terms of performance parameters, such as gain and efficiency. High operating temperatures can also severely limit the lifetime of the devices, or even catastrophically damage the device. Thus, designing a thermal environment, so that normal device temperatures under bias are maintained at specified levels, is critical for a MMIC designer to produce both reliable and cost effective circuits.

The primary goal of MMIC thermal design is to provide a means by which the dissipated heat can be carried away. This requires a low thermal resistance between the heat generation channels and the heat sink, which is usually a high conductivity metallic carrier, to which the GaAs chip is attached by a high conductivity bonding material. In most cases, the highest channel temperature is required to be below $125^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ in order to avoid the risk of failure by thermal runaway and to provide adequate overall reliability. Generally, the larger (or thicker) the heat sink is, the lower the channel temperature will be. Over design of the heat sink is not recommended, because of penalties associated with weight, volume and cost.

Figure 6.10 shows a typical MMIC power amplifier testing assembly. The test heat sink dimensions (length and width) are the maximum allowed values, because of the limitation of the real metal package. However, the thickness can be varied as a thermal design parameter. The material for the heat sink is Cu (hard temper alloy C10100). Some circuit details are illustrated in Figure 6.11.

There are two symmetric field effect transistors (FETs) on the chip: an input stage with 6 channels, and an output stage with 6 channels, as well. These structures are simplified to demonstrate FEA applications. Each channel has a width of $4 \mu \mathrm{~m}$, and a length of $100 \mu \mathrm{~m}$. The center to center spacing between any two adjacent channels is $100 \mu \mathrm{~m}$. The chip bonding material is standard $\mathrm{Au}-\mathrm{Sn}(80: 20)$ eutectic with a thickness of $25 \mu \mathrm{~m}$. Under a normal operating condition, the total power dissipation, which includes DC and RF components, is 4.0 W that is equally distributed in these channels. The testing assembly is placed on a flat plate of which the surface temperature can be controlled, as shown in Figure 6.10.

A three-dimensional one-quarter FEA model for this assembly has been developed with 5596 solid elements (Fig. 6.12a and 6.12b). Note that fine meshes are used only in power dissipating channel regions in order to obtain good resolution of the temperature gradient. For simplicity, the surface temperature of the base plate is controlled at $0^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$. Measurements in the

Figure 6.11 FET locations on the chip surface for the GaAs MMIC shown in Figure 6.10.
lab showed that if the base plate temperature is uncontrolled (initially at room temperature), the bottom temperature of the Cu heat sink was about $29^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ when the MMIC chip was operating at full power ( 4.0 W ). The maximum channel temperature under full power condition needs to be determined using FEA modeling.

Table 6.4 lists the material properties used for the modeling. A steady-state heat conduction analysis was performed and the temperature distributions of the chip are shown in Figure 6.13. The maximum channel temperature in Figure 6.13 is $89.7^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$. With this peak temperature value, the combined thermal resistance for this device can be estimated through the following expression:

$$
T_{\text {channel }}-T_{\text {bottom }}=P \sum \theta_{1}
$$

where $P$ is the full power and $\sum \theta_{1}$ is the total thermal resistance including the components of chip, bonding material and heat sink. Using the above values, the total thermal resistance is found to be $22.4^{\circ} \mathrm{C} / \mathrm{W}$. Note that this resistance is the sum of the three components, or overall resistance. Discussions relating to the estimate of each resistance component can be found in Fan (1992).

The overall thermal resistance for this assembly provides a convenient way to estimate the maximum channel temperature under any thermal environment. All we need to do is measure the temperature at the bottom of the heat sink, which is a relatively easy task. For instance, when the temperature of the flat plate is uncontrolled and the surface temperature is about $29^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ under full power operation, the maximum channel temperature obtained is $118.7^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$, using Equation (6.32). This temperature is still under the $125^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ limit, indicating a satisfactory thermal design for this particular ambient environment, although it is quite close to the limit. Nevertheless, good designs are environment dependent, i.e., the current

Through this example of thermal analysis, we can see that the overall thermal resistance is a key parameter for the design. Assuming structural and geometric variations are not significant and the thermal properties do not change over the working range of temperature, the total resistance approaches a constant. A good thermal design is one in which the overall thermal resistance along the heat transfer path is controlled, so that the maximum allowed temperature will not be exceeded for a given application environment. In actuality, it is desirable to evaluate the impact of variability in the parameters, whenever possible, through the use of the methods in this text.

Figure 6.13 Chip temperature distribution for the surface of the MMIC device shown in Figure 6.10.

In space flight or military applications, MMIC devices are required to go through a series of strict pre-deployment qualification tests, one of which is the thermal chamber cycling test. In this case, a certain number of temperature cycles ranging from $-55^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ to $125^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ are applied to the device assembly in the power off state. Detailed inspections are conducted after the test to ensure survivability and reliability for the field use. Due to high strength and stiffness of hard solders commonly used in MMICs, such as $\mathrm{Au}-\mathrm{Sn}, \mathrm{Au}-\mathrm{Si}$ or $\mathrm{Au}-\mathrm{Ge}$, a typical failure during thermal cycling is an overstress in which the GaAs chip cracks. This problem is magnified if the bonding layer is not uniform. However, producing relatively uniform bonding with hard solders is no longer a major technical problem, in most manufacturing environments, at present.

To evaluate the maximum stress in the GaAs chip during thermal cycling, we may conduct a thermal stress analysis with FEA. Because the power is off during the test, the concentrated heat dissipating regions are no longer significant in the thermal stress analysis. Thus we may build a one-quarter model with less elements so that the solving time can be reduced, as shown in Figure 6.14. Two issues based on the knowledge of static stress analysis were taken into consideration when building the stress model in Fig.6.14. First, the high stress region in the GaAs chip due to thermal mismatch with the hard solder must occur in the corner of the chip; secondly, the highest stress around the corner of the chip must be close to the interface of the solder. Thus, the relatively dense mesh is used around the corner of the chip only. Since

The one-quarter symmetry necessitates two symmetric boundary conditions along the two intersecting planes.

Figure 6.16 shows the distribution of maximum principal stress in the GaAs chip at $125^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ The highest stress occurs around the corner of the chip near the solder interface, which is found to be 128 MPa . Since the ultimate tensile strength for GaAs is 145 MPa , this chip is

In Figure 6.17, cyclic change of the maximum principal stress with the temperature is plotted.To remove large heat dissipation from MMIC circuitry, hard solders with high thermal conductivity are commonly used in practice. However, hard solders lacking any plastic deformation cause high stresses in the GaAs chip. This has caused many documented cases where the thermal stresses exceed the toughness of GaAs , resulting in microscopic defects in the material propagating into large cracks. Also such solders are not desirable for uniplanar GaAs MMICs, because of electromagnetic interference (EMI) between the solder and the coplanar wave-guides on the top surface of the chip, which reduces performance.

A possible solution is to use epoxy resin bonding, which presents no EMI problem, and does not require costly backside metallization. The problem with epoxy resin is its low thermal conductivity, that contributes to a large thermal resistance, causing potential thermal runaway. To circumvent this thermal problem, a recent study suggested using thicker GaAs chips, when epoxy resin is used for chip attachment (Nishihori et. al. 1997).

It was found that thermal resistance decreases with the increase of the chip thickness if epoxy resin is used, but thermal resistance increases with the increase of the chip thickness if using hard solder. By increasing the chip thickness from $150 \mu \mathrm{~m}$ to $250 \mu \mathrm{~m}$, using either bonding material resulted in nearly identical thermal resistance, which is sufficiently low for safe operation. Additionally, using epoxy resin as chip attachment can significantly reduce the risk of chip cracking.

As we can see from our discussions, many problems are faced in development. FEA provides a valuable tool for integration into design and reliability assessment. However, we must use this tool with some discretion, as we have discussed. Additional case studies are presented in Chapter 14, which employ FEA. In the next section, we discuss validation of FEA models through measurement of stresses and gradients, with whole field optical methods.

# 6.4 Whole Field Optical Stress Measurement for Model Validation

At this point, we have reviewed for the reader the fundamental application of finite element models. It is essential to reliability assessment and good design to understand the factors concerning accuracy and interpretation of modeling. Model validation is equally important. Experimental methods can be coupled with finite element modeling leading to a full understanding of the effects of loads applied to components. Optical methods have come to forefront, as they provide whole field measurements, that can be easily compared to a finite element analysis. Optical methods can be employed for mechanical stress analysis, as well as thermal loading and temperature distribution measurements.

Optical methods, in addition to providing a whole field view of the component stresses, offer several other advantages. Modern systems have become compact and easy to operate. In addition, software packages simplify the analytical processes necessary for reduction of the data. However, depending on the type of system, various limitations must be considered. As an example, various types of systems may have limitations concerning the size of components and resolution of the measurement.

Two of the most useful optical techniques are laser holography, using Electronic Speckle Pattern Interferometry (ESPI) for mechanical deformation measurements and infrared thermal imaging for spatial temperature distribution measurements. These whole field optical techniques are briefly explained and an example of each method is shown. Further information can be gained by consulting the references.# 6.4.I Laser Holography

Laser holography by electronic speckle pattern interferometry (ESPI) uses the principle of interference of coherent laser light. The object to be analyzed is entirely illuminated with laser light. The image of the object is recorded by a video camera. The light waves, which are reflected at single points on the object's surface, interfere and produce a speckle pattern. This represents the object's surface in combined form. A reference light superposes this speckle pattern. The interference between the reference light and the speckle pattern produces a new speckle pattern that contains the information about the shape and position of the object's surface. This speckle pattern is then stored in the image-processing computer as a reference image. The optical set up for an ESPI device is shown in Figure 6.18.

When measuring by ESPI, a small amount of the laser light is coupled out of the object illumination and directly guided to the camera. There, it is superposed with the light reflected from the object's surface. Object and reference light have passed through different path lengths from the laser to the camera. This produces a phase difference between both light waves, $\varnothing$. This phase difference produces the interference effects, which are recorded by the camera as the speckle pattern. When the object is moving, the light path, via the object's surface to the camera, changes and produces a new phase relation to the fixed reference light, $\varnothing+\Delta$. The difference between both states is the change of the object light path during the measurement. This is represented in correlation fringes. By counting the number of fringes, $N$, at every object point, the deformation of the object's surface, in the measuring direction is obtained in fractions of the laser wavelength. The measuring direction is in the center between the illumination and observation directions as shown in Figure 6.18

The measuring sensitivity can be calculated by the following formula:

$$
d=N \lambda 2 \cos (\alpha / 2)
$$

where:
$d=$ deformation component of the object point in the measuring direction
$N=$ fringe order at the measuring point
$\lambda=$ wavelength of the laser light
$\alpha=$ angle between the illumination and observation directions

Figure 6.18 Optical arrangement and principle of laser holography by ESPI. (Courtesy of Ettemeyer Qualitatssicherung)A complete speckle measuring system consists of the following components:

- the speckle sensor for the desired application
- the control and evaluation system
- the measuring and evaluation software

With the ESPI sensor, non-contact, full field deformation analysis can be provided. The sensor is applied in the case where full field and highly sensitive measuring information is required about the mechanical behavior of the components. As we have emphasized, the full field measurement offers great potential for comparison and verification of FEA, with the experiment. Models are then validated which extends their range of application and confidence in their results.

Sensors of this type are small and lightweight, which enables easy mounting. In the case of ESPI, vibration isolation can be avoided that is otherwise required for other optical methods. Systems of this type are generally rugged and easy to operate. Measuring sensitivity is about $0.1 \mu \mathrm{~m}$ with a measuring area up to $300 \times 400 \mu \mathrm{~m}$. The image analysis process is simplified with software.

As an example of the application of this technique, examine the component shown in Figure 6.20. This is a lifting lug for a large cast iron storage container for the transport of nuclear materials. The lug is being loaded by applying the force shown, in a laboratory environment.

The deformations were measured using an ESPI system similar to the arrangement in Figures 6.18 and 6.19. Deformations were measured in all three directions. As an example, the out-of-plane deformations are shown in Figure 6.21.

# 6.4.2 Infrared Thermal Imaging

Infrared thermal imaging can provide a whole field perspective of temperature distribution in a component under thermal loading. It provides a means of directly measuring temperature and spatial thermal gradients, when the technique is properly calibrated. Images thencan be directly compared to thermal finite element analysis. Instrumentation can be fitted to a microscope to provide micro-thermal images of electronic devices under operation, with a temperature resolution of approximately $0.02^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$.

Infrared imaging employs optics with detectors comprised of infrared sensitive arrays of Indium Antimonide or Mercury Cadmium Telluride. These sensor arrays can be cooled to liquid nitrogen temperatures to improve their sensitivity and spatial resolution for microscopy. Lens materials for infrared optical systems must be transparent to the infrared wavelength. They are usually manufactured from silicon, germanium, sapphire or zinc selenide.

The concept of infrared imaging is based upon the principles of radiation physics. In accordance with Plank's Law, all bodies emit thermal radiation as the temperature increases above absolute zero. Let's consider an object that is perfectly efficient in absorbing radiation. An object of this sort is referred to as a blackbody, as it will not reflect any visible light. Therefore, all radiation emanating from a blackbody is thermal.

Plank's Law states the magnitude of the emitted energy is then:

$$
Q=\frac{2 \pi c}{\lambda^{4}} \frac{1}{e^{\hbar / / \lambda T}-1}
$$

where $Q$ is the energy emitted in photons per second per $\mathrm{cm}^{3}$ at an absolute temperature $T$, where:

$$
\begin{aligned}
h^{\prime} & =\text { Plank's Constant } \\
k & =\text { Boltmann's Constant } \\
c & =\text { velocity of light } \\
\lambda & =\text { wavelength of emitted radiation }
\end{aligned}
$$

Infrared emissions within the measuring range of most applications are between $3-14 \mu \mathrm{~m}$ (Hudson 1969).

All bodies are not perfect emitters of thermal energy. We must consider the emissivity of the source of the radiation in order to estimate its temperature from Plank's Law. Emissivity is defined as the ratio of energy emitted, to that of a blackbody, at the same temperature. The emissivity is a material property and is a function of the wavelength of the emitted radiation.

As an example, consider a silicon microcircuit with aluminum conductors. The emissivity of aluminum in this application is about 0.1 . This is about half that of silicon. Appropriate considerations and emissivity corrections must be made in order to apply Plank's law to determine the surface temperature of the semiconductor device. In addition, background radiation from the surrounding environment must be compensated for, to achieve accuracy. Fortunately, elevating the component temperature above the ambient temperature reduces the effects of ambient radiation.

In thermal microscopy of semiconductor devices, for example, highly accurate temperature measurements are achieved by applying a pixel by pixel emissivity correction to a thermal image of the component (Macdonald and Albright 1997). A device is mounted on an opaque thermoelectric heated stage. Measurements are conducted on devices in the off states, at two elevated temperatures. The emissivity is then accurately determined without errors introduced from ambient conditions.

The device is then electrically operated and the operational temperatures and thermal gradients are easily correlated to the thermal image using the emissivities of the surface and Plank's Law. Software drives the calculation and whole field thermal images are then displayed with a spatial accuracy of about 5 microns.

Figure 6.23 Car audio system set up for thermal imaging during operation.(Courtesy of Daewoo Electronics Ltd.)

As an example of the application of thermal imaging, we can examine Figures 6.23 and 6.24. In Figure 6.23 we see a car audio system. Of concern are the operation temperatures and thermal gradients around the power integrated circuit near the heat sink, at the lower part of the image.

In Figure 6.24, we see the corresponding infrared images, at different times after powering on the system. The thermal gradients are clearly apparent from the image. As time progresses, we can see the steady state conditions, including the temperature distributions surrounding the finned heat sink. The spatial distribution of temperatures can be correlated to finite element simulations of this test to optimize the heat sink design and placement of components, which may significantly improve reliability by reducing thermal gradients and absolute operational temperatures.

# 6.5 Summary

Finite element analysis has become a very important aspect of system and component design and analysis. It can provide significant information regarding the magnitude and distribution of stresses in components under a variety of loads. Temperature distributions, stress, displacement and vibrational modes in components can be determined from finite element analysis, under thermal and mechanical loading. This information is then a critical part of determining the life and reliability of a component design in a given application. In addition, a validated model can be used to explore corrective action, design improvement and optimization.

For the non-expert, we have provided an understanding of the analysis process using a simple one-dimensional approach. However, the focus of this chapter is in the application of this method. Hence, we have presented information concerning errors and interpretation, as well as whole field methods of validation, along with several examples for structural and thermal modeling.

Figure 6.24 Infrared images of the car audio system shown in Figure 6.23. The images are at different times from the initial power on. Steady state is shown in the lower right. (Courtesy of Daewoo Electronics Ltd.)

# 6.6 Do's and Dont's in Design

Do carefully consider the following in FEM analysis and interpretation:

- Boundary Conditions
- Element Type and Mesh
- Material Properties

Do carefully consider the assumptions of the analysis, related to the above bullets.
Do carefully consider the appropriate constitutive models for the materials and conditions.
Do apply experimental methods to validate FEM.
Do apply whole field methods for validation of thermal gradients and mechanical deformation patterns.
Do test materials properties for new materials.Do not forget to check all assumptions comprising a FEM model when interpreting the results. Do not oversimplify:

- Time dependent creep
- Plastic behavior
- Boundary conditions

Do not forget Golomb's Rule of Modeling: We don't eat the menu.
