John W. Evans and Sun-wook Kim

Corrosion is the third of the four major categories of failures, which we will discuss. It is among the most common causes of failures in structural components and electronic assemblies. Fontana (1987), in his classic text on corrosion engineering, estimated that corrosion costs are in excess of $\$ 30$ billion dollars per year in the United States alone. It is essential to understand the nature of corrosion, types of corrosive attack and mitigation of corrosion in order to create reliable products The elements of these key ideas are presented in this chapter.

### 7.1 Galvanic Coupling and Susceptibility to Corrosion

Corrosion is an electrochemical process, which results in the deterioration of metal structures and components. Once the process is initiated, corrosion often rapidly leads to failure. Corrosion will also act in concert with fatigue to accelerate damage and fatigue failure. To understand the nature of this process, we must begin with a review of basic electrochemistry, remembering that reliability and the study of failure mechanics is inherently an interdisciplinary study.

### 7.1.1 Galvanic Cells

The basic model for an electrochemical cell or galvanic cell is shown in Figure 7.1. The primary components are the electrolyte or corrosive media, the anode and cathode. When two

Figure 7.1 A galvanic cell. The Magnesium-Silver galvanic couple.dissimilar metals are brought into contact, such as copper ( Cu ) and zinc ( Zn ), or silver ( Ag ) and magnesium ( Mg ), as shown in our figure, in an electrolyte, a potential develops. The magnitude of the electrode potential or voltage that develops, depends upon the nature of the electrolyte and the metals brought into contact. In the cell shown in Figure 7.1, we see that a voltage of 3.16 volts will develop at $25^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ in an electrolyte concentration of a 1 molar solution. These are the standard conditions at which the potential or open circuit voltage of Galvanic cells are measured. Under the standard conditions, we have the standard cell potential. Estimation of the standard potential and the potential under varying conditions is discussed further below.

The cell potential drives the corrosion process. As corrosion initiates, electrons flow from the anode to the cathode producing the corrosion current necessary to sustain damage to the anode. It is only the anode which deteriorates. As a result of electron flow or corrosion current, cations from the anode are released to the electrolyte causing the decay of the anode. The cations released to the electrolyte are then free to react with other species to form corrosion products. At the cathode, a variety of reactions may occur depending upon the nature of the electrolyte. However, the reaction at the cathode must consume the excess electrons transferred to the cathode.

This exchange of electrons is referred to as an oxidation/reduction reaction. Lets examine the oxidation/reduction reaction by separately assessing the processes as they occur at the anode and at the cathode. If the metal cations of the cathode are available in the electrolyte, the build-up of electrons will allow the cathode species to deposit on the surface of the cathode. This is a reduction process as electrons are consumed. This simple case is the basis of electroplating. However, cations of the cathode species are rarely available in the electrolyte in a corrosion process and other reduction reactions will occur. We will examine the various cathode reaction later.

At the other electrode of a cell, we have electrons being contributed to the process. The contribution of electrons in a chemical reaction is an oxidation process. Most metals may be subject to oxidation. Simply, we can write the oxidation reaction that may occur at an anode in a Galvanic cell as follows:

$$
M^{o} \rightarrow M^{n+}+n e^{-}
$$

$M^{o}$ is any metal and the superscript represents the metal in its native state. $M^{n+}$ is the cation where superscript $n^{+}$represents the valence of the metal cation. $n$ is then the number of moles of electrons that will form in the oxidation of the metal $M$. The reaction shown above is referred as a half reaction, as it represents half of the cell activity.

In corrosion engineering, we measure the potential difference of metals against the hydrogen electrode. If we insert a platinum tube through which we can bubble hydrogen gas into an electrolyte, along with our metal, $M^{o}$, the measured potential will be the standard electrode potential, under the conditions of a 1 molar electrolyte solution and a temperature of $25^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$. Hence, the hydrogen electrode has a reference voltage of 0.0 volts.

As an example, lets look again at Figure 7.1. The anode is Mg. The half reaction for the oxidation of Mg is written as follows:

$$
M g \rightarrow M g^{2+}+2 e^{-}
$$

The standard electrode potential for the half reaction or half cell potential is -2.36 V . The negative sign indicates that Mg is the anode relative to the hydrogen reference cell. The half reactions for the reduction of most metals is shown in Table 7.1Table 7.1 The Galvanic Series

| Electrode Reaction                                       | Standard Potential (V) @ $25^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ |
| :------------------------------------------------------- | :----------------------------------------------- |
| $A u \rightarrow A u^{+3}+3 e^{-}$                       | +1.50                                            |
| $P t \rightarrow P t^{+2}+2 e^{-}$                       | +1.20                                            |
| $P d \rightarrow P d^{+2}+2 e^{-}$                       | +0.987                                           |
| $A g \rightarrow A g^{+}+e^{-}$                          | +0.800                                           |
| $C u \rightarrow C u^{+2}+2 e^{-}$                       | +0.337                                           |
| $H_{2}(g a s) \rightarrow 2 H^{+}+e^{-}$(Reference cell) | 0.0                                              |
| $P b \rightarrow P b^{+2}+e^{-}$                         | -0.126                                           |
| $S n \rightarrow S n^{+2}+2 e^{-}$                       | -0.136                                           |
| $M o \rightarrow M o^{+3}+3 e^{-}$                       | -0.2                                             |
| $N i \rightarrow N i^{+2}+2 e^{-}$                       | -0.250                                           |
| $C o \rightarrow C o^{+2}+2 e^{-}$                       | -0.277                                           |
| $I n \rightarrow I n^{+3}+3 e^{-}$                       | -0.342                                           |
| $C d \rightarrow C d^{+2}+2 e^{-}$                       | -0.403                                           |
| $F e \rightarrow F e^{+2}+2 e^{-}$                       | -0.440                                           |
| $C r \rightarrow C r^{+3}+3 e^{-}$                       | -0.74                                            |
| $Z n \rightarrow Z n^{+2}+2 e^{-}$                       | -0.763                                           |
| $M n \rightarrow M n^{+2}+2 e^{-}$                       | -1.18                                            |
| $T i \rightarrow T i^{+2}+2 e^{-}$                       | -1.63                                            |
| $A l \rightarrow A l^{+3}+3 e^{-}$                       | -1.66                                            |
| $U \rightarrow U^{+3}+3 e^{-}$                           | -1.80                                            |
| $B e \rightarrow B e^{+2}+2 e^{-}$                       | -1.85                                            |
| $M g \rightarrow M g^{+2}+2 e^{-}$                       | -2.37                                            |
| $L i \rightarrow L i^{+}+e$                              | -3.05                                            |

This is known as the Galvanic Series, and is a useful tool for the evaluation of materials selection. In the event we want to couple two metals together, we can evaluate the resulting standard potential of the cell from the half cell potentials listed in Table 7.1, by the following equation:

$$
\Delta E_{\text {cell }}^{n}=E_{\text {anode }}^{n}-E_{\text {cathode }}^{n}
$$

The equation above applies when the electrode potentials are expressed for the oxidation reactions only, as shown in the Galvanic series. If the reactions are reversed, the reaction is then expressed as a reduction reaction and the sign of the potential is reversed to express the reduction reaction potential, $\varnothing$.

Then we can simply say that:

$$
E=-\varnothing
$$

The total cell reaction is the combination or sum of the oxidation and reduction reactions.
The Galvanic Series lists the most cathodic or noble metal to the most anodic or reactive metal. The farther apart on the series two metals are, the more likely they are to form a destructive couple. In other words, the greater the value of $\Delta E_{\text {cell }}^{n}$ the greater driving force for corrosion of the anode member of the couple.In a corrosion process, any number of reactions can occur at the cathode of the couple, depending upon the characteristics of the electrolyte. The cathode ions may be reduced and the cathode metal deposited from the solution. This is of course the basis of electroplating, as we mentioned above. However, this is not usually the case in a corrosion process. In an acid electrolyte, or low pH , we may have water formation. In the presence of oxygen in a near neutral to basic electrolyte solution we may have hydroxyl formation. This is common in many field environments to which a product is exposed. If conditions are anaerobic, water decomposition may be dominant, particularly in the presence of sulphur. The common cathode reactions are summarized below in Table 7.2. The table below expresses the cathode reactions as reduction reactions and the potential is the reduction potential.

A one molar standard solution is not usually likely in most environments. Electrolytes are usually more dilute. In addition, the temperature of the environment may be less than or greater than room temperature. In this case, we can calculate the half cell potentials for any condition using the Nernst equation. The Nernst equation is expressed as follows for a half cell oxidation reaction:

$$
E=E^{\mathrm{o}}+\left(\frac{0.0257 \text { Volts }}{n}\right)\left(\frac{T}{298 K}\right) \ln \kappa
$$

$n$ is the valance of the oxidized species, $T$ is the temperature in Kelvin and $\kappa$ is the chemical equilibrium constant.

The equilibrium constant, $\kappa$, for any reaction is a function of the reacting species chemical activity. In general we write a reaction in its equilibrium state as:

$$
a A+b B=c C+d D
$$

Then $\kappa$ is expressed as:

$$
\kappa=\frac{[\mathrm{C}]^{c}[\mathrm{D}]^{d}}{[\mathrm{~A}]^{a}[\mathrm{~B}]^{b}}
$$

The value or magnitude of $\kappa$ is then indicative how far the reaction will progress to the right. The bracketed quantities are the activities for each species in the reaction. The chemical activity for a solid element is generally taken as 1 . However, the activity in an aqueous solution is equivalent to the molar concentration. For gaseous species, activity is taken as the partial pressure of the reacting component. For a half cell oxidation reaction, $\kappa=C$, where $C$ is the molar concentration of the ion species undergoing the oxidation process.

Table 7.2 Cathode Reactions Expressed as Reduction Reactions with the Reduction Potential

|     |      Reaction Type       |                                         Cathode Reduction Reaction                                         | Environment <br> Characteristics | Standard Reduction Potential $\left(\phi^{\circ}\right)$ Volts |
| :-: | :----------------------: | :--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------: | :------------------------------: | :------------------------------------------------------------: | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
|  1  | Cathode Metal Deposition |                                   $M^{\circ+}+n e^{-} \rightarrow M^{0}$                                   |     $M^{\circ+}$ in solution     |                      See Galvanic Series                       |
|  2  |   Hydrogen Generation    |                     $2 \mathrm{H}++2 \mathrm{e}^{-} \rightarrow \mathrm{H}^{2}$ (gas)                      |               Acid               |                        0.0 (Reference)                         |
|  3  |    Hydroxyl Formation    |   $\mathrm{O}^{2}(\mathrm{gas})+2 \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}+2 \mathrm{e}^{-} \rightarrow 4(\mathrm{OH})$   |     Neutral to Basic Aerobic     |                            $-0.40$                             |
|  4  |   Water Decomposition    | $2 \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}+2 \mathrm{e}^{-} \rightarrow \mathrm{H}_{2}(\mathrm{gas})+2(\mathrm{OH})^{-}$ |            Anaerobic             |                                                                |
|  5  |     Water Formation      |                 $02+4 \mathrm{H}++4 \mathrm{e}^{-} \rightarrow 2 \mathrm{H} 2 \mathrm{O}$                  |           Acid Aerobic           |                            $-1.23$                             | Example 7.1 Lets consider Zn . What is the electrode potential of the half reaction for Zn at $60^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ in a solution containing 2 g of $\mathrm{Zn}^{+2}$ ions per liter of electrolyte? |

The atomic weight of Zn is 65.37 grams per mole. Then $C_{Z n}=(2 \mathrm{~g} / l) /(65.37 \mathrm{~g} / \mathrm{mole})=0.0306 \mathrm{M}$. The temperature is $273+60=333 \mathrm{~K}$. From the Galvanic series we see that $E^{\circ}=-0.76 \mathrm{~V}$. The valence for Zn is 2 . Then from the Nernst equation:

$$
E_{Z n}=-0.76+(0.0257 / 2)(333 / 298) \ln (0.0306)=-0.81 \mathrm{~V}
$$

Here we see the effect on the half cell reaction of a dilute solution of the corroding ion, relative to the hydrogen electrode, at $60^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$.

Let us now recall the concept of free energy. The free energy is a thermodynamic state function. When a chemical corrosion reaction occurs, a state change occurs, and the free energy change is the maximum useful energy resulting from the reaction. The magnitude may be thought of as the driving force of the reaction. If a reaction is spontaneous, the net change in free energy is negative.

The relationship between the free energy change and the electrode potential is:

$$
\Delta G=n E F
$$

$F$ is the Faraday Constant and $F=96,487$ Joules/Volt mol of $\mathrm{e}^{-}$.
We can now assess for any condition whether or not a corrosion reaction will take place or not, provided we know the concentration of the species involved in the corrosion process.

Example 7.2 Determine if Zn will corrode in a Hydrochloric Acid solution of $\mathrm{pH}=2$ with a $0.01 \mathrm{M} \mathrm{ZnCl}_{2}$ concentration at room temperature. Assume that the corrosion product is hydrogen gas.

The attack of Zn is an HCl solution is show below in Figure 7.2. This may be termed general attack. Lets examine this situation by looking at the half cell reactions and applying the Nernst Equation to calculate the cell potential, $E_{\text {cell }}$.

From the Galvanic Series, the anode reaction, expressed as the oxidation of Zn is:

$$
\mathrm{Zn} \rightarrow \mathrm{Zn}^{++}+2 \mathrm{e}^{-}
$$

The standard half-cell potential for the oxidation of Zn is -0.76 V .
Then from the Nernst equation

$$
\begin{aligned}
& E_{Z n}=E_{Z n}^{\circ}+\frac{0.0257}{n} \ln C \\
& E_{Z n}=-0.76+\frac{0.257}{2} \ln (0.01) \\
& E_{Z n}=-0.82 \mathrm{~V}
\end{aligned}
$$

The standard half-cell reaction for the oxidation of hydrogen is 0.0 V . This is the reference point for the Galvanic series as we discussed earlier. For a solution, we can recall that the pH $=-\log \left[\mathrm{H}^{+}\right]$, where $\left[\mathrm{H}^{+}\right]$is the hydrogen ion concentration. Then, the Nernst equation for the half cell reaction of hydrogen oxidation is expressed as $E_{H 2}=-0.0592 \mathrm{pH}$.

$$
\begin{aligned}
& E_{H 2}=-0.0592 p H \\
& E_{H 2}=-0.12 \mathrm{~V}
\end{aligned}
$$

Recalling that the half cell potentials are both stated as oxidation reactions:

$$
E_{\text {Cell }}=E_{\text {Anode }}-E_{\text {Cathode }}=-0.82-(-0.12)=-0.70 \mathrm{~V}
$$

Figure 7.2 Corrosion attack of zinc in hydrochloric acid (Hcl).

We can now examine the free energy change of the proposed cell:

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \Delta \mathrm{G}=n E F=2 \mathrm{~mol} \text { elec }(-0.70 \mathrm{~V})(96,487 \mathrm{~J} / \mathrm{Vmol} \text { elec }) \\
& \Delta \mathrm{G}=-135 \mathrm{~kJ}
\end{aligned}
$$

We can see that the proposed corrosion process will spontaneously take place with a large driving force.

One tool we may use to further study the themodymanics of corrosion is the Pourbaix diagram. This type of diagram is a plot of potential versus pH of the electrolyte, usually water, under standard conditions at $25^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$. The Pourbaix diagram will show the relative stability of the metal and its oxides, hydroxides, hydrides or other potential products of the corrosion process. The results of calculating cell potential from the Nernst equation can be examined for electrolytes of different pH .

Regions of immunity will be evident, as well as the potential for passivation. Passivation occurs when a thin resistant film forms on the surface of the metal, inhibiting corrosion. In fact, this is a necessary step in imparting corrosion resistance to stainless steel alloys. In this case, passivation is implemented into a surface treatment process.# 7.1.2 Types of Galvanic Cells

## Dissimilar Electrode Cells

The wide variety of materials and processes used in systems may lead to the formation of several types of cells in a corrosive environment. One of the most common types of cells is the dissimilar metal or dissimilar electrode cell. Two dissimilar metals in contact will result in corrosion of the anode in the presence of an electrolyte. There are many examples of dissimilar electrode cells in engineering practice. In microelectronic devices, gold wires bonded to aluminum bond pads form a potentially destructive couple. If we examine the Galvanic series, we can see Al and Au are quire far apart and that Al is lower in the series, or anodic. In this case, a small amount of moisture present in a microelectronic package will serve as an electrolyte and can result in severe corrosion of the aluminum bond pad, destroying the circuit.

Another example of a dissimilar metal electrode cell can be seen from observing galvanized or zinc coated steel. In this case, the Zn coating over the surface of the steel will be anodic to the Fe based steel. If the coating is damaged, the underlying steel is exposed to potential electrolytes. The Zn surface, however will corrode. As long as there is Zn present the steel is protected.

Example 7.3 Let's again examine coatings. It is common practice to coat electrical contact surfaces with gold (Au). Let's assume that a copper ( Cu ) alloy contact is electroplated with Au . Comment on the corrosion potential if the Au coating were damaged and the underlying Cu structure exposed.

In this case the coating is cathodic to the underlying structure, as we see from the Galvanic series. The standard cell potential is:

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \Delta E_{\text {Cell }}^{o}=E_{\text {Anode }}^{o}-E_{\text {Cathode }}^{o} \\
& \Delta E_{\text {Cell }}^{o}=0.34-1.5=-1.16 \mathrm{~V}
\end{aligned}
$$

Damage to the coating will result in corrosion of the base structure. A further problem here is that the anode formed is very small in comparison to the cathode. This disparity in area will greatly accelerate the corrosion process of the base structure, where the protective Au coating has been damaged.

## Stress Cells

Differences in the distribution of stresses can also result in the formation of an electrochemical cell. Grain boundaries, for example, will be preferentially attacked. Also, areas of a structure or component, which are cold worked, are anodic to the remaining portion of the structure. For example, if a bolt or nail head is formed by cold upset, then the head will have high residual stresses. The stressed region is anodic to the remainder of the component and would preferentially corrode.

## Concentration Cells

Differences in the concentrations of species involved in corrosion can also form a cell. An unprotected crevice will result in corrosion of a metal structure, at the site of the crevice. This kind of cell results from different concentrations of oxygen available to the structure. If we examine the following reaction from Table 7.2, we can expect from the Nernst equation, that variations in oxygen concentration will effect the electrode potential for this reaction.$$
2 \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}+\mathrm{O}_{2}+4 \mathrm{e}^{-} \rightarrow 4(\mathrm{OH})^{-}

$$

In regions where the oxygen concentration is higher, electron consumption or reduction is promoted over regions of lower oxygen concentration. Regions of lower concentrations of oxygen are forced to give up electrons and oxidation is promoted. Thus, the anode is the area deficient in oxygen. Recall that it is the anode that experiences deterioration.

This process is enhanced by entrapped residues in the crevice site. This can occur in joints which are spot welded and subsequently processed by electroplating or finishing. Entrapped residues can form a highly corrosive electrolyte, severely damaging the structure in a moist environment.

# Differential Temperature Cells

This type of cell occurs in a component manufactured of the same metal subjected to a temperature differential or thermal gradient. The hot side will be the cathode and the cold region will act as the anode. This type of cell can occur in boilers, heat exchangers, immersion heaters or other similar equipment.

## Impressed Voltage Cells

Finally, differences in applied potential in an electronic circuit may form an impressed voltage cell. As an example, we can expect that in the presence of an accumulation of surface moisture, a leakage current will form between two circuit lines of different potentials. In this case, it is always the element of higher voltage, that is the anode. As an example, if we consider a circuit line with an applied voltage supply of 5 Volts adjacent to ground potential, the 5 V line will be the anode in the event of leakage currents forming between the two lines. The various types of Galvanic cells are summarized below in Table 7.3.

Table 7.3 General Types of Galvanic Cells

|  | Galvanic Cell Types | Anode | Remarks |
| :-- | :-- | :-- | :-- |
| 1 | Dissimilar Metals | Member of the couple lowest <br> on the Galvanic Series | Common in many systems |
| 2 | Differential Stress | Areas of higher stress | Common when component is cold worked <br> Grain boundaries |
| 3 | Concentration/ <br> Differential Aeration | Lowest concentration or area <br> lowest in oxygen exposure | Crevice corrosion. Accelerated by entrapment of residual <br> chemicals, soils or accumulation of corrosion products. |
| 4 | Differential Temperature | Colder electrode | Common in boilers, heat exchangers, immersion heaters |
| 5 | Impressed Voltage | Highest voltage of coupled <br> electrodes | Common in connectors and on printed wiring board <br> assemblies |

### 7.2 Corrosion Rates

The expressions we have explored so far, tell us whether or not corrosion can occur, given a particular environment. We have used several thermodynamic quantities to explore the driving force for corrosion. However, the life of a component or structure in service will depend upon the rate of corrosion.# 7.2.1 Corrosion Current

Corrosion rates depend upon the current density over the corroding surface of the anode. To understand the current density generated in a corrosion reaction, we must explore electrochemical kinetics to assess the key variables that contribute to the process. First let's review briefly. In our treatment so far, we have utilized the Galvanic series to calculate our cell potential from the electrode potentials. We can apply, the Nernst equation to estimate the cell potential for essentially any set of electrode reactions at various electrolyte conditions. Hence, we can assess the relative driving forces for the corrosion process in any condition, provided we know the characteristics of the electrolyte.

But, we must keep in mind that this is the open circuit potential and represents an equilibrium condition. When the corrosion reaction begins, we are no longer at equilibrium. The anode and cathode come into contact and current flows. The potential of the cell will shift. The cell will reach a maximum current flow, which sustains the destruction of the anode. This is known as the process of polarization. A polarization diagram for the iron ( Fe ) and zinc $(\mathrm{Zn})$ cell is shown in Figure 7.3. $i_{\text {corr }}$ is the corrosion current density, governing the rate of anode deterioration.

Polarization behavior can be measured for various electrolyte conditions and electrodes. While electrochemical experiments are complex, we can visualize the elements of such experiments for our understanding of the kinetics of corrosion. If we place a variable resistance in series with our electrodes, we can simultaneously measure the potential shift and current flow. This simple arrangement is shown Figure 7.4 for a Zn electrode in relationship to our standard hydrogen electrode. Now, if we plot the measured voltage versus the measured current we can show the polarization behavior of the Zn electrode. At higher currents, a plot of the $\log$ of the current against the cell voltage will be linear.


Figure 7.3 Polarization behavior in the Fe-Zn couple.

Figure 7.4 Cell with variable resistance to measure electrode polarization behavior.

This linear polarization behavior of any electrode, relative to our standard hydrogen cell, will fit the following simple linear relationship, known as the Tafel Equation:


$$

\ln i=\ln i*{o}+\frac{E*{\text {Electrode }}}{\beta}

$$

$\beta$ is the Tafel slope which we directly extract from our experiments, $i_{*}$ is a constant known as the exchange current density. We can determine the corrosion current at the point of the corrosion potential directly from the cathodic polarization experiment.

At very low current densities, a direct Tafel extrapolation of the corrosion current density may not work. However, with known values of $\beta$ for both the anode and cathode electrode reactions of a Galvanic cell, we can estimate the corrosion current from the Stearn-Geary Equation:


$$

i*{\text {corr }}=\frac{1}{2.3} C^{\*} \frac{\beta*{\text {Anode }} \beta*{\text {Cathode }}}{\beta*{\text {Cathode }}+\beta\_{\text {Anode }}}

$$

$C^{*}$ is the inverse of the slope extracted from the linear region of a plot of the electrode potential versus the measured current density and the $\beta s$ are the Tafel slopes. This procedure is known as linear polarization analysis. Further details on electrochemical kinetics and associated measurements are presented in Fontana (1987). Our discusion here has simply introduced the subject.

With a known current density, we can calculate the depth of penetration of corrosion on the anode. This can be calculated simply from Faraday's Law. The expression in units of $\mathrm{mm} / \mathrm{yr}$ corrosion penetration rate, $\dot{\mathrm{P}} \mathrm{s}$, is as follows:$$
\stackrel{*}{p}_{\mathrm{s}}=\frac{0.00327 a_{w t} i_{\text {corr }}}{n \rho}
$$

$a_{w t}$ is the atomic weight of the corroding metal in units of $g \mathrm{~ms} / \mathrm{mole}, n$ is the valance and $\rho$ is the density in $\mathrm{gms} / \mathrm{cm}^{3}$. In the expression shown, $i_{\text {corr }}$ must be in units of $\mu \mathrm{A} / \mathrm{cm}^{2}$.

This assumes a uniform loss of material over the surface. If localized pitting attack occurs, the pitting factor, $P F$, for the metal and electrolyte conditions, must be known. The pitting factor at time, $t$, in the life of the component is the ratio of general surface loss, $p_{s}$, to the pit depth, $p_{d}$, formed at time $t$. This is shown in Figure 7.5.

Hence, the time to failure in years for any anode may then be expressed as the time it takes the corrosion process to reach a critical depth, $h^{*}$ in mm .

$$
t_{f}=\frac{h^{*}}{P F} * \frac{n \rho}{0.00327 a_{w t}} * \frac{1}{i_{\text {corr }}}
$$

$h^{*}$ is expressed as the critical pit depth in mm . If the $\mathrm{PF}=1.0$ then we can assume general surface attack and $h^{*}$ becomes the critical depth for surface loss. When pitting is of concern, the critical thickness becomes the thickness of the component, such as a pipe wall thickness or tank wall thickness. Pit depth, however, is statistically distributed in any sample and there is risk in taking a worst case pit depth from a small sample in order to project component life.

Example7.4 A 10 m section of cast iron pipe is used in a chemical handling facility. The outer diameter of the pipe is 10 cm with a 6 mm wall thickness. The pipe is gray cast iron and is used to transport corrosive deaerated acid. The current density in deaerated acid was determined to be $40 \mathrm{uA} / \mathrm{cm}^{2}$ by a linear polarization experiment. The pipe is subjected to a distributed external load of $240 \mathrm{~N} / \mathrm{m}$ including the weight to the transported material and pipe weight. Determine the time to failure if the pipe is an ASTM Type 20 gray cast iron with a tensile strength of 138 M Pa . If pitting is expected with an observed pitting factor of 5 , what is the life?

In this case, to determine the life of the structure to collapse, we must estimate the load and determine the bending stress as a function of internal diameter. The structure is shown in Figure 7.6 along with the nomenclature for our equations in this problem. As we can see, the internal diameter will increase as the pipe undergoes corrosion. We will assume the corrosion process is uniform over the internal surface.

Figure 7.5 Pitting parameters defined for pitting in the surface of a metal component.

Figure 7.6 Simple pipe, loaded as a beam, undergoing corrosion. In our example, we calculate the time to failure.

Recall that for a beam in bending, the stresses are a function of the moment generated by the load according to the following equation:

$$
\sigma=\frac{M c}{l}
$$

The stress is. $M$ is the bending moment and $c$ is the distance from the center to the outer most- point on the beam. $I$ is the moment of inertia of the circular section.

The maximum bending moment, $M$, is at the center of the beam length and for a distributed load:

$$
M_{\max }=\frac{w l^{2}}{8}
$$

where $w$ is the distributed load and $l$ is the length.
Given our circular section and substituting our tensile strength as the critical stress for a brittle material, like cast iron, we see that:

$$
\sigma_{c}=\frac{\frac{w l^{2}}{8} R_{o}}{\frac{\pi}{4}\left(R_{o}^{4}-R_{i}^{4}\right)}
$$

$\mathrm{R}_{\mathrm{o}}$ is the external diameter of our pipe and $R_{i}$ is the internal diameter.Solving for the internal diameter, $R_{i c}$, that will result in the critical stress, we see that:

$$
R_{i_{c}}=\left[R_{o}^{4}-\frac{w l^{2} R_{o}}{2 \pi \sigma_{c}}\right]^{\frac{1}{4}}
$$

Our critical thickness loss, $h^{*}$, is then our internal diameter at the critical stage, $R_{i c}$, minus initial internal diameter, $R_{i o}$. The time to failure for this structure is then:

$$
t^{*}=\frac{1000\left\{\left[R_{o}^{4}-\frac{w l^{2} R_{o}}{2 \pi \sigma_{c}}\right]^{\frac{1}{4}}-R_{i o}\right\} n \rho}{0.00327 a_{w t} t_{c o r r}}
$$

Substituting and solving we see that $t^{*}=6.4$ years. We see that in this case we had to construct our time to failure model from consideration of the failure mode and mechanism. The mode is structural collapse of the pipe and the mechanism is wear out by general corrosion attack in a corrosive media transported by the system.

In the case of pitting failure, the failure mode will not be structural collapse, but rather we are more likely to be concerned about leakage of the transported material from a pit. In this case we simply set the critical thickness, $h^{*}$, equal to the pipe thickness and solve for the time to failure using the given pitting factor. Then, with $h^{*}=6 \mathrm{~mm}$ and $P F=5$ :

$$
t_{f}=\frac{6}{5} \cdot \frac{2(7.86)}{0.00327(55.85)} \cdot \frac{1}{40}=2.5 \mathrm{yrs}
$$

A comparison of the two failure modes, shows that the piping system is likely to fail by pitting before structural collapse occurs. In either case the design is questionable, given the short life, and we may wish to consider an alternative material selection.

In this case, we have handled the calculation in a deterministic fashion. We can apply Monte Carlo simulation to estimate the failure distribution. We require some knowledge of the distributions of the parameters in the time to failure equation.

Another form of evaluating corrosion in structures and components is based upon weight loss. A weight loss test is conducted and the results are projected as thickness loss, over the corroding area. Weight loss tests may be conducted under accelerated conditions, such as increased temperature. The results are then projected to service conditions. The corrosion penetration rate can be related from the weight loss rate in testing, using the following equation:

$$
\dot{p}=87.6 \frac{\dot{w}_{\text {test }}}{\rho A}
$$

In the expression shown, $\dot{p}$ is the corrosion penetration rate in mm per year, $\rho$ is the density in $\mathrm{gm} / \mathrm{cm}^{3}$ and $A$ is the corroding area in $\mathrm{cm}^{2} . \dot{w}_{\text {test }}$ is the measured weight loss in milligrams per hour, under similar conditions to the environment expected in service. Considering a critical penetration depth, $h^{*}$ in mm, with a pitting factor, $P F$, we can express the time to failure for a component under corrosion, $t_{f}$, in years, as follows:

$$
t_{f}=\frac{h^{*}}{P F \cdot \dot{p}}=\frac{h^{*}}{P F} \cdot \frac{\rho A}{87.6 \dot{w}_{\text {test }}}
$$

While the units in these expressions may seem odd to the reader, they are generally the units of choice for testing and corrosion penetration rates (Fontana 1989, Uhlig 1971). Appropriate acceleration factors must be determined for tests at elevated temperatures.

A third expression is useful for impressed voltage cells. In this case we express the time to failure for parallel conducting elements as shown in Figure 7.7 by the following equation:

Figure 7.7 Parallel conductors in an impressed voltage cell. Similar conditions can occur on the surface of a printed wiring board.

$$
t_{f}=C \cdot \frac{1}{\Delta V_{a p p}} \cdot \frac{W_{z}^{2} h_{c} n F \rho}{4 a_{w t}} \cdot \frac{[\zeta]}{[\mathrm{z}]}
$$

In equation $7.29, \mathrm{C}$ is a constant, $\Delta \mathrm{V}_{\text {app }}$ is applied voltage difference, n is the valence, F is Faraday's constant, $\rho$ is the conductor density, and $\frac{[\zeta]}{[\mathrm{z}]}$ is the sheet resistance of the electrolyte.

# 7.3 Common Forms of Corrosion Attack

Fontana (1986) identifies eight forms of corrosion in which varies types of galvanic cells may be active. This classification is conveniently based upon the appearance of the corroded surfaces of the components. These eight forms will be briefly discussed in this section. In addition, a further discussion of corrosion in electronics may be found in Chapter 8. In addition to this classic description of the eight forms of corrosion, we can will also consider related mechanisms including stress sorption cracking of polymer materials, hydrogen embrittlement of steels and corrosion fatigue.

### 7.3.1 Eight Forms of Corrosion

The eight forms of corrosion identified by the Fontana classification include:

- Uniform Attack
- Galvanic Coupling
- Crevice Corrosion
- Pitting
- Intergranular Corrosion
- Parting
- Errosion Corrosion
- Stress Corrosion Cracking

## Uniform Attack

Uniform attack is the general and uniform loss of exposed metal surface. It is the most common form of corrosion. It is most easily characterized by the example of rust formation in the atmosphere on exposed iron or steel. This process generally involves most of the

Figure 7.8 Uniform attack of a metal component producing a loss of thickness, $h$, over time
exposed surface, which is lost at a relatively uniform rate, as shown in Figure 7.8. This form of corrosion is driven by random cathode and anode zones, which form across the surface of the metal due to microstructural variations. The uniform loss of surface is the most easily and accurately modeled corrosion problem and weight loss testing is often adequate to characterize the loss of material.

# Galvanic Coupling

Galvanic coupling is the formation of a dissimilar metal cell, as the result of two different metals that are adjacent in a component or structure. We have already discussed the galvanic series and its implications and the reader should review this discussion. An example of this type of attack is the couple formed between a protective finish and its base metal. For example, zinc coatings are used to protect iron and steel alloys. Exposure of the iron results in a dissimilar metal cell that causes the loss of the coating due to the formation of a dissimilar metal cell. This, of course, is generally the purpose of the protection. However, if the base metal is anodic, rapid penetration into the base metal can occur, such as with the use of tin plated steel surfaces. This is illustrated in Figure 7.9. An additional type of destructive galvanic cell is a fastener that is anodic to the pieces joined. This is highly undesirable. The improper use of fasteners and poor selection of metals for joining of parts in one of the more common, yet usually avoidable corrosion problems.

## Crevice Corrosion

Crevice corrosion results from the formation of a concentration cell in which there is a deficiency of oxygen in a region where two parts of a structure are joined together. As shown in Figure 7.10, a spot welded lap joint can experience this type of attack. In addition, bolted con-

Figure 7.9 Two type of galvanic couples. In a., the defects in the coating exposes the base which is anodic. This can lead to rapid penetration into the base metal. Destruction of the anode is enhanced when the anode area is small in comparison to the cathode. In case b., the coating is anodic and will sacrifice itself to protect the base metal.

Figure 7.10 Common crevice corrosion sites in a joint formed by spot welding.
nections or gasket sealed surfaces may be subject to crevice corrosion. Unfortunately, the crevice is the anode, potentially resulting in significant damage to joints. The entrapment of residual process chemicals and soils will intensify crevice corrosion by facilitating the formation of an electrolyte.

# Pitting

Pitting is a highly localized attack of the component. Pitting is initiated by a localized breakdown of the native oxides on the surface of the metal. It is autocatalytic in that the active ions tend to concentrate within the pitting site. Therefore, the process of corrosion by pitting can be quite rapid. Chlorine is often involved in pitting. The $\mathrm{Cl}^{-}$anion will rapidly breakdown native oxides on many metals and will contribute to rapid pit development, as illustrated in Figure 7.11, particularly in aluminum, stainless steel alloys and low purity iron. An example of pitting attack by chlorine on aluminum is shown in Figure 7.12. Pitting is perhaps the most insidious of the forms of corrosion.

## Intergranular Corrosion

Intergranular corrosion is also a highly localized form of attack. The grain boundaries of the alloy are preferentially attacked. This form of corrosion is most often associated with stainless steel alloys, which have been joined by fusion welding. Near the weldment, the alloy may become sensitized to corrosion due to precipitation of carbides.

Sensitization occurs when the alloy passes through a critical temperature range, in which the kinetics of carbide precipitation is optimal. Hence as Figure 7.13 illustrates, either side of the weldment will have a region of sensitized metal that may rapidly corrode by grain boundary corrosion.

In the sensitized areas, chromium carbides precipitate in the grain boundaries of the alloy. The formation of the carbide precipitates reduces the chromium content below the critical level of $12 \%$ in the region surrounding the grain boundary.

Figure 7.11 Schematic of pitting by chlorine.

Figure 7.12 Distribution of pits on the surface of aluminum following several months of service in the presence of residual chlorine contamination from foodstuffs.

Figure 7.13 Stainless steel component with a butt weld. Regions adjacent to the weld may be sensitized and subject to intergranular attack.Rapid deterioration then occurs along paths that follow the grain boundaries in the sensitized areas of the component. Proper post weld quenching and use of low carbon stainless alloys can help to avoid this form of corrosion.

The concept of grain boundary sensitization is shown in Figure 7.14. Consider an individual grain boundary in the sensitized region of a welded component. Within the grain boundaries, carbides have precipitated following the path of the boundary. Now, let's plot the spatial distance around the boundary, against the chromium content. We will find that the chromium drops rapidly near the grain boundary on either side of the boundary center line. The area immediately adjacent to the carbine precipitates, where the chromium is below $12 \%$, is sensitized and subject to corrosion.

# Parting

Parting is a unique form of corrosion that occurs when a single alloy constituent is leached from the alloy. This leaves a porous and weakened structure. This form of attack is most often associated with brass alloys. Common yellow brass is $70 \%$ copper and $30 \%$ zinc. Parting of the zinc or dezincification can occur in such applications as heat exchangers, leaving a porous structure of copper in the wake of the destruction of the component. Parting has also been associated with cast iron. Iron may be selectively leached from the component leaving behind the graphite. This is sometimes referred to as graphitization.

## Erosion Corrosion

Erosion corrosion occurs when the corrosive media is moving over the surface of the metal. Abrasive wear or mechanical contact may play a role is some forms of this attack mechanism. Pump impellers or other components used in the transport of corrosive fluids will be subject to erosion. Impingement of the corrosive media on the surface of the component, such as a pipe bend, will generally accelerate the erosion process in the presence of the impinging fluid.

Cavitation damage of pump impellers, propellers, turbines or other high velocity components involved in the transport of liquid media is one of the more well known processes of erosion. The collapse of vapor bubbles of the surface of moving components imparts very

Figure 7.14 Grain boundary sensitization.localized stresses of high magnitude, that deform the surface. The resulting deformations disrupt surface films and speed the process of localized corrosion in the region of the damage.

Another form of surface erosion is fretting corrosion. Fretting corrosion occurs when mating surfaces, with high contact stresses, experience small relative displacements under vibration. Contact forces cause the formation of wear debris and small particles. Wear debris accumulates and rapidly oxidizes. The aggregation of oxides promote further wear and additional surface destruction. This has been observed in certain kinds of electrical contacts and rotating machinery elements.

# Stress Corrosion Cracking (SCC)

Stress corrosion cracking (SCC) is a form of attack that results in brittle cracking and fracture of a component under tensile loads in specific chemical environments. Various alloys may be susceptible to SCC in the presence of specific chemical species. Susceptibility often increases with increasing concentration or when tensile loads produce high stress levels in components. Some alloys, such as brass exposed to ammonia solutions, will fail explosively under residual stresses in the component. For this reason, caution and careful attention must be paid to alloy selection for chemical transport and processing applications.

For an additional example we can look to the historical use of steels. Steel, under large tensile stresses near the elastic limit, will be susceptible to stress corrosion failure in alkaline water solutions. Alkalies were often added as inhibitors to water in boilers to retard general corrosion. According to Uhlig (1971), this accounted for many failures in the past of riveted boiler structures. Rivets gave way by brittle SCC failure, as residual alkaline water became trapped and concentrated in riveted joints. Of course riveting is no longer used for this type application. Yet SCC remains a concern particularly for the chemical processing and energy production industries.

Other materials that may under go SCC in specific environments are summarized in Table 7.4.

Figure 7.15 Fretting corrosion concept. A contact rubs against its mating surface under vibration causing the formation of oxidized wear debris.

The mechanism of SCC initiation and crack propagation will depend upon the alloy and the constituents in the environment promoting SCC. However, there are some general characteristics. The electrochemical nature of SCC has been demonstrated by applying cathodic protection to arrest crack growth. Cracking can be started and stopped by removing the protective current. Hence, using a sacrificial anode may be one way to prevent or inhibit SCC. Generally, failure in metals is by intergranular crack propagation, even though the alloy under attack may be relatively ductile. We can surmise that the anodic nature of grain boundaries is important to crack propagation. Dislocations, micro-segregation, localized plastic deformation and the presence of native inhibiting films may all play a role. When the chlorine anion is involved, it may concentrate in the region of the crack tip, promoting dissolution of the metal under attack.

Adsorption of the damaging constituent onto the metal at the crack site is also a likely contributing factor. The specific constituent promoting SCC may reduce the surface energy of the metal in its environment. When the load applied to the component produces sufficient strain energy to overcome the energy of new surfaces formed by cracking, crack propagation will be encouraged to proceed rapidly.

# 7.3.2 Related Mechanisms

In addition to the eight forms of corrosion, we must be aware of related mechanisms. Both hydrogen embrittlement and stress sorption cracking of polymers and metals are often discussed in the context corrosion, as they involve attack of the materials used in components by specific species in the use or processing environments.# Hydrogen Embrittlement

Hydrogen embrittlement is not electrochemical in nature, but is often categorized with SCC in the discussion of stress related corrosion mechanisms. High strength steels will be subject to rapid intergranular cracking after exposure to hydrogen. Hydrogen evolution on the surface of the metal during acid immersion or electrochemical finishing operations will often be sufficient to embrittle high strength steel. In particular, cadmium or zinc finishing to impart corrosion protection of fasteners, remains a failure mechanism of concern in these types of components. Fortunately, simply baking the components after finishing, will relieve the problem by encouraging absorbed hydrogen to diffuse from the metal. It is the authors experience, that even residual stresses in forming of components will be sufficient to cause cracking when hydrogen has not been relieved. As an example, high strength, coiled steel springs have been found cracked in their shipping containers, before they were deployed to the field. The cause was hydrogen embrittlement from cadmium platting, followed by cracking under tensile residual stresses in the component.

## Stress-sorption Cracking

Stress sorption cracking occurs in metals, glass and polymers. Various polymers may fail by cracking when exposed to solvents under tensile loading. In addition, structural alloys can fail catastrophically when exposed to other molten metals. Mercury will cause rapid intergranular fracture in titanium or brass (Uhlig 1971) and glass may fail when exposed to water in the presence of tensile stresses. The mechanism for these types of attack is related to the reduction in surface energy when exposed to the specific environment.

### 7.4 Corrosion Fatigue Interactions

The effect of corrosion on the fatigue life of components placed in service is profound. Generally, corrosion will degrade the fatigue life substantially. The greater the rate of corrosion, the greater the fatigue life will be lessened. In addition, we can expect that the fatigue limit that is present in structural steels, as discussed in Chapter 5, will disappear. These effects are illustrated in Figure 7.16.It should be noted that increasing the strength of a structural steel for a component may not enhance fatigue life in the event the component is undergoing corrosion.

Figure 7.16 Effects of corrosion on the fatigue life of a component.Figure 7.16 suggests that we can modify our stress life approach to fatigue by adding an additional factor for environment to our equation for modification of the endurance limit of a material during component design.

We will now turn out attention to corrosion prevention. Methods of prevention are discussed in the following sections.

# 7.5 Corrosion Prevention

When confronted with a potentially corrosive environment, engineers must design a system that will not be susceptible to the formation of destructive galvanic corrosion cells. Only compatible metal couples must be utilized when elements of a system or component come into direct contact. In addition, metals that are suspect to general atmospheric attack must be protected by electroplating or coating. Unprotected crevices should be avoided and adequate drainage provided as appropriate. Circuit cards should be mounted vertically and connectors should be mounted only on the sides of a electronic system chassis. Unavoidable couples or potentially destructive cells must be isolated from potential electrolytes.

The Galvanic Series is an initial tool to evaluate the compatibility of materials. As we have discussed, the driving force for the corrosion process will be proportional to the cell potential. A larger cell potential will mean greater risk when evaluating and comparing combinations of materials. The Galvanic Series in Seawater is shown in Table 7.5. This listing of the series can provide an indication of the behavior of materials in typical application environments, such as atmospheric exposure, and can also be used to assess galvanic compatibility. Metals are listed from the most active (anodic) to least active (noble). Materials near the top of the list are more likely to suffer general attack and the further the apart the metals are on the series, the more likely a detrimental couple will occur.

# 7.6 Summary

In this chapter we have explained the basic aspects of corrosion failure. The thermodynamics of oxidation-reduction reactions govern the potential for corrosion to occur in a component in service. Formation of one or more of the various types of Galvanic cells may induce one of the common forms of attack that manifest themselves in failure of components in service. The rate of corrosion and the time to failure depends upon the corrosion current developed in the cell. Modeling the process may be beneficial in many situations to validate the reliability of a component and the materials selected for its structure. Testing of materials used in harsh environments will also provide a great deal of insite into the potential for damage. In most circumstances we must prevent corrosion by the careful selection of materials and use of surface treatment and coatings.

### 7.7 Do's and Dont's in Design

Do evaluate the use environment
Do test for compatibility when corrosive electrolytes are present
Do analyze past failures and maintenance history
Do insulate dissimilar metals or seal metal couples
Do use caution when selecting fasteners
Do use coatings as necessary
Do seal electrical connectors
Do use conformal coatings on printed wiring board assemblies
Do specify completion of cutting, drilling or grinding prior to surface treatments
Do use compatible underplatings before final finishes are applied. Example: Use Nickel under Gold
Do ensure residues from assembly operations are removed. Examples: solder flux, cleaning agents
Do passivate Stainless Steel Alloys
Do use surface treatments such as chromate conversion coating or anodyzing and painting for aluminum
Do use low point drains for electrical cabinets, boxes and enclosures
Do use sealants to prevent fluid intrusion into cabinets, boxes or enclosures
Do use a shoe box style lid design for electronic enclosure for harsh environments
Do mount printed wiring assemblies vertically
Do mount connectors horizontally
Do use desiccant systems to reduce moisture as necessary
Do ensure good maintenance and periodic cleaning
Do evaluate potential entrapment of soils and avoid crevices
Do evaluate potential for pittingDo use corrosion testing on finished products and components such as humidity and salt spray
Do evaluate alloy compatibility with electrolytes and required equipment life
Do use gaskets and o-ring seals
Don't use dissimilar metals in contact if it can be avoided
Don't use sealants that outgas incompatible gasses such as acetic acid
Don't place graphite lubricants in contact with aluminum
Don't use top mounted lid fasteners for cabinets and enclosures in harsh environments
Don't mount PWBs horizontally in industrial equipment or products subjected to atmospheric exposure
Don't mount electrical connectors vertically or in the bottom of cabinets and enclosures
Don't use hygroscopic materials
Don't select alloys subject to pitting in harsh environments
Don't use organic coatings, plastic components or elastomer sealants that degrade with maintenance and cleaning, support fungal growth or outgas harmful and corrosive vapors

Michael Pecht, Patrick McCluskey and Jillian Y. Evans

Electronic assemblies consist of a hierarchy of interconnection as we see in Figure 8.1. Semiconductor devices, the chips or die, are most often packaged in plastic encapsulation and soldered to a printed wiring board. The board provides the supporting structure for the parts and the surface area necessary for the circuit. This interconnect structure may present many reliability issues for products and electronic systems. In this chapter, we continue to build our knowledge of the mechanics of failure, applying much of Chapters 4, 5, 6, and 7 to electronic assemblies and devices.

Once again, let's look at the packaging hierarchy shown in Figure 8.1. The lowest level consists of the semiconductor device itself, referred to as the chip or die. The enclosure for the chip may be a hermetically sealed package, often employed in low volume, high reliability systems. Most products, however, use plastic encapsulated microcircuits where the chip or die

## LEVELS OF INTERCONNECT

Figure 8.1 Levels of interconnect.is encased in plastic epoxy molding compound. When performance and size combine to become dominant design issues, multichip modules or hybrid circuits can be used, as an intermediate level of packaging. In either case, the die is bonded to the packaging and electrical interconnection between the die and the package is most often done by using wire bonding. The final interconnection is between the packaged device and the printed wiring assembly. Soldering remains the most often used process and eutectic or 60/40 tin lead solder the media of choice to achieve interconnection at this level.

Each level of packaging presents potential failure mechanisms. At the printed wiring board level, failure is often the result of corrosion processes or fatigue of the solder interconnection. In the next lower level, bonding between the chip and the package structure and the wire bonds serving the electrical interconnect function may be sources of failure. Fatigue, fracture and diffusion related mechanisms are common problems acting on device interconnects. Fracture of the package may lead to moisture penetration followed by corrosion on the surface of the die where metallization is exposed. At the die level, failures occur from electrical overstress, fracture of the die, hot electron build-up, ionic contamination, time dependent dielectric breakdown, electromigration or stress induced voiding. From a product design perspective, we need to be aware of loads on the system and their influence on these mechanisms.

In this chapter, we discuss the failure mechanisms most prevalent in electronic assemblies and devices. We begin our discussion with the assembly level and then discuss the package and die issues focusing on the most common mechanisms. As in our previous discussions of failure mechanics, we will describe the mechanisms, and present applicable models. This chapter serves as an introduction to failure mechanics of electronic assemblies and devices. More detailed descriptions and summaries of various mechanisms can be found in Pecht (1994) and Pecht, Dasgupta, Evans and Evans (1995).

# 8.1 Assembly Level Failure Mechanisms

Assembly level failures often occur by processes of corrosion or fatigue. Corrosion may effect the electrical traces, connectors and leads. Various sources of contamination drive the process or accelerate corrosion by lowering electrolyte resistance and enhancing current leakages, in the event an impressed voltage cell forms, as described in Chapter 7. Chlorine remains one of the most prevalent and insidious sources of contamination in electrical assemblies and devices promoting general attack of various surfaces and enhancing other forms of corrosion, such as localized pitting and attack.

### 8.1.1 PWB Level Corrosion Process

If corrosion is detected, ionic contamination has occurred at some step in the manufacturing process. In electronic assemblies, flux and flux residues are the most likely contributors to ionic contamination. Other sources include salt from human hands, plating solutions, and contaminated storage areas. Whatever the source of contamination, its presence indicates that the cleaning process was not thorough enough to remove the ions, particularly chlorine.

On the printed wiring board surface, the conductors are generally solder coated copper with connector surfaces on the board edge being finished with gold over nickel or perhaps tin. Lead surfaces are tin plated copper alloys and may be solder dipped. Unfortunately, all five of the various metals found on the PWB surface finishes may be attacked by chlorine residues. As conductor size decreases, general attack as well as current leakage becomes of considerable concern.Five metals - gold, nickel, copper, lead, and tin - commonly used in electronics can be corroded in the presence of chlorine. The corrosion products on the connector leads and in the epoxy between the leads undoubtedly results from decomposition of metal by chlorine and subsequent regeneration and migration of chlorine ions. Manko (1992) reports the following corrosion cycle in lead when chlorides are present:

Metallic lead is usually protected by an adherent and nonporous layer of lead oxide; however, in the presence of chlorine ions, lead oxide reacts to form lead chloride. Since lead chloride is not stable in a moist environment containing carbon dioxide, the lead chloride readily forms the more stable and porous lead carbonate, which produces the residue about the soldered leads that is shown in Figure 8.2. This reaction releases another chloride ion which is free to attack the lead oxide.

The corrosion cycle of copper when chlorides are present is as follows:

$$
\mathrm{Cu}+\mathrm{Cl}_{2} \longrightarrow \mathrm{CuCl}_{2}+\text { electrical energy } \longrightarrow \mathrm{Cu}+\mathrm{Cl}_{2}
$$

Cupric chlorides do not require the presence of oxygen to promote attack because their cations can be cathodically reduced. Multiple sites on the connector leads become anodes and other sites cathodes with aqueous cupric chloride as the electrolyte. Tin is not attacked by water and/or air, but in the presence of chlorides, tin forms stannous chloride.

# 8.1.2 Electrochemical Dendrite Formation

Electrochemical dendritic growth, essentially an electrolytic process, occurs on leads when metal dissolves at the anode region and migrates to the cathode region, redepositing there in a dendritic pattern. This phenomenon can cause an electrical short if complete bridging occurs between adjacent leads.

Figure 8.2 Lead carbonate corrosion product on PWB.The plating material most widely reported to undergo dendritic formation is silver, which is used for spot-plating copper leadframes in plastic packages. Depending on environmental conditions, other metals such as lead, tin, nickel, gold, and copper have also been found to undergo migration. Actually, almost any metal will form dendrites if subjected to the right combination of chemical contamination, moisture, and bias.

Copper has a lower electrochemical potential than silver, indicating that copper will go into solution and form dendrites more readily than silver. However, in the presence of oxygen, silver forms silver oxide $\left(\mathrm{Ag}_{2} \mathrm{O}\right)$ and copper forms copper oxide $\left(\mathrm{Cu}_{2} \mathrm{O}\right)$; the solubility product of silver oxide is larger than that of copper oxide, which increases the availability of free silver ions ( $\mathrm{Ag}++$ ), enhancing silver migration and dendrite formation. However, when packages are tested in an environment with large concentrations of sulfur impurities, heavy copper migration occurs instead. In the presence of sulfur, silver forms silver sulfide $\left(\mathrm{Ag}_{2} \mathrm{~S}\right)$, and copper forms copper sulfide $\left(\mathrm{Cu}_{2} \mathrm{~S}\right)$; the solubility product of silver sulfide is many orders of magnitude lower than that of copper sulfide. The increased availability of copper ions leads to the formation of copper dendrites.

The following conditions are necessary to form a dendrite:

- current density must reach high levels at the tip of the dendrite (e.g., $10 \mathrm{~A} / \mathrm{cm}^{2}$ ), through spherical and parabolic diffusion
- sufficient liquid (polar) medium such as condensed water must be present in the migration path so that adequate ionic flux is developed to sustain the required dendritic growth rate
- the applied voltage must exceed the sum of the anodic and cathodic potential in equilibrium with the electrolyte

These conditions dictate that the materials have a pore size distribution at interfaces that allow water condensation, to the extent that the current density requirement at the tip of the growing dendrite is satisfied.

The mechanism of dendritic growth is controlled by ionic transport kinetics and depends especially on (1) activation energy, (2) electric field, and (3) relative humidity. Dendritic growth also depends strongly on the state of the metal surface: oxidation and sulphidation can reduce metal migration susceptibility for some metals, as discussed above, while chloridation and low pH can greatly enhance it. Key surface factors effecting migration are (1) the ability of the metal to provide a surface barrier to ionic and electron exchange, (2) the pH of the medium, and (3) the nature and level of impurities (process residues or leachants) present.

Dendrite structures begin forming on leads at a high potential and grow toward adjacent leads that are at a lower potential. In the case of copper, the process consists of the dissolution of copper at the positive electrode, the anode; the passage of cupric ions through a conductive viscoelastic polymer (epoxy adhesive) containing $\mathrm{CuCl}_{2}$; and the deposition of copper at the negative electrode, the cathode. The reaction at the anode can be represented as

$$
\mathrm{Cu} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Cu}^{++}+2 \mathrm{e}^{-}
$$

The reaction at the cathode can be represented as:

$$
\mathrm{Cu}^{++}+2 \mathrm{e}-\longrightarrow \mathrm{Cu}
$$

Silver and tin readily form dendrites, as well, having loosely bound oxides. Dendrite structures continue forming and increasing in size as electrolysis progresses. Eventually, dendrite structures form a conductive bridge between two leads and cause an electrical short. A short due to dendrite formation is shown in Figure 8.3.

Figure 8.3 Dendrite formation on the surface of a PWB.

A model for dendrite growth, time to failure, $t_{f}$, was presented by Diagiacomo (1982). The model, shown below, describes the influence of the primary factors governing the process of dendrite growth.

$$
t_{f}=\frac{\left(\frac{P}{M C}\right)\left(\frac{2 r}{Z F D_{0}}\right)}{\beta\left(V_{\text {pot }}-V_{1}\right)(1 / k T) e^{-\Delta H / k T} \operatorname{erfc}(1 / 2 \sigma) \ln \left(\frac{k t(\ln H) r_{g r}}{2 \gamma \vartheta}\right)^{2}}
$$

The list of variables in the equation above is long and complex and may be summarized as follows: $\rho$ is the density of the dendrite, $M$ is the atomic weight of corroding species, $C$ is the ionic concentration, $Z$ is the charge or valence of the corroding metal ions, $D_{0}$ is the diffusivity, $F$ is Faraday's constant, $l$ is the distance between electrodes, $r_{d}$ is the dendrite radius, $\beta$ is the fraction of surface area promoting dendrite growth, $V_{\text {pot }}$ is the applied potential difference, $V_{T}$ is the critical threshold voltage for dendrite growth, $k$ is Boltzmann's constant, $\Delta H$ is the enthalpy of activation of the corrosion reaction, $\sigma$ is the variation in surface pore size, H is the relative humidity at which condensation occurs, $\mathrm{r}_{\mathrm{av}}$ is the average available pore radius on the surface, $v$ is the molar volume and $y$ is the surface tension, $T$ is temperature.

The model reflects the complexity of the dendrite formation process showing the need for exceeding a critical voltage to produce the dendrite, the influence of dendrite size, temperature, activation energy and surface issues. In practice, we can observe dendrite formation to occur rapidly when there is available electrolyte at common potential differences of $5-10 \mathrm{~V}$ on the printed wiring board surface. Silver dendrites will cross a typical line spacing within minutes.

# 8.1.3 Solder Fatigue

Fatigue of solder joints is a very common failure mechanism in electronic systems. The most common cause of solder fatigue is the strain imposed on the solder joint by uneven thermal expansions of the surfaces joined by the solder, which occurs when the device is heated, due either to environmental conditions (thermal variations in the ambient environment) or topower cycling (thermal variations caused by heat dissipation of the device within the package). While the fatigue life of solder joints is strongly dependent on operating conditions, the metallurgical mechanisms of joint failure are surprisingly constant.

Near-eutectic lead-tin ( $\mathrm{Pb}-\mathrm{Sn}$ ) solder, the most common choice for electrical interconnects, is mechanically soft and is used at a high homologous temperature (a large fraction of its melting point). For these reasons, deformation is introduced by plasticity and creep (stress relaxation) at both ends of the strain cycle. The cyclic deformation is affected by the fact that the solder contact is a thin layer bonded to relatively rigid materials with a complex intermetallic reaction layer at the bonding plane. The long-term deformation behavior is further complicated by the microstructure changes that inevitably occur in the solder as it is cycled and as it ages.

The lamellar eutectic microstructure is unstable with respect to reconfiguration into a mixture of equiaxed grains of Pb -rich and Sn -rich phases. The driving force for this reconfiguration is a decrease in the total area of interface, and hence, in the net surface energy. The reconstruction of the microstructure is significantly accelerated by plastic deformation: a eutectic $\mathrm{Pb}-\mathrm{Sn}$ solder is easily recrystallized into an equiaxed microstructure by deforming it, even at room temperature.

Upon aging, the solder microstructure coarsens, and a Pb -rich phase region forms at the interface between the solder and the intermetallic. Uniform coarsening of the solder would have little influence on the fracture behavior, due to the increase in ductility of the solder as it coarsens, which increases its resistance to fracture while the strength of the solder decreases. However, shear deformation in the irregular microstructure of eutectic $\mathrm{Pb}-\mathrm{Sn}$ solder is inhomogeneous. It is concentrated in planar bands in the shear plane of the joint, so the recrystallization of eutectic solder that is deformed in shear creates planar 'coarsened bands' that lie parallel to the interface and contain equiaxed and coarsened grains. The formation of coarsened bands is a catastrophic process. Since the recrystallized material is softer than the surrounding eutectic, strain concentrates in the coarsened band, causing further coarsening and strain concentration until fatigue cracks eventually form and propagate to failure.

Fatigue failure in tension initiates more rapidly than in shear, and tends to occur by crack growth through the brittle intermetallic layer. The final fatigue failure contains cracks through the intermetallic that are joined by cracks through the bulk solder near the interface. Bands of coarsened microstructure do not form in the striking way observed for fatigue in shear; the coarsening is more general and tends to concentrate along eutectic colony boundaries perpendicular to the interface. In summary, solder tensile fatigue cracks are observed in the intermetallic at the interface between the lead and the solder and solder sheer fatigue is observed in discontinuous bands containing larger solder grains.

To inhibit recrystallization within the deformed bands, chemical additives may be used that are known to delay recrystallization or grain growth in the $\mathrm{Pb}-\mathrm{Sn}$ system. Indium and cadmium are promising additives for this purpose. When Ni-thin-layer is plated on the lead wire, it suppresses the tin ( Sn ) diffusion in solder; as a result, fatigue life of solder is extended.

# Physical Solder Joint Changes

It is useful to understand the changes in joints as they undergo fatigue damage.

## Initial stress indications

Solder joint quality is normally determined exclusively from its visual appearance. High reliability assembly specifications require a smooth, bright or smooth, undisturbed appearance.The first visual evidence of cyclic damage to a solder joint is a dulling of the normally bright, shiny solder surface. This appears as an annular crazing or a frosty condition occurring in the higher stress areas of the solder joint. The effect is the result of physical slip displacements occurring within the solder matrix of the joint. These displacements occur in a relatively narrow slip band, normally within the smaller cross-sectional areas of the joint. As the solder is work hardened, grain growth and recrystallization occurs. Slips then occur in a slightly different (non-strain-hardened) position within the solder joint. This produces several slip bands until one is weakened due to Pb -rich phase alignment, then subsequent fracturing occurs.

# High stress, low cycle failure

A high stress (high strain), low cycle solder joint fatigue failure - defined as fatigue failure that occurs under 100,000 cycles - is evidenced by a complete fracturing of the solder joint with very little distortion of the surface of the solder (other than crack areas) or significant recrystallization of the solder structure in the high stress areas of the joint.

## Low stress, high cycle failure

A low stress (low strain), high cycle solder joint fatigue failure is evidenced by extreme dulling and crazing of the solder surface. Significant recrystallization and grain growth also occurs in the high stress areas of the solder joint. The Pb -rich phases will align themselves in the high stress direction within the solder matrix. Failure normally propagates through these aligned Pb -rich or softer phases within the solder matrix.

## Stressing conditions

It is important for corrective action to be able to determine the major stressing direction of the solder joint during thermal cycling. A visual examination can in many cases show these stress directions. The position of the component lead and the position of the fracture usually indicates the major stress direction. A component lead that pushes or pulls the solder into the through-hole will cause a compressive-shear loading of the solders with the joint fracture occurring near the top of the solder fillet and along the pin (Figure 8.4a). A component lead pulling the solder from the through-hole creates a tensile-shear loading of the solder, which produces a crack at $45^{\circ}$ to the pin and at a position lower on the solder fillet of the joint (Figure 8.4b). The weaker tensile-shear stress condition will also produce more separation of the solder.

Figure 8.4 Stressing conditions on plated through hole solder joint# Mechanical Properties

## Effects of Strain Rates and Temperature

The strength of eutectic tin-lead solder (Sn 63), and that of most other solders is very sensitive to both strain rates and temperature. Solder joint strengths are normally reduced very rapidly with slow strain rates or higher solder joint temperatures (Figure 8.5). In actual electronic assemblies, this relates to the rapidity of thermal profile changes and also to the temperature extremes of the profile.

## Stress Relaxation Properties

Solder joints not mechanically supported will creep very rapidly under applied loads (Figure 8.6), especially at higher stress levels and at elevated temperatures. The solder joint normally will relax stresses to the point where the stress rupture limit of the solder joint is reached or, in extreme cases, to the point where the solder joint fails.

Figure 8.5 Effects of temperature and test rates on Sn63 solder. Note that reduction in joint tensile strength with higher temperatures and lower strain temperature $\left({ }^{\circ} \mathrm{C}\right)$.

Figure 8.6 Stress relaxation properties. Note joint relaxation is very rapid, especially at the higher initial joint loadings.Figure 8.7 shows that as a joint going through thermal cycling, damages are induced into the solder joint due to creep-fatigue interactions. Onset of plastic deformations are observed through extrusions and intrusions on the surface of the solder joint. Stress concentration at the extrusion and intrusion sites leads to the initiation of microcracks. These microcracks coalesce to form a macrocrack. Cracks are initiated into solder joints due to the accumulation of stresses.

A failure mechanism model developed to address thermal solder joint fatigue for throughhole components mounted in single sided boards is described below. This required developing stress/strain and damage models in the following manner:

The displacement of the lead in the solder as a function of temperature cycle magnitude was determined as

$$
\begin{aligned}
& u_{x}=L_{x}\left(\alpha_{c}-\alpha_{b}\right) \Delta T \\
& u_{y}=L_{y}\left(\alpha_{c}-\alpha_{b}\right) \Delta T \\
& \theta_{x}=\arctan \left(u_{y t} u_{x}\right)-\arctan 45^{\circ} \\
& u_{z}=0 \\
& \theta_{x}=0 \\
& \theta_{y}=0
\end{aligned}
$$

Where $u_{x}$ is the displacement in the $z$-direction, $\theta_{x}$ is the rotational displacement in the x direction, $\theta_{y}$ is the rotational displacement in the $y$-direction, $\theta_{z}$ is the rotational displacement in the $z$-direction, $L_{x}$ is the length of the component in the $x$-direction, $\alpha_{c}$ is the coefficient of thermal expansion of the component, $\alpha_{b}$ is the coefficient of thermal expansion of the board, $\Delta T$ is the temperature cycle magnitude.

The net force at the solder joint was then determined by multiplying the displacements by the lead stiffness matrix, which increases with increases in the width and elastic modulus of the lead and with decreases in the lead height. The stress at the solder joint was determined by dividing the net force by the area of the solder joint which is a function of the pad radius, the hole radius, and the height of the solder.

The stress at the joint was then converted to strain at the joint by dividing by the elastic modulus of the solder. A more precise value can be determined by consulting the stressstrain hysteresis loop for the solder, but this is a constitutive property of the material which is often a function of the material history and was not available in this case.

The strain range equating to the $\Delta \mathrm{T}$ can then be placed into the Coffin-Manson equation

$$
N_{f}=\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{\Delta \gamma}{\theta}\right)^{1 / c}
$$

where $\theta$ is the fatigue ductility coefficient that is assumed to be 0.65 for $\mathrm{Sn} 63 \mathrm{~Pb} 37$ solder, $N_{f}$ is the number of cycles to failure, $\Delta \gamma$ is the strain range, $c$ is the fatigue ductility exponent which is a function of the mean temperature and the half cycle dwell time given by $\mathrm{c}=-0.442-6$ $\times 10^{-4} T_{\text {ave }}-1.74 \times 10^{2} \ln \left(1+360 / t_{D}\right)$ (Frear, et al. 1994).

A simple SMT case using simple shear strain dominated model is calculated by considering only in plane deformations due to a stiff component and PWB acting on a column of solder. This model assumes that the maximum strain occurs at a corner solder joint, the in plane deformations cause the damage and the out of plane warping is ignored, and that complete stress relaxation occurs during the thermal cycle. The solder joint quality is assumed to be good, creep fatigue dominates the damage mechanism and the local CTE mismatches are ignored. The model is characterized by the following equation:

$$
\Delta \gamma=F \frac{L_{D}}{h}\left(\alpha_{b}-\alpha_{c}\right) \Delta T
$$

Where $F$ is a correction factor, $L_{D}$ is $\frac{1}{2}$ the diagonal distance of the package and $h$ is the solder height. The life can then be estimated using equation 8.3 , when $F$ for the package style is known. 0) No stress. Joint bright and shiny

3. Slip evidence plastic deformation

4. Crack, 90 to 180

5. Near electrically open joint. Crack $>360$

6. Frosty (First indication of stress)

7. Crack initiation

8. Crack, 180 to 270

9. Proven electrical open

10. Frosty
    (More severe stress)

11. Crack, < 90

12. Crack, 270 to 360
