# 8.2 Failure Mechanisms of a Device Package

When a product's performance is no longer acceptable, it is said to have failed. Failure occurs when some failure mechanism - a chemical, electrical, physical, mechanical, or thermal process acting at some site in a structure - induces a failure mode, such as an electrical open, a short, or parametric drift.

Failure mechanisms fall into two broad categories: overstress and wearout. Overstress failures are often instantaneous and catastrophic. Wearout failures accumulate damage incrementally over a long period, often leading first to performance degradation and then to device failure. Further classification of failure mechanisms is based on the type of load that triggers the mechanism - mechanical, thermal, electrical, radiation, or chemical.

Mechanical loads include physical shock, vibration (e.g., underneath an automotive engine hood), loads exerted by filler particles on the silicon die (because of encapsulant shrinkage upon curing), and inertial forces (e.g., in the fuse of a cannon shell being fired). Structural and material responses to these loads may include elastic deformation, plastic deformation, buckling, brittle or ductile fracture, interfacial separation, fatigue crack initiation, fatigue crack propagation, creep, and creep rupture.

Thermal loads include exothermic die-attach curing, heating prior to wirebonding, encapsulation, postmold exothermic curing, rework on neighboring components, dipping in molten solder, vapor-phase soldering, and reflow soldering. External thermal loads lead to changes in dimensions because of thermal expansion, and can change such physical properties as the creep flow rate or cause burning of a flammable material. Mismatches in coefficients of thermal expansion often cause local stresses that can lead to failure of the package structure.

Electrical loads include, for instance, a sudden current surge through the package (e.g., in the ignition system of a car engine during start-up), fluctuation in the line current due to a defective power supply or a sudden jolt of transferred electricity (e.g., from improper grounding procedures), electrostatic discharge, electric overstress, applied voltage, andinput current. These external loads may produce dielectric breakdown, surface breakdown of voltage, dissipation of electric power as heat energy, or electromigration. They may also increase electrolytic corrosion, current leakage due to formation of dendrites, and thermally induced degradation.

Radiation loads are principally either alpha particles found in packaging materials from trace radioactive elements, such as uranium and thorium, or cosmic rays that can upset memory devices, degrade performance, and depolymerize the encapsulant. The problem is more acute in memory devices that are highly sensitive to alpha particles, in which even a minor alpha flux through the device can flip the binary state of a memory bit. Due to the stochastic nature of this failure mode, preventive measures usually are built in. A polyimide die coating of proper thickness is a simple measure that can block damaging rays. Compounding ultrapure fillers with low alpha residues in the resin is another way to minimize erratic device behavior due to ionizing charges.

Chemical loads include chemically severe environments that result in corrosion, oxidation, and ionic surface dendritic growth. Moisture in a humid environment can be a major load on a plastic-encapsulated package because of the permeability of moisture through encapsulants. Moisture absorbed by the plastic can leach catalyst residues and polymerization by-products from the encapsulant, then ingress to the die metallization bond pads, semiconductor, and various interfaces and activate failure mechanisms that degrade the package. For instance, reactive flux residues coating the package after assembly can migrate through the encapsulation to reach the die surface.

# 8.2.1 Die Level Corrosion

Along the metallization traces and edges it is possible for corrosion to appear. This will lead to an increase in resistance, electrical short or open, notching, electrical parametric drift, metallization shift, intermittence, intermetallics. The failure mechanism in this case can be either electromigration, oxidation, electrochemical reaction, interdiffusion, thermal mismatch. Also, on the die passivation, a stress concentration may occur from bearing of sharp edge of filler particle leading to transistor instability, corrosion of metallization, etc.

Another possible failure mode is called popcorning. Popcorning is due to the moisture entrapped in the device and above the boiling point of the moisture, a fracture in the package occurs. Popcorning leads to eventual loss of electrical function or even an electrical open. As per Figure 8.9 the crack in a device can appear at the bottom, on the side of the package, or on the top of the die. The patterns are sketched in Figure 8.9 and also shows when swelling and wire breakage occur.

Electrochemical corrosion takes place if all of the following conditions are present:

- moisture
- dc bias
- chloride $(\mathrm{Cl}-)$ or sodium $(\mathrm{Na}+$ ) ions to act as catalysts in the reaction

The dominant corrosion mechanism in semiconductor circuits is bondpad corrosion. It is generally accepted that it results from the transport of chlorine and moisture from the environment, typically along the lead pins, but moisture in plastic packages can also penetrate directly though the plastic. Chlorides, which accelerate corrosion effects, can come from fingerprints, spittle, etchants, fluxes used for tinning leads, plastics used for die-attach, molding compounds, or the operating environment. Chip bonding adhesives also are a source of chlorides. EDS can be used to detect the presence of the chlorides and characterize the chemical composition of corrosion by-products, thereby assisting in the identification and elimination

# Die Metallization Corrosion Models

Corrosion is the chemical or electrochemical degradation of a metal in contact with the surrounding environment. In an integrated circuit, corrosion occurs in the presence of an ionic contaminant and moisture at exposed regions such as the aluminum metallization on the bond pad. The ionic contaminants commonly found on the die surface include chloride from the encapsulants, phosphorus from the passivation, bromine and antimony trioxide from the flame retardants and sodium and potassium from semiconductor device processing. Time to failure $t_{f}$ due to corrosion in the plastic package is modeled as the sum of an induction time $t_{i}$ and a time for the corrosion attack and failure $t_{c}$.

$$
t_{f}=t_{i}+t_{c}
$$

The time required for moisture induction in non-hermetic packages is $t_{i}$

$$
t_{i}=-\frac{4 L^{2}}{\pi 2 D} \ln \left(1-\frac{P_{i n}}{P_{\text {out }}}\right)
$$

where $L$ is the length from the edge of the chip to the outside of the package, $D$ is the permeation constant, $P_{\text {in }}$ is the inside partial pressure and $P_{\text {out }}$ is the outside partial pressure. The corrosion time is given by

$$
t_{c}=\left(\frac{K_{1} K_{2} K_{3}}{K_{4}}\right)\left(\frac{w^{2} h n d F \rho}{4 M V Z}\right)
$$

where $M$ is the atomic weight of a metal conductor, $d$ is its density in $\mathrm{g} / \mathrm{cm}^{3}, n$ is the chemical valence, $V$ is the voltage applied, and; $\rho / z$ the sheet resistance of the electrolyte. $K_{1}$ represents the physical and chemical properties of the metallization materials and is a measure of the resistivity to corrosion, normalized to that of gold. $K_{1}$ for aluminum is set to 0.1 because aluminum corrodes approximately 10 times faster than gold. $K_{2}$ is the coating integrity index and accounts for the existence and integrity of the passivation layer covering the die metallization. A value of $K_{2}=100$ is assigned to a defect-free, completely bonded passivation layer and $K_{2}=1$ to unpassivated metallization. $K_{3}$ is the duty cycle correction factor related to power cycling. It reflects the reduction in the corrosion rate when the die temperature isincreased by power dissipation. The only temperature-dependent $K$ term is the environmental correction factor $K_{4}$, utilized to determine the time to failure for various temperature and humidity conditions. The $K_{4}$ term is modeled as

$$
K_{4}=\frac{\left(R H_{R}\right)^{n} \exp \left(E_{o} / K T_{R}\right)}{(R H)^{n} \exp \left(E_{o} / K T\right)}
$$

where $R H_{R}, T_{R}$ are reference relative humidity (\%), and reference temperature ( $K$ ), respectively, and $n$ is a constant. (Pecht and Ko, 1990)

# 8.2.2 Wirebond Failure Mechanisms

An electronic component essentially consists of a circuit and a case with interconnections. Historically, it is the interconnections that are the cause of catastrophic failure. The most common bonding wires used today are aluminum and gold. The aluminum often contains trace amounts of silicon or magnesium. The gold is typically $99.99 \%$ pure but may be slightly doped with beryllium for improved bonding. The gold ball bond can be formed by thermocompression or thermosonic bonding. Aluminum is primarily wedge-bonded ultrasonically. There are numerous failure mechanisms associated with wire bonds; the majority, however, may be grouped into three basic categories (see also Figures 8.11 and 8.12):

1. wire melting due to current overload
2. wire breakage due to thermal cycling during use
3. bond failure due to excessive intermetallic reactions

It is important to separate failure mechanisms that are related to degradation and aging (i.e., thermomechanical fatigue, current overload, and intermetallic reaction failures) from poor manufacturing practices or poor quality (i.e., loss of adhesion and ultrasonic agitation fatigue).

A common manufacturing problem encountered with both thermocompression and ultrasonic bonds is lack of bond formation due to contamination. The four major contaminants are

1. an $\mathrm{Al}(\mathrm{O})$ layer
2. F polymer-contamination
3. hydrocarbon residue
4. residual passivation ( $\mathrm{Si}-\mathrm{N}, \mathrm{Si}-\mathrm{O}$ )

Figure 8.11 Schematic of wire bond failure modes.

Figure 8.12 Bond schematic.

There is ample evidence that contamination can cause early bond failure, and an understanding of the influence of surface contamination is fundamental to the formation of a high-quality bond. Clearly, metal surfaces must be brought into intimate contact to allow interdiffusion of the wire with the metallization. Typically, impure metal oxides or organics at the bond interface act as barriers to a clean contact, thus inhibiting extensive metallic bonding. Metal oxide contaminants are usually removed by chemically etching the bonding surface. Organic contamination can be removed by ultraviolet-ozone cleaning procedures, although a significant improvement in bond strength can also be achieved if the temperature is raised to above $300^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$. TC bondability can be seriously reduced with only a few Angstroms of contamination on the surface.

Other manufacturing problems include cratering and wire sweep. Cratering, often referred to as overbonding, is characterized by damage to the semiconductor chip or underlying layers. Cratering failures are accompanied by holes or pits where the material has chipped out due to wirebond lift-off. Some common causes of cratering are improper bonding machine characteristics and setup parameters, including bonding force and tool-wire pad impact velocity; design errors such as improper bond pad thickness, bond pad hardness, or wire hardness, and intermetallics.

Selection of molding compounds based on shear dependence of viscosity should identify one that has the lowest viscosity at low shear rates and high cavity temperatures for wire sweep and/or paddle shift prone devices and in multicavity molds where complete filling before gelation is a concern (Pecht 1995). A material whose viscosity is more temperature insensitive performs better in all suboptimal tool designs.

# Current Overload

Current overload is a form of overstress failure. This is a common failure mode of wiring in microelectronic components is separation due to fusing, that is, melting open due to current overload. Resistance to fusing is determined by the wire material, cross-sectional area, length, and heat-dissipating capability. A 1 mil diameter gold wire has a resistance of $0.5 \Omega$ per

Figure 8.13 Photomicrograph of fatigue failure in bond wire.
centimeter. This determines the power dissipation of the wire for any given current level. The temperature rise due to the power dissipation is then controlled by the heat sink qualities of the bond and package. As the wire span is insulated by the surroundings, the majority of the heat is forced to dissipate down the wire to the bonds. The most likely point of failure is then the wire span. This is the point of smallest cross-sectional area and highest heat rise. Due to its inherent thermal and electrical conductivity properties, a 1 mil gold wire can handle considerably more current than a comparable 1 mil aluminum wire. Failures caused by current overload to a gold wire are obvious: when the gold melts, a ball is formed. Aluminum does not form such a ball; the wire simply separates, generally at midspan, with no evidence of fatigue.

Current pulse width is also an important consideration. Not only does the pulse width determine the average power, but it also determines the point of failure. Current pulses of short width will destroy metallization on the die rather than the wire. This is due to the smaller cross-sectional area and high resistance of the die metallization. The temperature rise is so abrupt that heat sink qualities of the die are of little benefit. As the pulse width increases, the die metallization is capable of dissipating more heat due to intimate contact with the silicon die. In this case, failure occurs in the wire where the temperature increases greatly due to the lack of adequate heat sinking.

# Wire Fatigue in Thermal Cycling

Expansion and contraction of internal wires in microelectronic components can be caused by two different driving forces. The entire device can be exposed to changes in the ambient environment on a gradual or rapid basis, that is, thermal cycling or thermal shock. Usually, however, there are an insufficient number of cycles to cause wire degradation due to this method alone. Second, expansion and contraction of the wire can be induced by self-induced heating during power cycling. In this manner, large numbers of cycles can be accumulated in relatively short times. Given that the thermal expansion coefficients of encapsulating materials such as silicones, epoxies, rubber, and other potting media are quite different than those of bond wires,stresses are imparted axially to the wires in plastic encapsulated microcircuits (PEMs) that result in accumulated damage. This failure mechanism does not occur in encapsulated packages or when a low modulus coating surrounds the wire. In cavity packages, the stresses are more flexural and are concentrated above the ball or stitch bond, as evidenced by the presence of slip plane damage in these areas. The wire invariably breaks in these areas, as all the force of expansion is concentrated at these points where the wire is tied down and immobile.

Thermal cycling is suspected as a failure mechanism if

- no evidence can be found of ultrasonic damage
- failure occurred at the heel of a stitch or wedge bond in a cavity package
- there is no evidence of mechanical tensile overload
- past history indicates that the device operates at high frequency and high current conditions

The wire used to connect die bond pads to leads in ICs can fail in cavity packages due to repeated flexing of the wire under cyclic temperature loading. The most prevalent failure site is the heel of the wire. The failure results from the difference in the coefficients of thermal expansion of the wire and the package, and it is exacerbated by delamination above the die surface. The time to failure is thus dependent on the temperature-cycle magnitude, the geometry of the wire, and its material properties, particularly its CTE. The stress in a wirebond interconnect has been modeled as a function of wire orientation. The cycle to failure estimate, $N_{f}$, is

$$
\begin{aligned}
& N_{f}(\text { cycles })=A\left(\varepsilon_{f}\right)^{n} \\
& \varepsilon_{f}=\frac{r}{\rho_{0}}\left[\frac{\operatorname{Cos}^{-1}\left(\left(\operatorname{Cos} \lambda_{0}\right)\left(\alpha_{w}-\alpha_{s}\right)\right) \Delta T}{\lambda_{0}}-1\right]
\end{aligned}
$$

where $r$ is the wire radius, $\lambda_{0}$ is the angle of the wire with the substrate, $\alpha_{w}, \alpha_{s}$ are the coefficients of thermal expansion of the wire and substrate, $\Delta T$ is the temperature cycle range encountered by the device, $\rho_{0}$ is the initial radius of curvature of a wire, and $A$ and $n$ are material constants. The forces and temperature applied during temperature cycling in operational life, lead to breaks and device failures. Axial fatigue during temperature and power cycling and is even greater concern in plastic-encapsulated packages in which the wire is encapsulated by a material with a higher coefficient of thermal expansion that the wire. This can result in the partial neckdown and eventual breakage of the wire (Pecht 1994).

# Excessive Intermetallics

A typical microelectronic component has a gold-aluminum interface either at the die or at the substrate/leadframe. Intermetallic compounds of gold and aluminum tend to form at this interface. These components are strong but brittle as a result of their complex crystal structures. Above temperatures of $125-150^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$, the growth rate becomes significant. This temperature range is lower than the maximum temperature specified in many storage and thermal cycling tests, and much lower than the temperatures at which thermocompression bonding processes and hermetic sealing processes take place. Thus, there is ample opportunity for intermetallic growth to occur. An example of intermetallic growth in a 3 years old device is shown in Figure 8.14.

Kirkendahl voids are formed as a result of the different diffusion rates of gold and aluminum into each other. Gold has the greater diffusion rate and as a result leaves behind vacancies on the gold side, which can coalesce into voids. This voiding effect is named after

Figure 8.14 Excessive intermetallic growth in a 3 years old PEM.

Kirkendahl because of his studies of the relative diffusion rates in a copper-zinc couple where such an effect was first observed. The process of metallurgical (Kirkendahl) void formation can lead to two kinds of failure: a mechanical stress-induced fracture along the locus of voids and through the brittle intermetallic, and an electrical open circuit caused by the coalescence of voids. Figure 8.15 shows the intermetallic growth sequence for ball bonds.

For the most common wire bonding system used in PEMs, (i.e. gold wire and aluminum bond pads) intermetallic compound layers can form over time at temperatures greater than $125^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$. Initially, $\mathrm{Au}_{5} \mathrm{Al}_{2}$ and $\mathrm{Au}_{2} \mathrm{Al}$ are formed, with a transition to $\mathrm{Au}_{2} \mathrm{Al}$ at high temperatures. These intermetallic compounds are called 'purple plague' because of the purple appearance of the $\mathrm{Au}_{2} \mathrm{Al}$ compound. However, high resistance and weakness of the bond can occur long before the 'purple' phase forms. This is because white intermetallic compounds are strong; they are also brittle and electrically insulating. In addition, intermetallic formation is often accompanied by Kirkendall voiding. Temperature and power cycling cause the Kirkendall voids to act as stress concentrators and crack initiation sites for fracture through the brittle intermetallic compounds. Generally, the bond strength is more a function of temperature cycling than of steady state temperature in the range between $-55^{\circ} \mathrm{C} \sim 125^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$, although the bond strength decreases as a function of temperature above $150^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ for goldaluminum bonds. The time to failure equation, developed by Kidson, describes an initial growth rate which follows the parabolic relationship common for diffusion controlled processes (Kidson 1961).

$$
\begin{aligned}
& t_{f}=\left(\frac{X^{2}}{K}\right) \\
& K=C \exp \left(\frac{-E_{o}}{k T}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

where $X$ is the intermetallic compound layer thickness, $t$ is the time, and $K$ is the rate constant.

Figure 8.15 Intermetallic formation in $\mathrm{Au}-\mathrm{Al}$ wire bonds.

# 8.3 Die Level Failure Mechanisms

### 8.3.1 Electrostatic Discharge/Electrical Overstress

Electrostatic discharge (ESD) is defined as transfer of charge between two bodies at different electrostatic potentials. This charge transfer results in a pulse of energy that can cause several types of electrical overstress (EOS) failure modes. The EOS failure modes seen in IC components include shorting due to the damage of the dielectric layers or device junctions, or opens due to damage of the metallization runs. Dielectric layers and device junctions are damaged by high voltage (low current) overstress. Metallization damage results from high current (lower voltage) overstress, due to resistive heating of a structure (up to and above melting temperatures) that is so rapid that the energy cannot be dissipated before damage occurs.Electrostatic charge is generated by either frictional contact between dissimilar insulators, known as triboelectric charge generation, or by the transfer of charge between a conductor and an insulator, known as induction charging.

EOS is typically defined as an event arising from inappropriate use of a component - typically during IC or system test procedures. If, for example, the test protocol forces a component pin to some potential (e.g. ground), while the logic state of the circuit drives that pin to some other potential (e.g. $V_{\mathrm{dd}}$ ), a contention state is established that results in a $V_{\mathrm{dd}}$-toground short across that pin. This condition, often transient, results in large current surges that can create significant damage. Similar contention states can be established within the circuit itself, if it is not specifically addressed in the chip design. EOS events are typically slower that ESD events, and involve a transfer of larger amounts of energy.

Pareto ranking of the failures in electronic components shows that ESD and EOS are major contributors. ESD/EOS are not only quality issues, affecting the components during manufacturing, testing and/or shipment, but are also principal reliability concerns because they often result in partial damage of the components. The partially damaged circuits then fail while in use, typically in the infant mortality portion of the product life cycle, due to interaction with other failure mechanisms. Addressing these problems affects many aspects of the components including their design, shipping and handling, and production and testing. The significance of ESD and EOS damage increases with the scaling of the chip feature dimensions, because the circuit sensitivity to these phenomena typically decreases. In addition the immunity of the MOS devices to these events is lower, and their increased usage has thus also increased the frequency of ESD/EOS failures.

# 8.3.2 Gate-Oxide Breakdown: Time-Dependent Dielectric Breakdown (TDDB)

Time dependent dielectric breakdown refers to the formation over time at temperature of low resistance paths through insulating layers, such as thermally grown oxide in MOS devices. Generally these paths are formed at a defect in the oxide layer caused by poor processing or uneven oxide growth. Fowler-Nordheim Tunneling-based Models for TDDB are based on the failure of oxides as a consequence of charge accumulation in the oxide. Breakdown of the oxide occurs when a critical charge density is reached in the oxide to trigger the breakdown process. The time to breakdown is thus represented by an apparent activation energy; $\mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{b}}$ represented as follows.

$$
t_{B D}(T)=\tau_{0} \exp \left(\frac{G X_{e f f}}{V_{O X}}\left(1+\frac{\delta}{k}\left(\frac{1}{T}-\frac{1}{300}\right)\right)-\frac{E_{b}}{k}\left(\frac{1}{T}-\frac{1}{300}\right)\right)
$$

### 8.3.3 Stress-driven Diffusive Voiding (S.D.D.V.)

Stress driven diffusive voiding refers to the creation of hillocks and voids in metallization lines as a result of metal migration driven by mechanical stresses. Opening of the conductor metallization occurs through the formation of slit-like or edge voids. The source of the stresses causing these voids are explained by various theories as follows.

- Silicon Nodule Formation theory - Large silicon nodules in A1 lines cause metal voiding during room temperature storage
- Coble and Nabaro-Herring Creep of A1 metallization theory - The migration force is generated by the thermal expansion mismatch, which is proportional to the length of the line, while the resistance to migration of the line is proportional to its width.- Passivation constraint theory - the voids in the metallization result from the device fabrication conditions, and the density of these voids is related to the residual compressive stresses created during the cooling of the passivation after deposition.

Okabayashi (1991) gave an analytical model for open-circuit failure for both wedge- and slit shaped voids, and accounted for the stress relaxation occurring during void growth. The time to failure for the metallization can be calculated by this equation.

$$
\begin{aligned}
& t=\frac{k G L W T \exp \frac{E_{g}}{k T}}{2 A E D_{0}(n-1)}\left(\left(\frac{\sigma(0)}{G}-\frac{E W \tan \Psi}{G L}\right)^{1-n}-\left(\frac{\sigma(0)}{G}\right)^{1-n}\right) \text { for } n \neq 1 \\
& t=\frac{k G L W T \exp \frac{E_{g}}{k T}}{2 A E D_{0}}\left(\ln \frac{\sigma(0)}{G}-\ln \left(\frac{\sigma(0)}{G}-\frac{E W \tan \Psi}{G L}\right)\right) \text { for } n=1
\end{aligned}
$$

where $\sigma(t)=\sigma_{0}\left(T_{d}-T\right)\left(\frac{W_{0}}{W}\right)^{m}\left(\frac{W_{0}}{W}\right)^{p}, G$ is the shear modulus of the metallization. $L / 2$ is the distance over which the stress due to void formation is relaxed, $T$ is the steady state temperature, $A$ is a factor independent of stress, temperature, and time, $E$ is the Young's modulus of the metallization, $D_{0}$ is a diffusivity constant, $E a$ is the activation energy for diffusion, $n$ is the stress-dependency exponent, $\sigma(t)$ is the stress at time $t, m=p=0.5, T_{d}$ is the passivation deposition temperature, $W_{0}$ is the normalization width, $H_{0}$ is the normalization thickness, $W$ is the line width, $H$ is the line thickness, $\sigma_{0}$ is the stress induced by a temperature change of $1^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ and $\psi$ is half the angle of the void. The lifetime reached a minimum at a certain temperature, $T_{m}$ and increased with an increase in the metallization width.

# 8.3.4 Electromigration

At a high current density $\left(10^{6} \mathrm{~A} / \mathrm{cm}^{2}\right.$ in Al$)$ in the metallization tracks, momentum transfer occurs between electrons and metal atoms. This momentum transfer can cause metal to pile up in the direction of the electron flow and provide voids upstream with respect to the electron flow. Electromigration-induced failure in thin film conductors usually appears in the form of voids and hillocks (see Figure 8.16). Voids can grow and link together to lead to open metallization line. Hillocks can grow and extrude materials, causing short circuit failure

a) Catastrophic failure

a) Non-catastrophic failure

Figure 8.16 Electromigration.between adjacent conductor lines. Mass transport during electromigration shifts from 'grain-boundary driven' to 'lattice driven' mechanisms at a threshold of $0.5 T_{m}$. At high temperatures, the main electromigration mechanism can become surface mediated. Since most devices operate at temperatures considerably lower that the melting point, electromigration is controlled by the grain-boundary diffusivity, and needs to be considered only along the grain boundaries (Pecht and Lall 1994). The time to failure equation has been developed by Black for grain boundary controlled electromigration (Black 1978).

$$
t_{M T T F}=A j^{-n} \exp \left(\frac{E_{A}}{k T}\right)
$$

$A$ is a factor depending on the geometry and microstructure of the conductor, and variables such as protective coating. $J$ is the current density and can be calculated by measuring the metallization cross-sectional area and the current. The $n$ is a empirical exponent in Black's equation. According to the current density range, several $n$ values were reported as follows.

$$
\begin{array}{ll}
0.5 \times 10^{6}<J<2.8 \times 10^{6} \mathrm{~A} / \mathrm{cm}^{2} & n=2 \\
10^{5}<J<10^{6} \mathrm{~A} / \mathrm{cm}^{2} & n=1.5 \\
10^{6}<J<2 \times 10^{6} \mathrm{~A} / \mathrm{cm}^{2} & n=4-5
\end{array}
$$

# 8.3.5 Die Fracture

Thermomechanical stresses are generated in a silicon die as a result of temperature cycling. Small nicks, cracks, and imperfections created in a silicon die during wafer dicing, can concentrate these stresses and act as crack initiation sites, leading to failure by die fracture. Die fracture is more prevalent in ceramic microcircuits, where gold-based eutectic die attaches are used, than in plastic packages, where silver-filled epoxy die attaches are used. The goldbased eutectic die attaches have high moduli and exhibit little plastic deformation, thereby transferring a large fraction of the stress to the die.

There are a number of models for die fracture which utilize the principles of linear elastic fracture mechanics to describe the fracture of the die. In these models, catastrophic failure occurs when

$$
K_{\mathrm{IC}}<Y \sigma(\pi \mathrm{a})^{0.5}
$$

where $K_{\mathrm{IC}}$ is the fracture toughness of the die, $\sigma$ is the applied stress and a is the size of the largest initial flaw. In the equation $\sigma$ is defined as either the tensile or the peeling stress depending on the type of flaw that is present in the die. The first type of flaw is a vertical crack through the thickness of the wafer. This type of crack causes a failure when a tensile stress is applied orthogonal to the crack as a result of thermal mismatch between the silicon die and the underlying copper die paddle. The second type of flaw is a horizontal crack which extends as a semicircle into the wafer. The same thermal mismatch stresses cause a peeling stress to occur orthogonal to this type of crack peeling it apart. The values for the tensile and the peeling stresses can be derived from the material properties and package geometric parameters according to stress analysis formulae developed by (Suhir 1986, 1987, 1989, 1990).

### 8.3.6 Die Attach Fatigue

For plastic packages, most of the stress between the die and the die paddle remains in the die attach, because of the low modulus of the silver-filled epoxy die attach that is com-monly used. As a result, these devices are more prone to die attach fatigue than to die fracture. Die attach fatigue for brittle die attaches follows a Paris fatigue crack propagation relation, such as :

$$
T T F=(1-\varepsilon / 2) C \sigma^{4} \pi^{\varepsilon / 2}\left(a_{\mathrm{c}}^{1-\varepsilon / 2}-a_{1}^{1-\varepsilon / 2}\right)
$$

with the stress calculated for transverse cracking through the die attach. The more ductile die attaches that are more common for the plastic packages, however, tend to follow a CoffinManson fatigue relation, similar to that for solders, where the number of cycles to failure is related to the plastic strain or corresponding stress.

$$
N_{\mathrm{c}}=C^{\alpha} \gamma^{\beta} \text { or equivalently } N_{\mathrm{c}}=\mathrm{C}^{\alpha} \sigma^{\beta}
$$

The plastic strain or corresponding stress are calculated from the material properties and the package geometry using the formulae in the tensile ductile and shear ductile die attach fatigue model.

The drawback of this model is the need to experimentally determine the fatigue coefficients of die attach materials along with the fact that most materials exhibit a combination of ductile and brittle behavior. In addition, the Coffin-Manson exponents are often actually a complex function of temperature, strain-rate and material relaxation behavior.

# 8.3.7 Hot Electrons

Hot electrons, or holes, are charge carriers that acquire energies from very high electric fields in excess of those that would be indicated by lattice or ambient temperature. Hot electrons are a phenomenon largely prevalent in high-density, small geometry, MOS memory devices because of small conduction channels and high voltages. It is accelerated at temperatures below $0^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ (Stojadinovic 1983; Woods 1980). Threshold voltage shifts or transconductance degradation can occur as renegade charge concentration build up over time (Ning, 1979). Penetration of the oxide by hot electrons can lead to excess gate and substrate currents (Takeda, 1983). There are three possible mechanisms by which the electrons or holes are injected from silicon into the silicon dioxide (Garrigues and Ballan, 1986):

Direct tunnel emission: Injection of electrons by direct tunneling is possible in thin oxides and large electric fields ( $E_{\text {ox }}>5 \times 10^{5} \mathrm{~V} \mathrm{~cm}^{-1}$ ).

Field-assisted tunneling: Electrons of energy close to but less than the energy barrier at the silicon-silicon dioxide interface may tunnel through the triangular energy barrier resulting from the field in the oxide. For larger electric fields, the energy bands of silicon are so slanted that direct tunneling can occur, regardless of oxide thickness (field emission or Fowler-Nordheim tunneling).

Injection over the barrier: Electrons may gain high potential energy due to high electric fields present in the conduction channel, and cross the potential barrier at the substrate-oxide interface. An electron in a conduction band of silicon can be injected over the energy barrier into the conduction band of silicon dioxide if its energy, $E$, is greater than the difference in the conduction band energies of the conduction bands in the silicon and silicon dioxide.

Electron injection through field-assisted tunneling or injection over the barrier is possible by stimulating the electron thermally, optically, or with an electric field; field stimulation is the most common form of electron stimulation (Garrigues and Balland 1986). The temperature dependence of the substrate current at fixed bias can have three origins: temperature-dependent channel current, temperature-dependent local electric field, and temperature-dependentionization rate. The low field mobility follows $-3 / 2$ power dependence on the temperature for typical n-channel MOSFETs (Sze, 1981). The reduced mobility increases the saturation voltage, which lowers the maximum-channel electric field at fixed-drain bias and results in a lower substrate current (Ko, 1980; Hu, 1983).

# 8.3.8 Slow Trapping

Slow trapping is a failure mechanism, observed only in standard MOS transistors and certain types of memory devices, programmed by the transport of charge from the source or the drain through the gate oxide to the gate interface. High temperatures, combined with a high electric field, provide electrons with enough energy to cross the silicon-silicon dioxide interface (Nicollian 1974; Woods 1980). Interstitial states at the silicon-silicon dioxide $\left(\mathrm{Si}-\mathrm{SiO}_{2}\right)$ interface trap electrons and hold them in the oxide, permanently shifting the threshold voltage of the device. The presence of electrons permanently trapped at the oxide interface decreases the speed at which the device can be programmed by creating a field that opposes further electron flow through the oxide interface. The failure mechanism of slow trapping decreases the circuit speed and causes functional failures. This mode is highly temperature dependent for temperatures greater than $175^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$. High temperatures combined with high electric fields causes electrons to cross the energy barrier at the device-oxide interface. A presence of trapped electrons creates a field that blocks the further electron flow and decreases device speed.

### 8.3.9 Ionic Contamination

Ionic contamination can result from packaging, interconnect processing, assembly testing, screening, and during operation. High temperature storage bake between 150 to $200^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ may heal failures due to high ion mobility. Ionic contamination causes reversible degradation phenomena, such as threshold voltage shift and gain reduction, due to the presence of mobile charge ions within the oxide or at the device-oxide interface, typically at temperatures above $100^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ (Schnable, 1988). A survey of published data shows that about $30 \%$ of microelectronic MOS device failures result from the ionic contamination caused by mobile ions in semiconductor devices (Brambilla, 1981; Johnson, 1976). Contamination can arise during packaging and interconnect processing, assembly, testing, screening, and operation. Sodium, chloride, and potassium ions are the most common contaminants. The most dangerous is sodium, which can cause failures in extremely small quantities ( $10^{11} \mathrm{per} \mathrm{cm}^{2}$ ).

### 8.3.10 Surface Change Spreading

Ionic charge is spread laterally along the oxide layer from biased metal conductors or through moisture on the device surface. This causes a formation of an inversion layer outside the active region of the device. The rate of change spreading increases with temperature between 150 to $250^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$. Surface-charge spreading, largely observed in MOS and memory devices, involves the lateral spreading of ionic charge, from the biased metal conductors along the oxide layer or through moisture on the device surface (Edwards 1982; Blanks 1980; Stojadinovic 1983). An inversion layer outside the active region of the transistor is formed due to the charge, creating a conduction path between the two diffused regions or extending the p-n junction through a high leakage region, resulting in leakage currents between neighboring conductors. The rate of charge spread increases with temperature. Surface-charge spreading failure, a wear-out mechanism, is usually observed at temperatures around $150^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ to $250^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ (Lycoudes, 1980). There are no existing physics-of-failure models to predict surfacecharge spreading failures.# 8.4 Do's and Don'ts in Design

- Do optimize the mechanical dimensions of the elements of the package structure with respect to one another (i.e., the size of the die in regard to the size of the die attach)
- Do optimize the package choice with respect to materials properties (consider the CTE mismatches between elements of the package, the stiffness coefficients between dissimilar materials, etc)
- Do optimize the package choice with respect to application environment (temperature, humidity, vibrations, etc)
- Do choose package compatibility with the available manufacturing capabilities in mind (do not choose a surface mount package if you only have mounted through hole capabilities)
- Do carefully choose the package weight requirements
- Do choose package materials compatible with circuit board material
- Do choose with part quality and reliability in mind
- Do consider part life-cycle status with respect to system life cycle expectancy
- Don't forget to design with thermal considerations in mind (choose heat sinks for high power devices)

The Do's and Don'ts of Using Power HEXFETs, Application Note \#936A, Government and Space Products Designer's Manual, International Rectifier, El Segundo, CA 1993.# Case Studies in Product Failure and Failure Analysis

John W. Evans

As we discussed in Chapter 4, failures occur when the applied loads on the system exceed the strength of the components, producing failure. The applied loads are any system load that include mechanical, electrical and chemical loads that produce the necessary stresses to drive failure processes. The applied loads and the strength of any component must be recognized as random variables. The potential for failure of a component is then related to the overlap of the load and strength distribution; this applies to overstress or wear out failures. However, in the later case we expect the degradation in strength to force greater overlap as time progresses. Overlapping distributions are illustrated in Figure 9.1. Greater overlap means greater probability of failure. In terms of field use of a product, such as a consumer appliance, this means more failures, potentially greater costs and loss of name brand recognition when early failures occur. This necessitates corrective action.

In this chapter, we explore how failures may manifest themselves in products and systems. We will examine several cases of both accelerated test failures and field failures in the overstress and wear out regimes. The case studies include a description of the failure circumstances, laboratory and analysis techniques used to ascertain the cause of failure and recommended corrective actions. This chapter is placed after our discussion of basic failure mechanics in Chapters 4 through 8 to enhance our understanding of failures and their

Figure 9.1 Concept of demanded load and available strength of a component in a system under load. An appropriate place to begin our discussion of failure case studies.causes in design. However, the reader, following Chapter 13 on Failure Analysis, should again visit this chapter, as each case includes a discussion of the general approaches used in failure analysis, as well.

The failures described below include a discussion of failures in mechanical, electronic and electromechanical systems. We can see the impact of several failure mechanisms and how they may manifest themselves in the system and how defects may play a role. These case studies have been selected as they represent some of the most common failure mechanisms and failure processes that occur in design and development of systems and products. If the reader is not familiar with the types of devices discussed, he may want to review a basic electronics text or mechanical engineering design text. The case studies presented are summarized in Table 9.1 below:

Table 9.1 Summary of Failure Case Studies in Chapter 9

| Failure Case Study | Description                                              |
| :----------------- | :------------------------------------------------------- |
| 9.1                | Microcircuit Life Test Failure                           |
| 9.2                | Television ESD Failure                                   |
| 9.3                | Spacecraft Filter Sub-system Vibration Failure           |
| 9.4                | Mounting Bracket Vibration Failure                       |
| 9.5                | Telecommunications System Printed Wiring Board Corrosion |
| 9.6                | Washing Machine Gear Box                                 |

The concept illustrated in Figure 9.1 governs strategies or test sequences that are applied in the failure analysis of components. In cases where critical field failures occur, we must examine failed components to determine whether the loading was excessive or the strength was insufficient using a systematic approach. Considering a mechanical component failure, this process breaks down, as shown in Figure 9.2, which shows the factors which must be examined to assess the root causes of failure in relationship to loading and strength, and the necessary sequence of analysis.

In the review of these case studies, we first discuss defects and overstress focusing on microelectronics. We then turn our attention to an electronic component under mechanical stress. All three cases present typical failures encountered in development of electronic assemblies. The next two cases show failures encountered in mechanical systems including a fastener fatigue failure and excessive bearing wear in rotating machinery. Finally, a case of corrosion failure on a printed wiring board of an electronic assembly is presented. The last case shows the influence of component selection on assembly failures and details the complexity of corrosion problems.

# 9.I Case I: Microcircuit Life Test Failure

In analyzing failures, we begin with a thorough understanding of the circumstances of failure for a given part or device. It is useful in the background investigation to also gain a good understanding of processes used to manufacture, test and assemble parts. In this case, a single microcircuit of low to medium complexity was analyzed following a standard accelerated life test, which was employed as part of normal reliability assessment for qualification and selection of parts for various new system developments.

Figure 9.2 Failure analysis approach developed from the load strength concept for a mechanical component of a system.

# Background

The part reportedly failed as a result of excessive electrical current leakage at input, PIN 4, subsequent to a standard life test of 1000 hours at $125^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$, under normal bias. Following the life test, a functional electrical test performed by Automatic Test Equipment indicated a leakage current of approximately 6 mA on PIN 4 at room temperature and at $-55^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ The maximum allowable leakage current for the device was specified at $0.1 \mu \mathrm{~A}$. The device type was a high speed CMOS digital inverter. The part had four bus buffer gates with 3 -state outputs. Theinput signal was required to pass through several stages of inversion and logic prior to reaching a final inverter. The maximum input current was specified to be $20 \mu \mathrm{~A}$. The minimum high level input voltage was 3.15 V at a supply voltage of 4.5 V . The part was passivated with silicon nitride and packaged in a 14 pin hermetic ceramic package.

# Preliminary Examination and Electrical Test

Initially, an external examination, radiographic examination and hermetic seal tests were performed on the part. These preliminary evaluations did not reveal any defects or anomalies. The procedures and equipment used were similar to those described in Chapter 13. An initial electrical test confirmed the failure. PIN 4, the suspect input pin, was found to have a 6000 ohm short to ground (PIN 7).

## Defect Isolation

Following the electrical evaluation, the part was de-lidded in the manner described in Chapter 13 to conduct an internal examination using optical microscopy. Initially, no obvious defects or overstress conditions were apparent, as are commonly observed in these kinds of failures. The silicon nitride passivation was subsequently removed using plasma etching by reverse processing to expose the underlying circuitry. Again, an optical inspection of the circuitry associated with PIN 4 and PIN 7 failed to reveal the location of the short circuit. Finally, microprobing was used to isolate portions of an N-channel MOSFET shorted to ground. Microprobing uses micromanipulators to place sharp tungsten probes directly on the circuit. This allows electrical testing of individual circuit elements using electrical test equipment, such as an oscilloscope or, as in this case, a curve tracer.

After isolating the short to a specific transistor, the metallization was removed and the portion of the gate underlying the ground stripes of the shorted N -channel transistor was carefully inspected using optical and SEM microscopy. These inspections revealed a particle in the protective oxide overlying the polysilicon gate. The gate structures are shown in Figure 9.3a.

The SEM micrograph in Figure 9.3b shows the appearance of the defect at high magnification. Some damage to the oxide was apparent adjacent to the embedded particle. No other anomalies were apparent in the oxide above the shorted gate structure. The embedded particle vas observed using backscatter imaging in the SEM. The particle was significantly brighter than the surrounding oxide silicon indicating the average atomic mass of the particle was greater than the average atomic mass of the surrounding oxide. This information coupled to energy dispersive spectrometry (EDS) of the particle to assess its chemical composition revealed that the particle was silicon. As a last step, the oxide was removed and the polysilicon gate was inspected. No defects were present on the gate structure.

## Failure Mechanism and Conclusions

From the analysis sequence performed, the conclusion can be drawn that the part failed subsequent to life testing as a result of a short between PIN 4 and ground. The short occurred in the oxide overlying a polysilicon gate of a N -channel MOSFET. A silicon particle was embedded in the oxide between the polysilicon gate and overlying ground metal, shown in Figure 9.3c. The presence of this particle, introduced during the manufacturing process, resulted in insufficient electrical insulation. This allowed dielectric breakdown to occur adjacent to the particle, over the course of the test, producing a short to ground. Here we see the critical role of a defect in producing early failure.

Figure 9.3 a Optical photograph of the polysilicon gate structures traced from PIN 4, after removal of the overlying ground metal connected to PIN 7. b SEM micrograph showing embedded particle and damage to the oxide surrounding the defect. c Sketch of the structure in cross section, showing the location of the particle.

# Corrective Action

In this case, no corrective action in the system design was necessary. The part was selected for various system applications. This corrective action was largely influenced by the fact that one device in a large lot failed. Rather, the corrective action centered on informing the manufacturer and assuring that the selected manufacturer of the device had an adequate quality system to avoid widespread defect content in the production of the microcircuits. Assurance that defects would not precipitate early failure was gained by specifying burn-in of the devices. The value of failure analysis in this case is shown clearly by allowing for proper deci-sion-making concerning the corrective action, thereby saving development cost.

### 9.2 Case II: Television ESD Test Failure

In this second case, we examine the impact of electrostatic discharge (ESD) into a television. In this case, a new television design was subjected to 25 kV in a simulated overstress test. The test was used to evaluate which components may be subject to electrostatic discharge failure. Typically, this level of voltage, or greater, can easily be developed by a person walking acrossa carpet. A consumer using a television may discharge a high level of electrostatic charge build-up on his body into the appliance. Reliability assessment of new product designs is essential in development to evaluate susceptibility to ESD and other failure mechanisms.

# Background

In this case, during reliability assessment testing of 32 television units, two failures resulted from the application of ESD type loads. In each case, failure was traced to a 64 PIN, medium complexity, plastic encapsulated microcircuit, as determined from system level electrical characterization. Failure analysis of the components was subsequently initiated.

## Electrical Testing

Failure analysis began with an electrical evaluation using a curve tracer. The curve tracer allows comparison of the current-voltage (V-I) characteristics of the device between each set of pins. This allows for an initial isolation of the failure site. In both cases, the failure was isolated to PIN 42 of the device. An example of the V-I curve for the device is shown in Figure 9.4. The trace clearly shows a resistive short circuit at PIN 42, as compared to a fully functional device. This is characteristic of electrical overstress.

## Internal Inspection

Decapsulation of the device was performed using automated decapsulation by acid dissolution of the epoxy encapsulation. This process is reviewed in Chapter 13. Following removal of the encapsulant, an internal inspection of the microcircuit was performed using high magnification optical microscopy. As shown in Figure 9.5, we can see significant damage to the input structures that are associated with PIN 42. This input was short-circuited to ground. Further analysis did not show any associated quality problems or defects in the device. We should note that the damage is relatively extensive for an ESD event indicating that a relatively larger amount of energy was delivered to the failure site than might be expected from the human body.

Figure 9.4 Curve trace showing V-I characteristics of a normal device and a shorted device, due to extensive ESD damage.

Figure 9.5 Extensive ESD Damage to input protection structures on a complex microcircuit. The energy of this event was greater than the energy that may be delivered in an actual field failure event. Hence, the damage is readily detectable.

# Failure Mechanism and Conclusions

In this case, the testing and analysis has shown that the device is susceptible to overstress failures in the system circuit. Two of 32 units failed by the application of ESD loads on the system. The result was significant damage to the input structures of the susceptible microcircuit. This caused an electrical short circuit to ground followed by a catastrophic loss of component function and system failure.

## Corrective Action

In general, any corrective action must be assessed based upon the level of risk acceptable to the manufacturer of the design. In this case, a risk of system susceptibility has been demonstrated to failure by ESD. For ESD prevention, corrective action might include designing protective measurers into the system circuits to prevent ESD damage to the susceptible components. Failure analysis of field returns and a careful assessment of consumer use of the product should corroborate the need for such corrective action.

### 9.3 Case III: Spacecraft Filter Sub-system Vibration Failure

We now turn to mechanical loads on a system, which have induced failure in an electronic component. Electronic devices must have adequate mechanical strength, as well as the electrical properties suitable to the application, when selected for a design. In this case, we see the structural elements of an electronic component failing from fatigue. Failure occurred in vibration during sub-system level testing and verification prior to the integration of communication sub-systems for a low Earth orbit spacecraft.# Background

An external lead wire of a single feed-through filter fractured following subsystem level random vibration testing, creating an open circuit through the filter array. The testing was conducted to simulate the launch environment for the spacecraft in which the sub-system would be used. The failure, shown in Figure 9.6a, was part of a large array of feed-throughs. Most of the feed-throughs had one interconnection wire soldered its lead. Two interconnection wires were soldered to the fractured lead wire. The failure was removed from the system for analysis, including the interconnection wires of the filter.

In this case, the component is a simple feed-through consisting of a stud mounted filter assembly. The structure included a discoidal ceramic capacitor and ferrite sleeve inductor housed in a tin plated, threaded brass stud filter. A schematic is as shown in Figure 9.6b. A 0.012 in . copper lead wire was soldered to the discoidal capacitor and provided the external electrical connection at either end of the stud. The remaining cavity in the filter was backfilled with epoxy to seal the unit and to provide additional mechanical support for the central lead wire.

## Preliminary Analysis and Visual Inspection

Failure analysis of the unit began with visual and radiographic inspections. This is a standard way to initiate failure analysis of a component. In such cases, every precaution must be taken to preserve the condition of the fracture for microscopic analysis. Visual inspection using low magnification streomicroscopy, as described in Chapter 13, showed that the lead fractured within the epoxy, at the solder joint fillet, between the lead and discoidal capacitor. The location of the fracture indicated that the epoxy did not provide any extra mechanical support to the lead during vibration. As explained, this was part of the intended function of the epoxy material. Also, it was evident that there was little plastic deformation of the lead wire around the failure site. This is characteristic of fatigue. Further, the fracture surface was perpendicular to the direction of applied bending stresses. As we have discussed in Chapter 5, this also characteristic of fatigue.

Figure 9.6 a Failure of the lead of a single filter in a filter array subsystem. The device and its separated lead are indicated by the arrows. b Sketch showing the type of device and location of fracture for the failure case study.# Scanning Electron Microscope Fractography

The fractured lead was examined using scanning electron microscopy. This is quite useful to ascertain the mechanism of fracture and mode of crack propagation and location of crack origin. This information may give crucial data about the strength of the material, defective alloy conditions and role of surface defects. The macroview of the fracture is shown in Figure 9.7. The fracture exhibited many of the classical features of fatigue crack growth produced by reverse bending, including the central shear lip. The details of the fracture, shown in Figure 9.8 at higher magnification, showed crack growth by mixed mode. Irregular striations are apparent along with ductile tearing. This is typical of low cycle fatigue in copper alloys. Finally, the lead wire was cross-sectioned. Optical microscopy did not reveal any problems with the grain structure or alloy condition.

Figure 9.7 SEM Macroview of the lead fracture shown in Figure 9.6. The fracture exhibits many of the classic features if a fatigue failure including a central shear lip indicated by the arrow.

Figure 9.8 SEM Fractograph showing crack growth by mixed modes. This typical of low cycle fatigue of copper alloys.# Load Analysis

Failure analysis may also require confirmation of load conditions. This can often be difficult, but basic engineering analyzes can be useful in looking at the potential for large stresses to occur. In this case, the exact accelerations were not known, so a range of conditions was investigated. A simple cantilever model of the component lead wire was constructed, which considered the mass of the attached lead wires. The stresses in the lead were estimated from the simple model to assess the potential loading in the wire.

$$
\begin{aligned}
\sigma & =16 K_{\mathrm{t}}\left(\frac{m l}{\pi D^{2}}\right) a \\
\sigma & =\text { stress in lead } \\
K_{\mathrm{t}} & =\text { stress concentration at failure site } \\
m & =\text { mass of lead and attached wires } \\
l & =\text { lead length } \\
D & =\text { lead diameter } \\
a & =\text { acceleration of lead and attached wires }
\end{aligned}
$$

The mass of the fractured lead wire, the solder connection and the attached interconnection wires was measured at 0.4 grams. For stress estimates, a mass of 0.5 grams was used. The actual stress concentration at the failure site was also not known, but a conservative estimate would be 3 . The result of this analysis is summarized in Table 9.2 and clearly shows the potential for large stresses. While this is not a rigorous stress analysis, we can see the benefits of examining the potential for failure to assist the failure analysis process. For reference, the typical endurance limit for copper is about $10,000 \mathrm{psi}$ and the typical tensile strength is about $32,000 \mathrm{psi}$.

Table 9.2 Lead Stress vs Acceleration for Failed Feed-through Filter

| Acceleration (Gs) | Stress Concentration Factor | Estimated Stress (ksi) |
| :---------------: | :-------------------------: | :--------------------: |
|        10         |              5              |           20           |
|                   |              3              |           12           |
|        12         |              5              |           24           |
|                   |              3              |           15           |

## Failure Mechanism and Conclusion

It should be noted in the discussion of the evidence that other factors can contribute to early fatigue failure. Surface irregularities, such as nicks, act as stress raisers thereby shortening fatigue life. Corrosive processes, such as those that may initiate due to residual soldering fluxes, will also reduce the fatigue life. However, there was no evidence to indicate these factors played a role in the failure of the filter lead wire. An additional problem, in this situation is the potential for resonance. Resonance could have occurred if the forcing frequency of the test encountered during random vibration was equal to the natural frequency of the wire lengths attached to the lead wire of the filter feed-through. In this case, very large accelerations would have been produced creating relatively large bending stresses.

In conclusion, the analysis of the lead wire of the feed-through filler showed that it failed in vibration as a result of low cycle fatigue. Analysis of the fracture surface indicated that large reversed bending stresses caused the failure. A simple stress analysis showed thatbending stresses, well above the typical endurance limit for copper lead wire alloys could be expected in vibration for the configuration of the failed lead. The presence of two interconnection wires on the lead and the fact that the epoxy surrounding the lead did not provide additional structural support served to accelerate the failure process.

# Corrective Action

In this case, corrective actions were necessary to reduce system failure risks during launch of the spacecraft. The potential for significant impact of failure drives the corrective action following failure analysis. Obviously the loss of a spacecraft during launch is a considerable loss. In this case, corrective action involved re-consideration of the part selection. A larger feed-through with a larger diameter lead wire was appropriate. In addition, investigation into the potential for resonance in the interconnect wire bundle was essential, leading to changes in the configuration of the interconnect wires attached to the leads of the feedthroughs in the sub-system.

### 9.4 Case IV: Mounting Bracket Failure During Vibration

Fasteners can often present significant problems in a new design. In this case, we see the impact of a fastener configuration design on the failure of a key structural component of an aircraft communications system mounting assembly.

## Background

Two bracket fasteners failed during a reliability assessment of a communications system. The system failed after 62 hours of random vibration. The failure of the fasteners caused a bracket to separate from the mounting platform. The communication system subsequently separated from its platform, resulting in severe system damage. The fasteners were required to be manufactured from low alloy steel exceeding 160,000 psi tensile strength (Class 8 Fastener).

## Visual Inspection and Optical Fractography

The fracture surfaces of the two bolts were very similar. Item A showed more corrosion indicating it probably failed first. The fracture surfaces were typical of fatigue failure as indicated by the smooth, flat fracture surface and lack of any evidence of general plastic deformation. The region of stable crack growth comprised about $85-95 \%$ of the fracture surface indicating moderate nominal stresses. Cracks initiated on one side of the fastener in the root of the thread, at several sites, as indicated by ratchet marks. The bracket and failed bolts are shown in Figure 9.9a. Bolt $B$ is shown in Figure 9.9b; the features of the fracture surface discussed above can be seen in this fractograph.

## Scanning Electron Microscope Fractography

Optical fractography is limited in depth of field and magnification. Hence, scanning electron microscopy can provide a great deal of information concerning the fracture surface details necessary to determine the mode of crack growth. In this case, crack growth was identified as microcleavage. This is undesirable in terms of materials performance in fatigue, since it is a brittle, low energy-absorbing mode of growth. However, it is not atypical of crack growth in high strength steels. Microcleavage fracture is shown in Figure 9.10.

Figure 9.9 a Structural bracket showing two fractured bolts, $A$ and $B$. b Optical low magnification fractograph of Bolt $B$. The fracture surface is typical of fatigue in fasteners. Corrosion is present on the surface of the fracture.

Figure 9.10 Microcleavage fatigue fracture of high strength quenched and tempered steel.

# Materials Analysis

Confirmation of the materials is an important part of failure analysis. Chemical analysis, microstructure evaluations by cross sectioning and mechanical property determinations are critical to materials characterization. In this case, Energy Dispersive Spectrometry(EDS), hardness testing and cross sectioning were employed. These tests showed the material to be a fully hardened and tempered, low alloy chromium steel with a hardness of 37 Rockwell C. The tensile strength was estimated to be $166,000 \mathrm{psi}$ from the hardness test. The material and subsequent heat treatment were adequate and in accordance with the specification.

## Failure Mechanism and Conclusions

The fasteners failed prematurely by fatigue as a result of cyclic bending and tension loads experienced during vibration of the system. Crack growth occurred by quasi-cleavage undermoderate to high stresses. Stress concentration at the root of the threads played a significant role in initiating the crack. Bending stresses, allowed by the bracket stand-off, played a significant role. Hence, improper fastener torque may have been a contributing factor. Improper torque would allow the relative motions necessary for bending, between the components of the mounting sub-system.

# Corrective Action

In this case, corrective action was needed to reduce the risk of failure during the useful life of the system. Stress reduction through the use of a larger bolt increased the life of the system substantially. In addition, assuring proper fastener torque reduced the likely hood of unwanted loading.

### 9.5 Case V: Telecommunication System Printed Wiring Board Corrosion

In this case, consecutive failures of communications equipment, during equipment level testing prompted the need for detailed failure analysis. As we have observed in other cases, knowledge of component materials and manufacturing processes is essential in determining the failure mechanisms that occur in system components. However, much of the process detail involving manufacturing of electronic devices remain proprietary, presenting difficulties. In this example, novel technology in packaging a glass body rectifier diode was selected for a rugged application requiring high corrosion resistance. While the device was selected from an approved supplier, in this instance, we can see the potential impact of process technologies used in components and their impact on the product and assembly, when consideration is not given to materials and process compatibility or adequate process control.

## Background

These failures occurred after 80 hours of system level tests initiated to evaluate the performance of a newly developed communications system. One test sequence exposed the system to $95 \%$ relative humidity at $60^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ followed by an 8 hour simulated rain test. These types of test sequences are typical of testing communications equipment for military or similar rugged applications. The equipment was operated intermittently during the environmental exposure test. The failures were discovered when the equipment failed to operate and were traced to open circuits on printed wiring assemblies. In both cases, the failures were associated with a single manufacturer power rectifying diode.

The entire failed circuit card was analyzed in the case of Failure Number 2 and Failure Number 1 was provided for analysis after removal from its circuit. This often the case in failure investigations where complete evidence of one or more failures may be obliterated in the haste of making repairs. In this case, it is fortunate that both devices were not removed from the circuit before analysis could begin.

For this part, packaging the die involved several key steps. First, the metalized semiconductor die was soldered to molybdenum slugs. This assembly was then cleaned in preparation for the application of the glass body. The glass was applied to the assembly as a slurry and fired at $600-800^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$. A $\mathrm{ZnO} / \mathrm{SiO}_{2}$ glass system was the basis of this process. For reference, the melting point of a typical glass of this type is about $1430^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$. To complete the package, tin plated leads were attached to the headers by welding or brazing to create a mechanically robust, sealed structure.A series of observations, tests and analyzes were performed on the failed devices in order to ascertain the failure mechanism. A planned series of laboratory analyzes of this type is usually necessary to accumulate enough information to determine the failure mechanism, the role of defects and the potential for design errors. In this case, the sequence of testing is described below with the results produced by the analysis described further on.

Initially, a visual inspection and analysis was performed. This involved removing failure number 2 from its circuit and carefully documenting all critical evidence on the printed wiring board. Both the failed diodes were then electrically tested. Corrosion products found in the failures were analyzed with scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and energy dispersive x-ray spectroscopy (EDS). In addition, similar parts from two different manufacturers were subjected to long term high temperature humidity testing for comparison. The simulation of failure environments can be useful in the analysis process to duplicate the circumstances of failure. Finally, surface analysis and cross sections were performed on the failures and tested samples. Again, we see that the most destructive tests are performed last in the sequence.

# Visual Inspections and Electrical Tests

The stereomicroscope is generally the first tool employed in the analysis of failures. In this case, Failure 1 was inspected over a range of magnifications and compared to diodes manufactured by the same vendor. Clearly, the glass encapsulation of the part had deteriorated significantly. Also, there were encrustations of black corrosion products on the device. The removal of Failure 2 from its circuit revealed many more interesting circumstances. The parts were mounted over a circuit trace in the configuration shown in Figure 9.11. After removal, many corrosion products were evident, including green, white and black deposits. In initial inspections of corrosion, it is important to note color and other properties of corrosion products. The circuit trace underlying the diode was completely corroded away resulting in an open circuit on the printed wiring board. This accounted for equipment failure and indicated that the circuit trace was an anode in the corrosion process. Electrical testing of the diodes showed that they met the specified parameters and were fully functional diodes.

Figure 9.11 Corrosion problem arising from mounting configuration of a diode. The diode packaging process produced a device incompatible with high moisture environments leading to failure.# Corrosion Product Analysis

The corrosion products on both failures were observed using scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and chemically analyzed using energy dispersive x-ray microanalysis (EDS). The black encrustation, comprising the bulk of the corrosion products, was associated primarily with varying concenlrations of Zn and Cu . The lesser amounts of greenish products were associated with Sn and Cu . Microscopically, these products were globular or botryoidal in appearance. The smaller amounts of white corrosion products were regular groups of crystals consisting of Zn and Mo.

## Humidity Testing

In order to assess the corrosion resistance of this type of component package, 10 samples from two different vendors were subjected to humidity tests. The tests were carried out under conditions similar to those in which the failures occurred. The parts were placed in a humidity chamber at $60^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ and $95 \% \mathrm{RH}$ for a period of 100 consecutive hours. Seven of the 10 specimens from Vendor A and 3 of the 10 specimens from Vendor B exhibited corrosion products that were similar to the white deposits of regular zinc bearing crystals on the surface of the failures.

## Post Humidity Test Analysis

A destructive physical analysis of the humidity failures was conducted which consisted of analysis of materials, corrosion products and cross sections. The materials analysis confirmed the structure and composition of structural elements of the diode, including the glass enclosure. The white corrosion products apparent on the humidity test failures were identical to the white deposits of regular Zn bearing crystals on the failures. Careful inspections of the $\mathrm{ZnO} / \mathrm{SiO}_{2}$ glass surfaces of the humidity test failures revealed the presence of numerous metallic inclusions. These inclusions were readily apparent using the backscatter signal detector(BSE) in the Scanning Electron Microscope (SEM) due to the high contrast made apparent by compositional difference. The composition of the inclusions was determined by Energy Dispersive X-ray spectrometry(EDS) to be metallic Zn. This was confirmed by cross section which showed the surface inclusions and their relative depth.

## Failure Mechanism and Conclusions

Electrochemical processes involving the package and underlying circuit trace resulted in equipment failure. Removing Failure 2 from its circuit board mounting, revealed that the failure mode was the formation of an open circuit trace due to severe corrosion. This open circuit failure mode caused the equipment to be inoperable. The diode itself did not fail electrically. However, the glass package played a significant role and was deteriorated.

The humidity tests of individual components revealed that the part has a marked tendency to deteriorate in humid environments through the formation of galvanic couples. Analysis of the corrosion products indicated that metallic Zn inclusions in the glass acted as the primary anode of the cell. A portion of the galvanic series, shown below, indicates Zn is anodic to the Mo present on the header and Sn plating present on the lead. This created two galvanic couples: $\mathrm{Zn} / \mathrm{Mo}$ and $\mathrm{Zn} / \mathrm{Sn}$. Moisture on the component surfaces served as an electrolyte. Evidently, enough inclusions were present to form a conductive path on the surface of the glass in the presence of moisture. This fact had important implications with regard to the equipment failures. The resulting galvanic cells produced white crystalline corrosion products on or near the Mo header. Extensive corrosion, deterioration and copious black corrosion products, as were evident on the actual equipment failures, did not occur.Simple galvanic interaction does not explain the equipment failures. Galvanic interactions were certainly present since similar corrosion products were found on humidity test failures of individual components and the two equipment failures. However, as Table 9.3 indicates, the solder coated circuit trace would be cathodic to the Zn inclusions in the diode glass and to the Mo header. However, the circuit trace clearly was the anode. Therefore, an external voltage differential was present between the circuit trace and diode; the diode being at a lower voltage, establishing an impressed voltage cell as described in Chapter 7.

Table 9.3 Half Reactions for Materials Present in the Diode Structure [Uhlig 1971]

|        | Half Reaction                               | Oxidation Potenrial $\left(\mathbf{V} @ \mathbf{2 5}^{\circ} \mathbf{C}\right)$ |
| :----- | :------------------------------------------ | :-----------------------------------------------------------------------------: |
| Active | $\mathrm{Zn}=\mathrm{Zn}^{++}+2 \mathrm{e}$ |                                      0.763                                      |
|        | $\mathrm{Mo}=\mathrm{Mo}^{+3}+3 \mathrm{e}$ |                                      0.200                                      |
| Nobel  | $\mathrm{Sn}=\mathrm{Sn}^{++}+2 \mathrm{e}$ |                                      0.136                                      |
