The presence of moisture on the diode and the Zn inclusions in the glass combined to create a conductive surface across the diode. The proximity of the diode to the circuit trace resulted in a path for extraneous currents from the circuit across the diode surface. The extraneous currents seen during equipment operation, resulted in corrosion of the circuit trace and the deterioration of the diode body. The loss of Zn from the surface of the diode produced the deterioration and appearance of the equipment failures. Copious amounts of corrosion products containing Cu and Zn formed as a result of this process and eventually an open circuit developed. The circuit board coating was inadequate protection to prevent failure. The presence of Zn inclusions in the glass was a critical factor. The exact origin of these inclusions was the reduction of ZnO during firing of the glass.

# Corrective Action

In this case, we see that a design change is warranted to reduce risks of failure in the communications equipment during use. The component selected for this application was incompatible with the requirement of durability in wet conditions. The options were to select an alternative diode configuration or change the circuit layout. In order to avoid subsequent failures, a rectifier utilizing a borosilicate glass was selected for use in the application. No subsequent failures occurred. For the manufacturer of the diodes and their packaging, a recommendation was made to investigate the firing and sealing processes to reduce the defect of free Zn inclusions. Here process changes would be necessary and process control needed to assure the end product does not contain the defect.

### 9.6 Washing Machine Gear-box Bearing Wear

This example presents a case study of an under-designed component. Whereas, other failures discussed in this chapter occurred in test environments, this case is an investigation of actual field failures. The component is the primary bearing used in a new washing machine design. This product experienced warranty claims from premature bearing failures. This necessitated failure analysis followed by a detailed reliability assessment. The details of the failure analysis are presented here. The overall course of corrective action and reliability assessment leading to a new design is presented in greater detail in Chapter 14 on product improvement.# Background

Bearing samples were obtained from field failures for detailed mechanical component failure analysis. A total of 11 units from a specific gearbox design were analyzed following service lives of 6-19 months. All the units failed as a result of various levels of excessive gearbox noise causing warranty claims or customer complaints.

## Visual Inspection

Bearing units were initially inspected by stereomicroscopy. Common to the bearings were various levels of damage to the races, as a result of spalling. Spalling is form of damage from excessive wear. The typical spalling condition is shown in Figure 9.12.

## Materials Analysis

Detailed analysis of the hardness and microstructure of the units indicated the bearings were properly heat treated 52100 bearing steel. The materials exhibited a tempered martensitepartially spheriodized microstructure with hardness ranging from 61-64 HRC. These are the common conditions necessary to impart the best wear resistance and strength to a 52100 alloy bearing. No material or process quality problems were apparent.

## Failure Mechanism and Conclusion

The conclusion of the analysis was that early wear-out of the bearings, resulting in excessive gearbox noise, was due to spalling or surface fatigue. Spalling is caused by relatively large localized stresses on the race of the component. Large stresses producing early wear-out, which are not associated with defective materials, are the result of under-design or loading of the component beyond is intended capability.

Figure 9.12 Spalling on the surface of a bearing race.# Corrective Action

As we mentioned in our discussion in previous cases, determining corrective action may require additional analysis and testing as part of the reliability assessment. Choosing effectively, the right courses of corrective action, is the subject of Chapter 14, which details case studies in product improvement. In the case of this bearing, corrective action to the design is necessary to reduce warranty claims and customer complaints. This means proper bearing selection and a detailed understanding of the loading in the system. The reader is referred to Chapter 14 to complete this case study.

### 9.6 Summary and Conclusions

In this chapter, we have observed how failures commonly manifest themselves under field and test conditions. Many failures often occur as a result of the mechanisms discussed above which include:

- Electrical Overstress
- Early Failure by Defects
- Fatigue
- Corrosion
- Wear

In each case we can see the role of design in influencing the failure process. In some cases, the design of the system needed to be corrected. Further case studies on design improvement are discussed in Chapter 14.

## Testing and Failure Analysis# 10 <br> Introduction to Testing and Test Effectiveness for Reliability Assessment

Steven L. Cornford

In Part I of the book, we have discussed crucial concepts to understand reliability assessment for design and in Part II we focused on some fundamental failure mechanisms that are often the root cause of many component failures and hence, system and product failures. We will now turn our attention to testing. We will begin by reviewing our perspective on relevant issues of product integrity and how the important concept of testing fits into development. Then we will focus on specific tests and test matrix design through Test Effectiveness Evaluation. The objective being to develop the methodology that will provide the most valuable and effective test program, to integrate into a physics of failure based reliability assessment process.

### 10.1 Introduction to Testing

Simply put, tests make measurements. They require a test article, which is then exercised or excited internally (and externally) and measurements are performed using sensors. Testing has a variety possible applications ranging from software to hardware to humans (remember exams?), to individual transistors on a chip, to an entire computer or spacecraft. The test goals and associated measurements of testing also vary widely from detailed performance characterization, to unmonitored 'burn-in', to automated spot checks of performance envelopes. The load environments in which tests are conducted may also vary: radiation, electromagnetic, constant acceleration, shock, random and sine vibration levels, temperature extremes, temperature excursion rates, number of cycles, etc. The duration of the test can vary from short duration functional tests to extended duration accelerated life testing, i.e. micro-seconds to years.

To further complicate the situation, consider that some (or all) of the goals of testing may be accomplished equally well through modeling, analysis, or preventative measures such as implementation of design decisions. This may eliminate the need for testing at all or merely change the location (and the objectives) of a test in a given process flow. Testing has been the historically preferred approach primarily because of uncertainty or lack of confidence in modeling or analysis, but also because of the belief that since the hardware under test is 'the real thing' there is no extrapolation required. Thus, many hardware developers and managers have a tendency to believe the results of a test with greater readiness than the results of an analysis. However, with the increasing complexity of today's technologies one must be certain of the test fidelity - which modes were tested, were the failures representative ofthose which will occur in the field, were the loading conditions accurately simulating that expected in the field.\*

With so many options available, and the variety of pros and cons alluded to above, how does one decide if, when and what to test? The answer lies in going back to the goals and objectives of testing. Once these goals have been established, one can select the test program as part of an integrated verification and validation program or reliability assessment process based on the translation of these goals into the failure modes being detected. It is at this level that one may intelligently tradeoff the relative effectiveness between the various available options to optimize the effectiveness of a particular test or of an overall test program. This systems approach to testing (which is itself a part of a systems approach to reliability) is the subject of Section 10.5 .

For now let's examine a roadmap for this chapter and what you will learn. This chapter will develop the tools the reader needs to understand the different types of testing available and how to then develop and implement an integrated test program. To accomplish this goal, the reader will learn about:

- Verification and Validation
- History of testing
- Levels of Assembly
- Failure Modes and Mechanisms
- Test Goals and Test types
- Test Environments and Stresses
- Test Effectiveness Analysis

The information within these Sections will then be combined to talk about the Development and Application of a Test Program (Section 10.5). This chapter will discuss the role of testing in the context of today's developmental environment with the impacts of significantly improved analysis capabilities and the goal of getting the most 'bang for the buck'.

# 10.1.1 Verification and Validation

Let us first examine some fundamental concepts and definitions useful for discussing testing. In designing and fabricating a product, the goal is to meet a set of requirements that provide the most value to the producer. The requirements may include functional performance parameters, environmental conditions, robustness (or the ability to perform within some specification outside of the intended operational constraints), and adequate durability and reliability.

In the course of translating a set of product requirements into a fabricated product, there are a number of assumptions and translations made. These assumptions usually involve material or component properties, which are assumed to be a given value, or range of values. For example, when one buys a lot of components one could assume that they all function perfectly, according to specification. When a torque wrench is used, one may assume that the calibrated torque readout is accurate. Thus, during the evolution of the product design, various working assumptions are made, which must be verified (bias voltage ripple content, adequacy of torquing, component temperature, etc.). Thus, verification is defined to be the process by which one proves (or disproves) the assumptions which went into the design. These verifications may be practical (or even possible) at every step of the process, as discussed below.

[^0]
[^0]: \* Remember that testing is in many cases also only a simulation and those who claim that testing is 'real' while analysis 'virtual' should remember that a 'real' test with wrong environment distributions is no longer 'real'.As a design is created, which is intended to meet the fundamental product requirements, there are points where these requirements must be interpreted into a set of internal, or derived, requirements. The number of interpretations of this type becomes particularly large in highly complex systems, which are in turn composed of a number of sub-systems, which in turn are composed of a number of assemblies, and so on. At each level of integration there will be a number of interface requirements generated which are intended to provide constraints and goals to ensure that when the product is integrated to the next level of assembly, the results meet the next higher level of interface requirements. As an example, a requirement to have a certain optical focal length might lead to a lower level, set of derived requirements, to use a certain type of lens in a certain configuration. These lower-level requirements were not the only solution to the original requirements, but have been derived to allow other parts of the design (procurement, layout, thermal and structural design, etc.) to proceed in parallel.

As the product is finally completely integrated, these derived internal and interface requirements are intended to ensure that the system now meets the fundamental requirements. In extremely high reliability, low volume applications such as interplanetary spacecraft, it has been historically routine to thoroughly check the performance at each level of integration and compare it to the interface requirements. In many cases, there are enough pockets of design margin in the requirements themselves, that performance which fails to meet a set of derived interface requirements may still be adequate for the product to meet its fundamental requirements. This propagation of actual performance values through the system may be used to generate a pass/fail criterion. On the other hand, the design margin may be uncertain to the extent that the original interface requirements may be the sole pass/fail criterion. This process of comparing the actual performance to the set of requirements, which were interpreted from the higher-level requirements, is defined to be validation. After this careful distinction, it should be noted that the words verification and validation are often used interchangeably in the industry! This is OK provided one just remembers both objectives.

Figure 10.1 illustrates the discussion regarding verification, validation, assumptions and interpretations by taking a simple example of a product, which requires two sub-divisions (called assemblies) to be produced. These are then to be integrated to produce the final product. Examination of Figure 10.1 reveals two key points. First of all, it is apparent that the more complicated the product, the more decompositions (and associated assumptions and interpretations) occur, and the more required verification and validation steps are required. Secondly, the risk (cost) of deferring verification and validation steps to later levels of assembly increases, as the cost and schedule impact of repair/rework grows significantly with each level of assembly. In cases where the processes, materials and components are known quantities (through previous verification and/or validation), and the design is mature, one may reasonably elect to defer the validation until the product is finished. In the ideal case, even this last step is not required. Thus the ultimate goal of product design is to eliminate the need for any validation and verification! In pondering the feasibility of this desired end state, consider that in previous centuries, a number of things we use today without even thinking about verifying required extensive verification at the time. Examples include the theory of electrical circuits, the behavior of matter in various load conditions, and the mathematical methods which lie underneath various calculations and computations. What has changed is that as various interpretations of nature become validated by everyday usage, one no longer feels the need to repeat the validation process; when was the last time you checked that vector notation or Ohm's Law was valid? As our technology, tools and capabilities evolve and mature, verification and validation should be required at fewer points in the product life cycle and should be focused only on the introduction of new, un-validated interpretations and unverified assumptions, as when new technologies emerge.

Figure 10.1 Verification and Validation. Note that the decomposition of the original product requirements into 'box level' or sub-system requirements introduces interpretations and the design process introduces assumptions. Subsequent testing simply verifies assumptions and validates interpretations.# 10.1.2 Evolution of the Testing Process

Having established the 'modern' definitions of verification and validation, let us examine the evolution of the testing process from this perspective.

As we know, when new concepts or designs are developed, there is uncertainty which arises from various interpretations and assumptions. Thus, materials testing and functional testing arose early in history. As a design or technology matures, the number of assumptions requiring verification and interpretations requiring validation decreases. However, usually the system becomes more complex, new technologies are developed and the process begins again. For example, the first transistor manufactured was only intended to provide amplification and this potential behavior required validation, partially because the theory of transistors did not even exist much less validated. As our knowledge base matured, the theory of transistors matured and the required verification and validation of fundamental performance characteristics was reduced. However, the introduction of digital logic required a new round of verification and validation. And so the evolution of what requires verification and validation continues as long as designs evolve. As these more functionally capable designs evolved, so did the complexity of testing. Today, testing every combination of test parameters for some Field-Programmable Gate Arrays (FPGAs) could require the 'age of the universe' to complete with today's technology. However, techniques for testing and deciding what to test have improved as well.

As technologies mature, one can try to achieve even more tightly controlled performance over a range of environmental conditions. This emerged the idea of environmental testing, in which the testing is performed in, or following, the introduction of various environments and associated loads. Whether it be coefficient of thermal expansion mismatch, or a drop in gain due to radiation damage, the introduction of these additional constraints usually results in another round of design, assumptions and interpretations. These in turn, again must be verified and validated by a new set of tests, which with an even larger set of test parameters. This process also continues as today we have under-the-hood electronics, vacuum and cryogenic operational mechanism and radiation-hard manufacturing lines to name a few examples. As these more robust products and technologies have evolved, so have the methods of environmental testing. Today vacuum, vibration, electromagnetic and thermal testing are considered fairly routine methods of environmental testing and others are used as well: for example, radiation, shock, and acoustic testing.

As environmental testing became more widely performed, it was noted that this type of testing also uncovered design and manufacturing flaws, as well as purely environmental effects. This led to some types of testing, particularly random vibration and thermal cycling, to become widely used as workmanship screens. This process was termed environmental stress screening (ESS). Note that in an ESS test the test levels and parameters may have no relation to the product usage environments, but are intended only to detect the presence of failure modes. As will be discussed later, some of this type of testing became almost 'religion' as they were applied routinely as the 'best workmanship screen' with little regard for the evolution of technology and process controls (IES 1984). To make matters worse, the test methods also evolved in such a way as to be unable to provide very little direct data regarding the effectiveness of the testing (Cornford and Plumb 1999, 1995).

Meanwhile, robustness (or margin) testing begin to develop. This testing was intended to demonstrate the robustness of the design - that is, the insensitivity of its performance to variations in external environment and aging. Robust designs can tolerate degradations in individual components, line voltages or environmental effects outside of those nominally anticipated. The efforts to understand how one can determine if a design is robust, and inwhat way, led to the implementation of testing using variations in temperature, voltage, current and clock frequency. As designs were investigated using this type of margin testing, it became apparent that some of failures being discovered were life related and the tests were actually simulating accelerated aging.

This led to today's approach of tailoring the test program (and associated test parameters) to the failure modes one wishes to detect. Finally, then, physics (and engineering ${ }^{\dagger}$ ) of failure based testing is essentially testing applied for good reason - this shouldn't be a new concept, but it is.

# 10.2 Testing and Failure Modes

This section will summarize the goals of testing by utilizing the concepts of verification and validation discussed above. This leads to a discussion of failure modes and in turn to a discussion of the concept of level of assembly which are the various levels of integration at which we can perform testing. This section culminates in a discussion of testing as part of an integrated reliability assessment program.

### 10.2.1 Failure Modes and Hierarchies

Testing is performed to verify/validate the product. Tests inevitably find problems and thus central to the reason(s) for testing is the concept of failure modes and failure mechanisms. Failure modes are essentially the different ways that failure manifests itself in a product or more simply put, the different ways something can 'fail', where failure is defined as 'failure to meet the requirements'. Thus, failures may range from having a gain 2 dB less than the requirement to an explosion of two materials coming into contact. Failure modes may also have a range of consequences, as is illustrated in the two examples provided. In addition, different product types may have different failure mode types, whose cause can cover the range of engineering and scientific disciplines. As we shall see later, these failure modes may be weighted by the likelihood of their occurrence (See Section 10.4.1) and by their impact on the requirements, to help focus a test (or test program) on the failure modes that are most important. These are the failure modes with the greatest potential impact on our product, component or assembly that we are designing (See Section 10.4.1).

Since failure mode impacts are characterized by their impact on the ability to achieve the requirements, one can think of failure modes as 'anti-requirements', or the ways in which a requirement can fail to be met. The requirements can occur at different levels of the hardware (discussed further in Section 10.2.2). For example, at the computer level, failure modes may manifest themselves by an inability to boot up, while a failure at the chip level may be observed as a missing clock signal. The failure modes observed in the test depend on the level of observation; that is, the level of the test, and the test instrumentation.

[^0]
[^0]: ${ }^{\dagger}$ Physics of failure is generally interpreted to have applicability to situations where failure mechanisms are physical phenomena. In the course of designing, errors can be introduced in the design itself (e.g. parts selection, mistaken assumptions, mistaken interpretations) by the engineers. Some of these errors may even require psychological models to get at the root cause (inspections require more light, critical components should be assembled on Monday morning, etc.). While it is not my intent to introduce the psychology of failure, I do like to broaden the definition of 'physics of failure' to include various engineering related failure models for which it is not useful to construct a model based on the underlying physics - sometimes a part fails because the wrong part was used and not because of any underlying physical principle.As we saw in Chapter 3, a failure mode diagram resembles a tree as the branches of different lower level failure modes meet at a higher level For example, we can imagine a number of possible failure modes, which could lead to a computer not booting up. A humorous example of a chain of failure modes may be found in a nursery rhyme:
'For want of a nail the shoe was lost, for want of the shoe the horse was lost, for want of the horse the rider was lost, for want of the rider the battle was lost, for want of the battle the war was lost.' Darn nail!

A good test will detect the latent ${ }^{\ddagger}$ failure modes within the test article. In order to design a good test, one must integrate the needs and insights of a variety of people involved in the development and eventually the production of the product or system. All of the participants in the production of a test article have failure modes which they are worried about. These are usually expressed as requirements, or measurement parameters. For example, a test article will have a responsible engineer who is trying achieve a collection of overall performance characterizations, but an electrical engineer for a sub-element of the box may wish to characterize the line voltage ripple, while the thermal engineer may wish to examine the temperature distributions across a particular printed circuit board. The questions to ask the people who are trying to meet the requirements are along the lines of: 'What failure modes will have the worst impact on your performance?, 'What failure modes are you trying to detect?', etc. This question is really just the opposite of 'What requirements are you trying to meet?', but can provide additional insight into the test design and selection of instrumentation and test parameters. An example of using insight of failure modes to specify the test parameters would be if the thermal engineer wanted only steady state temperatures, but was actually trying to ensure the devices do not overheat. This could lead to the addition of some hot power-on starts to the test plan and increase the required response time on the thermocouple acquisition lines, which are part of the test instrumentation.

Thus, it is useful to think about the failure modes when designing a test. There are a number of existing processes for identifying the failure mode tree, or the relationship between failure modes. The most obvious is to just write down the high-level failure modes as the ways in which the hardware could fail to meet its high-level requirements, and then logically refine the failure modes to the next lower level, and so on. Thus, one must tailor the evaluation to a product's particular requirements, using the expertise required to evaluate the various types of failure mechanisms. For a simple product a single smart individual may be sufficient, while for more complex products (e.g. mainframe computers) a team of people from a number of disciplines may work together to identify the various failure mechanisms, including the subtle 'cross-disciplinary' types such as electronic packaging failures and electromagnetic interference. In order not to miss any potential failure modes, and to expedite the process of identification, one can employ a combination of top-down (just described) and bottoms up ('For want of a nail, ...') evaluations one can easily generate the failure mode tree.

These failure modes may then be documented by using a fault tree or fishbone diagram, or more formally as a Failure Mode and Effects Analysis (FMEA) or a Failure Mode and Effects Criticality Analysis (FMECA). In using the fishbone method, the failure modes are written in a 'tree structure' with all of the causes of any one failure mode represented as lines connected to it. For more information about FMEAs and FMECAs, see Chapter 3.

The branches of the tree need only be identified down to the level at which corrective or preventative action can be performed. There have been various attempts to provide a

[^0]
[^0]: $\ddagger$ Latent defects are those which are present but currently undetected. When a defect is detected it is said to be precipitated.universal failure mode taxonomy but are doomed to fail because the tree will almost always have more than two-dimensional connectivity and unique relationships. However, one can try to identify a tree of possible physical failure mechanisms. These include mechanical (cracks, fatigue, etc.), electrical (over-current, arcing, etc.) and chemical (mold growth, electromigration), to name a few (Dasgupta et. al. 1992, Pecht 1995).

To provide a rough idea of the various failure mode types (and the difficulty in creating a universal 'failure mode taxonomy') consider the following simple example: an electronic box which has structural elements as well as circuit components (e.g. a radio or a spacecraft computer). The requirements of this hypothetical product may be considered to be purely electrical in nature (i.e. perform the function for a specified period over a specified environmental range). However, as one examines the failure modes at descending levels, one eventually finds that breaks in a wire (mechanical failure mode) may result in loss of signal (electrical failure mode). One may also find that an electrical failure mode (excessive peak current may lead to a mechanical failure mode (broken wire). Thus, an attempt to separate the possible failure modes into electrical and mechanical categories is not be feasible owing to the complexity of interactions. However, we can expect their to be a limited number of underlying physical processes or mechanisms that produce the modes. Fortunately, it doesn't really matter, but one must merely be certain to account for all of the relevant failure modes and their associated mechanisms of whatever type.

In summary, it is useful and straightforward to identify the various failure modes of a particular product. These failure modes can then be prioritized (Section 10.4.4) and the test can be designed to detect (through excitations and measurements) the presence of these failure modes. As discussed above, these failures manifest themselves differently at different levels of assembly. Thus, the concept of level of assembly is central to the goal of determining what failure modes to detect for and deciding at what level to implement what test.

# 10.2.2 Levels of Assembly

As a product is developed, it reaches various plateaus of level of assembly. One hierarchy of level of assembly was illustrated in Chapter 8, for an electronic 'box'. For a complete system, we might think of a spacecraft. It will have a collection of piece parts combined to form a higher level component. Components are combined to form a subassembly (i.e. circuitboard or gyroscope), and these subassemblies are combined to form an assembly. In the case of the spacecraft, this is the lowest level of a line replaceable unit or LRU (MIL-HDBK-344A 1993). In another example, the radio in an automobile would be considered an assembly and the various subassemblies of the radio would correspond to the mounting hardware and chassis, the internal circuit card, etc. while the knobs, dials, resistors, wire, etc. would be individual parts. Note that the concept of LRU would mean that in the field or during final system (car) testing, an anomaly in the radio would be immediately corrected by replacing the radio and the car would keep moving towards being shipped out the door. A central element of a systems based reliability strategy is what happens to the 'bad' radio? Ideally, the radio would be evaluated to determine it's root-cause failure mechanism and appropriate preventative measures would be then integrated into the process. This is called a closed loop corrective action system, (ISO 9000).

Returning to the car example, a collection of assemblies forms a subsystem which usually has a completely stand-alone function except for interfaces. In our case, the radio, speaker wire, speakers, and power amplifier (if a nice car) combine to form the sound subsystem. This has a stand-alone function which can be 'independently' tested/verified/validated by simulating the interface to the power subsystems (e.g. battery) by connecting to a power supply.There is a danger in assuming independence without sufficient knowledge of all the interfaces, including induced environments. In the car examples, we have been studying, the actual application may have the battery-to-radio line going through the engine. Without introduction of some inductance, the radio will 'play' the spark plugs firing, through EMI from the coil/distributor. Also, the shape of the car body may cause low frequencies to amplify excessively. This illustrates again the importance of test fidelity and robustness, as the best radio test would occur in the car itself, with the car running and powered by the battery or with seats and internal upholstery in place. However, this is a bit late in the development cycle to discover interference or resonance problems. One could have monitored the development of the spark plug firing assembly and measured, providing safety margins, as necessary, the observed interference levels, or measured these levels in a car with a 'similar' firing assembly (and added some uncertainty-in-similarity margin) or even built the radio/battery interface so robust that it didn't matter exactly what the EMI environment was. Or, in the case of the resonance one could have modeled the car's acoustical properties or made measurements with a sound generator on a prototype unit. Combinations of the options are always available and the selection should be based on effectiveness of the test for the failure mode under observation. In today's environment, one must also strongly consider the cost of each option and this optimization process will be discussed in Section 10.4, and is really the heart of the reliability function.

Concluding our car example and the discussion of levels of assembly, the collection of subsystems (sound, power train, transmission, etc.) forms the system known as the car. In the case of fleet of cars, or constellation of spacecraft, the level of assemblies may be continue even higher.

In summary, the detailed labels given to various levels of assembly is somewhat arbitrary, the discussion was intended to reveal that:

- Tests (and other activities) may be performed at different levels of assembly
- Options besides tests may do just as well or better
- Tests at lower levels of assembly have the benefit of finding problems earlier and being less complex, but may have reduced test fidelity, and
- Tests at higher levels of assembly have the benefit of finding more realistic problems and have less uncertainty in regards to having achieved test fidelity, but may result in problems being discovered late in the production process.

The judgment as when to test is part of an integrated reliability program and must be decided by the product development team.

# 10.2.3 Failure Mode Types

Failure modes may be looked at in a variety of ways: for example, one may look at the cause or the effect. They may grouped in a variety of ways. For example, they can be grouped by hardware sub-assembly, by failure mode cause types, by level of severity, etc) It all depends on what is the most convenient grouping for the evaluation at hand.

## Grouping Failure Modes by When They Occur

A grouping traditionally used is to describe failure mechanisms as being in three categories: early life, commonly referred to as infant mortality, useful life and wear-out. This originated from noting that graphical depictions of the hazard rate or failure rate for a wide variety of

Figure 10.2 Traditional 'bathtub' curve. This curve illustrates the phenomenon of initially high failure rates due to early life or 'infant mortality'. This rate gradually reduces until it reaches a constant failure rate which is known as the 'useful life' region. Finally, the failure rate again increase due to 'wear-out' effects. Note that while this curve may be accurate for a specific failure mechanism, the large number of possible failure mechanisms in a product may result in a failure rate curve for the box which does not resemble this bathtub curve at all. Recall that only overstress can result in a constant failure rate.
hardware, had a similar shape which is ideally depicted in Figure 10.2. This grouping was useful because in the high-volume marketplace, most of the early failures are due to manufacturing or processing defects and most of the end-of-life failures were due to fatigue, ablation and other life issues, which were part of the design process. The intermediate or useful life is sometimes referred as 'random's failures. It is intended to reflect the random probability of some device failing during the useful life regime. In an ideal product, the infant mortalities all occur before reaching the field, the wear-out failures all occur beyond the design life and there are very few (or no) random failures. In the low-volume business, this distinction may not be particularly useful, where design defects must be found during the development phase, and both design and manufacturing defects can escape into the field.

While thinking about failure modes in terms of where they occur in the product usage life cycle is useful, there are other groupings which are also useful. Thinking about failure modes in terms of the discipline in which it is most naturally evaluated can also be useful, as it can help manage the process by focusing the right individuals on the right problems. However, there are a number of interdisciplinary failure modes which may be optimally investigated by a system engineer or physicist.

The following is a partial list of failure modes (and in some cases we have included mechanisms as well) which may prove to be useful memory joggers when you try to develop a test program:

- Tensile failure
- Shear failure
- Stress rupture
- Parametric drift

# 10.2.4 Test Goals and Test Types

In general, the goals of a test in a test program is to find the right failures at the right level of assembly. More specifically, the goal of any test is to take the desired measurements in the desired conditions of a test article. The underlying goal of any test is to perform those verification and validation functions for which the test was designed. In addition, a test may also be intended to be able to detect unanticipated problems. These problems, or failure modes, may manifest themselves as electrical signals, structural behavioral characteristics, chemical deposition rates, etc. In other words, the test is merely a vehicle for performing measurements some of which may reveal the presence of a variety of failure modes; establishing the type and details of these physical measurements for a particular product, or product constituent, is the role of the test designer. These measurements may range from using electronic ground support equipment, such as amplifiers and receivers, to setting up and monitoring arrays of thermocouples (for measuring temperature), to measuring stresses and strains during the impingement of high levels of acoustic energy. The choice of measuring equipment depends on what you want to measure! Later in this chapter (10.3), some of the equipment associated with different specific test types will be discussed in further detail as part of the discussion of particular tests.

In addition to the wide range of possibilities of test measuring equipment, there exists an equally wide range of test objectives. As discussed previously, the measurements taken during a test may accomplish a variety of objectives ranging from electronic packaging and circuit performance qualification, to establishing product cleanliness (outgassing and particulates) to establishing the lifetime of a particular dynamic contact including lubricant aging and material galling. Thus, the test designer, or the test design team, must have a wide variety of disciplinary knowledge at their disposal. This allows the test design to uncover potential problems that would not have been anticipated within an individual discipline, particularly interactions such as thermal/structural, materials for performance versus materials for cleanliness, etc. This is particularly important on pre-production, or qualification, units where interactions which remain undetected into production could have significant cost and schedule impacts.

The philosophical distinction between verification and validation testing performed can be easily blurred when examining specific test types, since most tests accomplish both of these goals to some extent. Let us examine some of the principal test types.

Functional Testing or performance testing is probably one of the single most important tests which can be performed. As the design is being implemented, there are a number of parameters, which must be verified (or validated) to establish that the performance is adequate at nominal conditions. This testing should precede any other type of test because as Bob Conover of JPL quipped, 'If it won't function, it doesn't matter if it can survive'. Much of functional testing is performed as bench testing on engineering models or qualificationunits. This testing provides characterization of the performance over a variety of operating conditions and detects both functional, material and manufacturing failure modes.

The real challenge of functional testing is to measure the right collection of parameters to provide insight into the underlying performance without excessively increasing the complexity and cost of the test. The process for failure mode identification provided above can now be applied and higher-level functional failure modes can be seen to be manifestations of lower-level functional modes.

Life testing is intended to provide confidence that the product will meet, or exceed, it's design life. This may be testing to a particular standard, such as 5 years, or until $10 \%$ of the devices have failed. The selection of the standard is a reliability decision and may include uncertainty or statistical margins. However, test to failure is a higher fidelity approach as it provides sufficient information to perform statistical assessments of overall lifetimes, as well as identifying the various failure modes which are contributing to the life related failures. This information may then be correlated to various behavioral models for the hardware. It also has the practical advantage of precluding the usual possibility of having to run the test again when a different application warrants a longer life than the previous life test duration. Product validation is usually at a higher level of assembly (for example a radio or a black box). The principal recipients of life testing are mechanisms and electronic packaging, although in highvolume industry there may be reasons for life testing other hardware components.

Process Validation Testing is testing done to ensure that the results of a particular process (an assembly line, a mass reflow line, bonding application, etc.) are adequate for the intended application. This testing is most effective when the primary process variables affecting the process output are known. The output of the process is then tested to ensure it meets the requirements on the process (e.g. defect rates, lifetimes and tolerances). The performance of the process output may also be correlated back to process models either verifying the accuracy of the model or allowing model refinement.

Product Validation Testing is testing done to ensure that a particular product meets the product requirements. This product may be the result of a variety of process, or may done by a customer to ensure adequacy of a delivery. There are two principal approaches used here: Protoqualification or Qualification. Qualification testing refers to testing a particular design to ensure its ability to meet the design requirements. This testing is often destructive, or at least degrading, to the hardware under test and products which emerge from this type of testing are usually considered scrap. In order to test that a product can survive a given overstress condition, one usually accumulates damage on the product and in cases where margin is added onto test parameters to ensure robustness, the product may actually be destroyed and still prove that the design is adequate! Protoqualification testing is primarily used in parts of the aerospace industry, or other 'ultra-low' volume applications and entails testing a 'one-of-a-kind' unit which must be both qualified and deployed (for example, an interplanetary probe). Thus, the testing must prove the adequacy of the design without harming the product. This type of testing is very difficult and engineers must rely heavily on models and uncertainty margins.

Acceptance Testing is testing, which measures the product performance against its operational specification usually with some small additional margin. Acceptance testing usually follows qualification testing, and the simplest viewpoint is that qualification testing finds design flaws while acceptance testing finds workmanship defects; in reality, they both find both.

Integrated Testing is any testing which achieves the goals of some of the various test types by combining them into a single test. This may include combined environments (e.g. vibration while cold), or combining functional testing with thermal performance testing. As an additional example, Protoqualification testing is intended to achieve the objectives of both qualification and acceptance testing in a single test on a single unit.Possibly the most important attribute of the test is the test fidelity, or the degree to which the test realistically reproduces the desired usage scenario. For example, if the product is to operate in a vacuum, then a test done in an atmospheric pressure environments may not simulate the actual operation. As another example, software testing may be done through a set of random commands and not follow the command sequence which a user would naturally use. This is particularly critical when testing at lower levels of assembly and one is required to 'fake' the external mechanical, electrical and physical interfaces to other hardware pieces. A well-designed test will have addressed the extent to which this limits the test. For example, the extent to which the lack of a high-frequency vibration component will or won't modify the fidelity of the test or the extent to which a test heat sink will deviate from the heat sink used in the final application.

In addition, the test engineer should also have done an error propagation analysis for the measurement equipment to ensure that the various measurement tolerances are consistent with the measurements needed to identify failure modes.

# 10.2.5 Testing as Part of an Integrated Reliability Program

This chapter is primarily focused on testing, but let us return to the idea of testing as part of an integrated reliability program. The failure modes still present when a test is conducted is a function of what was done before. A mature design, or a collection of inspections, or bench testing may have already been implemented. This changes the population of defects present in the test article. Specifically, there may not remain any failure modes of the type detected by this particular test - then why do it? Thus, in this case one would implement a different test (or maybe no test at all). The goal of the test engineer is to select the test which will add the most value. That is, to select the test which will detect the most failure modes, which are actually present. Using the techniques discussed previously, one can identify the type and population of failure modes present and then select the test (or PACTs\*\*) which provides the desired level of detection and prevention. We will return to this 'mixing and matching' procedure in later sections of this chapter.

The PACTs already implemented will determine the distribution of failure modes which are present for the test to detect. If one imagines a big bar chart with the height of each bar corresponding to the number of failure modes of that type present, then the sizes of the different bars will go down (usually) but in varying amounts depending the PACT implemented. For example, a printed circuit board inspection will yield little information regarding electrical design failure modes, while a functional test will yields very little information about the sensitivity to high vibration levels. Different PACTs have different efficiencies at 'screening' out different types of failure modes. It is the ultimate goal of the reliability engineer to integrate the PACTs implemented at various levels of assembly to meet all of the requirements within resource constraints. Testing is an integral part of the this process: it's the ' $T$ ' in PACT! A graphical depiction of the interplay between testing and other design and development activities (PACTs) is illustrated in Figure 10.3.

In this figure, the solid arrows represent failure modes present in the hardware, while the dashed lines represent 'escapes' or failure present which were not prevented and are still undetected. There are at least four important insights to be gained by a more careful examination of this figure:
