[^0]: \*\* PACTs = Preventitive measures (design rules, component selection, redundancy, etc.), Analyzes (structural, thermal, electrical, reliability, etc.), process Controls (inspection, certification, process design of experiments, etc.), and Tests (bench functional, environmental, materials strength, etc.). PACTs are the collection of everything which can be done to detect or prevent the occurance of the failure modes.

Figure10. 3 Graphical depiction of the role of the various product development activities in detecting and preventing failure modes. Note that the boxes are not intended to be to 'scale'.

1. The solid line under Inspections/Verifications is a failure mode which was introduced by this PACT (i.e. ESD damage).
2. The solid line in the middle of the Figure 10.3, going directly to the System Testing box has only this one chance to be detected. If the System Test fails to find it, it will appear in the field. An even greater danger here is that in a resource crunch, part of this test may be modified or dropped and we run the risk of missing this failure mode with our one chance.
3. The solid line at the far right will go undetected and un-prevented by the entire development process. This is fairly rare, but more common in the production of 'fast track' development of single product builds. This is one of the situations we want to avoid unless the likelihood or impact is so small that not detecting this failure mode was a conscious choice.
4. At various points on this figure one can see several layers of boxes which represents different PACTs which are screens for the same failure modes. This could be because there are some new failure modes of this type being introduced, or it could be an attempt to make 5 different PACTs amount to the equivalent of one good PACT for this failure mode, it could mean that some of the PACTs get this failure mode 'for free', i.e. in the course of finding another, or it is most likely an oversight, in which the same tests are being run with little consideration as to the effectiveness of the various parameters within the PACTs on the failure mode in question.Optimization is the name of the game in today's competitive marketplace and we cannot afford to be ignorant as to why we are testing and what we are testing for. Think about the failure modes which need to be detected and how they can best be detected (or prevented) and spend some time thinking about the metrics one could measure to establish the effectiveness of the test - Is it cost per defect found? We shall return to this later in Section 10.6, but the answer is no.

However, let us first explore the various test environments and the stresses they induce.

# 10.3 Test Environments and Stresses

This section will summarize the application of test environments or environmental loads to induce stresses in system components. These test induced stresses that may precipitate, or induce, failures which might otherwise occur at more inconvenient times, such as during a system test or in the field. The stresses induced by testing loads may range from stresses typical of operation (e.g. power on, room temperature), to the extremes of typical operation (e.g. warm room with high humidity and handling), to extremes beyond typical usage (margined operation), to stresses intended entirely to precipitate design and workmanship defects. An example here being vibration testing of office computer equipment, even though it is not intended to launch on a rocket.

As test induced stresses increase, the likelihood of inducing a failure continues to increase, and the risk of overtesting, or inducing failures which would not have otherwise occurred in the field environment, also increases. This is discussed in further detail in Chapter 12. This variety of test stress levels has historically been grouped into three categories (listed in order of decreasing stress):

1. Stresses intended to demonstrate that the product meets its design requirements
2. Stresses intended to ensure the product exceeds its intended usage requirements
3. Stresses which occur in the usage environment.

Exposure to (1), or qualification levels, is generally considered to be life-consuming as the stresses may induce unintentional damage, or leave the product with insufficient life to meet its intended usage environment. The tested product is usually deemed unusable. Exposure to (2), or acceptance levels, is considered to be non-life-consuming as the stresses are only marginally outside the intended usage environment and may even be statistically possible. The tested product in this case is usually shipped. Exposure to (3), or normal usage, is intended to be reliable and is the goal of an integrated reliability program of which (1) and (2) are a critical element.

### 10.3.1 Environments

There are a variety of environments which can be used during testing to precipitate defects. As discussed above, these environments may simulate an actual usage environment or may be present only to produce stress on the article under test. For example, environmental stress screening (ESS) typically refers to using environments to cause stresses and identify workmanship problems but the environments may have nothing to do with the usage environment. For example, even in a vibration free application it may be beneficial to vibrate a piece of hardware to identify any loose connections or insufficient solder sites. This is in contrast to an aerospace application where the vibration testing is intended to ensure that the hardware will perform following launch (which produces enormous vibration input).Possible test environments include thermal (hot and cold), voltage/power (high, low, startup, turn-off), dynamics (shock, random, acoustic, sine), radiation (neutron, dose rate, single event upset), and EMC/EMI (isolation, radiated susceptibility and emissions, conducted susceptibility and emissions). These environments may not all be present or may not be deemed important for a particular application. For example, radiation environments are typically encountered near nuclear reactors, military applications or in space.

The thermal, vibration and electrical environments are very generic and are used across nearly all industries. This is because they represent the vast majority of usage environments. It is also because these tests have been found to be effective at screening defects, as well. Let us now examine some of these typical environments:

# Thermal Environments

The thermal environment, at a point $P$, may be parameterized by the temperature at a time $t$. However, since the temperature is invariably different at different locations, the temperature is a function of both time and space.

Under fixed boundary conditions, the temperature distribution is constant in time and can estimated by applying standard finite difference techniques (Chapman 1989). These are all equivalent to solving the Poisson equation. Although difficult in practice, all that needs to be known are heat sources and sinks and the thermal resistances of the constituent elements. Under time varying boundary conditions, the solution is more complex and requires additional heat capacity knowledge, which results in a variety of characteristic time constants. In order to get a converging solution in a finite amount of time, judicious care must be applied to selecting the elements and time steps in the finite difference techniques.

The sources (or sinks) of thermal energy may be both internal and external to the product. Solar illumination and surrounding air are examples of external thermal sources, while cryogenic fluids, deep outer space and surrounding air are examples of external thermal sinks. Internal thermal sources include dissipated electrical power and internal ambient air. Internal thermal sinks include radiators, cold fingers and refrigerators.

Thermal material properties range over many orders of magnitude across materials (for example, the thermal conductivity of periodic elements vary from 0.06 to $4.2 \mathrm{~W} / \mathrm{cmK}$ ) (Halliday and Resnick 1974). Even for a single material, the thermal properties may vary widely over temperature becoming particularly different near absolute zero or melting.

With this variety of materials properties, sources and sinks and the large number of possible configurations, performing a truly representative thermal test is difficult, if not impossible. Thus, thermal tests are usually intended to bound the environmental behavior and not to achieve precise fidelity. However, with careful attention to test fidelity details (heat sources and sinks, thermal boundary conditions and external fluxes) thermal tests may be used to correlate thermal models to actual product performance.

## Vibration Environments

The motion of a mass element is governed by the forces which exist on it, it's mass and the equations of Newton. These forces can be constant, have time dependence, or be the sum of both. In a real structure, a great number of these forces can be loads or torques from adjoining structural elements. These forces produce stresses and strains. These stresses and strains may then interact with other structural elements to induce additional stresses and strains. Under fixed boundary conditions, the behavior of an individual element can be characterizedby its stress and strain; the information required is it's dimensions, mass and Young's modulus. Under time varying boundary conditions, the response of and individual element is a function of frequency and techniques for estimating the normal modes (and frequencies) are commonly employed.

The sources of vibration can again be external (for example, the acoustic noise inside a rocket fairing, driving on a bumpy road, or a fall to the floor) or internal (for example, a vibrating wire, reaction wheel or resonating PCB). Also, the materials properties can vary widely across and within materials. Thus, once again the goal of the vibration test is not usually to allow complete model correlation, but rather to bound the expected (or design) levels.

Vibration environments are commonly simulated using pneumatic shakers which provide varying degrees of acceleration at different frequencies. These spectra are tailored to the test being performed. For testing at discrete frequencies, one can use a sinusoidal vibration of a given amplitude at a given frequency. However, one then worries about resonant frequencies which may have been missed and other consequences of discrete frequency testing. For this reason, random vibration testing is commonly used. This provides an output vibration level which is the integral of a continuous set of frequencies at different amplitudes. In either case, the size of the test article and the test equipment may unacceptably limited in both the lowand high-frequency portions of the spectrum (Forgrave et. al. 1999). Another way of simulating vibration environments is to use acoustic testing in which sound waves impinge directly on the test article. This testing uses horns and amplifiers to generate the sound levels and uses rooms and facilities designed to absorb reflected sound. This environment more accurately simulates the spacecraft launch environment (especially the low frequency portion) but is more expensive than random vibration testing and is thus mostly used only in the aerospace industry.

# Electrical Environments

The response of a product to electromagnetic stimuli is a function of frequency (ranging from DC to beyond optical), amplitude and phase. Components can be excited by an external magnetic field, induced noise, or the presence of multiple resistance and capacitance values in the overall configuration. Ohm's law, or extensions to cover time dependent effects, are commonly used in elementary circuit analysis, although Maxwell's equations may be required in higher frequency regimes (e.g. $>100 \mathrm{MHz}$ ).

The sources of electromagnetic stresses can be external (for example, power lines, neighboring motors, or signals from adjacent elements, such as voltages and currents). They can also be internal. The materials properties again vary widely over materials and within a material over frequency. Once again, the idea of the electromagnetic test is not to completely characterize the test article, but rather to bound its behavior and establish robust performance.

How this testing is accomplished depends on a number of parameters, including the frequency range and the failure modes which are intended to be detected. For complex systems, the test equipment and associated software can be nearly as costly as the system itself. Measurements of electrical performance invariably involves amplifiers, impedance matching networks, analog-to-digital (A/D) and digital-to-analog (D/A) converters and computer control. These electrical elements are integrated into a collection of test equipment, which can measure the performance parameters of interest under a variety of conditions. It may also act to simulate the performance of other product electrical components, which are not actually involved in the test (usually they are being developed in parallel). Design of a good simulator requires care and a good set of interface requirements.# Other Environments

Unique requirements may also involve unique test environments. These environmental parameters can include radiation (both particle and photon), pressure testing, contamination, humidity, zero-g to name a few. However, this chapter will focus on the three environments discussed above.

## Combined Environments

Combined environments may represent usage environments (such as the vibrations seen at hot temperatures in an automobile engine compartment) while in other cases, they may be used only to accelerate the precipitation of a particular failure mode. The approach of combining environments has become more popular as people realize that much of the value of testing is in precipitating failures and not just environmental simulation. Accelerating failure modes to occur before they normally would is, in many cases, accomplished by combining environments.

Designing a combined environment test can be difficult and is easiest when the objectives of the test are to precipitate a few specific failure modes. In this case, one can combine various types of analyzes (e.g. structural and thermal) to predict test levels which will induce the most stress. Examples include hot vibration tests (looking for creep and plastic deformation failure modes) and cold vibration testing (looking for various types of brittle failure modes).

### 10.3.2 Temperature Testing

Since many root-cause-level failure mechanisms can eventually be traced to material properties or chemistry, it is not surprising that temperature has been (and will probably continue to be) a preferred approach to accelerating failure mechanisms.

## Steady State Thermal Testing

Steady state temperature testing is the most well-known thermal test and has been dubbed 'burn-in' testing. Steady state temperature testing involves staying at one temperature for an extended duration of time. During this stay, one may be performing functional testing or other characterizations, or one may merely let the product 'burn-in'. Note that the utility of a burn-in is greatly increased by exercising the product during the test (Cornford et. al. 1998). Usually, steady state temperature testing will include several temperatures which are achieved sequentially. This 'burn-in' can accelerate Arrhenius failure mechanisms (see below), but it can also provide a chance to see the entire product functional performance in (possibly) extreme conditions which provides greater confidence in the product robustness. This test should be configured to provide realistic heat transfer paths to get a better idea of the actual component operating temperatures and associated performance.

In aerospace applications, this testing may be performed in a vacuum environment to provide a higher fidelity test. The vacuum environment can result in explosive decompression, outgassing (evolution of material from surfaces due to pressure differences) and different temperature gradients than those obtained where convection is a factor.

The Arrhenius relationship between hazard rate, or more often labeled failure rate in practice, and temperature arose from experimental observations in which many failure mechanisms were found to be accelerated by temperature according to the well known formula (Coffin 1973).

$$
F(T)=F_{0} \exp \left(-E_{a} / k\left(T-T_{r e f}\right)\right)
$$where $E_{a}$ is the activation energy of the specific failure mechanism (in electron volts, or eV ), $k$ is the Boltzmann constant $=1.38 \times 10^{-23} \mathrm{~J} / \mathrm{K}, T$ is the temperature at the failure mechanism site (in K), and $T_{\text {ref }}$ is the nominal operating temperature (in K ) for which the failure rate is $F_{0}$. The resultant failure rate, $F(T)$, is the accelerated failure rate due to the elevated temperature. Recall that the conversion from eV to J is a factor of $1.6 \times 10^{-19}$. Figure 10.4 graphically depicts the rise in Arrhenius failure rate due to increasing temperature for several activation energies. Note the dramatic increase in acceleration for higher activation energies.

Let's use the information from the figure to consider a specific example, where a product has four failure mechanisms with activation energies ranging from 0.3 to 1.0 eV as shown in Table 10.1 below, all of which will fail in 10,000 hours. Then assuming one performs a 50 hour test at 85 C we find that the different acceleration rates results in one of the failure mechanisms still remaining undetected.

Table 10.1 Comparison of accelerated times to failure for four different activation energies. The test is assumed to be for 50 hours at 85 C .

| Activation <br> Energy (eV) | Nominal time to <br> failure (hours) | Accelerated time <br> to failure (hours) | Detected in <br> 50 hour test? |
| :--: | :-- | :-- | :-- |
| 0.3 | 10,000 | 100 | No |
| 0.5 | 10,000 | 33 | Yes |
| 0.7 | 10,000 | 6 | Yes |
| 1.0 | 10,000 | 0.6 | Yes |



Figure 10.4 Graph of Relative Acceleration Factors versus Temperature (C) for various activation energies. These are in eV $(0.3,0.5,0.7$ and 1.0$)$ and are appropriate for different technologies. This graph assumes a default temperature of 25 C and compares accelerations for various temperatures. Note the temperatures are temperatures at the failure mode site.So, it is no surprise that with current defect rates approaching the parts-per-billion ( ppb ) level and test temperatures usually constrained to less than 50 or 100 C (for assemblies and piece parts, respectively) above ambient temperature, current residual activation energies are in the range of 0.3 eV . All of the higher activation failure mechanisms are tested out! This has led to the observation that temperature testing is not as effective at finding failure mechanisms as it once was. However, Arrhennius relationships between failure rates and temperature are still empirically found in boxes even where the defects found are not easily correlated to chemistry (Gibbel and Cornford 1997).

# Thermal Cycle Testing

Thermal cycle testing is still currently performed as a standard test, usually to find workmanship defects. However, there are questions as to its overall effectiveness in finding defects (Cornford and Plumb 1994). Like many of the original 'universal screening' tests, there is a reluctance to give up the universal application of thermal cycle testing. The evidence for its effectiveness (or ineffectiveness) is clouded by the fact that, in an effort to save money, much of the tested hardware is not even monitored until a pre-determined number of cycles has occurred (typically ten). At this point, functional testing reveals a number of failures and these are then attributed to the 10 cycles! What if, as usually is the case, these failure all occurred at cycle 1? The careful analysis of Cornford and Plumb (1994) concludes that thermal cycle testing is essentially in in-effective burn-in except for the few failure modes for which cycling is required. While this primarily addresses the effectiveness of thermal cycling for aerospace products, additional data from commercial industry studies have indicated the same lack of effectiveness (Gibbel 1997).

Failure modes which may be found with only a few cycles include CTE mismatches and hysteresis effects. Any failure mode which requires thermal stress reversal to excite can be found with thermal cycling. However, those which require a large amount of stress reversal (e.g. solder joint fatigue) are best revealed earlier in the design phase via focused life testing. This cannot be over emphasized: design life issues are best identified early using life testing on the intended package or configuration design. The usage of thermal cycle testing as a workmanship screen makes sense if one knows that the workmanship failure modes are accessible by a few cycles.

There are a great number of references on fatigue (both high and low cycle) and these will not be repeated here (Frear 1994). Instead, we will use Figure 10.5 to illustrate some of the challenges associated with fatigue life prediction and acceleration. For most metals, there is a power exponent which occurs in the simplified expression:


$$

\mathrm{N}_{\text {usage }}=\mathrm{N}_{\text {accel }}{ }^{\*}\left(\Delta \mathrm{~T}_{\text {accel }} / \Delta \mathrm{T}_{\text {usage }}\right)^{\text {exponent }}

$$

Where $\mathrm{N}_{\text {usage }}$ is the number of cycles anticipated in the usage environment over a temperature range given by $\Delta \mathrm{T}_{\text {usage }}$ and $\mathrm{N}_{\text {accel }}$ is the number of cycles until failure measured in the accelerated test environment over a temperature range given by $\Delta \mathrm{T}_{\text {accel }}$. The power law exponent is a function of the material being fatigued and is approximately 2 for most metals, but for solder joints it can range from 1.4 to 2.6 . Taking this equation and plotting Neq (the equivalent number of usage cycles) for different exponents and different ratios of $\mathrm{T}_{\text {accel }} / \mathrm{T}_{\text {usage }}$, we find a great difference in the predicted number of cycles: be very careful when extrapolating fatigue life! The best recommendation is to try to test with as small of an acceleration factor as possible.

Figure 10.5 Graph depicting the difference in predicted acceleration of fatigue life depending on the exponent.

# Hot/Cold Starts

Equipment operating in extreme environments may require testing to ensure that it can achieve nominal operation even when starting up in extremes. An obvious example is a car engine which needs to start at $-40^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$. When it is operating the engine will achieve temperatures at well over $300^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$, but it begins out at $-40^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ and may not even start which will not allow it to then reach its nominal operating temperature. In both the automotive and aerospace industries, hot and cold starting are an essential operational environment in which to validate performance.

Let us now summarize the discussion of this section by examining an actual thermal test profile. Figure 10.6 is an actual thermal vacuum test profile for a recent spacecraft which illustrates a number of important points. Note that the timeline includes a number of excursions over temperature with various specific operational modes (and corresponding measurements) specifically called out (numbers in circles). In particular, note how the intended usage has resulted in several temperature cases which are explicitly tested along with measurements performed during the temperature transitions. STV stands for System Thermal Vacuum test. Note also that in this particular test, an external illumination source is used to simulate direct solar impingement on the spacecraft. The intensity of this source is varied to simulate extreme conditions ( 1.6 suns for orbit near Venus and 0 suns for orbit near an outer planet).

### 10.3.3 Vibration Testing

The random vibration environment consists of stochastic instantaneous accelerations which are input to a spacecraft or other assembly, transmitted via a launch vehicle or usage

Figure10. 6 A typical thermal vacuum test timeline at the spacecraft level. Note that the timeline includes a number of excursions over temperature with various specific operational modes (and corresponding measurements) specifically called out (numbers in circles). In particular, note how the intended usage has resulted in several temperature cases which are explicitly tested along with measurements performed during the temperature transitions. STV stands for System Thermal Vacuum test. Note also that in this particular test, an external illumination source is used to simulate direct solar impingement on the spacecraft. The intensity of this source is varied to simulate extreme conditions ( 1.6 suns for orbit near Venus and 0 suns for orbit near an outer planet).
environment. Figure 10.7 shows a typical vibration spectrum where one can see the variations due to both variations in the input dynamic levels and the response of the test article. Random vibration input occurs over a broad frequency range, from about 10 Hz to 2000 Hz . In the space vehicle launch environment, random vibration is caused primarily by acoustic noise in the payload fairing, which is in turn induced by external aerodynamic forces due to dynamic pressure and reflection of rocket exhaust from the ground. In terrestrial applications, these environments can come from transport or other vibration sources.

Random vibration spectra are generally applied in each of three orthogonal axes, and have a Gaussian distribution of the instantaneous acceleration. Both the acceleration spectral


Figure10.7 Typical vibration levels transmitted to the flight article through the mounts. The goal of the well designed vibration test is to bound these levels with the induced vibration levels.

Figure 108 Typical Acoustic Noise requirements for a spacecraft assembly.
density and wideband acceleration are test parameters and should be within specified tolerances. Each assembly or subsystem should be in its launch configuration. Powered-on vibration, with attendant functional monitoring during testing, may be considered as an effective defect screening tool, although it is often cost-prohibitive. All tested subsystems should be attached to vibration test fixtures at their normal flight structural interfaces. As discussed previously, acoustic noise sources may also be used to perform vibration testing and a typical test spectrum is shown in Figure 10.8.

Test control accelerometer(s) should be located at fixture-to-test article interface(s). When more than one control accelerometer is specified, the test should be controlled by averaging the accelerometer signals. Automatic, closed-loop servo control should always be implemented with an electro-dynamic vibration exciter.

Vibration instrumentation for random vibration testing should include appropriately located accelerometers and strain gages. The accelerometers, strain gages and data acquisition system should have flat frequency response characteristics within $\pm 1 \mathrm{~dB}$ from 5 Hz to 2 kHz . Visual data available on site during actual execution of the test should include recordings of the time histories of the control and selected response channels. Additional quick-look analysis data in the form of Acceleration PSD plots should be available during testing as needed.

# 10.3.4 Electromagnetic Compatibility and Interference Testing for Electronics

Electromagnetic interference (EMI) produced by noisy electrical/electronic sources can degrade or hinder the performance or even damage sensitive portions of a product. The purpose of electromagnetic compatibility testing is to identify potential problems before final integration.

An electrically noisy article can generate interference noise either by conduction or radiation. The potential interference signals have a very broad bandwidth (ranging from 30 Hz to 40 GHz ) and can affect the operation of nearby circuits in receivers, data acquisition and telemetry circuits, various types of digital circuits as well as data buses and their associated circuitry. These noise signals can couple onto sensitive components through many paths including: power bus lines, signal bus lines, chassis box apertures, seams joints, connectors, a

Figure 10.9 Typical narrowband radiated emissions limits for spacecraft.


Figure 10.10 Typical broadband radiated emissions limits for spacecraft.
poorly designed chassis, as well as through poorly laid out, or fabricated, circuit boards. Representative test requirements for some typical spacecraft system level electromagnetic tests are given in Figures 10.9-10.11, as examples.

# 10.4 Test Effectiveness Analysis

Having established the concept of failure mode and having explored a variety of test types and test objectives, we now turn to test effectiveness evaluations. First we shall discuss how one establishes the metrics by which to determine effectiveness, followed by a brief discussion of defects and defect populations. We shall then perform some simple evaluations of test effectiveness, followed by a discussion of how to determine the relative importance of failure

Figure 10.11 Typical conducted emissions ripple limits for spacecraft power lines
modes. After a brief discussion of constraints and limitations, we will then discuss how to develop and implement a test program.

# 10.4.1 Metrics and Test Effectiveness

A metric is a measurement one can make which allows one to make comparisons, and ultimately decisions. Metrics are applied when we estimate the distance to an object, or decide which shirt to buy. Metrics are applied in the workplace to measure productivity, quality and which of two candidates to hire. In applying metrics to optimize a process, the rule generally stated is 'if you can't measure it, you can't manage it.' Without a relevant metric how do you know if things are going right, or wrong for that matter. Business management has generally recognized the need to apply metrics to various business processes, but somehow this has not become commonplace in the testing world. How do we decide which test to do? Unfortunately, the answer to this question is all too often a result of applying 'the same test as last time' or 'the one we've always done.' Let us explore some of the possible metrics one might use to measure the effectiveness of a test. Ultimately we are after the metrics by which we can evaluate the cost effectiveness of a test (or test program), but let us begin with a simple example.

A simple metric is the cost of the activity. In this case, the result of the application of this metric would be a list of activities and their costs. The decision would then be the activity with the lowest cost. Another simple metric would be the test which takes the least time, or finds the most defects. However, we shall see that these metrics do not always lead to the right answer. For the three simple examples above, the cheapest test may not be very effective and the cost of rework or additional testing may completely nullify any cost savings we thought we gained. Similarly, the test that took the shortest time to implement may result in schedule delays due to rework or additional testing, which completely nullify any schedule savings.Finally, the test which finds the most defects may be inducing them, or more subtlety, may not be finding the defects which have the greatest cost or schedule impact.

# 10.4.2 Defects and Defect Populations

The failure modes present in a given test article are generally known, although they may be specifically unknown. For example, a high volume manufacturing process, which is tightly controlled, may have a known total defect rate of $0.1 \%$ per unit. This does not mean that we know which unit(s) have the defect(s), or which type of defect(s) are present in each box. Thus, we are invariably led to statistical methods. The defect populations may then be characterized by a mean, standard deviation, skewness, etc. For the purposes of the discussion below, we will neglect everything but the mean value and it is left to the reader to perform the straight-forward extension to distributions. See Section 3 for more details.

### 10.4.3 Evaluating the Effectiveness of a Test

## Test Effectiveness for a Simple Test

Suppose we have N (say, 10) failure modes of type a present in a given test article. We could perform a test, Test a, which finds, say, $3 / 5(60 \%)$ of this type of failure mode. We thus define the effectiveness ${ }^{\dagger \dagger}$ of this test to be $\mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{a}}(=0.6)$, and we can find the number of failure modes of type a detected by the test, $\mathrm{Na}_{\text {found }}$, and the number of those which escaped detection, $\mathrm{Na}_{\text {out }}$, by forming the products:


$$

\begin{aligned}
& \mathrm{Na}_{\text {found }}=\mathrm{N}^{\*} \mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{a}}=10^{_} 0.6=6 \\
& \mathrm{Na}\_{\text {out }}=\mathrm{N}^{_}\left(1-\mathrm{E}\_{\mathrm{a}}\right)=10^{\*} 0.4=4
\end{aligned}

$$

Let us now use these notions of computing the number of detected failure modes and those which escaped detection.

## Evaluation of Cost Effectiveness for a Simple Test

Suppose a given test, say Test a, costs $\$ 375$ (including labor, fixtures, test plan generation, etc.), and each undetected defect costs $500 \$$ (i.e. cost to repair, or loss of partial function as a fraction of the total function value, see the next Section). Simply stated, the test found $\$ 3000$ worth of failure modes for only $\$ 375$ - Test a was value-added. One could also compute the cost/defect for the above simple example and obtain $\$ 375 / 6=\$ 62.50$, but as we shall see this simple metric is not actually very useful unless all defects have the same value. One could also go further and break up the costs with more granularity, evaluate multiple repetitions or combinations of tests, consider other prevention or detection activities, and optimize the value-added of the test program. This will be covered shortly.

## Tradeoffs

Consider another test, Test b, which only finds $30 \%$ of FMa but only costs $\$ 200$ to implement. Which is the more effective test, which is the more cost effective? As we shall see, the answers

The number of failure modes detected and which escaped from Test $\mathrm{b}, \mathrm{Nb}_{\text {found }}$ and $\mathrm{Nb}_{\text {out }}$, respectively, is given by:


$$

\begin{aligned}
& \mathrm{Nb}_{\text {found }}=\mathrm{N}^{\*} \mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{a}}=10^{_} 0.3=3 \\
& \mathrm{Nb}\_{\text {out }}=\mathrm{N}^{_}\left(1-\mathrm{E}\_{\mathrm{a}}\right)=10^{\*} 0.7=7

$$

and the cost/defect found $=\$ 200 / 3=\$ 67$ which makes this test better by the metric of cost/defect. But something tells us that this method of measuring test effectiveness may be leading us astray. Let us consider some other metrics. Suppose each defect found is counted positively, and each defect missed is counted negatively, then we can form the value of the test by

Net Value $=$ Value of all defects found - Cost of test, Unclaimed Value $=$ Value of defects not found
Let us examine some simple cases:
Table 10.2 is intended to clearly illustrate that one must be careful with the metrics used for effectiveness evaluation. Let us begin by comparing the implementation of Test a and Test b. The answer to which is the most cost effective depends on the metric by which the are being compared. If we apply the usual management metric then Test b wins because it costs the least to implement ( $200 \$$ versus $400 \$$ ). Even if we are more sophisticated and employ another common metric, cost/defect, we will still conclude that Test b is the best choice ( $66.7 \$$ versus $75.0 \$$ ). If we attempt to perform the selection by determining which finds the most defects, we will (correctly) conclude Test a is the best choice but our intuition would warn us that the test cost must somehow come into consideration. However, if we can establish a value for the defects being found (see Section 10.4.3) we can attempt to perform the evaluation by the best metric of all: the Net value of the test. Here the Net value of the test is defined as the value of the defects found minus the test cost. In this case, Test a appears to be the most cost-effective choice since it has the highest Net Value ( $2125 \$$ versus 1300\$).

Now let us explore combinations of tests and for simplicity assume that multiple applications of the same test is even more effective than a single application. Now we can compare the effectiveness of implementing Test a, or Test b, or Test a twice, or Test b twice, or Test a followed by Test b. Now the highest Net Value comes from implementing Test a twice (3000\$) even though it is the most expensive test combination! We could continue in this fashion and explore combinations of more than two types of test and let the metrics provide the answer, but let us proceed instead to a less simple case. The above analysis assumed that there was only one kind of defect, so let us expand our working example to the more realistic casewhere there are four different types of defects and Test a and Test b have a different relative effectiveness for different defect types.

First we need to introduce some notation for later convenience. Suppose there are i failure modes present and $\mathrm{N}_{\mathrm{j}}$ is the number of failure modes of type i present ${ }^{22}$. Then we let $\mathrm{Ea}_{\mathrm{j}}$ be the effectiveness of failure mode i for Test a. Then the term, $\mathrm{N}_{\mathrm{i}}{ }^{*} \mathrm{Ea}_{\mathrm{j}}$, yields the total number of failure modes of type i detected by the test.

Taking a specific example, contained in Table 10.3, let $\mathrm{N}_{\mathrm{i}}$ and $\mathrm{Ea}_{\mathrm{j}}$ be given for four failure modes. Then we can compute the number of failure modes of each type before and after the test and the totals. Note that a fraction of a failure mode present (e.g. 0.2) means that out of 5 test articles, one will have the failure mode. We use mean values here but the extension to include statistical distributions is straightforward (but somewhat tedious). Returning to the table, we see that there has been a reduction from 6 failure modes to only 1 . We could thus declare the test to be $83 \%$ effective. We could also do a more detailed metrics analysis (as was done previously) to determine the 'goodness' in terms of cost (or schedule). However, we shall keep to just the simpler evaluation of effectiveness.

Selecting another test, Test b, we could compare the two tests, a and b. Now let us perform an evaluation in which we want to determine a practical answer: what combination of tests provides the most value-added. This simple example consists of four failure modes (with varying values) and two primary tests, Test a and Test b, which have different escape probabilities (1- effectiveness) versus these failure modes. The table contains two evaluations with the only difference being the relative value of the failure modes. Note that the Test b is perfectly effective for the first three failure modes ( $0 \%$ escape probability) and perfectly ineffective for the fourth one ( $100 \%$ escape probability) and it illustrates a number of points:

1. In both of these examples, the lowest cost test is not generally the most effective
2. Two test combinations with very different effectiveness in finding defects, may have very similar cost effectiveness.
3. This variability in cost effectiveness and defect detection effectiveness is primarily due to the variation in importance of the failure modes.
4. Cost/defect is not generally a good metric.
5. The Net Value is the best metric by which to decide on a test or tests.

In order to take advantage of the best metric, Net Value, it is essential to have an estimate of the number and value for the failure modes which may be present. This is the subject of the next section.

# 10.4.4 Determining the Relative Importance of Failure Modes

Different failure modes may represent different concern levels for the reliability engineer. Both the consequence of failure modes and the likelihood of its occurrence may vary greatly. The consequence of a given failure mode, should it occur, may range from catastrophic (explosions, death, etc.) to insignificant (loss of 0.01 dB of gain, slight discoloration). These consequences should be considered when designing a test program or even when implementing a particular test. There is no point in implementing a test which screens out insignificant failure modes while leaving significant ones laying latent in the test article. As we have seen above, the value of a test is best measured by determining the relative importance of the failure modes under consideration.

To determine the consequence of a high-level failure mode one should look at the requirements. The ultimate cost of the occurrence of a failure mode includes lost performance and income, rework costs, embarrassment and injury. Ideally, one must decide what the relative weights of all of the various requirements are and thus establish the relative consequence of a failure to meet that requirement - this is really the best definition of a failure mode: the inability to meet requirements. Upon establishing the relative importance of a givenrequirement (could be expressed in monetary terms), one can establish the value of various sub-requirements and continue the process until the consequence of the failure modes under consideration can all be determined. As an example, consider the failure of a resistor and assume that we have a working electrical model which includes the resistor under discussion. We could then use a failed resistor in the model and see the consequences. These could range from total non-functionality to slightly increased noise. A model (virtual or real) allows us to measure the consequences of a wide variety of failure modes. Sometimes the costs of these models are determined to be non value-added, but one should be very careful to consider what failure modes might be prevented from occurring and measure its value using this information. It can be tough to appreciate the value of preventative measures since one can't be sure that the lack of its occurrence is due a particular prevention measure. Consequences can also be roughly estimated by establishing numerical values (say $0,1,3$ and 9 ) to correspond to qualitative assessments (say none, small, medium and large).

In addition to its consequence, a failure mode has an associated likelihood of occurrence which may range from certainty (more often than we might like to think) to impossible. Design flaws and software bugs will often occur with certainty; its just a matter of looking for them. For this reason, the value of ordinary functional testing cannot be overemphasized. Note that failure modes may occur with certainty provided a particular circumstance happens (e.g. error trapping in software, or a particular digital signal line). One could then characterize the likelihood of the occurrence of that failure mode by the likelihood of occurrence of that particular usage.

Estimating the likelihood of occurrence can be difficult but methods can be employed to obtain estimates of varying fidelity. For high volume applications, one can use the historical data from similar products but it is important to only use relevant data which represents similar failure mode distributions as that in the product under test. Assuming the data has been deemed relevant, one might be tempted to estimate the likelihood of occurrence from actual product data ( $\%$ of defects of this type out of total customer complaints). However, one should note that this likelihood of occurrence in the field is also a function of the PACTs (tests) which were performed prior to delivery. Thus, one should really integrate all of the occurrences in testing and in the field to estimate the likelihood of one being present at the onset of the testing process. If you are uncertain as to the likelihood of the failure modes occurrence you can try to look further back in the development process and see what kinds of defects were being found there. As a last resort, you can just assume the failure mode will happen with certainty.

It is actually the expected value of the failure mode's consequence which is the critical quantity. This is the product of the likelihood of occurrence and the consequence. As an example, if I have a $10 \%$ chance of losing $100 \$$ my expected value of loss is $10 \$$. Note that a $1 \%$ chance of losing $1000 \$$ and a $10 \%$ chance of losing $100 \$$ have the same expected value and thus deserve the same attention. Too often engineers worry about the failure modes with large consequences and very small probabilities and ignore the failure modes with medium consequences but much higher probability of occurrence.

Using any available spreadsheet package, one may estimate the expected loss due to a wide variety of failure modes and then sort them from high to low and generate a priority list for attention. Later, we shall see that the attention (effectiveness of testing) should really scale with the importance of a failure mode. Figure 10.12 shows a hypothetical example in which one had identified a list of failure modes which could be present, estimate the likelihood of occurrence and consequence and then sorted the results in a bar chart format.

Figure 10.12 Example of estimating the relative importance of various failure modes. The table computes the impact of each of six failure modes against each of three requirements where the failure modes may have a different likelihood of occurrence and each of the requirements have a different relative importance. The left plot is obtained by plotting each of the failure mode importance in the order in which the failure modes were listed, while the right chart plots the importance of each failure mode in order of importance (commonly called a pareto diagram). This chart should convince you (and others) that the test program should focus on FMe and not on FMd.

# 10.4.5 Constraints and Limitations

While much of this chapter has focused on the ideal approaches and methods for computing various quantities, the real-life engineer is often faced with a number of constraints and limitations. Data may be missing or irrelevant, a great test plan may get drastically shortened due to production delays but no corresponding delay in delivery to the customer - this is real life. For this reason, this chapter has attempted to indicated where cruder estimates may be used in a pinch. Furthermore, the valuable engineer takes advantage of their intuition and that of others to come up with the best answer given the constraints and limitations. One may even use mathematical combinations of expert opinions (so-called Delphi methods) to make likelihood, effectiveness and consequence estimates. Use the best information you can. Sometimes in the face of no data the only solution is to go get data. Preliminary tests and reviews of functional tests which have preceded the planned test may be useful sources of information for the test engineer. One can even plan a phased testing program where the fidelity of the tests is reduced in the early stages to save cost but the test can still provide a valuable 'heads up' into what the final test should attempt to accomplish.Even with all the data in the world, sometimes there are other constraints (available money or schedule) which can directly impact the application of a test program, especially since testing can commonly occur at the end of the production process and overruns are most likely to impact the test engineer! All one can really hope to do is to convince the powers-that-be to increase the needed resources or to tailor the test, or test program, to the available resources. Fortunately, both of these can be accomplished using the same techniques we have been exploring in this chapter. One merely optimizes the cost effectiveness (if cost is the issue) of the testing and convince someone that the cost of a test is more than paid for by the value of finding the failure modes. If the total money available to do the testing is still reduced, one simply performs linear optimization of overall cost effectiveness of testing subject to the cost constraint.

# 10.5 Development and Application of a Test Program

The reader should now be ready to think about developing and applying a test program. We have covered the tools necessary to do the job. Let us know write down the process for achieving this goal.
Step 1: Understand the product to be tested. This produces the background knowledge necessary to continue.
Step 2: Estimate the relative importance and numbers of the various failure modes. This will allow us to focus on the most important failure modes and be sure that if we have to miss some, we will miss the least important.
Step 3: Have, or develop, sufficient knowledge about the effectiveness and costs of the various test options within your corporate culture. Without this knowledge, it will be difficult to move beyond just 'doing what we always do.'
Step 4: Determine the constraints and metrics appropriate for evaluating the effectiveness of a test, or combination of tests. Some projects are more schedule-driven than others, while others have other unique constraints. Understand the needs of the product developer.
Step 5: Optimize the selection of tests (and more generally, the PACTs) which produce the most reliable product within the constraints provided.
Step 6: Implement the tests using your insight into the objectives of these tests and what they are trying to find. Be sure to focus on getting the instrumentation to accurately reflect the parameters you are trying to measure.
Step 7: Most importantly, follow this product through the rest of its development cycle and usage in order to calibrate the effectiveness for the next product.

Finally, most of the skills necessary for being a good test, or reliability, engineer come from learning while you work. Keep your systems perspective on the product and talk to everyone you can!

### 10.6 An Example: Test or not to Test Decision

The choice of whether to test or not and at what level of assembly is a complex one. It depends on a number of design decisions, desired reliability and available development resources. One of the biggest drivers for testing is the 1:10:100 rule. This rule of thumb captures the increasing cost of fixes as the level of assembly increases. For example, a fix in the paper design is obviously cheaper than performing a fix on the finished product coming off the line. The rule states that each increase in the level of assembly makes the fixes 10 times more expensive as at the previous level. Consider the following simplified example.Suppose a system consists of two assemblies and that the assemblies each contain 10 latent defects which are to be found during testing. The choice is whether to only do system testing or to do both assembly and system testing. The example will illustrate the enormous dependence of the answer on whether the rule is $1: 10: 100$ or $1: 2: 4$ which designing for reworkability can achieve.

Let each assembly test cost $100 \mathrm{k} \$$ and suppose each test has a $90 \%$ effectiveness with 2 'false alarms'. These false alarms arise from anomalies which are a result of operator or equipment errors and do not represent actual hardware failure modes. Suppose addressing each surfaced anomaly costs $10 \mathrm{k} \$$ (including the false alarms). The total cost of each assembly test is then determined from:

| $100 \mathrm{k} \$$ | Cost of performing assembly test |
| :-- | :-- |
| $10 \mathrm{k} \mathrm{\$} * 10 * 0.9=90 \mathrm{k} \$$ | Cost of fixing the $90 \%$ of anomalies found |
| $10 \mathrm{k} \mathrm{\$} * 2=20 \mathrm{k} \$$ | Cost of 'fixing' the false alarms |
| $210 \mathrm{k} \$$ | Total cost of 1 assembly test |
| $420 \mathrm{k} \$$ | Total cost of 2 assembly tests |

Note that there are 2 'escapes' from this level of testing which are to be detected at the next level of testing or in the field.

Now let the system test cost $600 \mathrm{k} \$$ and again suppose that the test has a $90 \%$ effectiveness with 2 'false alarms'. Now suppose that the cost of addressing each surfaced anomaly costs $10 \mathrm{k} \$$ *beta. Then the cost of doing system testing is:

| $600 \mathrm{k} \$$ | Cost of performing system test |
| :-- | :-- |
| $10 \mathrm{k} \mathrm{\$} * 2 * 0.9 *$ beta $=18 \mathrm{k} \mathrm{\$} *$ beta | Cost of fixing anomalies following assembly testing |
| $10 \mathrm{k} \mathrm{\$} * 20 * 0.9 *$ beta $=180 \mathrm{k} \mathrm{\$} *$ beta | Cost of fixing anomalies without assembly testing |
| $10 \mathrm{k} \mathrm{\$} * 2 *$ beta $=20 \mathrm{k} \mathrm{\$} *$ beta | Cost of 'fixing' the false alarms |
| $600 \mathrm{k} \$+38 \mathrm{k} \mathrm{\$} *$ beta | Total cost of system test following assembly testing |
| $600 \mathrm{k} \$+200 \mathrm{k} \mathrm{\$} *$ beta | Total cost of system test without assembly testing |

Note that there are 0.2 escapes following system testing with assembly testing, but there are 2 escapes following system testing only.

Now the total test costs are:
$1020 \mathrm{k} \$+38 \mathrm{k} \mathrm{\$} *$ beta
Total test cost for assembly plus system
$600 \mathrm{k} \$+200 \mathrm{k} \mathrm{\$} *$ beta
Total test cost for system only
Note for beta $=10$, the relative costs are: $1400 \mathrm{k} \$$ (s+a) versus $4400 \mathrm{k} \$$ (s) with reduced number of escapes for the first case. However if beta $=2$, then the relative costs are: $1096 \mathrm{k} \$$ (s+a) versus $1000 \mathrm{k} \$$ (s) with reduced number of escapes for the first case, but now the second case is cheaper.

One can thus see that as long as the 1:10:100 rule is in effect it always makes sense to find the problems early - Not only will you produce a more reliable product, but it will be cheaper to do so.

This simple example illustrates the importance of a systems based test strategy where consideration is given to the interplay between design decisions (in this case, ease of rework) and the testing decisions (in this case, whether or not to do assembly testing). One must understand the objectives of testing before deciding on a test program: Validation or Verification?, What failure modes are being checked?, Is the test to establish robustness or design life? Is the testing a workmanship screen?

# 10.7 Do's and Don'ts in Design

Do consider the critical purpose when implementing test methodology Do carefully assess available methods of testing the product under development Do plan a test program around effective methodsDo plan testing to precipitate failures
Do conduct testing at various levels and stages of program development
Do consider value of testing and evaluation methods
Do assess effectiveness of screening and other control methods in development
Do exercise a test effectiveness analysis early and development
Do failure analysis in an accelerated test program
Don't assume past practices are effective for new developments and new technologies
Don't rely on standards as the only source of test design
Don't assume all test methods are equally effective in assurance of quality and reliability
Don't select testing on the basis of cost to test only
