John W. Evans and Jillian Y. Evans

Statistical Experimental Design (SED), also referred to as Design of Experiments (DoE), is a valuable tool in reliability assessment. When properly set up and executed, designed experiments can serve to identify principal factors contributing to product unreliability or identify key factors on which to apply improvement and corrective action resources in manufacturing. In addition, designed experiments can be the basis of developing models for damage assessment by including multiple stresses or loading conditions, material properties and manufacturing variations.

There are many excellent references on the subject of experimental design. Our focus here will be on how to utilize a two level factorial experimental set-up in a typical reliability assessment. We will show in our following discussions why the simple two level factorial is often appropriate and the advantages and disadvantages of SEDs. Regression analysis is presented as the primary method of analyzing the output of a two level factorial experiments. Appropriate statistical tests are also presented to assess the significance of the results. As the reader gains ability in application of statistical experiments, he can refer to the reference list to develop a greater proficiency in this highly useful area of statistics.

It is interesting to note that these methods are the basis of the Taguchi approach to Robust Design and the eloquent approach to model development known as response surface methodology. But, engineers must give proper credit to the field of agriculture for the development of many of the concepts, where the experimental area was an area of ground for crop growth and a treatment was the application of fertilizer or other important farming chemicals.

### 11.1 Two Level Factorial Experiments

A factorial experiment gains its strength from the fact that we lay out the process of experimentation through observing the response at all of the combinations of factors that we want to control. A two level experiment, means we examine the controllable factors at two levels, set at a high level $(+)$ and a low level $(-)$. Hence, to examine all the combinations at two set levels of the controllable factors, the number of experimental runs, $i_{r}$, is as follows:


$$

i\_{r}=2^{k}

$$

where $k$ is the number of factors we want to examine. The combinations of high and low setting of the factors are called treatments.Lets consider an example. Suppose we want to assess the time to failure of a new dielectric material. As we can surmise by considering what we have learned about the mechanics of failure, we may wish to begin by testing the dielectric material under varying conditions of temperature and voltage loading. Here, we have two controllable factors of interest, voltage $(V)$ and temperature $(T)$. The number of runs for a two level factorial experiment is simply $i_{r}=2^{2}=4$. We set two levels for each of the controllable factors. Perhaps the material to be used is a thin insulating layer in a micro-printed wiring board in an automobile application and we might set our test conditions as follows:

- V-high: 25 V
- V-low: 10 V
- T-high: $200^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$
- T-low: $100^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$

We can quickly conceive of the four combinations of factors for this simple case by looking at the experimental space. Since we are considering only voltage and temperature, we can plot the experimental points as shown in Figure 11.1.

The experiment is now conducted by testing the dielectric material at each condition in the experimental space. In this case, we record the time to failure or number of hours it takes for a short circuit to occur under the test conditions. Hence, our response for this experiment is time to failure, measured in hours.

An examination of our experimental space shows us a key point about the SED approach to this problem. We can clearly see the SED gives us a full view of the experimental space. We can gain a maximum of information, particularly if we can be robust in selecting the ranges of our factors of interest.

It is useful to think in general terms when examining layouts of statistical experiments, so we can apply the layout to any type of reliability assessment. Below, we will show a few simple cases. In a tabulated SED layout of treatments, a ( + ) generally represents a high value for a factor and ( - ) a low value. Hence, if we consider any general, two level factorial experiment for $k=2$ factors, $x_{1}$ and $x_{2}$, the layout will follow Table 11.1.


Figure 11.1 Experimental space plotted for a simple two level, two factor experiment.Table 11.1 Layout for a $2^{2}$ Factorial Experiment

| Experimental Run <br> (Treatment condition) | Factor $\boldsymbol{x}_{\mathbf{1}}$ | Factor $\boldsymbol{x}_{\mathbf{2}}$ |
| :-- | :-- | :-- |
| 1 | + | + |
| 2 | + | - |
| 3 | - | + |
| 4 | - | - |

In the case of three factors, $i_{r}=2^{3}=8$. The corresponding layout for the 8 treatments is shown in Table 11.2.

Table 11.2 Layout for a $2^{3}$ Factorial Experiment

| Run | Factor $\boldsymbol{x}_{\mathbf{1}}$ | Factor $\boldsymbol{x}_{\mathbf{2}}$ | Factor $\boldsymbol{x}_{\mathbf{3}}$ |
| :-- | :-- | :-- | :-- |
| 1 | - | + | + |
| 2 | - | + | - |
| 3 | - | - | + |
| 4 | - | - | - |
| 5 | + | + | + |
| 6 | + | + | - |
| 7 | + | - | + |
| 8 | + | - | - |

Once again, we can easily visualize the experimental space for three factors as a cube where the vertices are the treatment conditions. This is shown in Figure 11.2.


Figure 11.2 Experimental space for a three factor, two level factorial experimental.Each column in our design layout is associated with the effects of our factor of interest. The columns in the design layout are referred to as contrasts. The effects of the controlled experimental factors on our dependent variable or response can be estimated from examining each contrast. The effect is the average of the differences in the measured response at each high and low setting of the factor. This leads us to the simple conclusion that we can sum the responses of each experimental run, following the signs of the contrast and divide by the number of pairs of data to determine the effect of a factor on our response variable.

Example 11.1 Lets refer to our simple two factor experiment designed to evaluate the effect of temperature and voltage on the life of a new dielectric material. Our treatment conditions and the response were as follows.

Table 11.3 Response Table for a Simple Reliability Experiment

| Experimental Run | Treatments |  | Response |
| :-- | :-- | :-- | :-- |
|  | Applied Voltage (V) | Temperature $\left({ }^{\circ} \mathrm{C}\right)$ | Life (hours) |
| 1 | $25(+)$ | $200(+)$ | 10 |
| 2 | $25(+)$ | $100(-)$ | 100 |
| 3 | $10(-)$ | $200(+)$ | 50 |
| 4 | $10(-)$ | $100(-)$ | 500 |

To evaluate the effects of the two independent variables on the life of the material, we examine the associated contrast. For the main effect of applied voltage we sum the responses following the signs of the contrast and divide by the number of pairs of responses:


$$

\text { Voltage Effect }=\frac{(10+100-50-500)}{2}=-220

$$

Temperature Effect $=\frac{(10-100+50-100)}{2}=-140$
Our initial analysis leads us to the conclusion that both effects reduce the life of the material as they have a negative sign and the effect of voltage is much more significant, given the ranges of the independent variables.

In example 11.1, we see a simple approach to analysis of a relatively simple experiment. But, we can easily surmise that we can develop more complex experiments to determine the effects of many factors, such as process parameters, geometric variables or materials properties, on our response. It may be of more interest to construct a model of the relationship between voltage and temperature on life. In this case, analysis of the results by regression would be more useful. We will discuss this in detail in later sections.

# 11.2 Interaction Effects in Two Level Factorials

Two independent variables might interact to effect our response. Therefore we may wish to analyze the effects of interactions of the independent variables and compare them to the main effects of our factors of interest. This can be of significant value in examining plant processes and process parameters and their impact on yield. However, we must use our knowledge of the basic physical mechanisms to judge the physical significance of interac-tions. Generally, they may tend to be insignificant or meaningless in reliability studies. The higher the order of the interaction, the less likely that there will be any physical or statistical significance.

In order to examine interactions of factors, we must construct the appropriate contrast for the interaction effects. We start with the basic design and then construct the interaction contrasts from the products of the principal factors, considering all possible combinations. If we have two factors $x_{1}$ and $x_{2}$, their interaction will be defined by the product $x_{1} x_{2}$. This would be termed a two-way interaction. The appropriate signs for each position in the interaction contrast is derived from the product of the signs of the main factor contrasts, associated with the interaction. It the treatment for run 1 is defined by a $(-)$ for $x_{1}$ and a $(-)$ for $x_{2}$ the product is $(+)$, and so on, for each treatment until the contrast is constructed for the interaction. If we re-examine Table 11.2, we can construct the full table of main effects, two-way and three-way interactions, as shown below.

The design table shows our main factors and the treatments for each run of the SED. When we expand the design table to add the interactions and the response to begin the process of analysis, the resulting table is called a response table.

Table 11.4 Response Table Showing All Interactions for a $2^{3}$ SED

| Run | Main Effects |  |  | Two-way Interaction Effects |  |  | Three-way Effect | Response |
| :--: | :--: | :--: | :--: | :--: | :--: | :--: | :--: | :--: |
|  | Factor $x_{1}$ | Factor $x_{2}$ | Factor $x_{3}$ | $x_{1} x_{2}$ | $x_{2} x_{3}$ | $x_{1} x_{3}$ | $x_{1} x_{2} x_{3}$ | $y$ |
| 1 | - | $+$ | $+$ | - | $+$ | - | - | $y_{1}$ |
| 2 | - | $+$ | - | - | - | $+$ | $+$ | $y_{2}$ |
| 3 | - | - | $+$ | $+$ | - | - | $+$ | $y_{3}$ |
| 4 | - | - | - | $+$ | $+$ | $+$ | - | $y_{4}$ |
| 5 | $+$ | $+$ | $+$ | $+$ | $+$ | $+$ | $+$ | $y_{5}$ |
| 6 | $+$ | $+$ | - | $+$ | - | - | - | $y_{6}$ |
| 7 | $+$ | - | $+$ | - | - | $+$ | - | $y_{7}$ |
| 8 | $+$ | - | - | - | $+$ | - | $+$ | $y_{8}$ |

After constructing the contrasts for each possible interaction, we can now use our simple averaging technique to determine the magnitude of each main effect and each interaction using our full response table. Interactions can also be considered in a regression model.

# 11.3 Standard Notation and Many Factor Designs

It is quite easy to visualize a $2^{2}$ or $2^{3}$ design, or even a $2^{4}$ design, and generate the appropriate design table that defines our treatments for each run. And, from the basic design, we can construct a full response table including all interactions, by the methods shown. While these simple designs cover many useful situations, as we increase the number of factors, it becomes increasingly difficult to construct a design table. Tabulated designs can be found in several references.

However, we can generate any full factorial experimental design by adopting some standard notations and considering the number of factors of interest. Further details of notations used for SEDs can be found in Montgomery (1984) and in earlier publications such as Natrella (1963). As an example, consider three factors. We will label them $A, B$ and $C$. We knowthat the number of required runs will be 8 . The treatment combination for each run can be generated by considering the application of the following standard notation. We will denote the combination of all factors set at their lowest levels to be a (1). The remaining treatments are then assessed by using small letter symbol. Condition $a$, is the treatment where its associated factor $A$, is set at its highest level and the remaining factors, $B$ and $C$ are set at the lowest levels. Condition $b$, is where B is set at its highest level and A and C are set at the lowest level. Condition $a b$ is where factors A and B are set at the highest levels. C is not represented in the symbol and it is set at the lowest level. Similarly, $b c$ represents B and C at their highest levels and A at its lowest. Our $2^{3}$ experiment is therefore represented by the following layout notation: (1), $a, b, a b, c, a c, b c, a b c$.

This layout notation includes small letter symbols denoting all the treatment combinations. By inspection, we can see it lends itself to an analogous comparison of determining all possible interactions that can occur. Hence, we start with small letters representing the main factors and construct the rest of the design symbols by determining the combinations. Each row of the design table is then constructed from the rules which we used to identify the treatment associated with each symbol. A $2^{4}$ experiment requires 16 runs. We denote the 4 factors as $\mathrm{A}, \mathrm{B}, \mathrm{C}, \mathrm{D}$. Then, we can construct our design as follows from standard symbols: (1), $a, b, c$, $d, a b, a c, a d, b c, b d, c d, a b c, a b d, a c d, b c d, a b c d$. Natrella (1963) suggests a standard ordering and we can rearrange: (1) $a, b, a b, c, a c, b c, a b c, d, a d, b d, a b d, c d, a c d, b c d, a b c d$. We can now construct each row of our design table from the notation, and if desired, add our interactions for a full response table.

# 11.4 Linear Models for Factorials

We have discussed the basic two level factorial experiment, its layout of treatments and a simple method of calculating the effect of each factor on the response. Of course, a major purpose of a designed factorial experiment is to determine a model from the relationship between the dependent response variable and the controlled independent variables that follow the experimental layout. This relationship may be determined by linear regression. We will discuss the process of regression analysis, as applied to factorial experiments later. First, we must be aware of the nature of the models which we can accommodate and fit by linear regression of a two level factorial experiment.

Two level factorial experiments are limited to simple linear relationships. The general linear model that can be fit by linear regression to a 2 level experiment can be expressed simply as follows:


$$

y=\beta*{o}+\sum*{i=1}^{k} \beta*{i} x*{i}+\delta\_{i}

$$

It is our objective in executing a design of experiments to determine the coefficients of the model or the $\beta_{i} s$ that relate the independent factors of the experiment, $x_{i}$, to our response variable $y$. The $\beta_{i} s$ represent the effect of the parameter of average response for a unit change in its associated $x_{i} . \beta_{o}$ is the regression constant and $\delta_{i}$ is the error. We discuss error in later sections.

We previously expressed the relationship between the experimental runs required and the number of factors of interest in Equation 11.1. Now, if we are interested in 3 factors, for example, we will require $i_{r}=2^{3}=8$ experimental runs, with treatments prescribed in accordance with Table 11.2.From this design we can fit the following polynomial:


$$

y=\beta*{0}+\beta*{1} x*{1}+\beta*{2} x*{2}+\beta*{3} x\_{3}

$$

where $\beta_{1}, \beta_{2}$ and $\beta_{3}$ represent the main effects.
It is important to understand the relationship between the number of experimental runs and the ability to perform a regression analysis and estimate the error. As we will see, we can estimate the error by calculating the confidence limits associated with a parameter, $\beta_{j}$, from the set of student-t distributions. Each student-t distribution is indexed by the number of degrees of freedom, $v$, that we have from the available data set. As we increase $v$, we increase our ability to estimate parameter error. This is because the variance of the student-t will decrease as $v$ increases. As $v$ becomes large, the student-t distribution approaches the Normal Distribution.

The correct student-t distribution must then be selected in accordance with the appropriate value of $v$. The degrees of freedom in a data set for calculating the error associated with a single parameter, such as the mean of a data set, is the sample size, $n$, minus 1 or:


$$

v=n-1

$$

But, for a regression analysis, we calculate more than one parameter from the data set. For analysis of a designed experiment, the degrees of freedom available from a data set, $v$, is simply the difference between the total number of data points, $n$, minus the number of parameters calculated from the data, $m$.


$$

v=n-m

$$

For a regression analysis used to analyze a full factorial with $k$ effects, without replication:


$$

v=i\_{r}-(k+1)

$$

where $i_{r}$ is the number of runs and $k$ is the number of main effects. We add 1 to $k$ because the basic linear model will include our regression constant $\beta_{0}$.

In our 2 level factorial example with our model shown by equation 11.5, we are determining 3 effects and there were initially 8 runs. Then:


$$

v=i\_{r}-k-1=8-3-1=4

$$

A minimum value of $v$ also decides whether or not we have sufficient data to support error analysis of a regression. The minimum value of $v$ needed to determine error in estimating the $\beta \mathrm{s}$ in our model is 1 . We cannot estimate error in our parameters without a minimum of 1 degree of freedom. To gain more degrees of freedom we can replicate the experiment by repeating the treatments.

As we have seen, one advantage of a full factorial is also to determine the second and third order interaction effects, between factors as well as our main effects. Consider the following model for our 2 level, 3 factor experiment:


$$

y=\beta*{0}+\beta*{1} x*{1}+\beta*{2} x*{2}+\beta*{3} x*{3}+\beta*{4} x*{1} x*{2}+\beta*{5} x*{1} x*{3}+\beta*{6} x*{2} x*{3}+\beta*{7} x*{1} x*{2} x*{3}

$$

The two way interactions are represented by $\beta_{4}, \beta_{5}$, and $\beta_{6} . \beta_{7}$ represents the three way interaction.

There are $m=8$ total parameters in the model. We should realize immediately that if we elect to try and fit the polynomial that includes all the interactions to the standard design, we will not have any degrees of freedom from which to estimate error. Thus, we must either replicate the design and repeat the experiments or sacrifice some of the desired information, by excluding effects that may not be of interest.Estimating two way and three-way interactions becomes important in process development, but may be less important in fitting linear models for developing relationships for reliability studies using failure mechanism models.

# 11.5 Linear Failure Mechanism Models

Two level factorial experiments are important in reliability studies, as many time to failure relationships are linear in nature. Hence, we can use a two level factorial SEDs for model development and to explore multiple variables and multiple test conditions. Many of our failure mechanism models can be classified into three different types:

- Simple Arrhenius
- Power Law Stress Models
- Mixed Models

All three types may be subject to a transformation to a simple linear model.
The simplest example of an Arrhenius model is the relationship between the rate of a chemical reaction and temperature. We therefore might represent the time to failure of a corrosion process as:


$$

t*{f}=A^{\*} e^{E*{A} / k T}

$$

The Arrhenius term is represented by the activation energy for the failure process, $E_{A}$, the Boltzmann constant, $k$, and the temperature $T . A^{*}$ is a constant.

Taking the natural log of both sides of the equation gives:


$$

\left.\ln t*{f}=\ln A^{\*}+E*{A}\right|\_{k T}

$$

This is a simple straight line relationship of the form:


$$

y=\beta o+\beta\_{1} x

$$

where:


$$

\begin{aligned}
& y=\ln t*{f} \\
& x=\left.1\right|*{T}
\end{aligned}

$$

and


$$

\begin{aligned}
& \beta*{o}=\ln A^{\*} \\
& \beta*{1}=\left.E*{A}\right|*{k}
\end{aligned}

$$

In a simple corrosion test, we could measure the time to failure as defined by a critical weight or thickness loss from at least 3 different temperatures and determine $E_{A}$ by regression analysis. As we indicate in Chapter $12, E_{A}$ is necessary to project test results to field conditions.

If we examine our basic S-N curve relationship for a material, we find it is also a simple linear model. Recall that we might express our average material fatigue strength versus cycles to failure as:


$$

S*{f}^{\prime}=C \prod*{i=1}^{n} k*{i} \bullet N*{f}^{b}
$$where $k_{i}$ represent the effects of component design and manufacturing. This is a typical power law model. We simply take the log of both sides and we see that:

$$
\ln S_{f}^{i}=\ln C+\sum_{i=1}^{n} \log k_{i}+b \log N_{f}
$$

This is the form of the general linear model shown in equation 11.4. Hence, a two level factorial is adequate for exploring the effect of many different factors on fatigue strength.

Evans, Hoang and Evans (1989) utilized factorial experiments for electromigration studies. Electromigration may be described by Black's Equation. This is a mixed model with a stress power law-Arrhenius relationship. Black's Equation is expressed as:

$$
t_{f}=A j^{-n} e^{E_{A} / k T}
$$

where the power law term is represented by the stress or current density $j$ and the current density exponent $n$. The Arrhenius term is represented by the activation energy for the failure process, $E_{A}$, the Boltzmann constant, $k$, and the temperature $T$.
Simply taking the natural $\log$ of both sides:

$$
\ln t_{f}=\ln A-n \ln j+\left.\left.E_{A}\right|_{k T}\right.
$$

This is of the following linear form:

$$
y=\beta_{o}+\beta_{1} x_{1}+\beta_{2} x_{2}
$$

where the independent variables are

$$
x_{1}=\ln j \text { and } x_{2}=\frac{1}{T}
$$

and:

$$
\begin{aligned}
& y=\ln t_{f} \\
& \beta_{o}=\ln A \\
& \beta_{1}=-n \\
& \beta_{2}=E^{A} / k
\end{aligned}
$$

In an electromigration experiment the current density and temperature would be controlled and the experiment would be exercised in accordance with a simple two level factorial layout. The dependent variable would be measured and the $\beta$ parameters determined by regression analysis. Once again, $n$ and $E_{A}$ are needed to project test results to field conditions.

An additional important value of two level SEDs is that they can be used to expand a model to evaluate discrete qualitative variables or additional quantitative effects. Hence, they provide the power to extend and expand an existing failure mechanism model, as well as building a new statistical based model. Different processes and materials can be compared by representing them as an added discrete variables. Then in the SED, a value of +1 represents a high level of a qualitative condition and -1 represent the lowest. Quantitative variables can also be added.

If we reconsider Black's Equation, we can add a discrete variable comparing two different manufacturing processes by expanding our layout from a $2^{2}$ design required to determine our model parameters to a $2^{3}$ design. Or, we can consider adding critical quantitative effects to the model. Evans and Evans (1989) suggested that we could improve Black's Equation by adding terms relating grain size and texture, which are also related to electromigration life-time by a power law relationship. Hence, Black's Equation might be effectively modified in equation 11.22:

$$
t_{f}=A^{*} \gamma^{-\eta} j^{-n} e^{E_{A} \mid k T}
$$

where $\gamma$ represents grain size of the film and $\eta$ is the grain size dependence for film life. The terms of this modified model could be determined form a $2^{3}$ factorial experiment. An additional example involving fatigue is shown below.

Example 11.2 A engineer wishes to compare the effects of surface finishing process improvements on fatigue life of a critical automobile components by running fatigue tests. Determine an appropriate experiment layout. Recalling Chapter 5, we can model surface effects on fatigue life according to:

$$
S_{a}=K_{a} S_{f}^{\prime}=C k_{a} N_{f}^{b}
$$

where $S_{a}$ is the applied alternating stress, $k_{a}$ is the surface factor and $N_{f}$ is the number of cycles to failure. $C$ and $b$ are constants representing material properties.

Now, we can simply take the natural log of both sides of the equation 11.23 and we see that:

$$
\ln S_{a}=\ln C+\ln k_{a}+b \ln N_{f}
$$

In a fatigue experiment we control the load which produces the alternating stress, $S_{a}$, in the component and measure the life, $N_{f}$ Therefore, solving for $\ln N_{f,}$, we see the following:

$$
\ln N_{f}=C^{*}-\frac{1}{b} \ln k_{a}-\frac{1}{b} \ln S_{a}
$$

This is of the following linear form:

$$
y=\beta_{a}+\beta_{1} x_{1}+\beta_{2} x_{2}
$$

From equations 11.25 and 11.26 , we see there are two factors of interest $x_{1}$ and $x_{2}$, representing surface finish and load conditions respectively. The number of runs required is $i_{r}=2^{2}=4$ runs required to determine the constants $C^{*}$ and $b$ and the effect of the process improvement.

We may not be able to directly control the surface finish factor, $k_{a}$. Rather, we may be primarily interested in comparing two different surface finishing processes. In this case, we may evaluate the effect as a qualitative variable and simply let $x_{1}=+1$ for the improved finishing Process $A$ and $x_{1}=-1$ for the original finishing Process $B$, when performing the regression analysis. $\beta_{1}$ would then represent the effect of process improvement. For load conditions, we substitute the values of alternating stress selected for the tests, with - representing the lowest value and + representing the highest value. $\beta_{2}$ would then represent the effect of load conditions. We can derive the constants for the $S-N$ curve.

The experiment would be conducted according to Table 11.5.

Table 11.5 Experimental Design Table to Compare Fatigue Life of Components

| Experimental Run | Finishing Process <br> $\boldsymbol{x}_{\mathbf{1}}$ | Load Conditions <br> $\boldsymbol{x}_{\mathbf{2}}$ |
| :--------------- | :--------------------------------------------------- | :------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| 1                | Process $A(+1)$                                      | -                                                  |
| 2                | Process $B(-1)$                                      | -                                                  |
| 3                | Process $A(+1)$                                      | +                                                  |
| 4                | Process $B(-1)$                                      | +                                                  | We would want to replicate this layout many times, particularly if we wished to estimate Weibull distribution parameters for each test condition. |

# 11.6 Fractional Factorials

If we examine equation 11.1, we will quickly see that the number of experimental runs and treatment combinations will climb dramatically as we increase the factors of interest. If we have 6 factors to examine in a fatigue experiment, we will need $i_{r}=2^{6}=64$ experimental runs to perform a full 2 level factorial experiment. On the other hand, we may only be interested in fitting a fatigue model that includes main effects. We can then elect to scale down the experiment by running a fractional factorial.

As an example, for an experiment with five factors $(k=5)$, our model will have $m=6$ regression parameters to include the 6 main effects and a regression constant. To fit a simple model with 6 regression parameters, we will need a minimum of 1 degree of freedom to examine error. This will require a minimum of 7 data points to analyze the main effects. We do not need the entire set of 64 runs and all treatments combinations to achieve our objective. In this case, we can reduce the experimental design by constructing a fractional factorial.

In doing so, we naturally expect to sacrifice our ability to examine all the interactions, but we will be able to perform a regression analysis to fit the model of interest and include the main effects.

As an example, we could construct $\frac{1}{8}$ factorial having $\frac{64}{8}=8$ runs, at treatments with 2 levels for our 5 factors. The experiment would be constructed using the following layout, leaving 2 degrees of freedom:

Table 11.6 Design Table for A Fractional Factorial with 5 Factors

| Experimental Run | Factor $\boldsymbol{x}_{\mathbf{1}}$ | Factor $\boldsymbol{x}_{\mathbf{2}}$ | Factor $\boldsymbol{x}_{\mathbf{3}}$ | Factor $\boldsymbol{x}_{\mathbf{4}}$ | Factor $\boldsymbol{x}_{\mathbf{5}}$ |
| :--------------- | :----------------------------------- | :----------------------------------- | :----------------------------------- | :----------------------------------- | :----------------------------------- |
| 1                | +                                    | -                                    | -                                    | +                                    | +                                    |
| 2                | +                                    | +                                    | -                                    | -                                    | -                                    |
| 3                | +                                    | +                                    | +                                    | -                                    | +                                    |
| 4                | -                                    | +                                    | +                                    | +                                    | -                                    |
| 5                | +                                    | -                                    | +                                    | +                                    | -                                    |
| 6                | -                                    | +                                    | -                                    | +                                    | +                                    |
| 7                | -                                    | -                                    | +                                    | -                                    | +                                    |
| 8                | -                                    | -                                    | -                                    | -                                    | -                                    |

Layouts for fractional factorial experiments may be found in many references.
We can easily construct a $\frac{1}{2}$ factorial by the method described by O'Connor (1991). First, we construct the full factorial layout. Then, we construct the full response table with all interactions. Next, we select an interaction that we will eliminate from the design. We can usually eliminate the highest order interaction, as it is unlikely to be significant or have much physical meaning. We eliminate all of the rows of the design in which the selected interaction has a $(-)$ value. We will be left with half of the required runs and treatment combinations. Similarly, we can again reduce the $\frac{1}{2}$ factorial to a $\frac{1}{4}$. Further reductions are possible depending upon the original size of the design table.

We need to be fully aware of the fact that we are losing information in the process of creating a fractional design and that we are incurring some risks. If we follow O'Connor's (1991)procedure, we will see that several contrasts in our resulting design will appear identical, after reducing the original design. In this case, we say that the effects associated with the like contrasts in a fractional design are confounded.

In other words, we cannot distinguish differences between the confounded effects. If higher order interactions are not significant, then this fact does not matter. We will distinguish the main effects. However, if these higher order effects are significant, we run the risk of the second or third order interaction contributing to the estimated main effect. We may draw an erroneous conclusion. Therefore, we should judiciously select interactions for elimination and carefully assess confounded contrasts based on engineering knowledge of the physical processes involved.

Example 11. 3 Let's consider our fatigue example again. As we have seen from Chapter 5, we can expect several factors to contribute to fatigue life reduction. Lets assume we wish to manufacture a component from a new material and we wish to examine 3 different factors on the fatigue life of the component. These factors will include:

- Surface Finish
- Temperature
- Stress Concentration

The following failure mechanism model governs our experimental design:

$$
S_{a}=k_{a} k_{d} k_{e} S_{f}=C k_{a} k_{d} k_{e} N_{f}^{b}
$$

and

$$
N_{f}=C^{*}\left[\frac{1}{k_{a}} \cdot \frac{1}{k_{d}} \cdot \frac{1}{k_{e}}\right] \stackrel{1}{S}_{a}^{\frac{1}{b}}
$$

If we transform our failure mechanism model, we can see it will fit the following linear form:

$$
y=\beta_{o}+\beta_{1} x_{1}+\beta_{2} x_{2}+\beta_{3} x_{3}+\beta_{4} x_{4}
$$

We will elect to include our factors of interest as discrete variables and we will vary the loading conditions at two different levels. Initially, we see that the full factorial will require 16 runs. Our model however, will require a minimum of 6 degrees of freedom. We will reduce our factorial experiment to a half-factorial to cut the cost. We will assign our standard notation as follows:

- $\mathrm{A}=$ Surface Finish Effect
- $\mathrm{B}=$ Temperature Effect
- $\mathrm{C}=$ Notch or Stress Concentration Effect
- D = Load Effect

Recall the general 4 factor design as: (1), $a, b, a b, c, a c, b c, a b c, d, a d, b d, a b d, c d, a c d, b c d$, $a b c d$. Using this notation we construct our design table and expand it to a full response table.

The contrasts labeled $A, B, C$, and $D$ represent our original design table. To create a fractional design, we select the highest order interaction and eliminate all rows in the design that are assigned ( - ) in the table. These rows are highlighted in lighter grey in Table 11.7. We are left with the rows that are shaded in darker grey. Since, we elected to include our design effects asdiscrete variables, we can assign the values in the contrasts as -1 and +1 and complete our analysis by regression using the method of least squares.

# 11.7 Analysis of Factorials by Linear Regression

To this point we have focused primarily on designing SEDs for reliability experiments. We will now shift our focus to analysis. Analysis of factorials can be performed by the simple procedure we have identified to assess the relative magnitude of the effects. We can also utilize sum-of-the-squares Analysis of Variance (ANOVA) techniques, which are discussed at length in Montgomery (1984). However, the most effective way to analyze an SED is by regression analysis. In the next sections we will introduce the principle concepts behind linear regression by least squares. This method is best executed by one of many available software tools. We have included a sample software in appendix. There are many sophisticated versions available.

Regression analysis is an invaluable tool for the investigative reliability engineer. Primarily it provides a method for correlating controlled experimental conditions to experimental results. Used in conjunction with SEDs, regression analysis will provide a model which will allow an estimation of the magnitude of the effect of independent variables on measured experimental results. In addition, such a model may be used to predict results over the range in which the model is valid.

In the case of relating a single independent variable to a set of measurements, a relatively simple procedure may be employed. In fact, many hand held calculators are equipped to develop a linear model from data entered through a keypad. However, when several independent variables must be related to a set of measurements, the analysis becomes much more complex and matrix methods must be employed. Several computer software packages are available for such purposes. The following discussion is a review of the statistics associated with regression analysis. A basic discussion of regression using matrix methods, regression statistics and statistical inference to evaluate parameter significance and error is presented.

### 11.7.1 Regression Equations

The objective of regression analysis is to develop a relationship between independent variables and a dependent response variable. The case may be as simple as fitting a straight line to a set of data. On the other hand, it may be as complicated as fitting a failure mechanism model to data collected via a statistically designed factorial experiment. In each case, a least squares technique may be employed to determine the coefficients of the desired model.

We can easily visualize the least squares method of regression analysis by considering the case of relating a single independent variable, $x$, to a dependent response, $y$. Let's consider a simple straight line model. In this simple case of fitting a line to a set of data, equation 11.29 can be used in the form of the model:

$$
y=\beta_{o}+\beta_{1} x
$$

where $x$ is fixed by the experimental process and $y$ is measured. $\beta_{o}$, as we know, is the intercept and $\beta_{1}$ is the slope of the line.

To develop this model, we will need to determine the two parameters, $\beta_{o}$ and $\beta_{1}$ for the line which will best represent the data. This is called the line of best fit.

As an example, we can look at Figure 11.3. We have measured time-to-failure for a component in testing at several different levels of stress. We would like to determine the parameters $\beta_{o}$ and $\beta_{1}$ for the line of best fit.

Figure 11.3 Example of a simple case of a line fitted to a set of data with a single factor and a response.

In order to determine the line of best fit we need to minimize the errors, between the experimental measurements, $y_{i}$ and the predicted values of the model, $\hat{y}$. We will minimize this error by minimizing the sum of the squares of the differences between all measured values and our model.

Our objective function is stated by the following equation:

$$
\min S S=\sum_{i}^{n}\left(y_{i}-\hat{y}\right)^{2}
$$

We substitute our model for the prediction of $y$ into the objective function.

$$
\min S S=\sum_{i}^{n}\left(y_{i}-\beta_{o}-\beta_{1} x_{1}\right)^{2}
$$

and to minimize the error, we must differentiate with respect to our parameters of interest, $\beta_{o}$ and $\beta_{1}$ and set the results equal to zero:

$$
\frac{\partial S S}{\partial \beta_{o}}=0 \text { and } \frac{\partial S S}{\partial \beta_{1}}=0
$$

This will yield two equations and two unknowns as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \sum_{i=1}^{n} y_{i}=\hat{\beta}_{o} n+\hat{\beta}_{1} \sum_{i=1}^{n} x_{i} \\
& \sum_{i=1}^{n} x_{i} y_{i}=\hat{\beta}_{o} \sum_{i=1}^{n} x_{i}+\hat{\beta}_{1} \sum_{i=1}^{n} x_{i}^{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

The summations are determined from the appropriate data sets. In this simple case, two equations are utilized to solve for the two unknowns, $\hat{\beta}_{o}$ and $\hat{\beta}_{1}$, which represent our least squares estimates of the model parameters.

In the multi-variable case, the situation becomes more complex. The sum of squares technique is still valid and a set of normal equations must be solved to determine the coefficients of the desired model equation. However, numerous simultaneous equations may have to be solved to find the appropriate set of parameters.

In order to visualize the problem, consider the following model in three dependent variables:

$$
y=\beta_{0}+\beta_{1} x_{1}+\beta_{2} x_{2}+\beta_{3} x_{3}+\beta_{4} x_{1} x_{2}+\beta_{5} x_{1} x_{3}+\beta_{6} x_{2} x_{3}+\beta_{7} x_{1} x_{2} x_{3}
$$

Data for such a model may come from several replications of a full two level factorial experiment. The SED requires eight experimental runs. Eight normal equations are required to solve for the eight regression parameters. Depending upon the number of experimental repli-cations, we may have a sizable amount of data to manipulate. However, the principle is exactly the same, as with the simple linear case.

In order to handle multi-variable equations and large data sets, matrix techniques are required. In the general case, equation 11.36 may be employed to solve for the regression parameters:

$$
B=\left(X^{T} X\right)^{-1} X^{T} Y
$$

The $X$ matrix consists of the data associated with the independent factors, as defined by the experimental treatments. The $\boldsymbol{X}$ matrix may be called the 'model' matrix and it is derived directly from the response table, for the SED. The $Y$ matrix represents the response data and may be called the 'data' matrix. $B$ represents the calculated regression coefficients.

In matrix form $X, Y$ and $B$ are expressed in the following equations. The mode matrix, $\mathbf{X}$, can be expressed as follows:

$$
X=\left[\begin{array}{cccc}
x_{1,1} & \ldots & \ldots & x_{1, m} \\
\ldots & x_{2,2} & \ldots & x_{2, m} \\
\ldots & \ldots & \ldots & \ldots \\
x_{n, 1} & \ldots & \ldots & x_{n, m}
\end{array}\right]
$$

For matrix analysis of an SED, $n=$ the total number of experimental runs, including each set of replications. If a $2^{3}$ full-factorial, with no replication, is to be analyzed, $n=i_{r}$. There will be 8 total runs. If it is replicated, $n=16$ total runs. $m$ is the number of parameters to be estimated, according to our model, including interactions if we wish to include them. If equation 11.35 were the model of choice, we would be calculating a total of 8 parameters.

Note that the first column in the matrix, $\left\{x_{1,1} \ldots \ldots \ldots x_{n, 1}\right\}=1$, when the regression constant, $\beta_{0}$ is included in the model. The remaining columns of the matrix correspond directly to each contrast in the response table, for the model of interest. The values of the treatment settings for each factor are used in place of each sign in the contrast. For discrete or qualitative factors a +1 or -1 may be appropriately entered, following the signs of the response table contrasts. The data matrix, $Y$, is expressed as:

$$
Y=\left[\begin{array}{c}
y_{1} \\
y_{2} \\
\ldots \\
y_{n}
\end{array}\right]
$$

$\left\{y_{1}, y_{2} \ldots \ldots \ldots y_{n}\right\}$ is the set of measured experimental responses for each run, from 1 to $n$ runs as called for by the design, including all replications.

The calculated B matrix contains the set of regression parameter estimates, associated with each factor in the design.

$$
B=\left[\begin{array}{c}
\hat{\beta}_{0} \\
\hat{\beta}_{1} \\
\ldots \\
\hat{\beta}_{m-1}
\end{array}\right]
$$

where $m$ is the total number of model parameters to be analyzed.
The quantity $\left(\mathrm{X}^{\mathrm{T}} \mathbf{X}\right)^{-1}$ is used to derive the covariance matrix. The diagonal terms of the co-variance matrix contain the variances of each parameter that are used to calculate the associated errors. We should recall, that a $T$ superscript indicates the transpose of the matrix while -1 superscript indicates the inverse.# 11.7.2 Regression Statistics

Earlier we mentioned error in our model. The error is the difference between the measured value and model prediction. We have developed our regression parameter estimation based upon minimizing the sum of the squares of the error. In applying regression analysis we are also making some important assumptions about the model error. We assume, the error is Normally Distributed with a mean of zero and the errors are independent and uncorrelated. We also assume that the variance of the error is equal to the variance of the dependent response, $y$. Hence:

$$
V[\delta]=V\left[y_{i}\right]=\sigma^{2}
$$

where $\sigma^{2}$ is the variance of the regression. We estimate $\sigma^{2}$ by calculating the unbiased estimate of the variance form our measured response.

We can also define a vector containing the set of errors for the regression as the residual vector. It is useful to develop a probability plot of the elements of the residual vector and examine their mean and distribution to evaluate the regression.

The unbiased estimate of the variance of the regression, $S^{2}$, may be calculated from the following matrix equation:

$$
S^{2}=\frac{Y^{T} Y-B^{T} X^{T} Y}{n-m}
$$

where $n=$ number of data points and $m=$ number of parameters to be estimated in the model.
The variance of the regression is used to determine the statistical significance of the regression parameters. In addition, it is an important quantity needed to calculate the confidence limits of the regression coefficients and any predictions made utilizing the model.

The correlation coefficient is calculated from the equation 11.42:

$$
R^{2}=\frac{B^{T} X^{T} Y-n \overline{y^{2}}}{Y^{T} Y-n \overline{y^{2}}}
$$

where $\bar{y}=$ mean of response data set, and $n=$ number of data points.

### 11.8 Statistical Inferences and Confidence Limits

In order to assess the impact of a particular independent variable on the measured response or dependent variable, it is necessary to determine whether or not the associated regression parameter is statistically significant.

To do so, we need to compare the magnitude of the effect to the variance of the parameter estimates. We can examine the covariance matrix to extract the variance of each estimated parameter:

$$
C=\sigma^{2}\left(X^{T} X\right)^{-1}=\left[\begin{array}{llll}
V\left[\hat{\beta}_{0}, \hat{\beta}_{1}\right]=\sigma^{2} \mathrm{C}_{1,1} & \operatorname{Cov}\left(\hat{\beta}_{0}, \hat{\beta}_{1}\right) & \ldots & \operatorname{Cov}\left(\hat{\beta}_{0}, \hat{\beta}_{m}\right) \\
\ldots & \mathrm{V}\left[\hat{\beta}_{1}\right]=\sigma^{2} \mathrm{C}_{2,2} & \ldots & \ldots \\
\ldots & \ldots & \ldots & \ldots \\
\operatorname{Cov}\left(\hat{\beta}_{0}, \hat{\beta}_{m}\right) & \operatorname{Cov}\left(\hat{\beta}_{1}, \hat{\beta}_{m}\right) & \ldots & \mathrm{V}\left[\hat{\beta}_{m-1}\right]=\sigma^{2} \mathrm{C}_{n, m}
\end{array}\right]
$$

Recall that we estimate $\sigma^{2}$ by calculating the unbiased estimate of the variance from our measured response.Hence, $V\left[\hat{\beta}_{i-1}\right]=\mathrm{S}^{2} \mathrm{C}_{i, i}$, where $\mathrm{C}_{i, i}$ is the diagonal element extracted from appropriate column of the $\left(X^{T} X\right)^{-1}$ matrix. Each column of the matrix is associated with a regression parameter. In equation 11.35 above, we provided an example for a model that includes a regression constant $\beta_{0}$.

Significance is decided by statistical inference using a standard $t$-test. Each student $t$-value, associated with each regression parameter, is as follows:

$$
t_{i}=\frac{\hat{\beta}_{i}-\beta_{i}}{\sqrt{V\left[\hat{\beta}_{i}\right]}}
$$

Initially a null hypothesis is formulated, in which the actual parameter is assumed to be zero and:

$$
t_{i}=\frac{\hat{\beta}_{i}}{\sqrt{V\left[\hat{\beta}_{i}\right]}}
$$

A critical $T$-value may then be selected from the student- $t$ tables. The value selected will be at the appropriate degrees of freedom, $v$, and at the preferred confidence level, $1-\alpha$, where $\alpha$ is the probability of error in our decision about the null hypothesis. The number of degrees of freedom, $v$, will be equal to the number of data points, $n$, minus the number of coefficients to be calculated, $m$.

If the following condition is met, the null hypothesis (that $\beta_{i}=0$ ) is rejected and the parameter estimate is deemed significant over the variance of the experiment:

$$
t_{i} \geq t_{\alpha_{i 2}}
$$

where $t$ represents the absolute value of the calculated student $t$-value and $t_{\alpha_{i 2}}$ is the tabulated value. Parameters whose estimates are not statistically significant, can be dropped from the model.

Once the issue of significance has been decided, the confidence limits for the significant regression parameter estimates, may be calculated from the equation 11.47 using the student $t$-value from the tables:

$$
\hat{\beta}_{i} \pm t_{\alpha_{i 2}} \sqrt{V\left[\hat{\beta}_{i}\right]}
$$

The confidence limits of any predicted value may be calculated from equation 11.48:

$$
y \pm t_{\alpha_{i 2}} \mathrm{~S}^{\wedge} \sqrt{a^{T}\left(X^{T} X\right)^{-1} a}
$$

where $\boldsymbol{a}$ represents the single column matrix of the values of the independent experimental factors at the predicted value of $y$.

For a model including a regression constant, $\beta_{o}$ :

$$
a=\left[\begin{array}{c}
1 \\
x_{1} \\
\ldots \\
x_{n}
\end{array}\right]
$$# 11.9 Coding Data

It is often useful to code the data in the model matrix. This makes the regression calculation balanced and reduces the error due to calculation, as a result of the matrix inversion of the $X^{T} X$ matrix. Coding is simply letting the value of the factors in the contrast of the response table equal +1 or -1 , just as we do when we wish to assign a discrete or qualitative variable to the model. Then, the scaled or coded factor becomes:


$$

x*{\text {coded }}=\frac{x-\left(\frac{x*{\text {High }}+x*{\text {Low }}}{2}\right)}{\frac{x*{\text {High }}-x\_{\text {Low }}}{2}}

$$

Example 11.4 Lets examine an experiment in which temperature is a factor. We have assigned $50^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ as the lower value and $150^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ as the upper value. We can perform the regression by inserting our actual values for temperature into the associated model matrix or we may elect to encode them, using equation 11.50 above. Our coded value at temperature of $50^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ is simply:


$$

x\_{\text {coded }\left(50^{\circ} \mathrm{C}\right)}=\frac{50-\left(\frac{150+150}{2}\right)}{\frac{150-50}{2}}=-1

$$

the estimated regression parameters are then associated with the coded factors.
The results of the transformation for a single contrast is shown in Table 11.9.

Example 11.5 MacPherson (1989) proposed that time to failure of plastic encapsulated semiconductors can be fit into the following model:


$$

An SED can be used to estimate the parameters of the model, for new types of devices or materials.

Lets consider the development of a new device. Two lots of this new device type were tested. Both lots used the same plastic encapsulation. The $\mathrm{Cl}^{-}$concentration was therefore assumed to be constant, among the devices. The time to failure model in equation 11.52, can be transformed:


$$

$$
Equation 11.53 is of the following linear form:


$$

y=\beta*{o}+\beta*{1} x*{1}+\beta*{2} x\_{2}

$$

There are two factors, Relative Humidity and Temperature. This requires $2^{2}=4$ experimental runs to estimate the model parameters. The experiment was replicated using each lot of prototypes using highly accelerated stress test (HAST) chambers. With our limited samples, we produce 8 data points. Example 11.6 A new synthetic lubricant has been selected for possible use by a manufacturer of diesel engines. The new technology offers a potential for cost reduction and improved recyclability. # 11.10 Summary

In this chapter, we have introduced the essential information needed to design, layout and analyze statistical experimental designs. SEDs provide an excellent method to develop and extend models, identify key factors in manufacturing processes and develop plans to address multiple test conditions. Two level factorials, as we have seen, are particularly useful for reliability experiments.


Figure 11.4 Factor plot graphically depicting the effect of lubricant type on engine wear, at two different treatments.# 11.11 Do's and Don'ts

Do consider the application of SEDs to multi-factor test situations.
Do apply SEDs to estimate failure mechanism model parameters.
Do include discrete and qualitative independent factors in the design.
Do consider expanding failure mechanism models using SEDs, to address new materials, technologies and processes. Do set factors level in a robust manner.
Do consider fractional factorial designs.
Do seek to understand the physical significance of interactions.
Do seek to understand the underlying causative relationship between factors and responses.
Do analyse SEDs using regression analysis.
Do estimate regression parameter error and statistical significance.
Do consider encoding factor data.
Do examine all sources of error and contributions to variance.
Do replicate.
Do randomize the runs of the SED when executing treatments in a design table.
Do use SEDs with Finite Element Analysis to develop stress models.
Do apply probability plotting techniques in conjunction with SEDs.
Don't forget to identify confounding contrasts in fractional designs.
Don't assume all factors will be significant in a regression model.
Don't forget that 1 degree freedom is needed to estimate error.
Don't assume that measurement and instrument precision are negligible.
Don't forget to consider the effects of acceleration in setting factor levels.

John W. Evans and Kyoung-Taeg Lee

In Chapter 10, we examined the basic elements of testing and test design issues. Then, in Chapter 11, we turned our attention to multiple factors, multiple test conditions and test design for model development using designed experiments. We will now address accelerated testing and the statistical analysis of data from accelerated tests.

Accelerated testing is the process of applying loads in testing that exceed the loads that are encountered in service. The result is a decreased time to failure of the material, component or system in testing. The benefit is a reduction in the test time, for the evaluations of product life by wear out failure mechanisms. It is unreasonable to expect to test a product in development under expected field loads, since we expect most products to last many years. Yet, we must assure their integrity in a short time, during design phases. In fact, virtually all life tests are conducted under some form of acceleration.

As an example, we may elevate the test temperature for a corrosion test leading to rapid deterioration of component test samples. Or, we may elevate both voltage and temperature in testing microcircuits, to evaluate the integrity of the deposited dielectrics used in the circuits. In any event, to understand the relationship of the test to the reliability of a system when it is fielded, we must be able to develop a relationship between test time and field life. To do this effectively, we must understand the impact of the accelerated loading conditions on the failure mechanisms active in the system.

In this chapter, we will discuss the development of acceleration factors for tests. In addition, we will discuss the analysis of data from testing and the projection of the data to field conditions. This is an essential and key aspect of effective reliability assessment and becomes necessary to confirm dominant failure mechanisms and to validate models used for design.

### 12.1 Acceleration Factors

The effects of acceleration must be examined for each dominant mechanism acting on the components in a system. An acceleration factor for a failure mechanism can be determined from the failure mechanism models we have developed in previous chapters. We can then apply the acceleration factor to data accumulated in test to assess the relationship between the test life and field life. In general, we can say the relationship between test time and field life can be expressed for a given failure mechanism (FM) as:


$$

A F*{F M}=\frac{t*{f(\text { field })}}{t\_{f(\text { test })}}

$$
In Chapter 11, we broadly categorized our models into three classes. Keeping in mind there are always exceptions, our models may fit into one of following three categories:

- Arrhenius Models
- Stress Power Law Models
- Mixed Models

Diffusion driven processes and chemical processes, such as corrosion, will often have an Arrhenius relationship or exhibit a mixed model with mechanical, electrical or chemical stresses acting in concert with temperature to accelerate failure. Power law models, on the other hand, represent fatigue and related processes. In fatigue, increasing the stresses in the component by increasing applied loads, accelerates failure by crack growth.

We can determine a relationship between loading conditions through an acceleration transform, developed from failure mechanism models of interest. Let us examine the simple Arrhenius expression. The time to failure for a corrosion process may be expressed as:


$$

t*{f}=A^{\*} e^{E*{A} / K T}

$$

Recall that $A^{*}$ is a constant, $E_{A}$ is the activation energy, $k$ is Boltzmann's Constant and $T$ is the absolute temperature at which the reaction is occurring. From Chapter 11, we can see that $E_{A}$ is determined by evaluating the time to fail at different temperatures.

Now consider that we have determined $E_{A}$ under a series of elevated temperature tests and we wish to project data to field conditions. Applying equation 12.1:


$$

\mathrm{AF}=\frac{t*{f \text { field })}}{t*{f(\text { test })}}=\frac{A^{_} e^{E\_{A} / K T(\text { field })}}{A^{_} e^{E\_{A} / K T(\text { test })}}

$$

Simplifying:


$$

A F=\exp \left[\frac{E_{A}}{K}\left(\frac{1}{T_{\text {field }}}-\frac{1}{T_{\text {test }}}\right)\right]

$$

Keep in mind that we have made several assumptions in deriving 12.4. The concentrations of the reacting species have not been considered. We have assumed that they have remained constant between the field conditions and the test conditions. If this assumption is not true, then we must derive a relationship that accounts for concentration differences.

Example 12.1 A heat exchanger was tested under accelerated conditions. The test was conducted at $215^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$, at operating pressures. A leak was detected as a result of pitting after 500 hours of test. The heat exchanger will operate at $125^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$. Assuming the process failure has an activation energy of 1.2 eV , determine the test acceleration factor and estimate the field life from the time of first failure.

Applying equation 12.4:


$$

\begin{aligned}
A F & =\exp \left[\frac{1.2}{86.1 \times 10^{-6}}\left(\frac{1}{398}-\frac{1}{488}\right)\right] \\
& =\exp (6.44) \\
A F & =626
\end{aligned}

$$
Then:


$$

A F*{F M}=\frac{t*{f(\text { field })}}{t\_{f(\text { test })}}

$$

and


$$

t\_{f(\text { field })}=626(500)=312,890 \text { hours }=36 \text { years }

$$

This is a simple example of an acceleration factor estimate and its application. Loading uncertainties and multiple failure mechanism have not been considered.

In general, equation 12.4 would apply to any Arrhenius relationship or mixed model in which the component stresses, other than temperature, remain the same between the field conditions encountered in application and the test conditions. Also, keep in mind that the field loads, in this case temperature, may not be known with precision. In application, as we discussed in Chapter 4, loading conditions are likely to have a lot of associated uncertainty.

Let's consider a power law relationship. Recall our simple expression for fatigue life of a material:


$$

S*{a}=C N*{f}^{b}

$$

where $S_{a}$ is the alternating stress, $N_{f}$ is the cycles to failure and $C$ and $b$ are material properties. Our acceleration factor expression is then:


$$

A F=\frac{N*{f(\text { field })}}{N*{f(\text { test })}}=\frac{C^{_} S\_{a(\text { field })}^{1 / b}}{C^{_} S\_{a(\text { test })}^{1 / b}}

$$

Simplifying:


$$

A F=\left[\frac{S_{a(\text { field })}}{S_{a(\text { test })}}\right]^{\frac{1}{b}}

$$

In the case of fatigue, we must know the exponent value $b$, for the material we are considering, to apply an acceleration transform. In comparing low cycle and high cycle fatigue recall that $b($ low cycle $) \neq b($ high cycle $)$. Hence equation 12.7 cannot be applied to transform low cycle fatigue test data to high cycle fatigue component applications. Equation 12.7 is also derived under the assumption that the components or samples used for testing would represent the components used in the field. As discussed in Chapter 5, factors such as manufacturing processes for surface finish and notch designs would contribute substantially to reducing fatigue life.

If we consider thermal cycling loads as a source of alternating stresses in the component, then the change in temperature is proportional to the stress amplitude:


$$

S\_{a} \propto \Delta T

$$

Equation 12.7 then becomes:


$$

A F=\left[\frac{\Delta T_{(\text {field })}}{\Delta T_{(\text {test })}}\right]^{\frac{1}{b}}

$$

Once again, 12.9 assume that the same fatigue process is active in the field as in the test. We cannot compare low cycle and high cycle fatigue or failure processes in which creep may dominate the deformation. In this case, more complex transforms are necessary.We have shown at this point that we can derive an acceleration transform from a failure mechanism model and we have derived some simple expressions for Arrhenius and Power Law failure mechanism models. These expressions are well known and often broadly applied. However, we must always keep in mind that the test conditions must represent the field conditions to apply an acceleration transform.

We are also interested in high levels of reliability, not necessarily in mean life. Figure 12.1 graphically depicts our objectives in interpreting accelerated test data. We test our components or systems at high loads inducing high stress levels. We then assess our test condition failure probability $p d f$. In following sections, we will discuss probability plotting methods for doing this task. Next, we want to assess field life from the data. However, we are most interested in low probabilities of failure. If we re-examine Figure 12.1, we see that we are interested in the lower curve that describes a low probability of failure for a component failing from a given failure mechanism. Hence, we need to restate equation 12.1:


$$

A F*{F M}=\frac{t*{f \text { field })}}{t\_{f p t}(\text { test })}

$$

where, $t_{f p f}$, is the time to failure, at an acceptable level of risk, as defined by the probability of failure. $p_{f}$

An alternative approach is to determine the hazard rate, $h(t)$, for a given failure mechanism acting on a component, by testing and applying probability plotting methods. We then apply the $A F$ to the $h(t)_{\text {test }}$ to estimate $h(t)_{\text {field }}$.

As an example, the hazard rate for electronic components may be expressed as a function of the applied stresses. The following equation or a similar relationship is applied:


$$

h(t)=e^{\left[C_{1}-E_{e} / K T\right]} e\left\{C*{2} \frac{V*{\text {Test }}}{V\_{\text {Applied }}}\right\}

$$



Figure 12.1 Illustration on the application of $\mathrm{AF}(\mathrm{s})$. We are interested in projecting the failure distribution to field conditions. Low probabilities of failure are of interest, not mean life. However, we are assuming the test distribution will resemble the field distribution and that we know the field loading conditions with certainty.where $E_{A}$ is the activation energy for the failure mechanism of interest, $T$ is the temperature of the device in the region of the active failure site, $V_{\text {Test }}$, is the voltage level applied in test and $V_{\text {Applied }}$ is the voltage level applied in the field $C_{1}$ and $C_{2}$ are constants. Equation 12.11 may be applied for a failure mechanism such as time dependent dielectric breakdown in which the activation energy may range from 0.2 to 1.0 eV (Sze 1988) depending upon the magnitude of the applied electric fields and the type of dielectric.

In applying acceleration transforms, we need to keep in mind that the transformation is valid for a single failure mechanism. The transform will be valid only for the mechanism we have precipitated in our accelerated testing. The same mechanism dominating the test conditions must be dominating the field conditions to accurately reflect field life. In complex systems and components, there may be competing causes of failure. In this case, we must separate each mechanism precipitated in testing by careful analysis of the data and application of failure analysis to the components. We can then apply the concepts illustrated in Chapter 3, to estimate field failure probabilities or reliability.

We should also recognize a conspicuous shortcoming of this method is that it does not reflect the uncertainties that may exist in field loading conditions. In actual use, considerable uncertainties may exist in system loading conditions, which will be reflected in the stresses induced in the system components. As Figure 12.1 reflects, we apply an AF assuming that we know the field loading conditions with certainty. While this is true for the test, it is often not the case for a system or product. As an example, consider a washing machine. The weight of the clothing the consumer places in the wash tub will probably vary considerably from consumer to consumer and with each use of the machine. In addition, the operation of an automobile accelerator will vary from consumer to consumer, depending upon such factors as age of the consumer. An alternative approach to $A F(s)$ is to apply a simulation technique. This is explored in greater detail in later sections.

# 12.2 Analysis of Data

It is essential to determine in the process of analysis which probability distribution that best fits a set of data accumulated from a single test condition. There are two approaches - qualitative and quantitative - that will be presented in this section. In accelerated life testing, the random variable of interest is of course time to failure of the components, sub-systems or systems subjected to the test loads. However, plotting techniques can also be applied to other random variables such as process parameters or strength. In this section, several different types of random variables will be used to demonstrate the analysis techniques and procedures.

### 12.2.1 Probability and Hazard Plotting

Although quantitative approaches, including the Chi-squared and Kolmogorov-Smirnov test have been developed, qualitative probability and hazard plotting methods are widely used in practice due to their simplicity. These techniques provide pictorial representations of the data, as well as:

- an evaluation of the reasonableness of the assumed probability model
- estimates of the percentiles of the distribution or probability of failure at different times
- estimates of the distribution parametersPlotting techniques are very simple to use and easy to demonstrate. For a given pdf, the data are plotted on special graph paper designed for that distribution. If the assumed model is correct, the plotted points will tend to fall in a straight line. If the model is inadequate, however, the plot will not be linear and the extent and type of departures can be seen. Once a model appears to fit the data reasonably well, percentiles and parameter values can be estimated from the plot. The procedure and underlying theory of probability plotting are illustrated first. Next, probability plots for normal, lognormal, Weibull and extreme value distributions are considered. Probability plot for singly censored data and hazard plots for multiply censored data are given at the end of the section.

# Procedure for Probability Plotting

The following steps are involved in preparing a probability plot from a given set of data:

- Step 1: Obtain the appropriate probability paper ${ }^{1}$ designed for the distribution under examination.
- Step 2: Rank the observations, $x_{(i)}^{\prime} z$, such as times to failure, from smallest to largest in magnitude. Thus, if $x_{1}, x_{2}, \ldots, x_{n}$, are the original unordered observations then the ordered observations, $x_{(1)}, x_{(2)}, \ldots, x_{(n)}$, are such that $x_{(1)} \leq x_{(2)} \leq \ldots \leq x_{(n)}$.
- Step 3: Plot the $x_{(i)}^{\prime} z$ on the probability paper versus plotting position, where the plotting position $=(i-0.5) 100 / n$.
- Step 4: If a straight line appears to fit the data, draw such a line on the graph 'by eye'.

If the selected $p d f$ is correct, the points should cluster around the line, although there will be some deviations. If the plot deviates appreciably from linearity, the chosen pdf does not adequately describe the given data. Systematic departures are indications that the model is inadequate and the another model should be used. The determination of what can and cannot be considered a straight line is a subjective matter, and two people using the same plot may arrive at somewhat different conclusions. But, the larger the sample size, the easier it will be to make the correct decision.

Example 12.2 In this example we will examine quality problem in which weight is the random variable to demonstrate the plotting concept. Lets examine a cement mix, which is packed in forty-pound containers. This product is expensive, and it is important to hold the weight close to forty pounds. The ordered values of the weights of 25 randomly selected containers and corresponding plotting positions are shown in Table 121.

An engineer has stated the weight follows the normal distribution. In order to examine his assumption, weights were plotted on a normal probability plot and are shown in Figure 12.2. The ordered container weights are plotted against plotting position (i- 0.5 ) $100 / \mathrm{n}$; the smallest weight value, 38.2500 pounds, is plotted on the data scale at the plotting position of 2.0 on the probability scale, the second ordered value, 38.4389 pounds, is plotted versus 6.0 , and so on. The highest value, 41.6327 , is plotted versus 98.0 . The plotted points fall close to the line drawn, and hence it can be said that the engineer's insistence is correct. And we may use the normal distribution to assess the quality of our product weight.
