# Theory of Probability Plotting

Consider that a large number of samples of size $n$ that are selected from a population with probability density function $f(x)$ and cumulative distribution function $F(x)$. After each sample, the observations are ordered and relabeled $x_{(i)}, i=1,2, \cdots, n$, where $x_{(i)}$ is the value of the $i^{\text {th }}$ smallest observation. Then, the expected value of $x_{(i)}$ can be shown to be


$$

E\left[x_{(i)}\right]=\frac{n!}{(i-1)(\mathrm{n}-i)} \int*{0}^{1} x*{(i)} f\left(x*{(i)}\right) F\left(x*{(i)}\right)^{i-1}\left[1-F\left(x_{(i)}\right)\right]^{n-1} d x\_{(i)}

$$

For example, if $x$ is uniformly distributed over the interval $(0,1)$, then equation (12.12) reduces to:


$$

E\left[x_{(i)}\right]=\frac{i}{n+1}

$$

For distributions for which $E\left[x_{(i)}\right]$ cannot be determined exactly, the following approximation is frequently used:


$$

E\left[x_{(i)}\right]=F^{-1}\left\{\frac{i-c}{n-2 c+1}\right\}

$$

where $F^{-1}\left\{\frac{i-c}{n-2 c+1}\right\}$ is the value of $x$, such that $\frac{i-c}{n-2 c+1}=\int_{c}^{x} f(u) d u$ and $E\left[x_{(i)}\right]$ is a number which depends on $n$ and $f(x)$.

For a sample of size $n$, the first ordered observation $x(1)$ is a one-sample estimate of $E\left[x_{(1)}\right], x_{(2)}$ is a one-sample estimate of $E\left[x_{(2)}\right]$, and so on. Thus the ordered observed values, when plotted against their expected values, would lie on approximately a straight line, and the linearity of the plot of the observations versus their expected values provides an evaluation of the adequacy of a chosen model for the $p d f$ of the data.

The construction of specially scaled probability paper has obviated the need for actually calculating expected values for each distribution. This paper is scaled in such a fashion that the ordered observations can be plotted directly against $(i-c) 100 /(n-2 c+1)$, without the need of determining $E\left[x_{(i)}\right]$. In general, the exact value of $c$ depends on $n$ and $f(x)$, but $c=\frac{1}{2}$ has been found to be generally acceptable for a wide variety of distributions and sample sizes.

Figure 12.2 Normal probability plot for measured cement container weights.# Normal Probability Plot

Normal probability papers are specially designed papers where the plotted points will cluster around a straight line if the data are from the normal distribution. If the plotted points tend to fall in a straight line, we can estimate percentiles $\left(x_{p}\right.$ satisfying $\left.P\left(X \leq x_{p}\right)=p\right.$, given $\left.p\right)$ and percentages failing by the probability plot.

To determine percentiles for any random variable we analyze, we enter the plot on the probability scale at the desired percentage and go to the fitted line and then to the corresponding point on the data scale to read the percentile estimate. To determine percentage failing, enter the plot on the data scale at that time. Go to the fitted line, and then go to the corresponding point on the probability scale to read the estimate. In fact, the methods of estimating percentiles and percentages failing are the same for all the probability plots, and thus the estimation of percentiles and percentages is omitted hereafter.

The mean and standard deviation are estimated as follows. The mean $\mu$ of a normal distribution equals the median ( $50^{\text {th }}$ percentile), since the distribution is symmetric. To estimate, $\sigma$, the standard distribution, estimate the mean and the $16^{\text {th }}$ percentile. The estimate of $\sigma$ is the difference between the mean and the $16^{\text {th }}$ percentile, since for any normal distribution the standard deviation equals approximately the difference between them.

Example 12.3 From example 12.2, we can estimate the percentiles and distribution parameters. From Figure 12.2, the estimate of the $50^{\text {th }}$ percentile (thus mean) is 40.05 . Also, since the estimate of the $16^{\text {th }}$ percentile is 39.22 , the estimate of $\sigma$ is $40.05-39.22=0.83$.

As a guide for the evaluation of normal probability plots, two sets each of random samples of sizes 20 and 50 have been selected from a standard normal distribution. Figure 12.3-(a) and (b) show the corresponding normal probability plots. In contrast, Figure 12.3-(c) and (d) show plots on normal probability paper for samples of size 20 and 50 , respectively from an exponential distribution whose shape differs dramatically from that of the normal distribution. We can note, from these figures, that:

- The variance of the points in the tails (extreme low or high plotted values) will be larger than that of the points at the center of the distribution. Thus, the relative linearity of the plot near the tails of the distribution will often seem poorer than at the center of the distribution even if the correct model has been chosen.
- The plotted points are ordered and hence are not independent. Thus the plot may consist of a series of successive points above and below the line, even if the chosen model is correct.
- Even though the correct model has been chosen, the plot appears to diverge from linearity due to random variations, especially when the sample size is small.
- When there is a systematic departure from a straight line, an examination of a plot can give some information about the shape of a more appropriate model. For example, the plots of Figure 12.3-(c) and (d) show that the values in both tails are too large, and thus the data suggest that a model skewed to the right should be chosen. Likewise, if the values in both tails of the normal probability plot had been too small a distribution skewed to the left would be suggested.


## Lognormal Probability Plotting

Probability paper for the lognormal distribution differs from that for the normal distribution in that the axis for the data scale is logarithmic instead of arithmetic. A lognormal probability

Figure 12.3 a-d Guide for the evaluation of normal probability plots. (a) and (b) show two populations of different sizes drawn from the Normal distribution. (c) and (d) are samples drawn from an Exponential Distribution and plotted on Normal paper. Note the dramatic departure from linearity.
plot can also be prepared on normal probability paper by using the logarithms of the observations and plotting these against ( $\mathrm{i}-0.5$ ) $100 / \mathrm{n}$. The procedure for estimating the parameters is similar to that for the normal distribution, except that the logarithms of the observed values are used. Thus the lognormal distribution parameter $p$ is estimated as the logarithm of the plotted $50^{\text {th }}$ percentile, and $\sigma$ is estimated as the difference between the logarithms of the plotted $50^{\text {th }}$ and $16^{\text {th }}$ percentiles.

Example 12.4 Lets now look at a reliability problem analyzing 30 times to failure or numbers of cycles to failure of Ball Grid Array (BGA) surface mount packages on printed wiring boards. The data are plotted on lognormal probability paper in Figure 12.4. From Figure 12.4, the estimate of median number of cycles to failure is 12,800 , and thus the estimate of $\mu$ is $\log (12,800)=4.107$. Also, from the figure, the estimate of $16^{\text {th }}$ percentile is 11,400 cycles and the estimate of $\sigma$ is $4,107-\log (11,400)=0.05$.

Figure 12.4 Lognormal Probability Plot of BGA fatigue test data.

# Weibull Probability Plotting

The importance of the Weibull distribution has been emphasized in Chapter 3. The Weibull distribution may be the most widely used lifetime distribution model. Its popularity maybe due to the flexibility of the distribution to represent many types of failure patterns. That is, the Weibull distribution hazard function is monotone increasing if $\beta>1$, decreasing if $\beta<1$, and constant for $\beta=1$ and for this case, the Weibull distribution reduces to the exponential distribution. In addition, if $\beta=3.5$, the distribution is similar to the normal distribution and it is similar to the lognormal distribution if $2.5<\beta<3.5$. So, in analyzing times to failure from testing or field conditions, the Weibull distribution is an excellent place to start.

In Chapter 2, the Weibull cumulative distribution function was defined as


$$

F(x)=1-\exp \left[-\left(\frac{x}{\mu}\right)^{\beta}\right], x>0

$$

where $\mu$ and $\beta$ are the scale and shape parameters, respectively. Therefore, we can obtain


$$

\frac{1}{1-F(x)}=\exp \left[\left(\frac{x}{\mu}\right)^{\beta}\right]

$$

and


$$

\ln \ln \left[\frac{1}{1-F(x)}\right]=\beta \ln x-\beta \ln \mu

$$

Thus, for any Weibull variate, $\ln \{\ln [1 /\{1-F(x)\}]\}$ will plot as a straight line against the natural logarithms of the observations. To avoid the need for computing $\ln \{\ln [1 /\{1-F(x)\}]\}$ and $\ln x$, the axes of the probability paper are scaled so that ( $\mathrm{i}-0.5) 100 / n$ can be plotted on the ordinate, corresponding to $\ln \{\ln [1 /\{1-F(x)\}]\}$, and the observed values can be plotted on the abscissa, corresponding to $\ln x$.The scale parameter $\mu$ is the $63^{\text {th }}$ percentile, since $F(\mu)=1-e^{-1} \approx 0.63$. In addition, from equation (12.17), the shape parameter $\beta$,is the slope of the fitted line. The slope can be estimated by


$$

\hat{\beta}=\frac{W*{2}-W*{1}}{z*{2}-z*{1}}

$$

where $W_{2}$ and $W_{1}$ are two values of $\ln \{\ln [1 /\{1-F(x)]]\}$ and where $z_{2}$ and $z_{1}$ are the corresponding values of $\ln x$ on the plotted line. In the commercial Weibull probability paper, $\beta$ can be estimated by using the point labelled 'origin', which will be explained below. In equation (12.18), the hat symbol, ${ }^{\circ}$, denotes the estimator of the parameter of interest, $\beta$.

Example 12.5 The data in Table 12.2 consist of the failure times of specimens of PET film in gas insulated transformers at $5,7,10$ and 15 kV . The purpose of the experiment was to estimate the insulation life at 4.7 kV where a nominal life of 20,000 hours was desired, and the distribution for 4.7 kV can be estimated by the an Arrhenius model with the Weibull distribution. We can refer to Nelson (1991) for a further discussion of the model.

The plotting positions are shown in Table 12.2, and the data for each voltage are plotted on Weibull probability paper in Figure 12.5. The plotted points for each voltage tend to follow a straight line, so the Weibull distribution appears adequate. Since the estimate of the $63^{\text {rd }}$ percentile is 5.2 , the estimate of $\mu$ at 15 kV is about 52 . To estimate $\beta$, we draw a line passing through the origin and parallel to the fitted line, as in Figure 12.5. The value where this line intersects the shape parameter scale is the estimate of $\beta$. For the 15 kV data, the estimate is 2.25 .

The fitted lines in Figure 12.5 are not parallel, owing to unequal $\beta$ 's. In particular, the slope of the 15 kV data is greater than the other slopes. This suggests that the failure mode at 15 kV may differ from those at the other test voltages. Careful failure analysis would validate this conclusion and should be used to corroborate the results of the statistical analysis.

In plotting data on the Weibull probability paper, there arise situations where the plotted points form a concave down plot, as shown in Figure 12.6. In this case, one should suspect that the item has a finite failure-free time under test. If strength is the random variable of interest, then we would expect a minimum strength. In either case, the data may better fit a three-parameter Weibull distribution, and he or she should estimate the failure free time or minimum strength and then transform the data to fit the Weibull probability paper to estimate the other Weibull distribution parameters.

Figure 12.5 Weibull probability plots for PET film data.

Figure 12.6 Typical Weibull Probability Plot for the case of a failure-free period. The concave -down curvature indicates the data fit the three parameter Weibull Distribution.

In order to transform such data into a straight line for analysis of the Weibull parameters, it is necessary to transform the three-parameter distribution to fit the two parameter plotting paper. The method of transformation is as follows:

- Draw equally spaced horizontal lines as shown in Figure 12.6 with the middle line intersecting the mid-point of the plotted data,
- Estimate the failure free-time;


$$

v=t*{2}-\frac{\left(t*{3}-t*{2}\right)\left(t*{2}-t*{1}\right)}{\left(t*{3}-t*{2}\right)\left(t*{2}-t\_{1}\right)}

$$

- Adjust data by subtracting $v$
- Replot using the adjusted data, and estimate $\beta$ and $\mu$ on two parameter paper

Example 12.6 Table 12.3 presents the shear strength test data for brass brake rivets. The data are plotted in Figure 12.7(a) and shows that the fitted line forms concave down plot. The mid-point on the probability scale gives $t_{2}=15.35, t_{1}=15.00$ and $t_{3}=15.80$ as shown in Figure 12.7(a).

Thus,


$$

v=15.35-\frac{(15.80-15.35)(15.35-15.30)}{(15.80-15.35)-(15.35-15.30)}=13.78

$$

Adjusted data are also given in Table 12.3, and they are plotted on the Weibull probability paper in Figure 12.7(b).

# Extreme Value Probability Plotting

If a random variable $t$ has a Weibull distribution, then $\log (t)$ has an extreme value distribution. Thus, an extreme value probability plot can be prepared on the Weibull probability paper by using the exponent of the observations and plotting these against (i-0.5)100/n.

Figure 12.7a, b Adjustment of Weibull probability plot. The raw data are concave down and indicate a minimum shear strength value for brass brake rivets. Adjusted data show a good fit to the Weibull with a minimum strength of 13.78 .

# Singly Censored Data

Often accelerated test data are censored. The test may be halted before all samples are run to failure and the data must be analyzed. Data are said to be singly censored if all failure times are before a single censoring time. The method of probability plotting for singly censored data is like that for complete data. In particular, plot the $i^{\text {th }}$ smallest failure time against the plotting position $(i-0.5) 100 / n$. Here $n$ is the total sample size including the non-failures. Nonfailures are not plotted, since their failure times are unknown. Only the early failure times are plotted, and they can be used to estimate the lower part of the life distribution. The lower end of the distribution is usually of greatest interest.

Example 12.7 Mann and Fertig(1973) give failure times of airplane components subjected to a life test. The data are Type II censored: 13 components were placed on test, but the test was terminated at the time of the tenth failure. Failure times of the 10 failed components were $0.22,0.50,0.88,1.00,1.32,1.33,1.54,1.76,2.50$, and 3.00 .

Figure 12.8 is a result of plotting the data on the Weibull probability paper. In this example, the sample size $n$ is 13 , but only ten data are plotted on the probability paper.

Figure 12.8 Weibull plot for Singly Censored Data

# Multiple Censored Data

Multiple censored data consist of failure times intermixed with several censoring times, as depicted in Figure 12.9. Such data are common and can result from:

- removal of units from use before failure,
- loss or failure of units due to different failure mechanisms or extraneous causes, and
- collection of data while units are still running(common for field failure data)

Probability plotting method can be used for multiply censored data, but it is very complicated and thus the use of hazard paper ${ }^{3}$ is recommended. The step by step procedure of using the hazard paper is as follows:

- Obtain the hazard paper designed for the distribution under examination
- Order the n data from smallest to largest without regard as to which are censoring or failure times. Label the data with reverse ranks; that is, label the first ordered data with n , the second data with $n-1, \ldots$, and the $n^{\text {th }}$ with 1 .
- Calculate a hazard value for each failure time as $100 / k$, where $k$ is its reverse rank.
- Calculate the cumulative hazard value for each failure time as the sum of its hazard value and the cumulative hazard value of the preceding failure time.
- Plot the cumulative hazard against failure time on the chosen hazard paper.

If the plot of failure times is roughly straight, one may conclude that the distribution adequately fits the data. The fitted line in the hazard paper can estimate then, percentiles and distribution parameters.

The theory of hazard plotting is similar to that of probability plotting, except that the cumulative hazard function is used instead of the cumulative distribution function. Before closing this sub-section, we will explain about Weibull hazard paper.

Figure 12.10 Cumulative Weibull hazard plot of failure times for an electrical device.The Weibull hazard function is


$$

h(x)=\frac{f(x)}{1-\mathbf{F}(x)}=\frac{\beta}{\mu}\left(\frac{x}{\mu}\right)^{\beta-1}

$$

and thus the Weibull cumulative hazard function is


$$

H(x)=\int\_{0}^{\infty} \frac{\beta}{\mu}\left(\frac{t}{\mu}\right)^{\beta-1} d t=\left(\frac{x}{\mu}\right)^{\beta}

$$

Then, time $x$ as a function of $H$ is


$$

\log x=\frac{1}{\beta} \log H+\log \mu

$$

This show that $\log x$ is a linear function of $\log H$. Thus, Weibull hazard paper is a log-log graph paper, and the axes of the hazard paper are scaled so that cumulative hazard value (calculated by the above procedure) can be plotted on the ordinate, corresponding to $\log H$, and the failure times can be plotted on the abscissa, corresponding to $\log x$.

For $H=100 \%$, the corresponding time $x$ equals $\mu$, which is used to estimate $\mu$ graphically. For example, the estimate of $\mu$ is 120 . The slope of the straight line equals to $1 / \beta$, and thus the shape parameter can be estimated by the formula similar to equation (12.19). When using the commercial Weibull hazard paper, $\beta$ can be estimated by using the dot in the upper left of the paper. That is, if we draw a straight line parallel to the fitted line, so that it passes both through the dot and through the shape parameter scale, the value on the shape parameter is the estimate of $\beta$. In Figure 12.10, the estimate of $\beta$ is about 2.

# 12.2.2 Goodness-of-Fit Tests

Goodness-of-fit tests are statistical hypothesis tests that are used to assess formally whether the observations are from a particular distribution. Goodness-of-fit tests can be used to test the following null hypothesis:
$\mathrm{H}_{0}: X_{i}^{\prime} \mathrm{s}$ are from a particular distribution $\mathrm{F}_{0}(x)$

## Chi-square Test

The most widely used goodness-of-fit test is the chi-square test, which was originally proposed by Karl Pearson (1990). To compute the chi-square test statistic, we must first divide the entire range of the fitted distribution model into adjacent intervals $\left[a_{0}, a_{1}\right),\left[a_{1}, a_{2}\right), \ldots$, $\left[a_{k 1}, a_{k}\right)$, where $a_{0}=0$ and $a_{k}=\infty$.

Then we tally
$N_{j}:$ number of $X_{i}^{\prime} s$ in the $j^{\text {th }}$ interval $\left(a_{j-1}, a_{j}\right)$
for $j=1,2, \ldots, k$. (Note that $\sum_{i=1}^{k} N_{j}=n$, where n is the sample size). Next, we compute the expected proportion $p_{j}$ of the $X_{i}^{\prime} s$ that would fail in the $j^{\text {th }}$ interval if we were sampling from the fitted distribution. Then


$$

p*{j}=\int*{a*{i-1}}^{a*{j}} f(x) d x
$$where $\mathrm{f}(x)$ is the probability density function of the fitted distribution. Finally, the test statistic is

$$
\chi^{2}=\sum_{j=1}^{k} \frac{\left(N_{j}-n p_{j}\right)^{2}}{n p_{j}}
$$

Since $\mathrm{np}_{\mathrm{j}}$ is the expected number of $n X_{j}^{\prime} s$ that would fall in the $\mathrm{j}^{\text {th }}$ interval if $\mathrm{H}_{0}$ was true, we would expect $\chi^{2}$ to be small if the fit is good. Therefore, we reject $\mathrm{H}_{0}$ if $\chi^{2}$ is too large. The precise form of the test depends on whether or not we have estimated any of the parameters of the fitted distribution from the sample.

# Parameter Known Case

When all parameters of the fitted distribution are known (usually of little practical use in reliability engineering), reject $H_{0}$ if $\chi^{2}>\chi_{k-1,1-\alpha}^{2}$ (Figure 12.11), where $\chi_{k-1,1-\alpha}^{2}$ is the $(1-\alpha)^{\text {th }}$ percentile for a chi-square distribution with $k-1$ degrees of freedom(df). Values for $\chi_{k-1,1-\alpha}^{2}$ can be found in the Appendix.

## Parameter Unknown Case

When some or all of the parameters of the fitted distribution are unknown, parameters should be first estimated to calculate $p_{j}$ of equation (12.24). The most popular estimation method is the Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE) and the estimation procedures for normal, lognormal and Weibull distributions are summarized in the Appendix. Then, when the number of unknown parameters is $m$, we reject $\mathrm{H}_{0}$ if $\chi^{2}>\chi_{k-m-1,1-\alpha}^{2}$.

Example 12.9 Table 12.5 shows 100 times to breakdown of an insulating fluid. We examine whether the failure time follows the Weibull distribution or not. From formulas (12.17) and (12.18), $\hat{\beta}$ and $\hat{\mu}$ are 9.867 and 13433.7. If we form $k=10$ intervals with $p_{j}=1 / k=0.1$ for $j=1$, $2, \ldots, 10$, then $a_{j} s$ are calculated by

$$
0.1=\exp \left[-\left(\frac{a_{j-1}}{\hat{\mu}}\right)^{\hat{\mu}}\right]-\exp \left[-\left(\frac{a_{j}}{\hat{\mu}}\right)^{\hat{\mu}}\right]
$$

$j=1,2, \ldots, 10$. The data are treated by following the above procedure and summarized in Table 12.6. When $\alpha$ is chosen as 0.05 (Statisticians usually choose $\alpha$ as 0.01 or 0.05 or 0.1 ), we can not reject the null hypothesis since $\chi^{2}=5.40$ is small relative to $\chi_{k-m-1,1-\alpha}^{2}=\chi_{7,0.95}^{2}=14.067$.

# Kolmogorov-Smirnov Test

Another goodness-of-fit test commonly used in reliability engineering is the KolmogonovSmirnov(K-S) test which compares an empirical distribution function with the fitted distribution function. To compute the K-S Statistic, we should first define an empirical distribution. That is, empirical distribution function from $X_{1}, X_{2}, \ldots ., X_{n}$ is

$$
F_{n}(x)=\frac{\text { number of } X^{\prime} s \leq x}{n}
$$

for all real values $x$. Thus $F_{n}(x)$ is a step function such that $F_{n}\left(x_{(i)}\right)=\frac{i}{n}$ for $=1,2, \ldots, n$. If $F(x)$ is the fitted distribution function, a natural assessment of goodness-of-fit is some kind of measure of the closeness between the functions $F_{n}(x)$ and $F(x)$. The K-S test statistic $\mathrm{D}_{n}$, is simply the largest distance between $F_{n}(x)$ and $F(x)$ for all values of $x$ and is defined by

$$
D_{n}=\max _{x}\left|F_{n}(x)-F(x)\right|
$$Clearly, a large value of $D_{n}$ indicates a poor fit, so that the form of the test is to reject the null hypothesis $H_{0}$ if $D_{n}$ exceeds some constant $d_{n, 1-\alpha}$, which can be found in the Appendix. Again, the precise form of the test depends on whether or not we have estimated any of the parameters of the fitted distribution from the sample. But, the difference of the critical values between parameter known and unknown cases is usually negligible in this case.

Example 12.10 Suppose that five numbers $0.44,0.81,0.14,0.05,0.93$ are generated from a random number generator. If we are willing to test that these numbers are really from the uniform distribution over the interval $(0,1)$, then the K-S test can be used. Since $F(x)=x$, the K-S test statistic is


$$

D\_{n}=\max [(0.2-0.05),(0.4-0.14),(0.6-0.44),(0.8-0.81),(1.0-0.93)]=0.26

$$

If $\alpha$ is chosen as $0.05, d_{5,0.95}=0.565$ from the tables in the Appendix and thus we may conclude that the numbers are from the uniform distribution.

# 12.3 Test Simulation Techniques

As we indicated, the application of acceleration factors to project test data does not address uncertainties that will exist in field loading conditions. For this reason, acceleration factors are not very predictive. An alternative approach is to apply simulation. The technique outlined in Chapter 3 can be applied to model the test conditions and test failure distribution.

We simulate test conditions through applying Monte Carlo simulation. A test simulation includes the primary sources of variability expected in materials properties and manufacturing processes, that affect the component we wish to evaluate. The simulation is exercised on the failure mechanism models, which represent the component. In testing, we will know the test loads with certainty and they can be considered as such in the simulation of the test. We then generate a simulated test distribution and compare it to our actual test data. Next, we assess the validity of our model. With a validated model, we now simulate the field conditions, allowing the loads to become random variables and considering their expected variations. Critical components for this process might be selected from a Failure Modes and Effects Analysis (FMEA) of the system or sub-system under development.


Figure 12.12 Test simulation compared to thermal cycling test data for fatigue in solder joints of ball grid array assemblies (Evans et. al. 1999).Test simulation has been employed by Evans et. al. (2000). In this case, solder attachments in ball grid array packages were evaluated. These types of packages are emerging as a standard method of packaging and assembly of high density semiconductors, in order to reduce size and cost. A primary wear out failure mechanism is solder joint fatigue, which occurs in thermal cycling. This is discussed in detail in Chapter 8. In Figure 12.12 we see a plot of actual versus simulated test data. The process of test simulation is summarized in Figure 12.13. This approach can be successful employed on a series of failure mechanism models that represent a component.


Figure 12.13 Process of test simulation and projection of test data to field conditions.# 12.4 Risks in Accelerated Testing

In the application of accelerated testing, we must be aware of the inherent risks that may lead to error. When elevated loads are applied to a component or system in testing, we run the risks of over acceleration and failure mechanism shifts. Over acceleration results when the dominant failure mechanism is no longer representative of what is expected in application or under field loading conditions. As an example, we can consider the effects of raising the temperature on diffusion processes. In a polycrystalline metal, grain boundary diffusion dominates at lower temperatures. The primary transport of atoms is along grain boundaries and interfaces. However at higher temperatures, bulk diffusion dominates and the primary path of diffusion is through the crystal lattice. Each of these two processes has different activation energy. Hence, if we measure activation energy for bulk diffusion, when in fact, grain boundary diffusion is the primary mode of transport, we would introduce significant error in projecting test results to lower temperatures.

Diffusion in polycrystalline silver for example, shifts from grain boundary to bulk lattice diffusion at about $700^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ and the activation energy for grain boundary diffusion is about half of the activation energy for bulk diffusion (Reed-Hill 1973). At this temperature, over acceleration is not a concern for product tests, but we need to be aware of the shift, if we are conducting materials tests to measure diffusion kinetics. On the other hand, aluminum shifts at much lower temperatures. In general, we should be concerned about temperature over acceleration for diffusion driven mechanisms in metals, when we exceed test temperatures of $0.5 \mathrm{~T}_{\mathrm{mp}}$ where $\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{mp}}$ is the melting point (Lall 1998).

Another concern is the potential to shift from one dominant failure mechanism to another when test loads are increased above application loading conditions. Let's examine Figure 12.14. This figure shows a plot of mission life versus normalized operating temperature for a


Figure 12.14 Plot of operating mission life versus normalized operating temperature for various failure mechanisms occurring in a microelectronic device. (Courtesy of CALCE Center, University of Maryland).microelectronic device. The mean life of the device is plotted for each potential failure mechanism. If we consider a test conducted at condition B, we can see that Time Dependent Dielectric Breakdown (TDDB) of the dielectric will dominate. Now, let's consider operating conditions at a lower temperature. At operating conditions, Point A shows that the dominant mechanism at the operating temperature is Stress Driven Diffusive Voiding (SDDV).

This clearly illustrates the risk of mechanism shifting under accelerated loads, when we have competing causes of failure. If we assess life based upon TDDB, as extracted from accelerated tests of the device, we would project a life in excess of $10^{6}$ hours. However under the field conditions, we might expect the device to fail from SDDV at about 20,000 hours. The risk of error increases with increasing complexity of the system or component and with the introduction of new technologies. In addition, our example does not consider uncertainty.

A comprehensive process of reliability assessment is needed to avoid error. As we discussed in Chapter 1, we must anticipate causes of failure. Modeling the failure processes then becomes essential, as Figure 12.13 illustrates. Following construction of models, we can appropriately design testing. For our example shown, we might elect to reduce the test temperature or run a series of tests at different temperatures. Following execution of testing, failure analysis must be used to confirm the failure mechanism and validate the modeling process. Comparison to field failure histories and known active mechanisms is also very useful.

# 12.3 Do's and Don'ts in Design

Do consider the limitations of acceleration factor models in projecting test data.
Do recall an acceleration factor applies to a single dominant mechanism.
Do model the accelerated test conditions and assess dominant mechanisms in test.
Do examine all data to assess field failure modes and mechanisms.
Do perform failure analysis of test items.
Do plot data at all test conditions and compare the slope of the plots.
Do failure analysis of outliers that do not fit models and plots.
Do begin analysis with the Weibull distribution and then evaluate other distributions as appropriate.
Do segregate failure modes from test data and apply censoring as appropriate.
Do consider the impact of sample size on fitting distributions and estimating parameters.
Don't perform plotting without a Goodness of Fit test.
Don't forget there is a risk of over acceleration when increasing loads, such as temperature and mechanical stress.
Don't perform accelerated testing without failure analysis of samples to confirm the failure mechanism.
Don't apply acceleration factor models without careful analysis, when there are competing causes of failure.

Michael Pecht and Patrick McCluskey

Significant improvements in the reliability of systems can be achieved by retrieving fielded assemblies and examining them to determine the root cause of failures and the extent of degradation which has occurred over time. In addition, it is important to examine root cause of failure as a result of accelerated testing to verify dominant failure mechanisms. Root cause failure analysis employs a number of non-destructive and destructive analytical techniques to identify the locations at which failures occur, characterize the modes in which failures occur, and provide clues as to the fundamental mechanisms by which failures occur. This information highlights the weak links in a system or product. These problems can then be modified, through corrective action to provide increased reliability. Because of the importance of failure analysis and degradation assessments in reliability growth, this chapter will focus primarily on describing the tools and techniques for systematically conducting such a failure analysis for reliability assessment.

The identification of the damage mechanisms, which are most likely to cause failure, and the sites at which the damage is the most pronounced in fielded assemblies is also a necessary part of a focused accelerated test program. Accelerated test programs can be used to qualify new assemblies, thereby eliminating those assemblies most likely to fail in the field. In addition, failure analysis becomes an essential part of to determining the expected life of a new assembly, or to determine the remaining life of an assembly, which has been stored or used for an extended period of time. The benefit of the focused accelerated test program is that it allows the proper test loads and stresses to be selected. This benefit is enabled by effective use of failure analysis in a reliability assessment program.

In this chapter, we will focus on failure analysis methods and tools. We initially examine an example of the overall process of failure analysis and then identify procedures, theory and information that each failure analysis tool can provide. Many examples in this chapter are specifically related to electronic assemblies and devices. However, the processes and tools are much the same for failure analysis of mechanical assemblies. The reader may wish to refer back to Chapter 9 to further see how these tools are implemented in the analysis of failures.

### 13.1 A Systematic Approach to Root Cause Failure Analysis

Root cause failure analysis is only successful if it is approached in a systematic way. The process begins with the most non-destructive techniques and then proceeds to the more destructive techniques, allowing the gathering of unique data from each technique through-out the process. This data, when properly analyzed, leads to the mechanism for the failure. The use of destructive techniques early in the process is discouraged, as it can result in the loss of valuable information that might be required later.

While a significant amount of failure information is available simply through optical microscopy, many analytical tools have been developed to enhance the failure analysis process. These include Environmental Scanning Electron Microscopy (E-SEM), Energy Dispersive Spectrometry (EDS), and Scanning Acoustic Microscopy (SAM). Each of these techniques are described in detail in the next few chapters, together with instructions for the application to the failure analysis of electronic assemblies.

Failure analysis begins with the least destructive method. The procedure for conducting a failure analysis of an electronic assembly is illustrated in Figure 13.1. A similar process can developed for mechanical components and assemblies using the same analytical methods. However, we will focus on electronic assemblies as our primary topic to illustrate failure analysis techniques, procedures and their relationship to defects and failure mechanisms. The reader can refer to Chapter 8 for a detailed understanding of failure mechanisms in electronic devices and assemblies. The process begins with non-destructive optical inspection and proceeds to evaluations requiring decapsulation and cross sectioning.

First, an examination is made of the external surfaces of the parts and the boards using both the unaided eye and optical microscopy. This examination, which is described in detail in section 13.2, is conducted to reveal obvious sites of corrosion; external package, solder joint, or printed wiring board cracks; and/or board warpage. We may also elect to perform a series of electrical tests to isolate failed components and later to assist in characterizing component failure modes. Electrical testing must be correlated to observations of the board and component surfaces, such as short circuit to a corrosion site or an intermittent open circuit correlated to a cracked solder joint. Electrical testing and its benefits are important to the process and are explained in further detail in Lee and Pabbisetty (1993), but will not be detailed further in our discussions here.

# Reliability Degradation Assessment Experimental Methods



Figure 13.1 Systematic procedure for failure analysis and degradation assessment.Next, components are desoldered from the boards and X-ray radiography is performed on these components to detect evidence of wire bond lift, wire fatigue, or wire sweep in the packaged integrated circuits (ICs). Wire bond lift is indicative of either poor bonding practice or the weakening of the bond interface due to oxidation, intermetallic growth or corrosion during aging. Wire fatigue is due to thermal cycling damage over time, while wire sweep is purely a manufacturing problem which results from poor molding practice. X-ray examination is described in detail in section 13.3.

After X-ray, scanning acoustic microscopy is performed to quantify delamination and cracking at the internal interfaces of any plastic encapsulated microcircuits (PEMs) and to quantify the die attach voiding in any IC packages. Both delamination/cracking and die attach voiding are manufacturing and assembly related defects which can increase the susceptibility of components to failure in storage or use, although they do not result from storage or use and do not constitute failures by themselves. Delamination and cracking can result in sheared or lifted wirebonds, passivation cracking, metallization shifting, and metallization/bond pad corrosion. Die attach voiding can lead to die cracking, die attach fracture, or thermal runaway due to poor heat dissipation through the die attach. Therefore, the purpose of this technique, which is described in further detail in section 13.4, is to uncover defects that could lead to failure, but may not constitute failure by themselves.

Having completed the non-destructive analysis, the next step is to use destructive sample preparation techniques to reveal the internal structure of the components. The two primary techniques are decapsulation or delidding to view the top surface of the die, and cross-sectioning. Decapsulation is usually performed chemically and consists of using red fuming nitric acid to dissolve the encapsulant, thereby permitting examination of the die surface and the wirebonds. Delidding involves mechanically sawing through the lid attach material to remove the lid from a ceramic single-chip or multi-chip package revealing the contents of the cavity inside the package. Decapsulation or delidding allows an internal examination by optical microscopy for wire fatigue and die fracture. It also permits subsequent examination of the die for bond pad corrosion, passivation cracking, ball bond lifting, stress driven diffusive voiding, electromigration, and metallization corrosion.

Cross-sectioning consists of encapsulating the device in a mold, and then grinding and polishing the molded sample until a surface is reached which reveals an important feature of the device, usually the intermetallics which form at the wirebond, in cross-section. The composition of intermetallic phases or of corrosion products at the bond pads can be determined using energy dispersive spectrometry. Cross-sectioning is not only used to examine the internal structure of components. It is also used to examine assemblies. Cross-sectioning combined with optical or electron microscopy reveals delamination between the resin and the fiber in a fiber reinforced PWB laminate as well as delamination between the laminate and the copper traces. In addition, cross-sectioning combined with optical or electron microscopy can reveal changes in the microstructure of solder joints associated with solder joint fatigue cracking. All elements of destructive analysis, including the decapsulation and cross-sectioning techniques together with the use of scanning electron microscopy are described in detail.

Finally, mechanical testing can be conducted on the decapsulated sample to measure the strength of the wirebonds or the die attach bond and compare this to the initial strength, thereby quantifying any degradation in bond strength. The strength of the wirebonds is determined using a wire pull test for wedge bonds and a bond shear test for ball bonds. The strength of the die attach bond is determined using a die shear test.# 13.2 Visual Examination and Optical Microscopy

Let's turn our attention to the actual analytical methods. Virtually every failure analysis, whether the item is a mechanical or electrical component begins with a through external inspection. The purposes of external visual inspection are to characterize any quality deficiency, assess degradation, and identify root causes of failure in a nondestructive fashion. External visual inspection can be performed either with the naked eye or with optical equipment at magnifications of $10-200 \mathrm{X}$. Low-power magnification ( $10-60 \mathrm{X}$ ) is achieved with a monocular, binocular, or stereo microscope using illumination at an angle of $30^{\circ}$ from the perpendicular; high-power magnification ( $70-200 \mathrm{X}$ ) is achieved with a transmission or reflection optical microscope. If the illumination is normal to the sample surface, the microscopy is termed bright field; if oblique, it is termed dark field. Visual standards (gauges, drawings, or photographs) are usually necessary as references to enable the human inspector or computer software to perform an effective examination and to aid in making decisions about the acceptability of the sample. Adequate fixturing is required when handling electronics in order to permit efficient inspection without inflicting damage. If the circuits are electrostatic-sensitive, adequate safeguards such as grounded wrist straps and table mats are also required.

The advantage of external, visual inspection is its nondestructive nature. The disadvantage is that resolution is limited; this can be mitigated by an appropriate choice of test conditions, such as the type of lighting used for inspection.

### 13.2.1 Principles of Operation

The basic principle behind any visual optical microscope is that light reflected from or transmitted through the sample passes through objective and imaging lenses in order to form an enlarged image either on the retina in the human eye or on a photographic film. A schematic of a conventional optical microscope is shown in Figure 13.2.

Depending on the application and type of sample, light is either reflected from the object surface (reflected-light microscopy) or passes through the object (transmission-light microscopy). Reflected-light microscopy is used to analyze opaque samples, and transmis-sion-light microscopy is used to analyze optically transparent materials. There are two classes of reflected-light optical microscopy common to electronics failure analysis: stereo (low magnification) microscopy and metallurgical (high magnification microscopy.

## Stereo Microscopy

The stereo microscope is a bifocal, reflected-light instrument used for low-power threedimensional viewing of objects. Each eyepiece has separate optics allowing stereo viewing of samples mounted on a movable stage. The placement of the lighting source can dramatically accentuate any anomalies in the sample. The illumination sources can include ring lighting and externally manipulated fiberoptic lighting.

## Metallurgical Microscopy

A metallurgical, high magnification microscope consists of an inverted stage on which are positioned mounted and polished samples. The use of special objectives, light sources, and filters can greatly aid in locating and documenting packaging-related failures. There are three basic kinds of illuminating arrangements: bright field, dark field, and polarized light.

Figure 13.2 Optical microscope.

# Bright Field

This is the most common configuration for examining samples, the majority of which are opaque and reflect light. Light passes through the objective: the light that hits the flat areas on the sample is reflected and reenters the objective; the light that hits sloped, lower surfaces is diffracted away from the objective. In this way, contrast is generated that simulates normal vision. The illumination aperture can be made larger to increase the depth of field, but at the expense of lower resolution. Figure 13.3 shows an example of a bright field image.

## Dark Field

This type of microscopy uses diffracted light for image formation, which makes low, sloped surfaces bright and makes high, flat surfaces dark. This illumination accentuates surface


Figure 13.3 Bright field image.

Figure 13.4 Dark field image.
irregularities on samples. It is useful for examining integrated circuits (ICs) and hybrids for contamination and defects in the metallization. When using dark field, a powerful light source is required because a majority of light is not reflected into the objective. Figure 13.4 shows an example of a dark field image.

# Polarized Light

Filters are frequently used to enhance optical images and can be used with transmitted and reflected light instruments. Polarizing filters are placed in the optical path between light source and the objective (polarizer) and between the objective and the eyepiece (analyzer). Rotating the analyzer filter can result in a range from complete transmission of light to extinction of light. A polarizing system can be useful for locating interfaces and examining the grain structure of metals.

### 13.2.2 Uses in Failure Analysis

The distinctive feature of each type of microscope makes is uniquely suited to characterizing specific failure mechanisms, as described below.

## Low Magnification Stereo Optical Microscope

The primary advantages of low-magnification inspection are that it is fast and easy to perform and requires no sample preparation. The part under inspection is examined 'as received.' Failure mechanisms and accelerators easily identified by the low-power stereo microscope include the following:

- contaminants on the package surface that can cause electrical leakage
- fractured or broken seals
- fractures in weld seams, blow holes, or voids
- broken leads or loose feed-through pins
- lead corrosion
- board warpage
- solder joint cracking/liftoff
- poor adhesion of board metallization
- corrosion of board traces# Medium to High Power Optical Microscope

The medium- to high-power optical microscope is generally used to provide further information after the low-power microscope has detected some unusual situation. The limited field of view and shallow depth of focus make this inspection specific to a previously detected area of concern, rather than a general inspection. The medium-to-high power optical microscope is especially effective for examining the following:

- dendrite formation
- fractures in leads, platings, or glass-to-metal seals
- small defects in weld zones
- metallization/bondpad corrosion

This microscope is also used to carry out microstructural examination of cross-sections of electronic components and printed wiring boards (PWBs). It can reveal defects within the material that cannot be identified using superficial visual inspection. The key to successful use of this technique is in the preparation of the sample, such that the true microstructure is revealed, which is discussed in detail in section 13.5. Microstructural examination of polished electronic components can reveal a wealth of information about defects and failure mechanisms in such key components, as the following:

- chip resistors - reveals ink adhesion, ink thickness, and end termination integrity
- ceramic substrates - reveals conductor adhesion, thickness, porosity
- connector pins, lead frames - reveals thickness, composition, quality of plated layers
- solder joints - reveals composition, microstructural coarsening, fatigue cracking, fillet shape, and extent of wetting
- printed circuit boards - reveals plating quality in plated through holes (PTHs), evidence of barrel cracking, and board delamination
- metal welds - reveals the depth of the weld metal (nugget), the heat-affected zone (HAZ), and the base metal
- wirebonds - reveals intermetallic layers, voiding, and porosity


### 13.3 Radiography

X-ray radiography is the next tool used in degradation and failure analysis, as it permits nondestructive assessment of internal damage, defects, and degradation in microelectronic devices. The X-ray microscope is used regularly in process monitoring. Illuminating a sample with X-ray energy provides images based on material density that allow characterization of solder voiding, wirebond sweep, and wirebond breakage in components. In addition, using an X-ray microscope, such as that shown above in Figure 13.5, to inspect a sample from a die attachment process can reveal anomalies such as die attach voiding, solder pooling, or die shifting that can be quickly corrected. It should be noted that the defects detected by X-ray examination are the result of poor manufacturing, not aging, but they have been correlated to increased degradation and susceptibility to failure over time in field storage or use.

### 13.3.1 Principles Involved in X-ray Radiography

X-rays are generated by an X-ray tube (Southworth 1975). Under a high-voltage potential, electrons are emitted from a heated tungsten filament and are accelerated and focused onto ametal (e.g., tungsten or copper) anode. The primary beam electrons decelerate as they collide with the atoms of the target anode, and X-rays are generated due to the energy released by these collisions. About $1 \%$ of the energy is released as heat that must be dissipated via a water cooling system. The generated X-rays are emitted in all directions, so the X-ray beam is directed onto the sample by allowing the X-rays to escape from the tube only through carefully positioned windows. X-ray tubes are usually evacuated to pressures of the order of about $10^{-4}$ Torr in order to minimize the collision of electrons with gas molecules, and permanently sealed tubes are often used to avoid the need for a vacuum- pumping system. The quantity of X-rays emitted by the tube is controlled by varying the current heating the tungsten filament, while the lower wavelength limit of the X-rays is determined by the magnitude of the accelerating voltage.

X-rays are used for nondestructive internal imaging because when an X-ray beam passes through different materials, these materials absorb X-rays to varying degrees. The beam's intensity is thereby reduced different amounts by different materials. The linear absorption coefficient is determined by the atomic number of the material and the X-ray wavelengths. For example, there is a difference of about one order of magnitude between the absorption coefficients for polyimide and gold. This difference provides a good contrast for imaging electronic packages. It is preferable to use continuous Bremstrehlung radiation instead of the characteristic radiation for imaging purposes.

Contact microscopes are widely used for both manufacturing and research in electronic packaging. In contact radiography or microscopy, the specimen is placed in contact with an X-ray image receptor, such as a film cassette or a CCD camera, at a certain distance from an X-ray source (Figure 13.5). The X-rays transmitted through the specimen form an image on the receptor at effectively 1:1 magnification. The resulting film or recorded image is then


Figure 13.5 Schematic of X-ray contact radiography.examined under an optical microscope. The entire internal structure of the specimen can be viewed on the X-ray film, provided the film has sufficient resolution. Selected areas may subsequently be enlarged photographically.

# 13.3.2 Uses in Failure Analysis

The principal advantage of X-ray radiography (also called X-ray microscopy) for failure analysis lies in the nature of the image contrast that X-rays produce as a result of differential absorption of the primary X-rays by different materials in the specimen. The degree of absorption depends both on the species of atoms in the specimen and on their atomic number. It is thus possible not only to reveal the presence of different microstructural features, but also to obtain information about their composition.

The most common defects observed using this technique are wire sweep, wirebond lift, die attach defects, and die misalignment. Cracks in solder due to fatigue and improper bonding can also be observed. X-ray radiography is effective in characterizing uniformity and voiding of die attach, even though the die attach itself is quite thin. This is because the common die attach materials contain elements of relatively high atomic number. Examples are the Au content of eutectic die attaches and the Ag fillers in epoxy and glass attaches. Even glass die attaches typically have a high Pb content, which makes X-ray radiography easily applicable. For this reason, the presence or absence of die attach material can be readily determined.

Another advantage of the X-ray microscope is the comparatively deep penetration of Xrays into thick specimens, which enables detection of the internal structure of electronic packages or components. Furthermore, the package or component can be examined in its natural state; neither a conductive coating nor a high vacuum is needed, as they are with conventional electron microscopes. No medium, like water or oil, is required either, as it is for the scanning acoustic microscope (SAM).

### 13.3.3 Data Provided by X-Ray Radiography

After producing film images of the internal structure of a specimen using X-ray radiography, an optical microscope can be used to enlarge the negative images captured on the film to examine the package for wire sweep, wire breakage, ball bond shear, and other defects in the specimen. Figure 13.6 is a picture of the top view of six plastic encapsulated microcircuits (PEMs). Under the microscope, it is possible to examine each wire attached from the die to the lead frame. In this figure, there is no wire breakage or ball bond shear. It should be noted that the packages are of the same type, but they contain two different sized die and lead frames.

Figure 13.7 contains enlarged pictures from the X-ray microscope. The top-view image clearly shows the wires, and the central area of the projection shows the die, die attach, paddle, and molding compound. The side-view image shows the interfaces between any two-package elements. The die, die attach, and molding compound can be clearly seen in the side-view image. Plastic/die interfacial delamination can be detected using these side-view images.

### 13.4 Acoustic Microscopy

Acoustic microscopy is a nondestructive technique for detecting internal defects in microelectronic devices. Acoustic techniques create images based on physical properties of materials at interfaces and based on their mismatches. Acoustic microscopy uses acoustic

Figure 13.6 Top view of six PEMs at one-to-one magnification.


Figure 13.7 Top and side view of magnified 18-pin plastic package, showing the wires.
waves to image the surface and internal structure of a specimen. The resolution and penetration depend on the materials examined and on the wave frequency, higher-frequency waves achieve higher resolution. Acoustic waves cannot penetrate as deeply as X-rays at comparable resolution, but can detect smaller cracks.There are two main types of acoustic microscopes: the scanning laser acoustic microscope (SLAM) and the scanning acoustic microscope (SAM). Each differs in application and principle of operation; however, both produce images that reveal the inner structural features of a sample by using very-high-frequency ultrasound. Figure 13.8 shows a representation of the basic acoustic microscopy technique.

Commercial scanning acoustic microscopes are capable of imaging in three modes: A, B, and C. In A-mode acquisition, the transducer remains stationary at a single point above the sample and is focused to a specific depth within the sample. In B-mode acquisition, the transducer mechanically rasters in the x direction and scans increments in the $z$ direction; B-mode scanning generates a cross-section image of a package. In C-mode acquisition, the transducer mechanically rasters in the $x$-direction and scans increments in the $y$-direction; C -mode generates a x-y planar image at a specific depth within the sample.

To perform a test, a focused acoustic wave pulse at frequencies from $10-100 \mathrm{MHz}$ is applied to a sample device through a liquid medium such as water or a gel. Water is typically used, since it is a safe, nonhostile environment for most electronic packages. The acoustic microscope transducer is capable of movement in $x, y$, and $z$ directions: the $z$-axis is used to focus the ultrasonic pulse at particular depths within a sample; the $x$ and $y$ axes permit acquisition at various locations in the plane of focus, analogous to using a high-powered optical microscope.

As an acoustic wave approaches interfaces, such as voids and delaminations, it is partially or totally reflected, depending on the impedance discontinuity at the interface. Transmitted waves are used in SLAM; reflected waves are used as signals in SAM. In the SLAM technique, a plane acoustic wave is introduced to one side of the sample and travels through to the opposite side. The intensity of the transmitted wave is detected by a scanning laser beam to produce an image. In SAM, the transducer receives and records echoes. Echoes are produced at the sample surface and at the interfaces within the sample, the time of flight of which are functions of the distance from the interface to the transducer and of the speed of the acoustic wave in the sample. An electronic gate is used to image an interface at a specific depth level, using the time of flight, the signal amplitude, and the signal polarity to identify the interface of interest.

Defects in ceramic packages that are targeted by SAM include: voids, pinholes, and delamination in wirebonds, substrate metallization, dielectric layers, element attaches, and lid seals. SAM can also detect die attach field failure mechanisms induced by improper die mounting and deadhesion. Acoustic microscopy is also very effective for examining plastic packages, since it can detect typical defects such as those illustrated in Figure 13.9, including: delamination of the molding compound from the leadframe, die, or paddle; molding compound cracks, die attach, die tilt, and voids in the molding compound and die attach. In the field,

# 13.4.1 Principles Underlying Acoustic Microscopy

When an ultrasonic wave impinges on an interface between two dissimilar materials, part is transmitted and part is reflected, as shown in figure 13.10. The amplitude, position in time, and polarity of the reflected signal provide useful information about the level from which the signal is being reflected. Every material has a physical property called acoustic impedance (Z), which is the ratio of the acoustic pressure to the particle velocity per unit area and is defined as the product of the density $(\rho)$ and the speed of sound $(v)$ in layer $i$ :


$$

Z*{i}=\rho*{i} v\_{i}

$$

Table 1 shows impedance values used in the analysis of plastic packages.
To understand the phase inversion phenomenon, consider the simplified example of plane reflection at normal incidence at an ideal interface. The incident plane wave has the sinusoidal acoustic pressure amplitude PI and reflected and transmitted waves have the relative pressure amplitudes PR and PT, respectively. The materials are assumed to be ideal elastic


Figure 13.10 Reflections at normal incidence of a plane wave at a delamination (left) and at a bonded interface (right) (Courtesy of ASM).solids. As a result of the boundary condition that the acoustic pressure and particle velocity in both materials must be equal at the interface, the frequency remains unchanged across the interface, and the reflected and transmitted pressure amplitude can be described as functions of the acoustic impedances, $\mathrm{Z}_{i}$, of the two materials. For an ultrasonic wave impinging on the boundary between materials with acoustic impedances $\mathrm{Z}_{1}$ and $\mathrm{Z}_{2}$, the theoretical reflected and transmitted amplitudes are therefore computed as shown in Equations 13.2 and 13.3:

Table 13.1 Acoustic Impedance for Materials Found in Plastic Packages

| Material | Acoustic Impedance <br> (Units of $10^{6} \mathrm{~kg} / \mathrm{sec}-\mathrm{m}^{2}$ ) |
| :-- | :-- |
| Air/vacuum | 0 |
| Water | 1 |
| Plastic | 2.0 to 3.5 |
| Epoxy resin | 3 |
| Mold compound | 6 |
| Glass | 15 |
| Aluminum | 17 |
| Silicon | 20 |
| Copper | 42 |
| Alumina | 21 to 45 |
| Tungsten | 104 |


$$

\begin{aligned}
& \mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{R}}=\frac{\text { reflected }}{\text { incident }}=\frac{\left(\mathrm{Z}_{2}-\mathrm{Z}_{1}\right)}{\left(\mathrm{Z}_{1}+\mathrm{Z}_{2}\right)} \\
& \mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{T}}=\frac{\text { transmitted }}{\text { incident }}=1-\mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{R}} \text { or } \frac{2 \mathrm{Z}_{2}}{\left(\mathrm{Z}_{1}=\mathrm{Z}_{2}\right)}
\end{aligned}

$$

For example, when a signal travels through water and strikes the top of a plastic module ( $Z=3$ ), approximately $+33 \%$ of the energy is reflected, the balance continues to travel into the materials below. Ignoring frequency-dependent signal attenuation in the plastic, the $+67 \%$ of the original signal that travels into the plastic can strike one of two surfaces, a copper leadframe (Case A) or an air gap or delamination (Case B). In situation A, the sound goes from a material with a Z of $\sim 3.0$ to a material with a Z of 42 . Using the above formulae, $\mathrm{R}=87 \%$, which translates to $+87 \%$ of $67 \%$, so $58 \%$ of the total energy is reflected from that interface. Compare this with situation B, in which $\mathrm{R}=100 \%$ and $\mathrm{T}=0$. Here, $-100 \%$ of the original $67 \%$ incident signal is $-67 \%$, which is the signal, relative to the original beam, that is returned from the delaminated interface. The magnitude of this signal varies only slightly from that returning from copper, but the polarity is reversed. With a polarity detector, it is possible to differentiate between these two signals. The simplified plane wave model (Equation 13.2 and 13.3) is useful in describing the phase inversion of reflected acoustic pulses at delamination and cracks.

The intensity reflection coefficient, IR, is defined as


$$

\mathrm{IR}=\left(\left[\mathrm{Z}_{2}-\mathrm{Z}_{1}\right] /\left[\mathrm{Z}_{1}+\mathrm{Z}_{2}\right]\right) \* 2

$$

IR indicates the fraction of incident energy that is reflected at the interface; the balance is transmitted, assuming absorption at the interface is negligible.

Polarity analysis of acoustic echo signals provides information about delamination at internal interfaces in plastic-packaged ICs. Figure 13.11 shows typical examples of acoustic echo signals from an area with good adhesion and from a delaminated area.

Figure 13.11 Typical acoustic echo signals ( 15 MHz ) from an area of good adhesion (solid) and a delaminated are a (dashed) at the encapsulant-to-die interface in PEMs.

In each of the two echo signals in Figure 13.11, a reflection from the top surface of the package and a later subsurface reflection from the interface between the mold compound and die can be seen. Note the $180^{\circ}$ inversion of the signal at the delaminated area, and the deeper, partially resolved, reflections in the signal from the die surface area with good adhesion to the package.

Attenuation losses in plastic packages can often obscure the increase in the amplitude of signals reflected at delaminations. Phase inversion is therefore critical for reliable detection of delamination and cracks in plastic packages. Various factors can contribute to signal losses in the package. One of these factors is the natural attenuation of the signal caused by scattering and absorption by the materials through which the sound passes. This attenuation is a complex function of such factors as grain diameter, energy, wavelength, and frequency.

In addition to attenuation, some package features can obstruct signal transmission totally. For instance, when a package contains a tilted obstruction, the sound can be reflected off this obstruction at an angle greater than the capture range of the transducer. This feature therefore is not visible directly in the acoustic image, and underlying features are hidden by it. For this reason, a tilted feature has the same characteristics as a void and can be misinterpreted as a void or delamination. Another method of viewing tilted features in a sample is to allow reflections originating only from certain depths in the sample to create the image.

Plastic voids in the bulk of the molding compound can also cause signal loss. When focusing on the leadframe, a void in the plastic can shroud the leadframe from view. As a result, the signal is scattered from the irregular shape of the void, leaving an area where no leadframe is visible. The voids appear as shadows over an otherwise bright field. If the C-SAM is focused on the level in the plastic at which voids reside, they can, to some extent, be directly imaged. They may look similar to a delamination, since the void is just an irregularly shaped air pocket.

The $x-y$ resolution of the acoustic microscope varies with the materials that the sound travels through and the frequency of the sound. For example, in a plastic package, the resolution for a 15 MHz transducer is approximately 0.13 mm . For the upper frequency practical in plastic, 50 MHz , the resolution is approximately 0.05 mm . Dispersion from signal obstructions, such as $\mathrm{SiO}_{2}$ particles in the molding compound, tends to reduce the apparent resolution. In the $z$ direction, the machine can be sensitive to minute delamination, sinceeven a very thin air gap will reflect $w 100 \%$ of the signal. The literature suggests that gaps of less than a micron can be successfully detected. In an area with only partial delamination, the signal may not completely reverse to a large negative polarity but, rather, the intensities of the peaks can change slightly. Such delaminations are known as pre-delaminations or partial delaminations.

Mold compound attenuation varies considerably from one formulation to the next, and this dramatically affects the lateral resolution. Nevertheless, acoustic attenuation in a typical mold compound has been reported to $40 \mathrm{~dB} / \mathrm{cm}$ at 15 MHz and to increase rapidly with increasing frequency. As molding compounds preferentially attenuate the higher frequencies, acoustic inspections of standard PLCC packages are limited to roughly 20 MHz . However, thin packages ( $<0.5 \mathrm{~mm}$ ) are often inspected at frequencies up to 90 MHz .

Attenuation also affects depth resolution, especially in plastic package inspection. The decay period for a broad-band echo pulse is roughly $1.5 \lambda$, which creates a 'dead zone' after each reflection in which later reflections cannot be resolved without the use of frequency domain analysis methods.

The resolution and penetration of a given C-SAM system is defined by the frequency and the focal length of the transducer. Spatial resolution at 100 MHz is typically 25 microns. As the frequency is decreased, the spatial resolution is degraded to upwards of a few hundred microns. Although higher frequencies give increased resolution, (Figure 13.12) the penetration is decreased, whereas lower the frequencies provide deeper penetration (Figure 13.13).

# 13.4.2 Comparison Between X-ray and SAM Techniques

When it is necessary to maintain a sample's integrity, the two primary choices for flaw detection and material characterizations are x-ray and ultrasound techniques. SAM has the following advantages over conventional x-ray imaging when applied to IC packaging:

- detects subsurface delamination
- detects defects and flaws in nonmetallic material
- is not hazardous to operations or to nearby personnel, and has no effect on equipment and materials in the vicinity
- has volumetric scanning ability, enabling inspection of volume of metal extending from front surface to back surface of a part


Figure 13.12 Spatial resolution becomes finer at increased transducer frequency.

Figure 13.13 Depth of acoustic signal penetration is smaller at increased transducer frequency.

- operation is electronic, which provides almost instantaneous indications of flaws - only one surface need be accessible
- has greater accuracy than other nondestructive methods in determining position of internal flaws, estimating their size, and characterizing their orientation, shape, and nature
- given the speed of sound in molding compound (about $2900 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$ ), the approximate depth of a feature creating a peak on the scope can be determined
- depth-specific information can be obtained, whereas X-ray has no depth information
- small voids (e.g., in die attach) can be imaged that are invisible to X-ray
- very thin delamination (e.g., in die attach or plastic packages) can be imaged
- images can be obtained through materials opaque to X-ray (e.g., copper-tungsten)

The disadvantages of SAM compared to X-ray include the following:

- manual operation requires careful attention by experienced technicians
- extensive technical knowledge is required for development of inspection procedures
- parts that are rough, irregular in shape, very small, or thin are difficult to inspect (flat is best)
- discontinuities that are present in a shallow layer immediately beneath the surface may not be detectable
- couplants are needed to provide effective transfer of ultrasonic-wave energy between transducers and parts being inspected
- reference standards are needed, both for calibrating the equipment and for characterizing flaws
- SAM has limited resolution and penetration
- resolution reduces with depth of penetration into a material
- imaging is not possible where an air-gap exists, (e.g., inspection of die attach through the metal lid of a ceramic package)
- interpretation of images can be subjective and difficult


# 13.4.3 Defects and Mechanisms Detected by SAM

Quantifying delamination and cracking in plastic packages is probably the most common use of acoustic microscopy in failure and degradation analysis of electronics. Delamination and cracking occur while a device is being mounted to a circuit board. When surface-mount parts are soldered onto boards, the entire package body is exposed to soldering temperatures. Atthese temperatures, moisture absorbed from the air during shipping and storage vaporizes and expands, creating internal stresses that, when combined with thermal mismatch stresses at package interfaces, produce delamination and package cracking. The crack scatters the signal and appears like a ring of disturbance around the die pad. Wave-soldering of dual inline packages (DIPs) delivers comparatively less thermal stress to the body of the package than that experienced by surface-mount packages, so this phenomenon, often termed 'popcorning,' is a problem primarily with surface-mount packages.

# 13.5 Decapsulation and Cross Sectioning

After completing the external and nondestructive examination phases of the failure analysis and degradation assessment, the next step is to perform a high-magnification internal examination of the packages and boards. This first requires destructive sample preparation techniques for opening or decapsulating the package and cross-sectioning the package and boards. Then high-resolution techniques for examining the internal features and microstructures of the packages and boards and for performing associated chemical and/or elemental analysis, can be used. The examination techniques are environmental scanning electron microscopy (ESEM) and energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS).

### 13.5.1 Delidding a Ceramic Package

Delidding a cavity-type hermetic package is more straightforward than removing plastic encapsulants. To delid a ceramic package with a ceramic lid, the following procedure is used:

- grip the base of the package in a vise or clamp
- remove the lid by tapping a slot-head screw driver or a sharp chisel on the glass seal using a hammer or mallet

To delid a ceramic package with a Kovar lid, the lid is sawed off at the level of lid attach using a diamond saw. Similarly, a diamond saw can be used to cut the top off a welded hermetic metal can package to expose the die.

### 13.5.2 Decapulation of Plastic Encapsulated Devices

Decapsulation is the removal of the encapsulant from a plastic encapsulated microcircuit (PEM) so as to expose the die and the interconnects for failure examination with the aid of other techniques, such as optical microscopy, scanning electron microscopy (SEM), environmental scanning electron microscopy, energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy, and mechanical ball bond testing. Detecting the following failure modes requires components to be decapsulated before examination:

- wirebond fatigue
- wire fatigue
- bondpad and metallization corrosion
- die fracture
- dendritic growth on the die surface and bondpad
- electromigration- and stress-driven diffusive voiding- electrical overstress
- electrostatic discharge

Decapsulation can be performed mechanically or chemically. Mechanical decapsulation is performed by sanding the back of the package to reveal the back of the leadframe, heating the package on a hot plate to $200=\mathrm{C}$ to soften the molding compound, and then prying the paddle and die from the package with a scalpel. This type of decapsulation is preferred in instances where there is concern about exposing the die surface to chemicals, perhaps because of fear of corrosion.

More commonly, however, a chemical decapsulation approach is used to reveal the die surface. This involves removing the plastic encapsulant with an appropriate acid. The acid used is either red fuming nitric or sulfuric acid or a mixture of the two, depending upon the type of molding compound and lead frame or wire material. For example, for the most common plastic encapsulants used today, red fuming nitric acid is generally used because it etches away the epoxy novalac encapsulants, while doing little damage to underlying aluminum metal on the device. If urethane-based encapsulants, PVC, ABS, or epoxy anhydrides are to be etched, sulfuric acid must be used. For packages with copper lead frames or copper wire, mixed acids are used to limit damage to the copper. The chemical decapsulation approach can be done manually; however, there is an instrument that can perform this process automatically as shown in Figure 13.14. Examples of decapsulated parts are shown in Figure 13.15.


Figure 13.14 Schematic of the decapsulator [B \& G Corporation].
