# 13.5.3 Cross-sectioning

Cross-sectioning is an invaluable tool for examining the internal construction and microstructure of electronic parts and their component materials. It is especially useful in characterizing the following degradation and failure mechanisms:

- solder joint fatigue
- intermetallic growth and voiding at wire bonds
- board delamination
- plated through-hole (PTH) fatigue

Exposing the true material microstructure and potential device damage requires carefully preparing a specimen that is truly representative of the system being examined. The definition of a properly prepared cross-section is that it must have the following attributes:

- be flat and free from scratches, stains, and other imperfections that mar the surface
- be sectioned, ground, and polished so as to minimize the amount of disturbed material caused by mechanical deformation and thus allow the true microstructure to be revealed
- show no chipping or galling of hard and brittle intermetallic compounds
- be free from all traces of disturbed metal
- be flat enough to permit light optical microscopic examination at high magnification
- be polished so that inclusions and phases are preserved intact and not in relief
- be prepared in such a way that its edges are preserved to reveal surface details

To ensure achievement of true surfaces, preparation must be carried out not only with accuracy, but also with a clear understanding of what must be accomplished during each stage of preparation.

The cross-sectioning process is divided into a logical series of steps, each of which is discussed in detail in subsequent sections:1. Sectioning. A representative sample is removed from the parent piece.
2. Coarse grinding. An initial flat surface is produced.
3. Mounting. The sample is embedded in a plastic medium for ease of manipulation and edge preservation and to avoid damaging fragile components.
4. Fine grinding. The deformation caused by sectioning and coarse grinding is removed by fine grinding using a sequence of progressively finer abrasive sizes in order to limit the depths of new deformation introduced during this stage.
5. Rough polishing. The deformation zone produced by fine grinding is removed.
6. Final polishing. The deformation zone produced during rough polishing is removed. Any damage produced at this stage should be minimal and generally is removed during subsequent etching.

# Sectioning

Sectioning is the removal of a representative area from the parent electronic assembly. If the assembly or some component on it has failed, a specimen should be selected that encompasses the failure region. Depending on the type of failure, it may be necessary to take several specimens from adjacent areas.

The technique of low-speed sectioning for metallographic and related-type specimens is patterned after principles used in the precious gem industry. Small-diameter, 4-6-inch dia-mond-rimmed wheels are used. The speed range is $0-1,000 \mathrm{rpm}$, and the load range is $0-1,000 \mathrm{gm}$. The technique is applicable to many types of materials. Response is excellent to metallic as well as to nonmetallic materials, and to soft, hard, brittle, ductile, porous, simple, or complex configurations. This is the method most commonly used for electronic components and assemblies.

## Coarse Grinding

The purpose of coarse grinding is to remove deformation that is produced during sectioning and create a flat surface. The process is performed using abrasive belts or disc-covered rotating wheels with a grit size of $50-180$. The abrasive action is very aggressive with this grit range, and careless coarse grinding can lead to altered microstructure and potential analytical errors. Water is recommended as a coolant to prevent overheating the specimen and to flush away the surface removal products, thus keeping sharp abrasive grain exposed at all times. Abrasive belts and discs are available in silicon carbide and aluminum oxide, with resin bond for wet or dry operation. Garnet-coated materials are only available with glue bond and must be used dry. With higher-speed coarse grinding, the resultant surface finish for a given grit size approaches that produced by finer grit sizes. For example, a surface finished with $60 \mathrm{grit} / 5,200$ SFM would be equivalent to one produced by $120 \mathrm{grit} / 2,500$ SFM. A surface that appears smooth and bright does not necessarily have the least (or shallowest) amount of deformation, however. An apparently improved appearance can be due to rubbing or smearing of the surface by the abrasive particles. Grinding with worn or loaded abrasive surfaces also produces more extensive surface deformation.

## Mounting

The primary purpose of mounting metallographic specimens is for convenience in handling specimens of difficult shapes or sizes during the subsequent steps of the metallographic preparation and examination processes. A secondary purpose is to protect and preserveextreme edges or surface defects during metallographic preparation. The mounting method should in no way be injurious to the microstructure of the specimen. Mechanical deformation and heat are the most likely sources of injurious effects. The different mounting methods used are compression mounting and cold mounting.

# Compression mounting

A common metallurgical method, compression mounting uses pressures and heat to encapsulate a specimen in a thermosetting or thermoplastic mounting material. Common thermosetting resins include phenolic (Bakelite) and diallyl phthalate. Methyl methacrylate is the most common thermoplastic mounting resin. Both thermosetting and thermoplastic materials require heat and pressure during the molding cycle. For thermosetting materials, some shrinkage of the resin from the specimen surface may occur on cooling; thus, it is recommended that the temperature be lowered to about $50^{\circ} \mathrm{C}\left(130^{\circ} \mathrm{F}\right)$ before ejecting the sample from the mold. Thermoplastic materials remain molten at the maximum molding temperature and must be cooled under pressure before ejection.

## Cold mounting

Cold mounting is the most commonly used method for mounting electronic components. The materials used for cold mounting require neither pressure nor heat and are therefore recommended for mounting specimens that are sensitive to heat and/or pressure. Epoxy resins are the most widely used cold-mounting materials. They adhere tenaciously to most metallurgical, mineral, and ceramic specimens. They also exhibit lower-volume shrinkage than either polyesters or acrylics and are very useful for impregnating porous structures or cracks by vacuum methods. For minimal shrinkage, epoxy mounts should be cured at room temperature for 8-12 hours. Hard filler particles can be added to enhance edge retention.

## Fine Grinding

The fine grinding operation is used to reduce the depth of deformation to such a level that polishing will be able to produce the final surface finish. The abrasives used for fine grinding are silicon carbide, emery, and aluminum oxide. Generally, fixed-type abrasives are used; that is, the abrasive grain is bonded to a paper or cloth backing. The bonding material may be glue, resin, or resin over glue. Silicon carbide and aluminum oxide materials can clog with removal products, so flushing with water is used to keep the cutting edges of the abrasive grains exposed. Silicon carbide abrasive grain when used wet has a removal rate twice that of a corresponding grade of emery and provides a much shallower deformation depth. Use of a closely graded series of abrasives is often called for in the preparation of soft materials. The true microstructure is achieved at the completion of this stage.

## Rough and Final Polishing

Polishing is the most important stage in the entire cross-sectioning preparation sequence. The nature of the abrasive type employed should permit accurate sizing and separation by various methods into fractions of uniform particle size.

## Abrasives

Diamond abrasives are preferred because they permit this sizing and separation. Other favorable properties are high hardness, inertness, and low coefficient of friction. Diamondparticles retain their shape and size during abrasion and produce a uniform and high rate of material removal while inducing minimal surface damage.

# Suspension Medium

The suspension medium for diamond powders is very important because it contributes to better lubrication and a faster removal rate. Some adjustments in viscosity of the medium must be made for various particle sizes to compensate for possible drastic changes in heat generation. Oil- or water-soluble media promote superior lubrication and removal rates in comparison to slurry suspension. Dispersing the suspension as a paste facilitates convenient charging of the polishing cloth surface. Addition of an extender contributes to even particle distribution. Figure 13.16 depicts a cross-section of a multi-layer ceramic capacitor, while figure 13.17 depicts a cross-section of a ball bond, showing the intermetallic layer and the voiding.


Figure 13.16 Cross-section of a multilayer ceramic capacitor.


Figure 13.17 Cross-section of a ball bond. The arrow indicates intermetallic layers.# 13.6 Scanning Electron Microscopy and Energy Dispersive Spectrometry

After the sample has been prepared by delidding, decapsulation, or cross-sectioning, the scanning electron microscope (SEM) can be used to perform a high-magnification internal and microstructural examination. The advantages of SEM are high levels of magnification, large depth of field, and the resultant ability to examine rough surfaces at high magnification in their original state. SEMs began to appear commercially in the mid-1960s. In the early instruments, the primary limitations of SEM, as a general imaging and analytical technique, were the restrictions it imposed on samples by requiring a high vacuum environment. The samples had to be clean, dry, and electrically conductive. Nonconductive specimens had to be coated with a conductive film to avoid specimen charging.

The environmental SEM or ESEM, pictured in Figure 13.18, was developed in the mid1980s. Its primary advantages lie in permitting the microscopist to vary the sample environment through a range of pressures, temperatures, and gas compositions. The environmental SEM retains all of the performance advantages of a conventional SEM, but removes the high vacuum constraint on the environment. Wet, oily, dirty, nonconductive samples may be examined in their natural states without modification or preparation. The ESEM offers high-resolution secondary electron imaging in a gaseous environment of practically any composition at pressures as high as 50 Torr and temperatures as high as $1500^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$.

### 13.6.1 Principles of SEM/ESEM

All SEMs consist of an electron column that creates and focuses a beam of electrons, a sample chamber where the electron beam interacts with the sample, detectors that monitor a variety of signals resulting from the beam-sample interaction, and a viewing system that constructs an image from the signal.


Figure 13.18 A schematic representation of a SEM. The electron column accelerates and focuses a beam of electrons onto the sample surface. Interactions between the sample and the beam electrons cause a variety of signal emissons. The signals are detected and reconstructed into the virtual image deployed on a CRT.An electron gun at the top of the column generates the electron beam. In the gun, electrons are thermonically emitted from a very small region on the surface of a heated tungsten filament cathode and then directed by an electrostatic field through a small spot called the crossover. The gun accelerates the electrons down the column toward the sample with energies typically ranging from a few hundred to tens of thousands of electron volts. The wavelength of the electrons, and thereby the resolution of the microscope, is inversely proportional to the accelerating voltage. The electrons emerge from the gun as a divergent beam. A series of magnetic lenses and apertures in the column reconverges and focuses the beam into a demagnified image of the crossover. Near the bottom of the column, scan coils deflect the beam in a scanning pattern over the sample surface. The final lens focuses the beam into the smallest possible spot on the sample surface.

The beam exits from the column into the sample chamber. The chamber incorporates a stage for manipulating the sample, a door for inserting and removing the sample, and access ports for mounting various signal detectors and other accessories. As the primary electron beam penetrates the sample, it loses energy, which is emitted from the sample in a variety of ways. The two most commonly used electron signals, shown in Figure 13.19, are called 'secondary electrons' and 'backscattered electrons.'

# Secondary Electrons (SE)

Secondary electrons are electrons that have been ejected from the sample as a result of interactions between the sample and the primary beam electrons. They generally have very low energy (by convention, less than 50 electron volts). Because of their low energy, they can escape only from a very shallow region at the sample surface. As a result, they offer the best imaging resolution of the sample topography. Topographic contrast causes peaks to appear bright and valleys dark, since more secondary electrons can escape for a point at the top of a peak than for a point at the bottom of a valley. This makes the interpretation of secondary images very intuitive. They look just like the corresponding visual image would look in bright field optical microscopy.


Figure 13.19 The interactions of beam electons and sample atoms generate a variety of signals, including secondary electrons and backscattered electrons.# Backscattered Electrons (BSE)

Backscattered electrons are primary beam electrons that have been scattered back out of the sample by elastic collisions with the nuclei of sample atoms. They have high energy, ranging (by convention) from 50 electron volts up to the accelerating voltage of the beam. Their higher energy results in a larger specific volume of interaction, which causes the resolution of backscattered electron images to be less than that of secondary electron images. Contrast in backscattered images comes primarily from point-to-point differences in the average atomic number of the sample. High atomic number nuclei backscatter more electrons and create bright areas in the image. Backscattered images are not as easy to interpret, but properly interpreted, can provide important information about sample composition.

Unlike the light in an optical microscope, the electrons in an SEM never form a real image of the sample; instead, the SEM constructs a virtual image from the signals emitted by the sample. It does this by scanning the electron beam line-by-line through a rectangular (raster) pattern on the sample surface. The scan pattern defines the area represented in the image. At any instant in time the beam illuminates only a single point in the pattern. As the beam moves from point to point, the signals it generates vary in strength, reflecting differences in the sample. The output signal is thus a serial data stream. Modern instruments include digital imaging capabilities that convert the analog data from the detector into a series of numerical values. These values are then converted into an image. This process allows the user to perform significant image refinement.

### 13.6.2 Advantages of ESEM

Some of the advantages of the ESEM are:

- Gas ionization in the sample chamber eliminates the charging artifacts typically seen with nonconductive samples, so the specimens do not need to be coated with a conductive film.
- By eliminating the need for conductive coating, ESEM allows the imaging of delicate structure and permits subsequent energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) compositional analysis.
- The ESEM can image wet, dirty, and oily samples. The contaminants do not damage the system or degrade the image quality.
- ESEM can acquire electron images from samples as hot as $1500^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ because the detector is insensitive to heat.
- The detector is also insensitive to light: light from the sample - for example, incandescence from heated samples, cathodoluminescence, and fluorescence - do not interfere with imaging.
- ESEM can provide materials and microstructural information such as grain size distribution, surface roughness and porosity, particle size, materials homogeneity, and intermetallic distribution.
- ESEM can be used in failure analyzes to examine the location of contamination and mechanical damage, provide evidence of electrostatic discharge, and detect microcracks.
- ESEM can be integrated into quality control screening: comparing good and bad samples, determining material thickness, and verifying dimensions.
- ESEM permits the acquisition by EDS of X-ray data from insulating samples at high accelerating voltage.
- Eliminating the need for sample preparation, particularly the need for conductive coating, makes it possible to investigate dynamic processes such as deformation, crack propagation, heating, cooling, freezing, melting, hydration, dehydration, and sublimation.# 13.6.3 Failure Mechanism Studied Using ESEM

ESEM is used to analyze the following failure mechanisms:

- Intermetallic growth, voiding, and corrosion at the bondpad under the gold ball bond
- Electromigration and stress-driven diffusive voiding of the on-chip metallization
- Metallization corrosion
- Wirebond fracture
- Passivation cracking
- Delamination at the die/die paddle interface
- Dendritic growth
- Die fracture
- Electrostatic discharge/electrical overstress
- Wire fatigue
- Solder fatigue

Images of ball bonds and their defects are shown in figure 13.20 and 13.21.


Figure 13.20 a ESEM image of a ball bond. Good ball bond: good shape, no intermaetallic growth or corrosion. b Bad ball bond intermetallic growth between ball bond and bond pad.


Figure 13.21 ESEM image of cross-section of ball bond. Bad interface: crevice between ball bond and die pad.# 13.6.4 Energy Dispersive Spectrometry(EDS)

As mentioned in the section on ESEM, an electron beam creates a number of signals when it interacts with a sample. The signal of critical importance for EDS is the characteristic X-ray emission which is superimposed on a background of continuum X-radiation. Using this signal, EDS can identify the composition of a small selected area of the sample where the electron beam is directed.

A device that produces pulses proportional in height to the X-ray photon energy detects the X-ray emission. Electronic pulse-height analysis is then used to sort the pulses and produce an X-ray spectrum. Energy-dispersive spectrometry was pioneered by Dolby (1959, 1963), who used a gas-filled proportional counter to detect ultralight element X-rays. Solidstate detectors, which give better resolution, are used today. Their resolution is still inferior to that of wavelength dispersive spectrometers, which use crystals to separate X-rays based on Bragg diffraction at particular crystal orientations for given lattice spacings. However, the EDS technique does have certain advantages, in particular, 'parallel' collection of the whole spectrum (whereas wavelength dispersive spectrometers operate in 'sequential' mode) and greater X-ray collection efficiency. An EDS acquisition screen with a typical spectrum is seen in Figure 13.22.

The fact that it is easy to attach an energy-dispersive detector to a environmental scanning electron microscope has led to the widespread adaptation of these instruments for analytical


Figure 13.22 EDS acquisition screen with typical spectrum.purposes; indeed, there are far more ESEM-EDS instruments in use than true electron microprobes. Qualitative analysis (identification of elements present in a sample) is especially quick using EDS. Quantitative analysis is also possible (for concentrations greater than 0.1 weight percent), by comparing the intensity of characteristic X-ray emission (that is, the number of X-ray photons per second) from an element of interest in the specimen with intensity of characteristic X-ray emission from a standard of known composition (often, for convenience, the pure element).

The X-ray emission spectrum generated by a beam of energetic electrons, when it impinges on a target, consists of a background of X-rays (continuum X-rays) that extend up to a limiting energy corresponding to the incident electron energy, together with superimposed peaks at discrete energies (characteristic X-rays) that are a function of the target composition. The relationship between the energy of characteristic X-ray emission lines and atomic number of the target is related by Equation 13.5:


$$

v=2.48 \times 10^{15}(\mathrm{Z}-1)^{2}

$$

where $v$ is X-ray frequency and Z is atomic number. This equation refer to the $\mathrm{K} \alpha$ series, although similar relationships are found for $\mathrm{K}_{\beta}, \mathrm{L}$ and M spectra when these are generated.

X-ray spectra are produced by elements spanning most of the periodic table. Intensity of characteristic X-radiation emerging from a sample is strongly affected by sample composition, which governs both the strength of the signal generated and the attenuation of that signal by absorption in the sample. The probability of a generated X-ray being emitted being is given by Equation 13.6


$$

I \alpha=I\_{0} \exp [-(u / \rho) \rho z \operatorname{cosec} \psi]

$$

where $I_{0}$ is the incident X-ray intensity, $m$ is the linear coefficient of absorption, $\rho$ is density, $\psi$ is X-ray take-off angle, and $\rho$ zcosec $\psi$ refers to mass thickness. The total intensity emerging at this angle is expressed in Equation 13.7:


$$

I=\int\_{0}^{\infty} \varnothing(\rho z) \exp [-(\mu / \rho) \rho z \operatorname{cosec} \psi] d \rho z

$$

where $\int_{0}^{\infty} \varnothing(\rho z) d \rho z$ is the total generated intensity.
Special methods have been developed that enable peak identities to be determined. The energy of an unknown peak may be ascertained by finding the channel containing the maximum number of counts for that peak and converting channel number to energy. Referencing a table of energies that may be stored in computer memory can identify the peak. Aids are usually provided in the EDS system, such as a movable cursor on the display that can be aligned with the unknown peak to select it for identification. Since there is an uncertainty of at least one channel in the peak position, identification may be ambiguous, in which case the computer will suggest several possible alternative lines. In order to decide whether a given peak is a K, L or M line, the computer may be employed to display the complete K, L, or M spectrum in question with the correct relative peak heights: it is then easy to see if the peak coincides with the computer-generated spectra.

A useful facility for identifying phases is the ability to compare the spectrum just recorded with one recalled from the computer memory, where a library of relevant spectra may be stored. If two such spectra can be displayed simultaneously with a small vertical offset, similarities and differences can be appraised very easily.# 13.7 Specialized Mechanical Tests

Several specialized mechanical tests may be employed in failure analysis. In microelectronics, these may include:

- Wire Bond Pull
- Wire Bond Shear
- Die Bond Shear

The wire bond pull test is the most widely used method for assessing the quality and degradation of wirebonds and providing assurance that semiconductor devices will not fail in the field due to weak bonds. Specific test procedures and pull-force values are called out in MIL-STD-883 as well as in numerous documents used internally in the electronics industry. The wire bond pull test has been used to assess and determine the strength of wire bonds in semiconductor devices since their introduction by Bell Laboratories.

Although the wire bond pull test is effective in evaluating aluminum wedge bonds, it is not as valuable in evaluating ball bonded systems, due to the large interfacial weld areas. This is especially true in gold ball bonding (i.e., either thermosonic or thermocompression), where a ball of relatively large diameter compared to the wire diameter forms an effective bonding pad attachment many times stronger than the breaking strength of the wire. Since these interfacial weld areas are nominally at least 6-25 times the cross-sectional area of the wire (the nominal permitted ball size by MIL-STD-883C is $2.5-5.0$ times the wire diameter), it is apparent that the destructive pull test provides little information on the strength and quality of the ball-to-bond-bonding pad interface. Even in poorly made ball bonds, if the actual interfacial weld area is greater than approximately $10 \%$ of the possible weld area ( total area based on maximum ball diameter), the wire will break in pull testing prior to the ball lifting. In addition, the wire above the neck of the ball bond is totally annealed and recrystallized, and it becomes the weakest part of the ball-bond wire wedge-bond system. In a pull test, the wire often breaks at this point, depending on the bond geometry and where the hook is placed. Only in cases of catastrophic failure, such as low-temperature impurity-driven intermetallic growth, will the destructive wire bond pull test yield information other than the relative breaking strength of the wire at this weakened neck area.

Therefore, although the wire bond pull test has historically provided much useful information, today it is usually combined with a test that examines the integrity of the gold wire bond-aluminum bonding pad interfaces. This test it the microelectronic ball bond shear test, which was first developed in 1967. The ball-bond shear test consists of bringing a mechanical shearing ram (or tool) up to the outside of a bonded ball and applying a force to the ball, parallel to the bonding pad metallization, of sufficient magnitude to push the ball off the pad and/or substrate metallization, and then recording the value of this force and the mode of failure. The ball bond shear test provides the necessary interfacial stress; with proper care and control it can be used to determine wire bond quality as well as provide a response parameter for bonding machine setup and optimization, hybrid process development, and long-term reliability studies.

There is a variety of test equipment available commercially. Features of the equipment, regardless of manufacturer, include calibrated load cells or force gauges; methods (with appropriate tolerances) for positioning both the sample and the shearing ram or tool; methods for determining (and recording) the maximum shear force; and a microscope for inspecting the mode of failure. Figure 13.23 shows a typical bond tester, while Figure 13.24 shows vertical and horizontal shear tester configurations respectively.

Figure 13.23 Wirebond test Systems.


Figure 13.24 Horizontal and vertical shearing ram configurations.# 13.8 Summary

Failure analysis is essential to reliability assessment, product improvement and reliability growth. It is necessary to analyze accelerated test failures to correlate failure mechanisms to field conditions. Yet its discussion is often neglected in many texts on reliability. In this chapter, we have outlined the basic process applicable to reliability assessment in development and for analysis of field failures and assemblies. We have detailed the process for an electronic assembly. The techniques used in failure analysis are explained in detail along with the information derived from the technique to provide a detailed understanding of failure analysis. While most of the examples focus on electronic devices, similar steps can be exercised to tailor these methods mechanical components. At this point, the reader may want to once again review Chapter 9 , to see details of several failure analyzes applied to different components.

### 13.9 Do's and Don'ts in Design

Do analyze accelerated test failures to assess dominant failure mechanisms
Do compare failure analysis of field failures and test failures.
Do handle all failed specimens with care.
Do an adequate background investigation prior to initiating any laboratory procedures.
Do plan the course of analyzes and tests to be performed.
Do perform failure analysis systematically from least destructive to most destructive analyzes.
Do utilize electrical testing to characterize electronic component failure analysis.
Do use low voltages in electrical testing.
Do utilize SEM to characterize crack growth modes when fractures are involved.
Do mechanical testing last.
Do hardness testing on mechanical failures.
Do keep a good reference of failures.
Do write a good report.
Don't jump to conclusions
Don't place fracture surfaces together when fractures are involved.
Don't handle failed microelectronics without ground protection.
Don't skip a very careful visual inspection at the start of the analysis
Don't forget to correlate models to failure analysis conclusions.
Don't forget to carefully document each phase of the analysis.

John W. Evans, Jillian Y. Evans and H.S. Jeon

During development of new technologies or the design of the next generation of a new product, we necessarily execute reliability assessment to evaluate the design. The results of the assessment may lead us to improving the next design or may necessitate corrective action development. In this chapter we explore two such case studies in product development.

The first case is a discussion of improvements developed from reliability assessment of a consumer product. Here we see the value of failure analysis and modeling coupled to focus on root cause and proper corrective action. The primary driver of the assessment was the need to reduce unexpected warranty claims for early wearout of a mechanical subsystem in the product. The second case deals with reliability assessment of a new electronic packaging technology. In this case, we see the value of up front reliability assessment, including the need for materials testing and the application of modeling to properly interpret accelerated test results. We also see the value of reliability assessment in focusing corrective action for the design and fabrication of the product. Inherent in both of these case studies, is the direct consideration of design uncertainties.

### 14.1 Case I: Consumer Product Development

This case reviews product improvement efforts performed on various models of washing machine gear mechanisms. The effort focused on assessing root causes of failures encountered in the field by the customer and the impact and effectiveness of design changes on these failures. In general, the aim of this effort was to evaluate the feasibility of increasing component life and reducing failure rates in washing machine products. Effective corrective actions, aimed at root causes, reduced warranty claims and associated costs, and improved brand image, resulting in increasing product competitiveness in the consumer market were the results. Failure analysis of mechanism components, coupled to modeling and analysis were used to focus on root cause of the failure mode. Recall that root cause can be defined as understanding the failure mechanisms and the driving forces of the mechanism. Samples for detailed study were obtained from failed units. The samples were subjected to detailed failure analysis. Finite element analysis and closed form models followed this.

The washing machine was typical of many designs used around the world for washing machine products. The gear mechanism for this machine was driven by an electric motor. The load was taken off the mechanism by the wash tub of the unit. A simple schematic of the

Figure 14.1 A simple schematic of the critical components for purposes of discussion. The actual design cannot be shown.
key components is shown in Figure 14.1. The gear mechanism was designed to perform the functions necessary to facilitate the various cycles of the washing machine, from agitation during the wash cycle through the spin cycle.

Over the course of the study, two models of this basic gear mechanism design were included in the evaluation: Model A and a potential improvement, Model B. These units contained many common components and shared a common basic design. The major difference was in the primary or upper bearing assembly and the mechanism housing, specifically the housing cover and bearing support. For this discussion, we will refer to the bearings as Type K and Type N. The improved Model B gear mechanism employed the Type N bearing. Two different bearing support structures or case designs were used on the Model B assembly, a standard 1.6 mm thickness housing cover and a potential new 2.0 mm thickness. The reliability assessment yielded the necessary data to assess quantitatively the benefits of the potential design improvements suggested for Model B.

# 14.1.1 Failure Analysis of Field Assemblies

As this case involved product failures, the assessment process was initiated with detailed failure analysis. The failure analysis of the bearing assemblies is discussed in Chapter 8 and is summarized below. Bearing samples were obtained from field failures. A total of 21 units were analyzed following service lives of 6-19 months. Several critical results were obtained from the analysis. Common to the Type K type bearings used on the Model A assemblies was severe damage to the races of the major ball bearing, as a result of spalling. Spalling is an indication wearout failure from surface fatigue of contacting rolling surfaces in the bearing.

In the absence of defective materials, overstress or early wear out of a component would indicate under-design or applications of large loads beyond the intended capability of the component. The conclusion of the failure analysis was that spalling of the Type K units was due to relatively large localized stresses on the race of the component, indicating the need for design modeling and analysis.# 14.1.2 Modeling and Design Analysis of Bearing and Cover Assemblies

## Bearing Life Estimates

The life of a bearing is dependent upon the applied loading and operational speed. Bearings will be rated for a critical basic load at which evidence of failure will not be expected for at least $10^{6}$ cycles of operation in $90 \%$ of the bearing population or in other words reliability of 0.9. This basic rated load is dependent upon configuration factors such as ball diameter, ball pitch and total number of balls. The relationship between the life, the rated load and the applied load can be expressed in the well known bearing design equation as follows:


$$

\frac{\mathrm{C}_{\mathrm{B}}}{\mathrm{~F}_{\text {app }}}=\left[\frac{L_{D} n_{D}}{10^{6}}\right]^{\frac{1}{3}}

$$

In this expression $\mathrm{C}_{\mathrm{B}}$ is the rated load, $\mathrm{F}_{\text {app }}$ is the applied load and $L_{D}$ is the rated life at $n_{D}$ operational angular velocity in rpm. The rated load for the assemblies analyzed, which included the $N$ and $K$ style bearings, was 1080 kgf for Type $K$ bearing and 1030 kgf for Type $N$ bearing respectively. The applied load must be estimated from the operational conditions of the equipment. Equation 14.1 is well known to mechanical designers and is often employed with a safety factor approach to design of bearings.

The reliability of a bearing assembly will fit the Weibull distribution. Under given conditions, the bearing life will be limited by the applied load and the probability of failure of a ball bearing at a point in its life can be estimated from the following equation given by Shigley and Mitchell(1983):


$$

F=1-R=1-\exp \left[-\left(\frac{L}{6.84 L_{10}}\right)^{1.17}\right]

$$

$F$ is the probability of failure, $R$ is the reliability, $L$ is the demanded life under the applied load conditions and $L_{10}$ is the available life at rated load conditions or life at $C_{B}$.

It should be noted that misalignment is a critical factor. While roller bearings can tolerate some degree of misalignment, bearing life can be significantly degraded if misalignment is significant, particularly for grooved ball bearing assemblies. The severity of bearing life reduction due to misalignment can be estimated from the following equation:


$$

\eta=-167 \delta+1

$$

Eta is the life reduction factor and delta is the angular misalignment of the shaft in radians. Equation 14.3 above represents the most severe loading effects of misalignment for line contact bearings and applies when misalignment exceeds approximately 0.001 radians.

A typical washing machine unit is designed to operate with a spin cycle of approximately 800 rpm for a total of 3 minutes. The distribution of mass in the washer drum will induce an unbalanced load during the spin cycle. However, the design compensates for the unbalanced load and limits the total unbalanced load that can develop in the wash tub during the spin cycle.

A free body diagram of the gear mechanism shaft is shown in Figure 14. 2. From a simple dynamic analysis of the spin cycle and a static analysis of this diagram, the loads on the shaft bearings can be estimated. In this study, the unbalanced load developed on the shaft was estimated at 120 kgf . Allowing for a $20 \%$ overload condition to occur for the most aggressive customers using the washer, the unbalanced load on the shaft would be 144 kgf . Under these conditions, the bearing assembly loads were estimated and the rated life under operation was determined from the above equation. The results of these estimates are shown below in Table 14.1.Figure 14.2 A free body diagram of the gear mechanism shaft, separated from the housing, with bearings shown.

However, as seen from service data, wearout of assemblies in the field occurred in less than 2 years, leading to frequent service and repair. This lead to the conclusion that further analysis was needed and that other contributing factors must be the root cause. Most notably, the analyses conducted to this point assumed that the bearing has a rigid support and there was no misalignments.

# Bearing and Support Structure Finite Element and Design Analysis

A finite element analysis of the support structure was conducted to further study the load distributions in the assembly. The analysis included the shaft, bearing and external case assembly. Two different support cover assemblies were analyzed including the 1.6 mm thickness and 2.0 mm thickness The applied load for the finite element analysis was $20 \%$ greater than the estimated nominal loading.

The analysis was conducted assuming the mechanism was rigidly attached at its mounting bolt holes. The bearing was considered to be a solid element. The second simplifying assumptions does not allow for accurate assessment of stresses in the bearing, however, it is a reasonable assumption to analyze the deformations in the system and stresses developed in the support structure and case due to load transfer from the shaft. The material properties used for the analysis are summarized in Table 14.2. The case behavior was considered to be elasto-plastic. Materials property and geometric variations were not treated in this analysis.

The results of the analysis were highly significant to assessing the mechanism's design. Most significant were the deflection of the shaft and the associated deformation of the supporting case assembly. Figure 14.4 shows the deflection of the shaft with the 1.6 mm case cover for Model B, with the N type bearing. The finite element results estimated an angular shaft deflection of approximately 0.003 radians. The shaft deflection has a similar effect as a static misalignment of the assembly. Hence, the estimated life reduction factor from the shaft deflection, at $20 \%$ over load, is approximately 0.50 or $50 \%$ of the nominal life.Table 14.2 Materials Properties Used for the FEM Analysis

Figure 14.5 shows the shaft deflection patterns for the thicker support structure. The applied load conditions are the same as for the 1.6 mm . The heavier case produced significantly less deflection. The estimated angular deflection of the shaft with the 2.0 mm cover was 0.0015 radians. The estimated load reduction factor from the shaft deflection is 0.75 or $25 \%$ reduction from the nominal condition.

The effects of the shaft deflections and support structure deformation on the bearing life of Model B can be estimated in field use. Once again, the appliance life will depend on


Figure 14.5 Shaft deflection of Model B with housing cover thickness of 2.0 mm .customer usage. The results of this analysis are shown in Figure 14.6 for a desired bearing reliability of 0.99 near the end of life. The impact of case and support structure deformation can be compared to the assumption that the case is rigid. At a usage of 1 load per day, the 2.0 mm thick support structure would provide approximately 11 years of life for the N bearing while the 1.6 mm would provide 7 years of life. The expected repairs would be 1 unit in 100 at the end of life. The life of the assembly would drop significantly with increasing usage under the load of 144 kgf . Lower shaft deflections and less life reduction would be expected under the nominal load of 120 kgf .

The cover and shaft deflections for Model A were not directly analyzed. However, the deflections can be assumed to be similar to the deflections of Model B in order to estimate the effects of support structure deformation on the Model A mechanism life. The results of this analysis are summarized in Figure 14.7. The thin cover and support structure would deflect and reduce the life to less than two years, at a usage of two loads per day, under the applied load of 144 kgf . The expectation of repair is 1 unit in 100 at the end of life for these conditions. This result was consistent with the service data and identified that the Model A design with a K bearing was inadequate.

# 14.1.3 Case I Discussion and Summary

Failure analysis, coupled to modeling and design analysis, were used to critically assess options for the case design and bearing assembly. The analyses showed that early wearout occurs in the K type bearing, used in the Model A assemblies, due to excessive case deflection, which produces misalignment in the bearing-shaft coupling. One in a hundred units ( $1 \%$ ), used 2 or more times per day, would be expected to fail from early bearing wear out in less than two years. This is based on a load of 144 kgf and represents an upper bound for the given load. These result correlated with the wearout period of the K bearing samples collected from the field. Increasing case thickness to 2.0 mm would improve the design, but a


Figure 14.6 Model B bearing life analysis. The thicker supporting case structure yields sufficient life, greater than 7 years, under light usage of the product, based on a selected reliability of 0.99 at end of life.

Figure 14.7 Model A bearing life analysis. Analysis shows warranty claims are to be expected under heavy use conditions.
nominal life increase to 7 years would not be expected for machines fitted with the Model A mechanisms, that were used more than 1 time per day, at a unit reliability of $99 \%$.

Employing the N bearing in the Model B gear mechanism and the 2.0 mm case would provide a 7 year life on units nominally loaded and used less than 2 times per day, at a reliability of $99 \%$. Heavy users would, however, experience wear out earlier. For example, 1 unit in 100 ( $1 \%$ ) used more than 3 times per day and heavily loaded by the user, would fail in 3 years. Thus, Model B with the case design improvement is an adequate design for nominal washing machine use, but not heavy use of more than 2 times per day.

Here we see the value of proper failure analysis in pointing the direction to focus on the component in the subsystem responsible for failure. Modeling and design analysis yielded the root cause of early wearout of this component. In addition, we see that reliability analysis directly incorporated uncertainty in the use of the product. The end result is selection of appropriate design improvements and directions needed for future development.

# 14.2 Case II New Technology Development: Multichip Module Thin Film Process ${ }^{1}$

Effective allocation of resources to product improvement requires a solid understanding of the relationship between sources of manufacturing variability and product reliability. Sources of variation that effect reliability include material properties, dimensional variations and defect content. The link between these factors and reliability is the key to achieving the goal of built-in reliability and cost-effective corrective action when it is necessary to improve the design.

[^0]
[^0]:    ${ }^{1}$ The editors are grateful to the University of Maryland CALCE Electronic Packaging Center for their contribution to this case study and the IEEE for permission to republish in part the journal article Designing and Building in Reliability in Advanced Mcroelectronic Assemblies and Structures appearing in IEEE Transactions on Components, Packaging and Manufacturing Technology-Part A, Vol. 20, No. 1 March 1997.This critical connection can be established through effective reliability assessment, including modeling the failure processes that a product will experience in use. The contribution of design and fabrication variability to the failure process can then be evaluated. The primary sources that contribute the most to product unreliability become the focus of improvement. The use of modeling becomes an essential tool in producing the data necessary to make rapid upstream decisions effecting product improvement. These techniques include Monte Carlo simulation and statistical experimental designs coupled to failure mechanism models.

This case study presents the implementation of these concepts through an examination of an advanced development for microelectronic packaging. In the development of dense circuitry for size and performance enhancements, thin films and multilayer dielectric systems are integrated in a high density circuit structure. A high performance circuit of this type is shown in Figure 14.8. In order to facilitate interconnection between layers of circuitry, a via is created by a combination of etching or laser drilling through the dielectric, followed by electroplating a suitable conductor.

The reliability of this type of structure and related structures-plated through holes or PTHs- in printed wiring board assemblies, is highly important to electronic systems and devices. A cross section of a series of vias is shown in Figure 14.9. This section was taken through a polyimide dielectric using standard sectioning techniques described in Chapter 13. Polyimide is generally the dielectric selected for this type of application due to manufacturability and dielectric properties. Fatigue of vias, occurring as a result of thermomechanical loading, is a dominant failure mechanism and has been widely explored in the literature (Pecht, Dasgupta, Evans and Evans, 1995).


Figure 14.8 A high performance MCM circuit compared to a conventional printed wiring assembly. (Courtesy of General Electric).

Figure 14.9 a A cross section of a series of vias b Finite Element Model of via stack. The inset shows the results of one of a series of thermomechanical analyses of via stresses and strain. (Courtesy of CALCE Center.)

# 14.2.1 Accelerated Testing, Finite Element Analysis and Fatigue Modeling

Microelectronic devices are subject to thermomechanical fatigue at a variety of potential failure sites. Hence, accelerated thermal cycling tests are an integral part of accelerated testing of new technologies and devices. Thermal cycling tests are highly effective in their ability to precipitate failures in microelectronics. The interpretation of the results of these tests, however, requires adequate fatigue models of the failing structures. In this case, via structures were caused to fail in a highly accelerated test conducted from -65 to $+125^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$. The early prototype devices showed significant resistance increases and intermittent open circuits in 100 250 cycles.

Failure analysis attributed this to via fatigue with the location of cracking as indicated in Figure 14.10.

Figure 14.10 Via fatigue cracking. (Courtesy of C. Pagel Naval Surface Weapons Center.)

Materials testing indicated that the polyimide dielectrics had a out-of-plane coefficient of expansion of $112 \mathrm{ppm} /{ }^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ as compared to $17 \mathrm{ppm} /{ }^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ for the copper via structure. This difference is significant and drives the fatigue process for the copper via structure. Here we see the value of adequate materials testing in understanding the physical processes which comprise failure mechanisms.

As mentioned, the process of fatigue in this structure is driven by the significant difference in the out-of-plane coefficient of thermal expansion between the polyimide dielectric and the electroplated copper via structure. The differences in coefficient of expansion induce strains as the ambient environment changes temperature and as the circuit is cycled through its operational duty cycle. To interpret the results of the accelerated tests, an adequate fatigue model is needed to project the behavior of the via in operation thermal cycling that is encountered in product application.

The reliability of via structures in thin film polyimide was investigated using finite element analysis by Prabu et. al.(1995). In this case, FEA was used to predict the strain developed in a copper via structure as the temperature changes from equilibrium conditions. This strain was then an input to a fatigue damage model allowing an estimation of life for various thermal cycling conditions.

As we have seen in Chapter 6, the accuracy of FEA models depends largely on accuracy of constitutive behavior of the materials. In this case, viscoplastic, time dependent materials behavior was used to model the polyimide, while elastoplastic modeling was used to model the copper. The elastic assumption is not valid in this case for anything but a first approximation. Appropriate constitutive relationships were developed from test data of the polyimide and adhesive materials. Several analyses were executed to estimate the total strain in the copper via at different conditions including the test conditions.

Manufacturing defects, in the form of irregularities or flaws in the copper via walls were apparent from the failure analysis of the prototypes. The influence of these defects on the total strain in the via is significant and was accounted for explicitly in the analysis (Prabu 1995). The effects of notches on fatigue were discussed in Chapter 5. In examining various notch configurations, the maximum total concentration factor for defects of the size observed was estimated to be $3.0-3.5$. A notch strain analysis becomes essential as finite elements analysis cannot easily account for small geometry variations in a structure.The strain concentration from these irregularities was estimated by applying Neuber's rule for notch strain analysis, which gives the relationship between the stress, strain and total concentration factors:


$$

K*{t}=\sqrt{K*{o} K\_{\varepsilon}}

$$

Values of $K_{t}$ can be extracted from appropriate tables and $K_{\varepsilon}$ can then be calculated using the elastic-plastic constitutive relationship appropriate for copper.

For example, recall that constitutive relationship for plastic strain behavior fits the power law:


$$

\sigma=\mathrm{C} \varepsilon^{n}

$$

Applying our relationship for stress and strain concentration:


$$

\begin{aligned}
& \sigma=\sigma*{n o m} K*{o} \\
& \varepsilon=\varepsilon*{n o m} K*{\varepsilon}
\end{aligned}

$$

We can easily show:


$$

K \sigma=K\_{\varepsilon}^{n}

$$

The value of $n$ for electroplated copper is about 0.215 . Now, we can determine the strain concentration factor using equations 14.4 and 14.7. A detailed description of notch strain analysis can be found in Fuchs and Stephens ( 1990).

Under plastic deformation, via wall irregularities were found to increase the local strain by a factor of 8.6. Under elastic deformation, the strain concentration is equivalent to the total concentration factor, $K_{t}$ of 3.0.-3.5. These factors were applied to the equivalent strain from the finite element analysis to estimate the total strain range:


$$

\Delta \varepsilon*{\text {total }}=K*{\varepsilon} \varepsilon\_{e q(F E A)}

$$

The strain analysis was used as an input to subsequent fatigue estimates. The fatigue model selected was a variation of the Manson-Coffin fatigue model developed by Engelmaier.

The Engelmaier Fatigue Model for Plated copper can be expressed as follows:


$$

\Delta \varepsilon*{\text {total }}=N*{f}^{-0.6} D*{f}^{0.75}=0.9 \frac{S*{u}}{E}\left[\frac{\exp D_{f}}{0.36}\right]^{0.1785 \log 10^{5} / \mathrm{N}\_{f}}

$$

In the expression above, $\mathrm{N}_{f}$ can be estimated if the ductility, $D_{f}$, ultimate strength, $S_{u}$ and elastic modulus, E, are known.

The subsequent fatigue analyses revealed the limitations of the structure, as shown in Figure 14.11. The plot shows the life strain relationship estimated for the via. The model closely matched initial test data for early prototypes and test vehicle devices tested in thermal cycling at the range of -65 to $+150^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ and at the range of -40 to $+125^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ Here the life of the structure at use conditions, where the temperature range is $40^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$, exceeds $10^{6}$ cycles, showing that the structure evaluated is adequate for many applications. But the effect of sources of variation in manufacturing, which contribute to uncertainty in the life, are not included in the plot and require further study. In addition, we have not identified the key parameters in design and manufacturing for statistical control and perhaps improvement for increasing structural life for rugged conditions.

Figure 14.11 Fatigue analysis including the effect of strain concentration.

# 14.2.2 Virtual Experiments. Determining Key Sources of Unreliability

These initial results reflected observations of defects in the via structure, which created significant stress concentration. In the region of nominal elastic stresses in the copper, the stress concentration factor ranged up to 3.5 , based on the defects observed in the via. in addition, the potential ranges of other variables and their associated parameters, used in the modeling process are shown in Table 14.3. These parameters reflect the primary sources of variability occurring in the processing of the via.

A statistical experimental design was built around this data. (Ogunjimi et. al.1995.) A full factorial design was used. As we saw in Chapter 11, a two level design is often sufficient to describe a fatigue process. Hence, a total of 32 runs were needed for the 5 factors shown above. After layout, a virtual experiment was conducted based on the design. In this case, the temperature range was kept constant at $40^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$.

An initial analysis, using an analysis of variance (ANOVA), indicated the dominance of the defect size, as reflected by stress concentration variations and plating thickness. Thus, via wall preparation and electroplating are the most critical processes to control, to achieve built in reliability. Clearly, achieving adequate plating thickness and uniformity is essential to the reliability of the structure. Whereas, variations in plating ductility, adhesive thickness and wall angle of the via are not as important at the operating range of $40^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$.

Table 14.3 Ranges of Manufacturing Variables for an HDI Via [Prabhu et. al. 1995, Ogunjimi et. al.1995, Evans et. al. 1997]

| Factor | Units | Low Value | High Value |
| :-- | :-- | :--: | :--: |
| Via Wall Thickness | Microns | 2 | 5 |
| Adhesive Thickness | Microns | 8 | 16 |

| Wall Angle | Degrees from Verticle | 0 | 45 |
| Strain Concentration |  | 1 | 3.5 Elastic |
| Factor |  | 3.5 | 8.6 Plastic |This work was extended to derive a closed form model using a regression analysis. (Evans, Evans and Ryu 1997). As previously shown, fatigue is in general a power law relationship between strain and cycles to failure. A regression was performed using the natural log of each factor contributing to the strain. The natural log of the cycles to failure was used as the dependent variable. The regression was performed using a step-wise procedure to obtain the model best fitting the data. Best fit was determined from the correlation coefficient and an examination of the residuals. The correlation coefficient of the model with the two most significant factor was $94 \%$. In the models below, $N_{f}$ represents the cycle to failure, $t_{p}$ is the plating thickness, $K_{e}$ is the strain concentration factor, which represents the influence of defect size.


$$

N*{f}=\frac{e^{24.3}}{t*{p}^{0.88} K\_{e}^{7.38}}

$$

# 14.2.3 Exploring Variability by Monte Carlo Simulations

The model shown above was embedded in a Monte Carlo simulation. Since the actual distributions of the parameters of interest were not known, simple triangular distributions were constructed using the data shown in Table 14.3 above and the procedures discussed in Chapter 2. The initial simulation on both models was intended to explore the sensitivity of the variability in the life, $N_{f}$, to the variability of the parameters of interest. The results of the simulation are shown in Figure 14.12 as curve A.

The peak value, or most likely life for the via structure is $3.6 \times 10^{6}$ cycles. The minimum life is approximately $6.6 \times 10^{5}$ cycles. It is interesting to note the differences between this approach and the results of Prabu et. al (1995). In applying finite element analysis from a deterministic viewpoint, a 'worst case life' at an environment of $40^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ temperature range was $1.5 \times 10^{6}$ cycles.

Overall the range of life was significant. By inspection of the plot and data, the life could extend from $6.6 \times 10^{5}$ to $1.9 \times 10^{10}$ cycles (overall probability of 1.0 ). in fact, it is not unusual for fatigue data to extend over several decades, particularly at lower stress levels.

An additional simulation was performed on both models after changing the input distribution for the strain concentration factor. The new strain concentration factor distribution reflects the effect of improving the process through reducing defect size and defect size vari-



Figure 14.12 The results of Monte Carlo simulation applied to the fatigue of the via structure.ability. In this case, the most likely strain concentration factor was reduced to 2.0 and the maximum was reduced to 3.0. The impact to the via life is reflected in the probability density function represented by curve $B$. The data reflect a substantial increase that could be achieved by improving the processes of via preparation and electroplating to reduce via wall irregularities. The most likely value increased by more than a factor of 10 to $4.9 \times 10^{7}$ and the minimum value increased to $2.7 \times 10^{6}$ cycles to failure. Clearly, focusing manufacturing improvements on reduction in defect size through enhancing plating uniformity and reducing via wall roughness could yield a significant payoff in increased product reliability.

Each probability density function generated above was fit to a Weibull distribution. The parameters are shown in the Table 14.4 below. The relatively good fit implies that the parameters shown can be used to estimate reliability or unreliability of the vias for various expected service lives.

Further analysis showed other interesting results. Increasing via wall thickness is an intuitive approach an engineer would take to increase fatigue life. However, inspection of equation 14.10 above shows, that over the range of interest, fatigue life will decrease with increasing wall thickness. These effects were explored further and the results are shown in Figure 14.13. As we increase thickness, stress distribution changes. Hence, we see a decrease in life beyond 4 to 5 microns in wall thickness. The implication is there is an optimum thickness for stress management that is not apparent from intuitive engineering. Here we see the value of adequate reliability assessment.

# 14.2.3 Case II Discussion and Summary

Building-in reliability to achieve robust products requires an assessment of manufacturing variabilities and their relationship to reliability. The relationship between specific product characteristics influenced by the manufacturing processes and reliability can be achieved through understanding the failure mechanisms which are present in the product. A relationship between product life and manufacturing variabilities may require some development through a reliability assessment process using techniques such as virtual experiments and Monte Carlo simulation. Product improvements to achieve the goal of robustness can be made after clearly understanding the influence of the variability of product characteristics on reliability.

Figure 14.13 Effects of increasing via wall thickness of via fatigue life. These results are due to a change in stress distribution and are not intuitive.

# 14.3 Conclusions

The two cases studies show the value of reliability assessment as we introduced it in Chapter 1. The various concepts explained through out the book are brought together in these case studies. The primary theme shown is to understand root cause of failure and act to improve the design to meet product integrity objectives, including product life and risk of failure. An understanding of root cause is achieved through an interdisciplinary process of assessment. To review some key points, effective reliability assessment leading to root cause correction or improvement during design and development requires:

- Understanding the loading on the system or product
- Materials testing and characterization
- Knowledge of fabrication methods
- Accelerated testing
- Failure analysis
- Design modeling which addresses uncertainty and identifies critical factors

The benefits yielded include the detailed knowledge required to make effective design decisions and when necessary, effective improvements in the product.

Statistical treatments of uncertainty abound ${ }^{1}$, and I will only attempt to provide a set of formula useful for approximately Gaussian distributions of error. Using some results from calculus, one may show how uncertainties or deviations in a given value will affect the uncertainty of the product. We will derive on type of function in detail and then provide the results for others.

The reader has previously seen a discussion of the mean and standard deviation for a Gaussian distribution (Section 3) so it will not be repeated here. It is assumed that the user has a measure value with associated mean and standard deviation. In the experimental world, it is customary to write the value plus or minus the standard deviation. Let $x$ and $y$ represent measured values which have some value of uncertainty, in the measurement:


$$

\begin{aligned}
& x=0.5 \pm 0.2=\bar{x} \pm \Delta x \\
& y=2.0 \pm 0.2=\bar{y} \pm \Delta y
\end{aligned}

$$

Then, the product of $x$ and $y$ will also have an error associated with it - The mean value is clearly 1.0 but what is the uncertainty? One usually talks about the root-mean-square value, or rms, value of the deviations, which means square the individual error contributions, sum them and then take the square root to be the rms of the result. Using the techniques of the Taylor series of calculus, one can calculate the partial derivatives of the product with respect to $x$ and $y$, to obtain the individual contributions to the total error and will obtain, to first order:


$$

x y=(\overline{x y})+\left(\frac{\partial(x y)}{\partial x} _ d x\right)+\left(\frac{\partial(x y)}{\partial y} _ d y\right)=1.0+y^{_} d x+x^{_} d y

$$

Now the contribution to the total error from $x$ is $y^{*} \mathrm{dx}$ and the contribution to the total error from $y$ is $x^{*} \mathrm{dy}$. Upon replacing $\Delta x$ and $\Delta y$ with, and , respectively, and taking the rms to obtain the total error one obtains:


$$

\Delta x y=\sqrt{\left(y^{_} \Delta x\right)^{2}+\left(x^{_} \Delta y\right)^{2}}=\sqrt{\left(2^{_} 0.2\right)^{2}+\left(0.5^{_} 0.2\right)^{2}}=0.41

$$

And thus, the result of the product of $x$ and $y$ is given by:


$$

x y=\left(\bar{x} \* \bar{y}\right) \pm \Delta x y=1.0 \pm 0.41

$$

Notice that the error is now about $41 \%$ of the total ( 0.41 out of 1 ), while the individual errors were $40 \%$ and $10 \%$, respectively. There is usually a net increase in the percentage error sincethe deviation represents the 1-sigma value of the product and must include outlyers of both $x$ and $y$. It is worth noting an alternative representation of the errors resulting from a product obtained by dividing by the product $x y$, one then obtains:

Multiplication: $\left(\frac{\Delta x y}{x y}\right)^{2}=\left(\frac{1}{x y}\right)^{2} *\left(\left(y^{*} \Delta x\right)^{2}+\left(x^{*} \Delta y\right)^{2}\right)=\left(\frac{\Delta x}{x}\right)^{2}+\left(\frac{\Delta y}{y}\right)^{2}$
Now it is more clear that the error in the product is a weighted sum of the relative error of the constituents and that is why the example worked above had a $41 \%$ error which was dominated by the $40 \%$ error in the variable $x$.

By following the same partial derivative, rms technique used above one may compute the standard deviations associated with the elementary functions:

Addition and subtraction: $(\Delta(x \pm y))^{2}=(\Delta x)^{2}+(\Delta y)^{2}$
Note that the $\pm$ used here is intended to refer to either the addition or subtraction operation. Further note that the absolute error, not the percentage error, appears in the formula for addition and subtraction. As an example, note that repeated measurements will result in a smaller percentage error for the average of the measurements. This technique is often called signal averaging and is a common noise reduction technique.

Division: $\left(\frac{\Delta(x / y)}{x / y}\right)^{2}=\left(\frac{\Delta x}{x}\right)^{2}+\left(\frac{\Delta y}{y}\right)^{2}$
Note that the weighted error contributions are exactly the same as for multiplication.
Powers: $\left(\frac{\Delta\left(X^{b}\right)}{x^{b}}\right)^{2}=b^{2} *\left(\frac{\Delta x}{x}\right)^{2}$
Note that higher powers tend to contribute more and that the reason the division formula looks like the multiplication formula is the fact that the power (e.g. -1 ) is squared and becomes positive.

Other functions may be calculate similarly and is left as an exercise for the reader.# Maximum Likelihood Estimation for Normal, Lognormal and Weibull Distributions

There are many types of estimation methods, but the most popular estimation method is the Maximum Likelihood Estimation(MLE) because it has several desirable properties often not enjoyed by alternative methods. Details on the MLE can be found in any statistics textbooks, and we will only give the estimation procedures for three widely used lifetime distributions. Let $x_{1}, x_{2}, \ldots, x_{n}$ be the sampled data.

## (1) Normal Distribution

The maximum likelihood estimators of $\mu$ and $\sigma^{2}$ are


$$

\begin{aligned}
& \hat{\mu}=\bar{x}=\frac{1}{n} \sum*{i=1}^{n} x*{i} \\
& \hat{\sigma}^{2}=\frac{1}{n} \sum*{i=1}^{n}\left(x*{i}-\hat{\mu}\right)^{2}
\end{aligned}

$$

## (2) Lognormal Distribution

If $X$ has a lognormal distribution, then $Y=\log X$ has a normal distribution. Thus, if we put $y_{i}$ to be $\log x_{i}$, the maximum likelihood estimators $\mu$ of and $\sigma^{2}$ are


$$

\begin{aligned}
& \hat{\mu}=\frac{1}{n} \sum*{i=1}^{n} y*{i}=\frac{1}{n} \sum*{i=1}^{n} \log x*{i} \\
& \hat{\sigma}^{2}=\frac{1}{n} \sum*{i=1}^{n}\left(y*{i}-\hat{\mu}\right)^{2}=\frac{1}{n} \sum*{i=1}^{n}\left(\log x*{i}-\hat{\mu}\right)^{2}
\end{aligned}

$$

## (3) Weibull Distribution

The estimator of $\beta$ is the solution of satisfying the following formula:


$$

\frac{\sum*{i=1}^{n} x*{i}^{\beta} \log x*{i}}{\sum*{i}^{n} x*{i}^{\beta}}-\frac{1}{\beta}-\frac{1}{n} \sum*{i=1}^{n}\left(\log x\_{i}=0\right.
$$To solve the above formula, an iterative search method such as Newton's method should be used. The estimator of $\mu$ is

$$
\hat{\mu}=\left(\frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} x_{i}^{\hat{\theta}}\right) \frac{1}{\hat{\beta}}
$$# Normal Distribution Table
